issues.title: Recommend use of mid-range values as default priority in implementations
issues.author: englishm
issues.body:
The text we landed for [draft-05](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-05.html) to define priorities (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/470) indicates that we should use a 8 bits (`x (L)` where `L` is `8`) to convey subscriber priority and similarly a byte to convey publisher priority.

> `Subscriber Priority (8),`
( https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-05.html#section-6.4.2-2 )

> Publisher Priority: An 8 bit integer indicating the publisher's priority for the Object
 ( https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-05.html#section-6.11.1 )

The text also indicates that lower values have higher priority which I read as meaning 1 (`0000 0001`) should be sent before 10 (`0000 1010`), ~~but we don't seem to explicitly indicate anywhere whether we expect these values to be interpreted as signed or unsigned integers.~~

~~Should `1000 0101` be sent before or after `0000 0101`?~~ (After)

~~Is `1000 0101` -5 (i8) or 133 (u8)?~~ `1000 0101` is 133 (u8)

Edit: We should probably recommend that implementations use a mid-range value like `127` as a default to allow for prioritizing both above and below it. (The MoQT spec doesn't need to **define** a default since these values are currently always explicit on the wire, but I think it would be helpful to provide guidance here.)

comments.author: englishm
comments.body:
I have a slight preference for treating these priorities as signed values because it makes `0` a good default for implementations to choose. That way it's possible to go above or below the default.

The same is possible with unsigned values, too, but if we go that direction we may want to provide some guidance to that effect (recommending something like `127` or `128` as a default mid-range value).

comments.author: englishm
comments.body:
Oh, nevermind, @mengelbart noticed some text I missed in section 4: "with 0 being the highest priority" which would imply these are unsigned int values, `u8`.

It may still be helpful to make that more explicit and recommend a default mid-range value.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I'm fine with some editorial text here if that's how we want to resolve it? (PRs welcome @englishm )

I'm also ok with it being signed, since it it nice for 0 to be a 'default' value, but we don't use signed integers anywhere else in MoQ, so I'm a bit concerned that using them in exactly one spot could be confusing or error prone?

issues.title: Simplify naming by removing the distinction between Track Namespace and Track Name
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
Alan's PR https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/498 introduced a N-tuple construct for namespace, in which the namespace is made up of an ordered sequence of between 1 - 32 byte arrays. This allows us to construct namespaces in the form

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice`

Alice would publish tracks under this namespace called audio|video|catalog leading to the final track identifiers being

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `audio`
`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `video`
`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `catalog`


At this point, the distinction between the track name and last stanza of the namespace is arbitrary and I would argue, unnecessary.

We could remove the separate concepts of TRACK-NAMESPACE and TRACK-NAME and instead coalesce this down to a single construct of TRACK-NAME, which would hold the same definition as a bounded N-tuple. So under the simplified scheme, the TRACK-NAMES would be 

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `audio`
`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `video`
`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice` `catalog`

Alice as the publisher would ANNOUNCE the _minimum prefix_ which uniquely describes describes the content she is responsible for, in this case, she would announce

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice`

This schema then allows for easy aggregate subscription. We could remove the need for SUBSCRIBE-NAMESPACE. For example, a subscriber wanting to receive everything produced by Alice would SUBSCRIBE  to 

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123` `alice`

Someone wanting to receive all feeds from meeting abc123 would SUBSCRIBE to

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123`

If we standardize some means of communicating a null (*) stanza, and if different publishers produced

`example.com` `meeting` `abc123`
`statistics.com` `metrics` `abc123`

the someone wanting both the meeting and metrics for abc123 could SUBSCRIBE to 

`    ` `    ` `abc123`

issues.title: Change in publisher priority is underdefined
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
The current text says "When two or more subscriptions have equal subscriber priority, the original publisher priority is considered next and can change within the track, so subscriptions are prioritized based on the highest priority data available to send."

There are two issues here.  The first is that "data available to send" is not well-defined for a protocol running over QUIC, in the sense that it's unclear as to when the data should be deemed "unavailable" (does it become unavailable after we put it into the QUIC buffer? after we send it? after it gets acked?).  The second is that doing this requires extra bookkeeping to keep track of the current publisher priority per subscription (@martinduke implemented this in our MoQT prototype, and it was definitely quite a bit of complexity and overheard that seems unnecessary, to me at least).

(As an aside, I am not quite sure as to where the "publisher priority of a track is the max priority for all objects in the track" came from; I remember myself arguing for "publisher priority of a _stream_ is the max priority for all objects in the track" at the interim, but that point was moot since we don't actually allow specifying different priorities on a single stream in the current wire format anyways.)

I can see at least two ways we can simplify this:
1. Make the publisher priority of a track to be equal to the priority of the latest (=highest sequence number) object in the track.
2. Make it so that the publisher priority of a peep/datagram is just what is in its header, and does not retroactively change priorities of other peeps and datagrams on that track.  This effectively makes publisher priority have the same expressive power as peep priority, so we may want to merge those if we decide to go this way.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think option 1 doesn't accomplish what people want in some cases.  For example, if you have a high priority peep and a low priority peep for a group, the intent is to deliver the high priority peep first.  However, the low priority peep might have the highest Object Id.  Also, couldn't this cause the priority of a track and hence the related streams to be constantly changing as new Objects arrive?

Option 2 seems sensible to me and I believe has much more consistent behavior.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Under the status quo, the priority of a track can constantly change as new objects arrive.

A third option would be just to completely separate the concept of track-level and object-level publisher priority. A publisher can assign completely different values to each (and send the former in the SUBSCRIBE_OK)

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
Yeah, I think that option 2 makes more sense.

Let's take a real use case, let's say we have high priority for active speaker, and low priority for other audio tracks.  Let's examine how it behaves when a speaker transitions from active to inactive (high -> low priority) under diferent approaches.

Current approach: the speaker's audio will remain at high priority for as long as there is any higher priority data in the buffer.  This risks unnecessarily sending low-priority audio as high-priority.

Option 1: the speaker's audio will get to low priority as soon as the first low priority object is encountered.  This risks unnecessarily sending high-priority audio as low-priority, causing it to be "truncated" at the end.

Option 2: the speaker's audio when active will he always treated as high-priority, and when inactive, as low-priority.  That sounds like the desired outcome here.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This is related to #512

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
Re option 2 -- I remembered that there is group ordering in between publisher priority, and the individual peeps, so merging them does not quite work.

So we get `(subscriber priority) -> (publisher priority) -> (group ID) -> (peep priority) -> (object ID)`

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I have no idea what the publish priority of a track is. Publisher are setting priorities for objects. I think the confusion on this may have crept in on how the quic priority for a quic stream is set when the stream is created. 

I agree that subscriber priorities greatly increase the bookkeeping in a relay. They probably result in each subscriber needing a separate priority queue. I'd be fine with removing them but I recognize most the working group will wand to keep them. However for the use cases I care about, the publisher being able to set different priorities is critical.

issues.title: Do tracks need their own publisher priority?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
In #517 and #512 we discuss details about how priority should work.

In https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/518/files#r1744303191 @afrind suggested that there be an explicit publisher priority.

Do we need one?  It might make things simpler, despite adding another attribute to prioritization, because we could only consider subscriber and publisher priority when picking which track to prioritize, and then within a track, we can use group order and peep/object priority to decide what data to send.

@vasilvv may have thoughts as well?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: The only reason I can imagine having a publisher priority attached to the subscription and not individual things on it is if we wanted to let publishers update it, including changing priority of previous objects.  That is logistically complicated, and I don't think it's the desired behavior in any use cases I can think of.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
Publisher specified priority on objects being published is needed to support the cases where there is uplink congestion from the publisher to the relays , home wifi(relays) to cloud relays , for example. 

Also in cases where publishers and subscribers are in a controlled settings, only publisher set priority will ever be needed.  

My thinking from our discussions in Seattle has been along the following lines
- objects carry publisher priority
- the algo to pick the next object when there are more than one object available to send, will consider publisher priority and per subscription priority.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: SVC transmission is another use-case where the publisher would want the ability to set priorities between tracks since it would be critical to their correct transmission between relays.   A catalog can always be used for the publisher to communicate relative track priorities to a subscriber and hence have subscriber-only priorities, but these are not read by relays and hence we need some way to optimize the transmission between relays.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
In my opinion, priority should flows _down_ through the object model.

track > group > object

- The track with the higher subscriber priority is sent first.
- If there's a tie, the track with the higher publisher priority (in SUBSCRIBE_OK) is sent first.
- If there's a tie, the group with the highest ID is sent first if the subscriber indicates DESC, reversed otherwise.
- If there's a tie, the group with the highest ID is sent first if publisher indicates DESC (via SUBSCRIBE_OK), reversed otherwise.
- If there's a tie, the object with the lowest ID is sent first.

I think SVC should be done via multiple tracks with different priorities. The most obvious reason why is so you can choose to unsubscribe to enhancement layers. But a secondary reason is that it prevents object priority from bubbling up and trumping track priority (publisher only?)

issues.title: Ad Insertion
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body: How does insertion of advertisements work and do we need any changes in MoQT to support that ?

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: @wilaw thoughts ?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: We're at the point this is an important topic to discuss, but I'm not an expert on it.  It's possible we don't need to do anything special for MoQ transport to enable this, but I'm not sure.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
I don't have a good answer for this.

HLS makes it "easy" to perform ad insertion because there's a decoupling of the manifest and edge server. You can run a custom manifest server that, on a per segment basis, instructs viewers the URL of the next segment. This doesn't require any cooperation with the CDN that actually serves the segments.

However due to the subscription-based nature of MoQ... it's more complicated. The only idea I have is to create a new track at possible ad insertion points and force the viewer to resubscribe, consulting the ad server for the name of the new track. It's kind of gross but it could work.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
I have though about this a bunch because support for advertising is crucial for the commercial viability of MOQT-based streaming formats. I had a side meeting with Yospace CTO David Springall  a few months back to talk through some conceptual ideas. He provided this diagram of how MOQ might integrate into a low latency ad insertion workflow:

![PastedGraphic-1](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ee875ea7-8e0c-4723-afb9-c2c9726caa62)

The OTT ad industry is moving towards server-guided ad insertion, a mode of insertion which the client performs the insert but using instructions provided by a server. 

There are some key points in all of this:
1. We need the concept of a playback session. Luckily, we have a good proxy for this with our Wt or QUIC session establishment. We assign this session a random ID and it registers itself, either via HTTP or MOQT (I am in favor of the latter) with an ad backend. This backend will understand the previously registered broadcast and then be able allocate ad placement opportunties to each individual session. 
2. Interstitial ads are VOD content, even when placed into live streams. This means we can FETCH them. 
3. MOQT encoders will need to be SCTE compliant, as those markers are the dominant placement signaling mechanism in use today.  In my draft design of a timeline track, I [showed](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1MgcASdH_b8gUpMHjO-05Gbk_0CP8yw0RQO9gVO0UHrg/edit#slide=id.g21bc8d0f159_0_23) how an off-the-shelf SCTE-35 marker could be embedded. 
4. It is important that we are compliant with existing ad inventory. This is almost universally stored as ISOBMFF or TS files. It would be possible to create a proxy gateway to these ad systems which vend MOQT track variants of these assets, including trans-packaging to LOC or other container formats. 
5. We can use catalogs to instruct clients on when to insert ads. In order to provide user-personalized advertising, we need to be able to generate unique catalogs for each user. This must be done at the edge. To enable this, we should introduce the concept of an application layer at the outermost relay server. This app layer will provide functionality similar to the serverless edge compute offered with HTTP today. It will be able to subscribe to a base catalog and then modify it for each connection. It should also be able to modify Objects themselves. We can use this for many customization features (per-session watermarking, codec/format restrictions based on device type, content offering suggestions etc). 

MOQT offers some benefits for advertising that we don't have in the HTTP workflow:
1.  Having millions of client report ad playback quartiles during synchronized ad placements means that the ad reporting services need to be highly scalable. Today this is done with separate data collection networks. The directional nature of MOQT connections means that client-side ad reporting can be made though the same distribution network which is serving the media. This affords much richer, reliable and easily scalable reporting. 
2. The parallel nature of MOQT means that more flexible ad displays can be implemented. Overlays are possible MOQT can also carry image assets for advertising, it does not need to be A/V. 

Yospace have signaled interest in participating in some early proofs-of-concept to start exploring these ideas.

comments.author: kota-yata
comments.body: What about SSAI? MoQT principle of not modifying stream content on the path and SSAI doesn't seem to fit together. I'm thinking something like this for SSAI-like insertion, but I don't feel like this is efficient or viable for personalization

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
@kota-yata  - what I had in mind is explained in the diagram below. The original publisher would publish a catalog (or equivalent list of tracks). This would include the audio and video content as well as a timeline track. The timeline track describes the history of the audio and video from that publisher and its common for all subscribers, so I don't want to put any ad related data in it. For that, we add a new track which I'm calling an 'Ad insertion track". It will be filled with a list of instructions of which ads to insert and when. This ad insertion track is not coming from the original media publisher (green), but from another original publisher I'm calling the "MOQ compliant ad decisioning system" (blue). When the client subscribes to this ad track, it appends its userID to the subscription. This allows the ad decisioning system to customize an ad pod for that user. The track returns a set of insertion instructions of which ads to insert and when. This ad content is provided by a third original publisher I'm terming the "advertising content origin" (purple). 

This architecture allows the same catalog to be consumed by all end-users (good for scale) while allowing the ad insertion instructions to be customized for each end user based on their identifier which makes it compatible with current interstitial solutions (good for interop and to leverage existing ad inventory and decisioning systems). 

Let me know if you have opinions. 


![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cb2bafa9-25c9-4c5e-b853-adde5b7ec3b6)

comments.author: kota-yata
comments.body:
Thanks.
To support ad insertion at dynamic timings like the end of an inning in a baseball game, the decisioning system needs a mechanism where the ad insertion track delivers the ad content in advance, while the exact timing for insertion (i.e., timeline placement) is notified later. This way the content could be preloaded and ready, and the actual insertion point can be determined in real time based on the state of the live event or stream.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
wilaw
comments.body:
> @wilaw your solution requires the client to explicitly subscribe to the ad tracks. It is not SSAI, is it?

Indeed. It's Server Guided Ad Insertion (SGAI) which is where the OTT ad industry is moving with both Interstitials in HLS and AlternativeMPD in DASH. This has shown to be flexible and scalable. comments.author: riedlse
comments.body:
SO I still think SSAI still makes a lot of sense over SGAI at least in Paramount sense and the way our stitcher works and scales. I was c hatting with ChatGPT about having individual timelines and it was quite optimistic. I'm happy to have any of the esteemed folks on this chat tell me where it started hallucinating as I am told it can do time to time...

MoQ is not only useful when “everyone watches the same moment.” It was designed to support both live fan-out and individualized timelines, including pause, rewind, and “off-timeline” playback, without dropping out of MoQ.
Here’s the sharper breakdown:
1) Independent timelines (pause/rewind/DVR) are built into MoQ
MoQ’s core transport lets a subscriber FETCH arbitrary ranges of past media (“Standalone Fetch”), and—crucially—“Joining Fetch” lets a client backfill from the past and then flow straight back into the live subscription contiguously and without overlap. That’s exactly what you need for pause/DVR time-shift. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
Clients also choose Group Order (ascending or descending) per subscription/fetch, which is handy for “catch up” behavior (e.g., newest-first to close a gap). ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
Net: With a live SUBSCRIBE + periodic JOINING FETCH (relative or absolute), you can implement pause, replay 30s, or join-midstream catch-up entirely over MoQ. No HLS/DASH manifest gymnastics required. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
2) Personalized ads do not require leaving MoQ
MoQ is publish/subscribe by track name/namespace; a server “stitcher” can publish a per-viewer track (or a shared program track + personalized ad objects) and the client just stays subscribed. The protocol makes no assumption that all viewers get identical bytes; that’s an application choice. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
If you want server-side SSAI that’s indistinguishable to the client (your goal), you simply interleave ad objects at Group boundaries on the same track. The client never switches protocols or tracks. (Operational note: like per-user HLS SSAI, personalization reduces cache dedupe; that’s an economics/architecture trade-off, not a MoQ limitation.) ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
3) Where HLS/DASH are still strong (and why you may pick them)
The HLS/DASH ecosystem is mature for pure VoD, very long DVR windows, offline/downloads, and deep CDN cache leverage; tooling and players are everywhere. If you don’t need sub-second or interactive latency, they’re a safe, boring choice. ([nanocosmos](https://www.nanocosmos.net/blog/webrtc-latency/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Streaming Media Magazine](https://www.streamingmedia.com/Articles/Editorial/Featured-Articles/Media-Over-QUIC-and-the-Future-of-High-Quality-Low-Latency-Streaming-167165.aspx?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
But for low-latency live with time-shift and individualized experiences, MoQ gives you a single transport with built-in catch-up (Joining Fetch) and per-subscription scheduling/priority—no manifest surgery. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
4) Practical MoQ patterns for “independent viewing” you asked about
Pause/DVR: Keep a live SUBSCRIBE to video/main + audio/main. When the user seeks back 30s, issue Relative Joining Fetch for N groups behind the live edge; when done, let playback run back to the subscription’s live edge seamlessly (the draft defines this contiguity explicitly). ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
Late join catch-up: Start a SUBSCRIBE in Descending group order for the last few groups to fill the buffer quickly, then switch to normal playback order. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
SSAI on one track: Stitch ads at Group (GOP) boundaries in the same track; no client switch, no protocol switch. (If you also mirror ad cues via a tiny “events” track using DATAGRAMs, beacons fire on time but the media still stays on one MoQ track.) ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))

Bottom line
MoQ ≠ “broadcast-only.” It supports individualized timelines (pause/rewind) with FETCH + Joining Fetch, per-subscription ordering, and deadlines/priorities. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))
You don’t need to “go off MoQ” for personalized ads. Your stitcher can publish a per-viewer stitched track; the client stays on the same MoQ subscription. The trade-offs are about caching/ops, not protocol capability. ([IETF Datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/))

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
So the intent is:

```
track    == rendition
group    == gop
subgroup == layer
object   == frame
```

However, without the ability to subscribe to a specific subgroup at different priorities, I don't think this will actually work for SVC. Yes, the publisher can indicate a different priority per subgroup (aka SVC layer), but the subscriber can't.

My proposal is instead:
```
track    == rendition/layer
group    == gop
subgroup == 0 (or <deleted>)
object   == frame
```

The client would subscribe to each SVC layer/track independently, joining them based on the group. It makes it very easy to signal the priority of base/enhancement layers and use different settings (ex. delivery timeout).

The only architecture I can think of is to run an "active intermediary Relay" [#527 (comment)](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/527#issuecomment-3131106213)

No, I'm describing something a little bit different.  I would consider it SSAI because the client has no way of getting the original broadcast, similar to SSAI via HLS playlist rewriting.

publisher produces:
```
content-abc123:  ------
ad-break:              |
content-def456:         -------------------
```

The names of these tracks and the position of the ad-break are made available to the ad signaling service via some means. They are NOT known by the client, hence the random suffix.

The ad signalling service tells all clients to `SUBSCRIBE content-abc123`. When the ad break is triggered, it tells clients:
- no fill: `SUBSCRIBE content-def456` (no content missed)
- fill: `FETCH some-ad-id`, `FETCH another-ad-id`, followed later (in real-time) by `SUBSCRIBE content-def456`.

You absolutely could pretend like the ads are live and use SUBSCRIBE instead of FETCH. I just think it quickly becomes too complicated/expensive without explicit CDN cooperation. And from personal experience, you're likely leaking something else that can be used to determine if it's advertisement (ex. VAST tracking, click URLs, "advertisement" banner, etc). 

At Twitch, we realized that we couldn't avoid leaking if an ad was active and settled for "at best, an ad blocker can show a black screen over an ad". The critical part is that `content-def456` is either unguessable or gated behind authentication only provided by the ad service.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
@kixelated  - I like your approach described above, however wouldn't it fall squarely in the Server-Guided bucket, since the the client is receiving real-time instructions (guidance) on which content to play? Here are my classification

- Client-side ad insertion: client is given the primary content address, ad content address and information on when to render the ads. It is trusted to perform the insertion operations. 
- Server-guided insertion: the client receives dynamic information on which content (primary and ad) to request and is still trusted to to request the correct content at the right time. 
- Server-Side ad insertion: the server performs all the work of inserting decisioning, retrieving ,and inserting the ads and the client passively plays a single stream of content. The client may be untrusted.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
At the last interim, we presented several presentations on advertising and debated these concepts at length.

[Advertising with MOQT ](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1DenP4DWcZSe42QVlrF1oyas-V8WNYVAMla2v8-1YqsQ)- Will
[Ad Insertion and Blackout Management in MOQ ](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/128-O-Hr-jvpdsXuArlV7b-8bjP-ccZFvH7j0VRPGPNQ)- Gwendal

This [slide ](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1DenP4DWcZSe42QVlrF1oyas-V8WNYVAMla2v8-1YqsQ/edit?slide=id.g39f93a06033_1_300#slide=id.g39f93a06033_1_300) summarized the requirements on the core transport (which is the subject of this thread). The WG consensus was that _**there was adequate message capability within draft-16 to enabled client-side and server-guided ad insertion, as represented by various diagrams in this issue thread**_. The was no-consensus and in fact rejection of the notion of defining "application-like" behaviors for relays, such as would be required to implement a pure SSAI solution in a standard relay, in which tracks were multiplexed relay-side in a manner which was imperceptible to the client. An implementer can always build a relay which performs such an action, but it's behavior and interface would not be standardized by this transport specification. It could be implemented via a separate draft which defines an extension point. 

With these conclusions in mind, we'd like to close this issue.

issues.title: Clarify "abruptly closed" on control stream
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Section 3.3 says:

"The control stream MUST NOT be abruptly closed at the underlying transport layer. Doing so results in the session being closed as a 'Protocol Violation'."

I know we have multiple transports, but it would be good to clarify what an abrupt close is. Presumably any sort of RESET_STREAM, but what happens if there's a FIN? Is this a "clean close" of the session? Does it imply or force a reset of data streams?

issues.title: Allow padding streams
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: Since we currently don't allow unknown frame types and unknown stream types, there is no way to inject padding on the application level.  I believe it would be useful to allow for at least padding unidirectional streams (i.e. streams where receiver ignores everything past the stream type), those could be used for probing (e.g. sending a unidirectional stream at the lowest priority to determine if the connection could sustain more application data).

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
As a publisher, one can publish a track like what you're describing, but it sounds like you want it built into the transport.

Understanding how it might be used would be helpful.  Is the subscriber trying to see if it has more bandwidth so it can increase quality?  If so, why not just subscribe to the higher quality at a lower priority?

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: Agree with Ian . We already do a mix of these things today ( hi/low tracks, low priority probe-like stuff) .. May be I am lacking to understand the requirement here ?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
> Understanding how it might be used would be helpful. Is the subscriber trying to see if it has more bandwidth so it can increase quality? If so, why not just subscribe to the higher quality at a lower priority?

Those are valid if you have one publisher and a lot of subscriber, but for 1:1 scenarios, you would typically have the sender produce only one video stream (and then adjust its bitrate unilaterally), so that's not really an option.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: For 1:1 scenarios where the sender is only producing a single stream, the publisher/sender can decide to probe for more bandwidth unilaterally.  The simplest but effective approach is to just retransmit data you've already sent, aka world's simplest FEC.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Victor's ABR design should be discussed at a hybrid Interim.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
There was a discussion in the slack channel about this issue, which AI has summarized thus:

The discussion revolves around ensuring the congestion controller isn't app-limited in BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) congestion control algorithm. @kixelated mentions sending QUIC PADDING or PING frames periodically, specifically during the BBR ProbeBW_UP phase, to fill the congestion window until a target bitrate is achieved.

For WebTransport clients, creating a "padding" stream with a high sendOrder (lowest priority) is suggested. However, timing the padding with ProbeBW_UP (~1/8th of the time) is crucial for it to be effective with BBR. @vasilvv mentions BBRv1 adjusts cycles depending on whether you're app-limited or not, and ensuring the probe is at least 8 RTTs long can also help.

The goal of padding is to increase bandwidth, and it should be used when the padding rate is smaller than the maximum bitrate. Constant padding can minimize wasted bandwidth, but padding only during ProbeBW_UP is more efficient.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
The danger of application padding is that the underlying QUIC library MUST deprioritize any padding stream otherwise it'll start impacting the broadcast. As I result, don't think you should use padding streams today with WebTransport (upload) because `sendOrder` is only a hint and not even implemented in Chrome yet. It's highly dependent on the underlying transport too; I don't think you want padding streams with WebTransport over HTTP/2 or QMux.

Additionally, QUIC PADDING frames are not subject to flow control, so you can't accidentally hit MAX_DATA early and block real data. PADDING frames are not retransmitted, unlike application level padding which will be retransmitted with highest priority after congestion.

I think bandwidth probing is the type of feature that requires explicit support from the underlying QUIC stack unfortunately. The timing and duration of padding also depends on the underlying congestion control algorithm.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
> `sendOrder` is only a hint

That isn't entirely true, if there are two streams with different send orders, one of them will starve another, and that is not an optional behavior of the current W3C spec.

> not even implemented in Chrome yet

That is correct, though MoQ already does rely on send order working in order to operate well under poor network conditions.

> I don't think you want padding streams with WebTransport over HTTP/2 or QMux.

Why not?

> bandwidth probing is the type of feature that requires explicit support from the underlying QUIC stack unfortunately

Well, we don't have this feature guaranteed to be in every QUIC strack, and given we do need some form of probing up, I am not sure that saying "guess we just can't do this" and giving up at this point is an option.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The WG was largely supportive of closing this with no action, though Victor commented that I didn't fully explain what he was trying to describe in this issue, because a Track that's all padding is different and slightly more costly than streams where the payload is discarded.

Unless we're also going to add a way to request the proposed "Padding" streams be sent (ie: a control message?), I'm unsure how we could use them in MoQ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @vasilvv this issue is blocked on you.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
My proposal is:
- Add a new unidirectional stream type.
- The stream has to be all zeroes.
- The receiver has to discard all data on the stream.

That's what we currently do in our implementation, at least.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> My proposal is:
> 
> * Add a new unidirectional stream type.
> * The stream has to be all zeroes.
> * The receiver has to discard all data on the stream.

I support this approach. The advantage of enabling this versus an application-provided stream of zeroes, is that the application provided stream must be routed from the original publisher all the way through the network to the edge, when its really only needed at the dge. This is wasted mid-gress traffic and midgress cache. Being able to have the edge relay spawn this stream would be more efficient. I would extend the design to enable the Subscription to this special stream to specify the desired bitrate i.e SUBSCRIBE (padding, 1.2Mbps)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @vasilvv can you write a PR for this?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I left a comment on the PR, but I'm not sure if a stream is the best option due to retransmissions?  Are datagrams better?

issues.title: No mention of H3 GOAWAY or WT drain
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body: MoQT defines its own GOAWAY drain, thats fine. But it probably needs to refer to H3 and WT in a similar way that WT does in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-10#section-4.6. In other words, MoQT is building a 3rd mechanism and any folks that might use the other two could be in for a surprise. So I think there needs to be some text about the expected interactions.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Hopefully we don't need to mention H3 GOAWAY specifically, and WT will handle that bit for us (and any other protocols on WT), and it ought to mean "You can't make any new WebTransport sessions above the parameter in GOAWAY".

We do need to address DRAIN_WEBTRANSPORT_SESSION, but unfortunately I don't think we can completely remove moq GOAWAY, since raw QUIC has no equivalent.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Yeah I think MoQT does need it's own GOAWAY and just a small amount of text is needed. 

However, I'm not sure you can completely omit mention of H3 GOAWAY. WT makes it pretty clear that if you receive one, it's an indicator to start closing all webtransport sessions. There's a bit if a race here, if a client receives H3 GOAWAY, it won't know the URI to migrate to and it might have to wait indefinitely. We should consider some text for a) whether a client should wait on receiving MoQT GOAWAY (and for how long) before deciding to tidy up WT state b) whether it can safely assume that it can retry with the same URI or not.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I wish QUIC had it's own GOAWAY.  I generally think of the WebTransport and QUIC API surfaces being identical and this is a spot they clearly differ.  And ALPN, but in theory that's fixed?

issues.title: Extending QUIC notation
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
In https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-1.3 three new notations are presented thst extend the usual QUIC notations defined in RFC 9000.

Personally, with no hats, I don't see much value in adding all the notation. It introduces overlap and divergence from how we already use the existing notation to convey similar types e.g. the `x (b)` form

> SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE_ERROR
{
  Track Namespace Prefix (tuple),
  Error Code (i),
  Reason Phrase (b),
}

vs two separate fields

> CONNECTION_CLOSE Frame {
  Type (i) = 0x1c..0x1d,
  Error Code (i),
  [Frame Type (i)],
  Reason Phrase Length (i),
  Reason Phrase (..),
}

The `x (tuple)`  format seems potentially useful but grates me a bit given its just a group of things, where the group size is restricted to 1..32. It could be represented for example as a type

``` 
Track Namespace Parameters {
  Parameter Count (8) = 1..32,
  Track Namespace Parameter (..) ...,
}

Track Namespace Parameter {
  Track Namespace Paramater Length (i),
  Track Namespace Parameter Value (..),
}
```


Personally, I don't quite think the value of the new things overcomes the additional cognitive load that readers need to carry. There's many other folks that already use or consume RFC 9000 notation. This issue is sort of already present in MoQT, where the `Parameter` type doesn't use the `x (b)` form even though it could to cover the length and value parts.

```
Parameter {
  Parameter Type (i),
  Parameter Length (i),
  Parameter Value (..),
}
```

So one suggestion is to remove the special notations and go back to RFC 9000 style. This shouldn't change the wire encoding at all.


A different suggeation, if I'm in the rough and the MoQ WG has consensus that there is value in extending the notation and dealing with the overlap and cognitive load, it's possible other WGs might too. Having to import MoQT for a notational convention is messy. So it might make sense to spin them out into a separate I-D that could update RFC 9000, and send that over to the QUIC WG to manage.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I don't really care what we do here either but I would like to point at what I suspect is one of the root causes of all the pain around this is given 

```
Track {
   Len (i), 
   Val (..),
  } 
```
  
It is not possible to write a encoder/parser for that because the length of val may or may not be encoded in Len. You have to have extra information to know how to write an parser for that structure. That seems like a pretty big lacking in any formal syntax.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I agree with your point. However, knowing what exactly to do also depends on the context of the parsing. There could be redundant length fields etc.

And there's formal syntax and there's formal syntax :-) despite what our friends in the formal methods world might wish for, I don't think anyone wants to devolve into Z notation etc. 

We've done pretty ok with the existing notation plus normative language across a number of RFCs. It's flexible while providing a natural mapping to many common languages. That might be good enough, or there might be an opportunity to take feedback to the QUIC WG and let them consider it. Adding notation inside MoQT seems like the least best outcome to me

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
No strong opinion. Other than (b) which is a simplification, the draft currently defines 2 new notations
1. Boolean
2. Tuple
I feel those 2 are still needed as RFC9000 doesn't really define them.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The boolean `x (f)` is used in two places, for example

> SUBSCRIBE_OK
{
  Subscribe ID (i),
  Expires (i),
  Group Order (8),
  ContentExists (f),
  [Largest Group ID (i)],
  [Largest Object ID (i)],
  Number of Parameters (i),
  Subscribe Parameters (..) ...
}

This especially sticks out because the `Group Order` field is also a bit field but it uses a different value range.

> Group Order: Indicates the subscription will be delivered in Ascending (0x1) or Descending (0x2) order by group. See [Section 4](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#priorities). Values of 0x0 and those larger than 0x2 are a protocol error.

> ContentExists: 1 if an object has been published on this track, 0 if not. If 0, then the Largest Group ID and Largest Object ID fields will not be present.

You can substitute the `x (f)` notation e.g. `contentExists(8),` and add the statement `values other than 0x0 or 0x1 are a protocol error`.

The other common way of defining message variants, that may or may not contain an optional field, is to use the type value itself. For example, 

> CONNECTION_CLOSE Frame {
  Type (i) = 0x1c..0x1d,
  Error Code (i),
  [Frame Type (i)],
  Reason Phrase Length (i),
  Reason Phrase (..),
}

> Frame Type: A variable-length integer encoding the type of frame that triggered the error. A value of 0 (equivalent to the mention of the PADDING frame) is used when the frame type is unknown. The application-specific variant of CONNECTION_CLOSE (type 0x1d) does not include this field.

This approach is used in several RFCs. It avoids needing to send an entire byte for the field.

As noted above, the tuple type can already be represented with existing notation. As I read more, I think the notation actually causes a disservice to implementers because the tuple size is represented as a varint but MoQ allows only values in the range 1-32. That constraint is stated once in https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-2.4.1. There is no language to state what happens when other values are received. By creating a generic notation, MoQT actually made things harder to decipher.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The point is, `x (f)` is not required. If you want to constrain the set of values permittednin a field, use this from RFC 9000:

> x (L) = C..D:

>   Indicates that x has a value in the range from C to D, inclusive, with the length described by L, as above

The `x (f)` notation seems to be invented here specifically to optimise for messages that are defined in a way that diverge from common convention. That seems like a pretty weak argument to me.

And if we uplevel further, the use of a boolean to describe variants of a message is a common design approach already. But it is already commonly solved by using two different types instead, for example:

QUIC ACK frames
QUIC STREAM frames
QUIC MAX_STREAMS frames
QUIC STREAMS blocked frames
QUIC CONNECTION_CLOSE frames
QUIC DATAGRAM frames
HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE frames

I'll also highlight that the notational convention is defined as 

> A value of 0 indicates the flag is false or off, while a value of 1 indicates the flag is true or on. Any other value is a protocol error and SHOULD terminate the session with a Protocol Violation ([Section 3.5](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#session-termination)).

So actually this is a MoQT specific notation in its current definition. 

The more I poke at this stuff, the stronger my opinion grows that these extensions are bad for the overall health of IETF documents.I think we need stonger justification for extending the notation in this way.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Most of this is fixed by #550 except for tuple's use of x(b).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See #1192 which removes x (tuple) and x (b).

issues.title: Include message type in definitions to match QUIC notation style
issues.author: LPardue

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Good point, that would also prevent us/me from forgetting to allocate a codepoint for new messages.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I would prefer it to look more like: 

```
GOAWAY_Frame {
Type (i) = MSG_TYPE_GOAWAY,
Length (i),
Stream_ID_Push_ID (i),
}
```
( I don't care about if we are camel case, snake case, or whatever, but using space as a separator is really confusing as it s the separator when want to put two labels in text. I don't care if this is how quic did it, this is not quic ) IfYouWantToUseSpaceAsTheSeperatorForPartsOfALabelNameThenWeNeedToStopUsingThemIntheText. 

Then in an IANA table with all the message types,  define MSG_TYPE_GOAWAY = 0x07. This make it easier to have a label to talk about the type and makes it easier to ensure 7 is not assigned to two messages.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
FWIW, the PR to close this issue was already merged in https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/550.

To address the comments though:

>  I don't care about if we are camel case, snake case, or whatever, but using space as a separator is really confusing as it s the separator when want to put two labels in text. I don't care if this is how quic did it, this is not quic )

 I humbly disagree. There's a family of related documents that are building on each other, QUIC, HTTP/3, Capsule Protocol, other extensions, WebTransport, and then MoQT on top of those. Adding inconsistency in the documentation presentation just adds friction. Implementers are likely to be the same people. 
 
 In code, I'm going to represent this as a subtype of Message. In Rust, I can do it like 
 
 ```
 enum Message {
   GoAway { newSessionId: Vec<u8> },
   Unsubscribe { subscribe_id: u64 },
   ...
 }
 ```
 
There's never anything labelled GOAWAY_Message in that model (no matter how it might be capitalized) . Sure, other programming languages are different but again, the approach we have taken so far has been widely implemented and nobody seemed to have an issue.
 
 > Then in an IANA table with all the message types, define MSG_TYPE_GOAWAY = 0x07. This make it easier to have a label to talk about the type and makes it easier to ensure 7 is not assigned to two messages.
 
 So a few thoughts here:
 
 1) How often are message type concrete wire values talked about in text?  My very quick scan indicates zero times. In common parlance, my experience is people talk about messages "I sent you a GOAWAY Message", rather than "I sent you a MoQT message and it had the type MSG_TYPE_GOAWAY". When it comes to IANA, I expect we would register a MoQT Message registry and have entries like 
 
 | Value | Message Type | Status | Reference | Date | Change Controller | Contact | Notes |
 | 0x10 | GOAWAY | Permanent | RFC XXXX | YYYY-MM-DD | IETF | MoQ WG | |
 
 and if we had that style, I don't really see where the label `MSG_TYPE_GOAWAY` really fits in. 
 
 I agree there's a problem using the same value twice. That's why we should already have had IANA tables :D
 
 2) My implementation experience from QUIC etc is that its very convenient to have the pertinent information close at hand. Having the concrete value off in a different part of the document means needing to flip back and forth, which is doable but a bit annoying. Especially because of the lack of hyperlinks in our diagrams (a tooling issue). In contrast, its nice IMO to see in a single glance the objects full structure and expanded constants.
 
 3) All that said, having a layer of indirection in concrete values has proven useful for other documents while they are in a churn phase. Especially if they need to be renumbered (which I expect will happen for MoQ). For example, in RFC 9297,   in early drafts we used indirection (https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-masque-h3-datagram-05.html#section-4.4.2 `Type (i) = CLOSE_DATAGRAM_CONTEXT,` and in the IANA text defined  CLOSE_DATAGRAM_CONTEXT). Then for the RFC we removed the indirection. 
 
 On balance, I could support type indirection for I-Ds and then a removal of indirection when it comes to RFC. Would that be an acceptable compromise? If so, lets spin it out to a different issue and PR.

comments.body: The linked PR has closed

issues.title: Consider using different terms to disambiguate control messages with a type, from untyped messages on dedicated streams
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The spec uses the term `Message` for two different forms of things. Control messages share a single stream type and all need to contain a type in the message itself. IIUC, the things sent on streams of type OBJECT_DATAGRAM, STREAM_HEADER_TRACK, and STREAM_HEADER_TRACK are homongenous, so don't need an explicit type field. 

Calling both of these things `message` is mildly confusing since they have fundamentally different formats.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: While the control messages are defined as `Control Messages` in https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-control-messages, this isn't consistently used throughout the document. So perhaps that is the solution here.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Although we want to get rid of STREAM_HEADER_TRACK, it's necessary to have a type byte on unidirectional streams from STREAM_HEADER_SUBGROUP at this time.

IIRC, there is some thought about using Datagrams for another thing, and at the very least it's necessary to keep the OBJECT_DATAGRAM codepoint as an extension point for any such scheme.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I do agree that the doc needs an editorial pass, as until recently the control plane/data plane distinction was not as clean as it is now.

issues.title: Why define a boolean type but be lenient with its usage?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-1.3-5.4.1 states 

> Indicates that x is a flag and is encoded as a single byte with the value 0 or 1. A value of 0 indicates the flag is false or off, while a value of 1 indicates the flag is true or on. Any other value is a protocol error and SHOULD terminate the session with a Protocol Violation ([Section 3.5](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#session-termination)).

This seems at odds with the QUIC design ethos of being very strict about receiving things that are obviously broken. This matter is wrapped up in https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/536 and the proposed change (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/543), so I wanted to track the question separately.

I suspect we might want a bigger pass over the recomendations about when to detect a protocol error and how to handle it but I don't want to miss this specific issue in case it was done for a good reason.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I don't think this is editorial, since it affects the expectations on what a receiver is expected to do

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
To clarify, the proposal is to change the SHOULD terminate to a MUST terminate?

I expect that's what everyone will do anyway, so this SG

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Yes that would be my proposal here.

And in addition, a separate review of other fields for consistency.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Discussed in today's interim. MUST rolled into https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/543 and merged. So closing issue as done.

issues.title: Error code definitions use proper English
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
There are several error cocdes defined in MoQT which state a code and a reason, that is proper English. This contrasts with the QUIC and HTTP/3 specs, which define error codes using Upper Case format. E.g. "Foo Bar" vs. "FOO_BAR".

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Just a note on the characterization of this as QPACK-like.  I don't think that's accurate.  QPACK reserves the highest value in the first octet as a marker for there being more bytes.  After that, it uses the high bit on subsequent bytes.

Given @fluffy's constraints it seems like there are other options to consider...

First byte, up to 250 is directly encoded.  A value of 251 indicates that there are two more bytes that follow, 252 means four, 253 means eight, 254 means sixteen, 255 means thirty-two.  Choose a different cut point and a different mapping to integer size if you prefer (this doesn't need to be powers of two or even a simple sequence; I can see this being 2, 3, 4, 8, 16).  You can add 251 to those values if you want better bit-efficiency, but that might not be a good trade for this protocol.

The main drawback of that is that you lose alignment.  The advantage is that you have a straight table off the first byte, rather than having to do the two-way mapping in Alan's sample implementation, or a call to [`leading_ones`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html#method.leading_ones).

If you like, there's a testbed in https://github.com/martinthomson/quic-int that you can tweak to test byte-packing efficiency and encode/decode performance.

I would expect my proposal to perform roughly equivalently to QUIC integers since it uses an O(1) lookup table to determine the integer size, just one with 16 entries instead of 4.  I will see if I can adapt my implementation to your benchmark.

Given current architectures I think anything that's longer than 64 bits needs to be encoded as a bit string rather than an integer.  It's an equivalent number of bytes on the wire for an MOQT parameter or extension, it just means we won't support 128 bit Group IDs, Object IDs and Aliases, etc in this version.

issues.title: Better compression of VarInts
issues.author: fluffy

A one byte VarInt can only 64 values but most variable length encodings could express twice that many values. 

The bandwidth of MoQ could be reduced, helping reduce global warming, by a better VarInt design for MoQ.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
QUIC varints use 2 bits in the first byte to express if the number is 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes long.

Protobuf varints use 1 bit *per byte* to express if the number continues to the next byte. This is probably similar to what you're referring to.

QUIC is usually more efficient when encoding numbers greater than 2^14. Protobuf is only more efficient encoding numbers between 2^6 and 2^7.

Regardless, you already need a QUIC library for MoQ and it often comes with a VarInt encoder/decoder for free.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
So if I understand the problem statement, the issue is that reserving the 2 MSBs means that a value of 64-127 needs 2 bytes rather than 1 (and values 16384-32767 need 3 bytes rather than 2 etc). 

Is there any idea how much this would affect MOQT traffic? If its isolated to a few message types, rather than defining another new primitive variable-length integer, we could consider structured variable-length messages. I.e. a VAR_FOO message would have two (or more) variants that support different length thresholds

8-bit version
```
VAR_FOO Message {
Type (i) = 0XF00,
Length (i),
Field that is commonly 0..255 (8)
}
```

16-bit version
```
VAR_FOO Message {
Type (i) = 0XF01,
Length (i),
Field that is commonly 256..65535 (16)
}
```

issues.title: ANNOUNCE (and maybe SUBSCRIBE?) infinite loops
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
I believe that if we're not careful, we can end up with ANNOUNCE infinite loops today.

If there are three relays connected: A -> B -> C -> A, then we need to ask relays to see if they've already seen an ANNOUNCE before forwarding it along to applicable SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACEs.  Similarly, I can imagine an ANNOUNCE/UNANNOUNCE loop, which aren't as trivially prevented by ensuring you don't forward the same ANNOUNCE twice.

SUBSCRIBE has a temporal ordering, so this feels more tractable, but given we allow arbitrary gaps in Objects and Groups, tracking everything you've already forwarded for a subscription is potentially very costly/complex.  If a relay is subscribing to the same track twice because two different relays announced it, I think it needs to keep state to ensure it doesn't forward the same Object multiple times?

BGP has loop prevention mechanisms and so do QUIC stateless resets.

Possibly deployments can ensure data flows in only one direction, but given this is pub/sub, not request/response, it's a lot easier to create loops.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
Typical feedback. Good to call this out as we are already are keeping state for both subscribes and announces.   Subscribes do have the same problem. 

The relay needs to maintain state that it sent the announce and subscribe. I agree it is costly with MOQT. This is not the only costly state requirement that MOQT requires the relay to maintain.  Unfortunately, MOQT is pretty heavy in state at many levels.   Having to maintain state without protection measures can lead to exploiting resources to cause a DoS.   It also adds latency/join times.  

 While not required to mitigate loops, it would help if both announce and subscribe had the originating relay ID included to enable features such as Reverse-path forwarding (RPF).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Seems like the solution is to disallow sending the same announce twice on the same session.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
One problem is the discretion we have to forward ANNOUNCE.

Suppose SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE flows C->B->A but C and A are directly connected.

A gets an ANNOUNCE for that namespace from upstream and forwards it A->B->C.

C did not get a SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE but decides to send it to A. Then even if A's upstream goes away, it will think it has a route to the namespace.

Worse yet, A might even have sent SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE to C, which would further encourage A to send an ANNOUNCE.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: The 1/22/25 interim indicated there is no interest in solving this problem; routing between relays is out of scope for the WG. I will add some text to #643 warning that this is not a relay routing protocol.

issues.title: How to use ANNOUNCE_OK, ANNOUNCE_ERROR, and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
QUIC provides reliability, so I know the peer received the ANNOUNCE (or UNANNOUNCE).

We have almost no text on what might constitute an ANNOUNCE_ERROR and the only text on ANNOUNCE_CANCEL is you're supposed to send it if you're not going to send subscriptions to the publisher for something you sent an ANNOUNCE_OK for previously.

As it's written today, I don't see why an implementation would send or take any action based on any of these messages?

I believe there is some functionality we'd like in MoQT, which is we don't want anyone to be able to announce a track without appropriate auth, but I don't think this trio of messages gives us that, certainly not in the current draft.  I'd hope pretending to be authoritative for an entity you're not would be rare, and closing the session or another more abrupt approach would be fine.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

ANNOUNCE_ERROR was intended tell the publisher their auth failed.  I suppose closing the session is an alternative, but a potentially harsh one?  ANNOUNCE_OK Is basically the opposite.  Not all implementations (eg browser webtransport) offer callbacks on QUIC acks, and in H3 we decided that transport ACK was insufficient to communicate application ACK.  But it's mostly a debugging thing.  You could assume ANNOUNCE_OK unless you got an error, there's no action to take on it.

UNANNOUNCE is needed to support SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (eg: the relay needs to tell a client that previously ANNOUNCEd publisher is gone).

ANNOUNCE_CANCEL I think was added to make the state machine more complete for the publisher.  It might have a future use if we add something like MAX_ANNOUNCE_ID, which I think we will, since ANNOUNCE can cause the peer to add state.  Or maybe it could have a use in make-before-break, like "I am not going to route subscriptions on this session because I have a different path".  But agree that right now I don't have a reason to send it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
We've been punting auth for a bit, but maybe the upcoming interim is a time to prioritize discussing it, because I think once we understand our auth model better, we'll be able to understand if we need all the ANNOUNCE messages we have.

I started thinking about this in detail when I was trying to propose replacing SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE with sending a SUBSCRIBE for announces.  If we did that, I believe it would remove any functionality these three messages provide.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I am unclear of the state machine for these messages.

A publisher sends ANNOUNCE, which may or may not be in response to SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES (which has its own state machine which is orthogonal?)

If ANNOUNCE_ERROR comes back, we're done. If I get a later SUBSCRIBE, is that an error?

If ANNOUNCE_OK comes back, then we are serving any subscriptions, until I send UNANNOUNCE. So there's some sort of "ANNOUNCE_ACTIVE" state where the ANNOUNCE has been OKed but not canceled or UNANNOUNCED.

Does ANNOUNCE_CANCEL do the same thing as UNANNOUNCE, but in the opposite direction?

What does this state mean? As a relay, does this mean I'm prewarming it with a subscription? Does a relay not send its own ANNOUNCE_OK until it's gotten one from downstream (which might be a server in an upload scenario)? Does an uploading client give up if it gets ANNOUNCE_ERROR?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Here are my preferred answers:

- In terms of state, SUBSCRIBEs are totally divorced from ANNOUNCEs. It is never a protocol error to SUBSCRIBE to anything regardless of the state of any ANNOUNCE lifecycle, although of course a subscription can be refused, which is not a protocol error. [This is a change from the current language in ANNOUNCE_CANCEL].

- ANNOUNCE triggers ANNOUNCE_OK/ANNOUNCE_ERROR because ANNOUNCE_ERROR is a useful signal, certainly in the upload case.

- Publishers SHOULD send UNANNOUNCE to avoid useless SUBSCRIBEs, unless the subscriber has sent ANNOUNCE_CANCEL.

- Subscribers SHOULD send ANNOUNCE_CANCEL in case the publisher is maintaining state (again, likely in an upload scenario). Again, this doesn't preclude future SUBSCRIBEs, though those are likely to fail.

I think the only thing inconsistent with the current text is removing the protocol error.

comments.author: VMatrix1900
comments.body:
> Subscribers SHOULD send ANNOUNCE_CANCEL in case the publisher is maintaining state (again, likely in an upload scenario). Again, this doesn't preclude future SUBSCRIBEs, though those are likely to fail.

How does the subscriber know that the publisher is maintaining state?

issues.title: What is the data type of PATH?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
> Each parameter description will indicate the data type in the Parameter Value field.

It's implicit what the type is, but the section should state exactly what it is. 

https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-6.2.2.2

> The PATH parameter (key 0x01) allows the client to specify the path of the MoQ URI when using native QUIC ([[QUIC](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#QUIC)]). It MUST NOT be used by the server, or when WebTransport is used. If the peer receives a PATH parameter from the server, or when WebTransport is used, it MUST close the connection. It follows the URI formatting rules [[RFC3986](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#RFC3986)].

> When connecting to a server using a URI with the "moq" scheme, the client MUST set the PATH parameter to the path-abempty portion of the URI; if query is present, the client MUST concatenate ?, followed by the query portion of the URI to the parameter.

A protocol violation and so a CONNECTION_CLOSE?

I'd expect there to be similarities, where possible, to how HTTP would handle bad paths.

issues.title: Is there any reason to use 2MSB in x(tuple) in Track namespace?
issues.author: yuki-uchida
issues.body:
At this time, x(tuple) is only used in Track namespace, but Track namespace is limited to 32.
The 2MSB defined in RFC9000 can be used up to 62 bits, but since the Track namespace is limited to 32 bits, the 2MSB is effectively used only for 00.
In Track namespace, 8 bits are sufficient to represent N, so why not use 8 bits to represent N?
It is easier to understand than expressing with 2MSB.



```
x (tuple): Indicates that x is a tuple, consisting of a variable length integer encoded as described in ([RFC9000], Section 16), followed by that many variable length tuple fields, each of which are encoded as (b) above.

Track namespace is an ordered N-tuple of bytes where N can be between 1 and 32. The structured nature of Track Namespace allows relays and applications to manipulate prefixes of a namespace. Track name is a sequence of bytes.
```

comments.author: martinduke

comments.body:
> That makes sense but I think it would be nice to get this done before Dublin IETF

issues.title: Alternate Priority Clarification Proposal
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
This is an individual technical proposal for modifying the priority algorithm added in draft-05 (herein called "Seattle").

Draft-05 contains the following text:

> When two or more subscriptions have equal subscriber priority, the original publisher priority is considered next and can change within the track, so subscriptions are prioritized based on the highest priority data available to send. For example, if the subscription had data at priority 6 and priority 10 to send, the subscription priority would be 6. 

My interpretation of this text is that when a relay receives a new object with higher priority than any queued objects on that subscription, it elevates the publisher subscription priority to this new higher priority.  When it receives objects with lower priority than any queued objects, there is no impact to the publisher subscription priority.  When the relay dequeues an object of higher priority than remaining queued objects, it lowers the priority of the subscription.

Maintaining the subscription priority in this way is complex and potentially computationally expensive. The following proposal is intended to address that while otherwise maintaining the properties of Seattle algorithm, specifically selecting the next group within a prioritized subscription before selecting a subgroup from that group.

**MoQ Priority Proposal “Boston”**

The proposal supports the following priority signals:

1. **Subscriber Subscription Priority**: Subscriber specified priority of a subscription relative to other subscriptions
2. **Publisher Subscription Priority**: Publisher specified priority of a subscription relative to other subscriptions
3. **Subscriber Group Order**: Subscriber specified group order preference within a subscription, Ascending, Descending or Default to Publisher
4. **Publisher Group Order**: Publisher specified group order preference within a subscription; only considered when Subscriber Group Order is Default to Publisher.
5. **Object Priority**: Publisher specified priority of subgroup and datagram relative to other subgroups/datagrams in the same group

When “highest” and “lowest” are used to compare priorities, “highest” means the highest priority, which has the lowest numerical value, and vice versa.

**The priority algorithm is:**

* A relay selects the subscription with the highest **Subscriber Subscription Priority**;
	* If more than one subscription has this priority; select the subscription with the highest **Publisher Subscription Priority**;
		* If more than one subscription has this priority; the implementation chooses, with the assumption that every subscription makes some progress

* From the selected subscription, use the **Group Order** to choose the group to send from (either highest or lowest available).  

* If using stream-per-track, send the object with the lowest Object ID.

* If using stream-per-subgroup, select the subgroup with the highest **Object Priority**
	* if more than one subgroup has the same priority; choose the one with the lower subgroup ID.

* If using datagrams, select the Object with the highest **Object Priority**
	* if more than one datagram has the same priority; choose the one with the lower Object ID

**Analysis:**

The proposal in #518 uses the Object Priority as both the Publisher Subscription Priority and Object Priority.  In order to express increased importance of a particular subscription or track, it must also elevate the priority of the subgroup or datagrams relative to the subgroups and datagrams in the same group and other groups.  

Both Seattle and 518 can only change subscription priority by sending new subgroups or datagrams, although the wire format proposed below could also address this.

The 518 proposal also relegates Group Order to a less significant place in the priority hierarchy.  Consider a track with a single subgroup per group.  The subscriber may have asked for Group Order Ascending, but the publisher sets Object Priority as follows:

```
Group 0, Subgroup 0, Priority 1
Group 1, Subgroup 0, Priority 3
Group 2, Subgroup 0, Priority 2
```

Assuming queuing happens at the relay, it will send the groups 0, 2, 1 which is neither ascending nor descending, and overrides the subscriber preference.

In the new proposal, when the relay receives a new publisher priority signal, all unsent data in the subscription updates to that priority, the send order of groups and objects within that subscription remains unchanged.  Subscription Priority can be changed at any time and does not require producing an object or beginning a new subgroup.

“Boston” Wire Format changes:

Identical to draft-06 with the following additions:

1. - Subscribe OK contains a mandatory field for **Publisher Subscription Priority**
2. - One or more new messages to change the **Publisher Subscription Priority**:

* A new Object Status “Family”, eg: 

`UPDATE_PUBLISHER_SUBSCRIPTION_PRIORITY 0x100 - 0x1FF` where the last 8 bits are the new priority

* A new unidirectional stream header

```
UPDATE_PUBLISHER_SUBSCRIPTION_PRIORITY {
	Subscribe ID (i)
	Priority (8)
}
```

* A control message 

```
UPDATE_PUBLISHER_SUBSCRIPTION_PRIORITY {
	0xTBD
	Length (i)
	Subscribe Id (i)
	Priority (8)
}
```

Any of these messages could work but they have tradeoffs that can be discussed.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I don't think the algorithm proposed here is what we want.

The biggest problem I see with it is that the group order takes precedence over any priority assigned to individual subgroups, which means that all subgroups of a given group will be delivered before any subgroups of the subsequent group.  This sounds like the opposite of desirable for SVC (we presumably want the base layer in the next group before enhancement on the current one).

The other thing it does is it introduces a track-wide publisher priority, which, given the use cases I've heard described so far (see my analysis [here](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/517#issuecomment-2329283158)) is probably not what we want.

Speaking as someone with a non-caching relay implementation:

SUBSCRIBE_OK will return 2-1
SUBSCRIBE (Latest obj) begins with 2-2

I haven't implemented FETCH yet, but I think FETCH can set the end object to 2^62-1.  The question is, what comes in the FETCH OK?  Since I don't have a cache, I can just forward upstream (side question: should the relay rewrite the upstream FETCH end object to 2-1?).  If I had a cache, I'm not sure. comments.author: englishm
comments.body:
With Joining Fetch (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/638) now merged, it's especially important to clarify this now. It doesn't matter _too much_ where we draw the line, but it's important that we're consistent and that 2-1 be accessible on one side or the other.

Delivering all of 2-1 on the Subscribe side would mean keeping at least a "current object" cache as part of subscribe implementations. Some may prefer purely fanout implementations with no cache and this might be a slightly burdensome requirement.

Delivering all of 2-1 on the Fetch side could mean waiting for all of it to become available (particularly in the case of a Joining Fetch) which could mean blocking the Fetch until that object is fully in-cache or preemptively starting delivery of the Fetch range, but accepting that it may get blocked once it reaches 2-1 and have to drop from line rate delivery to application rate delivery. This could potentially have implications for CC / BWE algorithms if they expect Fetch to always deliver at or close to line rate. For small enough objects and large enough Fetch ranges this may be a non-issue in practice, but for very large objects and smaller Fetch ranges, it could have a larger impact.

As someone currently thinking a lot about implementation requirements for minimalist fanout relays, I'm slightly inclined towards the position which says 2-1 belongs on the "past" / Fetch side of the line.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Delivering all of 2-1 on the Subscribe side would mean keeping at least a "current object" cache as part of subscribe implementations. Some may prefer purely fanout implementations with no cache and this might be a slightly burdensome requirement.

Remember that Objects can have arbitrarily long durations and also large sizes. We tend to think of them as video frames, but they could be 10 minutes in duration and carry data at 20Mbps. If we want to enable non-caching fan-out relays, then the requirement to hold the current object in memory could be more than "slightly burdensome". We could set normative limits on the memory size of an Object (which may constrain some applications), or we could make holding the current Object optional, which leads to indeterminate behavior between relay networks.

>  I don't really understand the meaning of "deliver partial objects" perhaps

There's no way to send an Object via either SUBSCRIBE or FETCH unless you transmit *the object from the beginning*.   For a non-caching relay, this means that when a SUBSCRIBE comes and part of 2-1 has been received and forwarded, the new subscriber cannot get 2-1, except via FETCH.

Now, if if's a caching relay and it does have the beginning of 2-1 cached, it's possible that it could deliver it to the new subscriber via subscribe.  Then this gets tangled up with #758, but even with my interpretation of Latest Object, this is still fine so long as the relay puts 2-0 in SUBSCRIBE_OK.  If we add All Object filter type as suggested in #853, in that mode it wouldn't matter what value is put in SUBSCRIBE_OK; the caching relay can deliver 2-1 via subscribe regardless.

issues.title: Subscriber has to look up subscriptions by both track alias and subscribe ID
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
The subscriber needs to index all of its subscriptions by track_alias, because this is how objects will arrive. After the brief period waiting for SUBSCRIBE_OK/ERROR, the only time it needs to lookup a subscription by subscribe_id is when SUBSCRIBE_DONE arrives.

There is no reason this couldn't be the track_alias instead.

An implementer could just iterate through all its subscriptions to find the matching ID, or set up a separate map of subscribe_id to subscription. But that's pointless.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE also uses Subscribe ID, so I'd prefer using the ID for any state changes to SUBSCRIBE, and track alias is only for object delivery.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
This is an issue for messages that arrive at the Subscriber. The subscriber has no choice but to set up a map of track alias to subscription to manage incoming messages.

It has to keep a much smaller map of subscribe ID to subscription for subscriptions still waiting for SUBSCRIBE_OK and SUBSCRIBE_ERROR.

Having SUBSCRIBE_DONE use Subscribe ID means that all subscriptions need to be in two maps: one by track alias, one by subscribe ID.

Personally, I'd prefer we just get rid of track alias and use subscribe ID, since the latter has flow control implications. The next easiest thing to implement would be to always use track alias after the initial SUBSCRIBE.

FWIW, 

I'm in favor of keeping track alias over subscribe ID. Either way, both are not needed. 

tl;dr

 The original use-case, as I understand it, was that subscribe ID was to support multiple tracks (e.g., full track namespace and name = track alias) at the same time.... but that was when Fetch didn't exist and subscribe was used.
