issues.title: SUBSCRIBE(current group) splits past and future
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
One of the principles the group seemed to agree on is that FETCH is for the past and SUBSCRIBE is for the future.  Draft-07 however left in SUBSCRIBE(current group) which spans both and seems to violate the principle.  I understand that subscribing starting from the current group is likely to be a very common use case, as groups are MOQT join points.

My concern is that all the reasons we decided FETCH semantics were good for past data are being discarded here.  If the current group consists of an large number of subgroups or datagrams, the sender can overwhelm the receiver.  If the relay has a cache with gaps, we have not explained the interaction.

My strawman is to respond to SUBSCRIBE(current group) with both a FETCH OK and SUBSCRIBE OK, and objects from (current group, 0) to (current group, live edge) are returned in a FETCH stream using those semantics.

A large number of datagrams is a congestion issue, but not a flow control one.  For congestion, I'd expect the relay could lower the subscriber priority once it had too much data for a subscription?

If there's only one peep in a group, then starting at the current group doesn't create any problems.  If the peeps were all going to be open at once anyway (ie: 3 or 4 enhancement layers), then the stream usage is no different than starting at the current object.  As the number of peeps increases, it does start being problematic.  If you're doing one Object per peep, for example.

I'd rather not add a 3rd way to retrieve Objects, but I can see an argument for merging the existing functionality of FETCH and SUBSCRIBE and saying:
- You're getting things before the latest Object on a single stream, and ones after it in peeps or datagrams.

If we want to use track alias, I think we still need to prohibit having two "JOINs" that end beyond the current object?  Alternatively, we could just say that you'll only receive one copy of things after the current object, even if there are multiple matching JOINs/SUBSCRIBEs/etc?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
I distinguish the _present_ to the past and the future. The present is the current group, as seen by the Relay, i.e. the latest object it got from its parent. Let's call it current_ID (in Will's figure, current_ID = 2). Any object with a group ID lesser than current_ID is in the past. They should be obtained by FETCH. Any object with a group ID greater than current_ID is in the future. They typically trigger an error if referenced in a FETCH. The objects with a group ID equal current_ID are the present.

In the present, the Relay has a normative behavior: The Relay sends objects in the current group _in the order of the subgroups_ to each subscriber. Those with a high network connection will be at the latest object, while some subscribers with a much lower connection will be late. In Will's schema, it means that some subscribers are still downloading 2-0 while some others are at 2-1. If we extend it, it means that the Relay must store the ID of _the latest sent object within the group_ for all subscribers. When a new subscriber joins, it is at object 0 while all others will be somewhere between 0 and X (the latest object). It is not a problem, it is the normal behavior.

Yet, I'd see a problem with _ascending order_ in SUBSCRIBE. The subscribers with a slow network will cumulate drift and will eventually be far in the past, at the point that the Relay serves some subscribers in the present (2-1 and 2-0 in Will's schema) and some late subscribers in the past (1-X).

As I pointed out at one virtual interim, I think the past/future problem is one we already have, it's just not as bad.

Specifically, if one issues a SUBSCRIBE and FETCH and the FETCH has a higher priority (think lowish latency live sports) to fetch data from the recent past (ie: 15 second jitter buffer), the latest object could be in the next group or later by the time it can start sending Objects for the subscription

One could close the subscription with too far behind in this case, but you risk closing the subscription right around the time the video playback gets to the live head.

issues.title: What is the use case for DATAGRAM as an immutable property?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
We are close to getting rid of original-publisher defined forwarding preferences.

The stream mapping of FETCH is derived from the fidelity requirements of the Subscriber, not the Original Publisher. Once we made it possible for the subscriber to express this, Track forwarding preference was obsolete.

Similarly, the use case for DATAGRAM (AFAICT, "my latency requirements are so low you shouldn't even try to retransmit") seems to be a subscriber requirement rather than an immutable property of the track. This tells me it should be something subscriber determined (or sender calculated based on timeouts) rather than a track property.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Cullen's point about multiple subscribers to the same track with different delivery timeout properties is valid.  The subscriber with the longest delivery timeout will determine the relay -> upstream timeout, so subscribers joining/leaving at the relay could impact what is seen by other subscribers.

>  if there's a property of the track that one is trying to express by saying it only goes over datagrams, we should make that clear.

Datagrams have 3 properties

1. Shorter than 1 MTU
2. Not retransmitted
3. Not flow controlled

We don't need forwarding preference to convey 1, but having an end-to-end publisher signal to convey 2 and 3 seems right to me.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

1. There's a 4th property of datagrams, which is that they can be silently dropped -- dropping a stream once it's begun transmission requires a RESET.
2. I'm sort of ignoring flow control and stream limits for subscriptions because I don't think they make much sense - I think moq subscribers will set high limits to avoid running into them.

3. Martin what is your goal?  Do you want to enable datagrams as an optimization for originally-stream based tracks for low-timeout subscribers?  Or do you want to disallow publishers to control the delivery properties that datagrams afford?

The optimization case seems more-or-less fine to me:

Let's say the original publisher made the track based on streams, but a last mile subscriber A set a delivery timeout=0.  It seems like the relay should be able to optimize and send any objects < MTU as datagrams to this subscriber, since it will clearly never be able to retransmit them.  This will also save the overhead of sending a reset if the stream detects loss.  Subscriber B, with a higher delivery timeout, can still receive the same track via streams. 

As an aside - we should probably add text about how relays set delivery timeouts upstream, and possibly SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE needs to be able to change the timeout.  Does the upstream timeout need to be at least the MAX of the current downstream subscribers, or is ok for it to be smaller?

I think Suhas and Cullen are arguing for retaining publisher influence of delivery properties because they wouldn't want a rogue subscriber with a long timeout to impact other subscribers with shorter timeouts - potentially generating rxmits and resets on the uplink that the original publisher didn't want.

Good point, but this is, again a performance optimization that individual senders (not Publishers) can choose to make or not.

> 2. I'm sort of ignoring flow control and stream limits for subscriptions because I don't think they make much sense - I think moq subscribers will set high limits to avoid running into them.

OK. To the extent it matters, why should Publishers dictate to relays whether they need flow-control or not?

> 3. Martin what is your goal?  Do you want to enable datagrams as an optimization for originally-stream based tracks for low-timeout subscribers?  Or do you want to disallow publishers to control the delivery properties that datagrams afford?
> 

I don't think DATAGRAM is strictly necessary at all, but I understand why individual senders in the chain might choose to send them on a hop-by-hop basis under certain conditions. I think all of those conditions are local to the sender and cannot sensibly be controlled at the individual publisher.

The current framework actually *prevents* relays from making the local optimization decision to send DATAGRAM.

Furthermore, if we can completely eliminate the concept of forwarding preference, it simplifies the spec and the code. Implementations don't even have to support Datagram, if that's an obstacle.

> The optimization case seems more-or-less fine to me:
> 
> Let's say the original publisher made the track based on streams, but a last mile subscriber A set a delivery timeout=0. It seems like the relay should be able to optimize and send any objects < MTU as datagrams to this subscriber, since it will clearly never be able to retransmit them. This will also save the overhead of sending a reset if the stream detects loss. Subscriber B, with a higher delivery timeout, can still receive the same track via streams.

I agree, but this is specifically forbidden by the spec, because the Original Publisher sets this, and it must be obeyed.

> 
> As an aside - we should probably add text about how relays set delivery timeouts upstream, and possibly SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE needs to be able to change the timeout. Does the upstream timeout need to be at least the MAX of the current downstream subscribers, or is ok for it to be smaller?

Agreed. I have little insight on this.

> 
> I think Suhas and Cullen are arguing for retaining publisher influence of delivery properties because they wouldn't want a rogue subscriber with a long timeout to impact other subscribers with shorter timeouts - potentially generating rxmits and resets on the uplink that the original publisher didn't want.

The original publisher would always be free to send DATAGRAM all the time, if it wants, and its immediately connecting clients support DATAGRAM.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> I agree, but this is specifically forbidden by the spec, because the Original Publisher sets this, and it must be obeyed.

I'm agreeing with you that this optimization (stream -> datagram) is potentially something we should consider.  However, the scope needs to be narrowed further to *subgroups* where the length < MTU.  If a small object arrives at a relay in a stream but not the FIN, it may not be safe to forward as a datagram because another object with a dependency might still be coming. 

> The original publisher would always be free to send DATAGRAM all the time, if it wants, and its immediately connecting clients support DATAGRAM.

If you add another hop then this breaks down.

```
Pub -> Relay 1 -> Relay 2 -> Sub1 (timeout=0, prefer datagrams)
                         +-> Sub2 (timeout=1000, streams ok)

  Datagram     ???   
```

I think it's fine or even necessary to have publisher control/influence here.  I'll offer a more flexible spelling option - which is letting the publisher specify a MAX_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT value.  Setting to 0 would force datagrams through the delivery chain.  Values larger than zero may afford a relay to streamify an incoming datagram, but the safety of that seems questionable unless stream limits and flow control are effectively disabled.

> if we can completely eliminate the concept of forwarding preference, it simplifies the spec and the code. 

Given that we need to be able to send Objects in both streams and datagrams, what would eliminating preference actually simplify?  The wire image is the same, but the decision about how to forward becomes more complex.  In moxygen I recently [removed ForwardingPreference from the API](https://github.com/facebookexperimental/moxygen/commit/5195b9bf9a19ea67c5fa1e54f3c705afe96ba085).

> Implementations don't even have to support Datagram, if that's an obstacle.

I think all QUIC implementations have this so we shouldn't sweat it.

comments.body:

One use case for descending was to ensure you always got the most recent data, but now that priorities are clarified (#518), I think the correct thing will happen with ascending and delivery timeout. comments.author: englishm
comments.body:
> You wouldn't want to skip over the last object or two of the previous group to start sending the first object(s) of the next group.

This is behavior that has been explicitly described as desirable in the past. Prioritization equivalent to descending group order was present even in the earliest WARP drafts because Twitch's player preferred to optimize in favor of low latency by skipping ahead and dropping frames at the tail of a GoP, providing a way for clients to catch-up to as close to the live edge as possible.

This tail drop behavior isn't desirable for all use cases, but assuming we still want to support this Twitch-like skip-to-live behavior, I don't see how we can do it with priorities and timeouts alone.

SubGroup priorities are still bounded to groups and publisher/subscriber priorities apply to the track level.

Due to temporary congestion on the last mile hop, a relay may have objects ready to send: 
- {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 58}
- {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 59}
- {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 60}
- {Group: 4, SubGroup: 0, Object: 0}

If we can apply group order descending, then that relay will put {Group: 4, SubGroup: 0, Object: 0} on the wire first and the player can skip ahead, catching up as close as possible to the live edge. Then the relay sends {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 58}, and possibly also objects 59 and 60 if the delivery timeouts permit and the subscriber has not sent QUIC STOP_SENDING for the stream carrying objects of {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0}. It's possible that more objects from Group 4 may be ready to send before the remaining objects from Group 3 are sent, so they may be interleaved or eventually starved off up to a delivery timeout or QUIC STOP_SENDING from the subscriber. Importantly, if the temporary congestion clears and there's room to send those objects in time, they can still be sent.

If we were to try to force the relay to send {Group: 4, SubGroup: 0, Object: 0} using only priorities and timeouts, we would need to set a delivery timeout for the subscription short enough to expire {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 58}, {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 59}, and {Group: 3, SubGroup: 0, Object: 60} as soon as {Group: 4, SubGroup: 0, Object: 0} is available. 

If our objects are frames being produced approximately every 33ms, we could set a very tight delivery timeout matching that rate and get {Group: 4, SubGroup: 0, Object: 0} to be sent in this scenario rather than any more objects from Group 3, but we would then preclude the possibility of ever sending the remaining objects from Group 3 when conditions improve.

I think delivery timeouts are more useful as a backstop to prevent unnecessary queuing when congestion is present for more prolonged periods of time. Maybe our application has a buffer a handful of frames in length to account for brief periods of congestion, but eventually we do want to skip ahead to a new group. The delivery timeout might be something like 165ms, but we'd still want group order descending to make sure that a keyframe from a new group is sent as soon as it's available.

If we instead had a very tight delivery timeout, we'd risk creating worse problems because we'd end up more likely to expire the heads (object 0) of new groups when encountering congestion, essentially starving end subscribers of objects that can be decoded and played back.

It's a subtle difference, but I do think there's some meaningful behavior we would be precluding by dropping group order descending with our current priority scheme.

comments.author: englishm

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
So clearly we need order for fetch, but for subscribe, it has never made much sense to me. So few things 

First thing: if some people want this, I happy to keep it even thought I don't think it will be used because I don't think it adds much complexity. 

That said .... First keep in mind that is the order is descending, but there is not congestion, all the data will arrive in ascending order. I've played with implementations of this and what happens is if the subscriber is operating at near the limit of bandwidth available ( which is the optimal situations ) you end up with the last frame of group X nearly always gets delayed until after the first frame (or more) of group X+1. This is because the first frame of the group is typically larger than other frames. This results in the last frame of group X having huge jitter. The jitter buffer compensates for this by uping the depth of the jitter buffer. 

So in summary, in playing with implementations of this, I find that descending increases jitter and latency over ascending but does not increase quality of overall user experience. 

We clearly need order for Fetch, but for subscribe, I don't think we need order, but if other people want it, I am perfectly fine with keeping it.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
+1 to the FETCH use case of visual scrubbing in DESC order, especially when combined with a filter to only pull objects containing I-frames. 

While we definitely need GROUP ORDER for FETCH, I don't think we need GROUP order for SUBSCRIBE. @englishm gives the best motivation for why using delivery timeouts alone would be difficult to produce the head-of-line skipping for newer content. However even Luke, who was the originator of this approach, backed off citing poor performance when testing. An  alternate strategy using priorities would be to put all the I-Frames (Object 0) in their own subgroup with a high priority and then the p-frames in a separate subgroup with a lower priority. This would mean that under congestion, your I-Frames are delivered ahead of your p-frames, which is the skip-ahead visual behavior that you want. I'd prefer to remove GROUP order for SUBSCRIBE now and then add it back in later if experimental evidence shows that it really is the path to better real-time performance under congestion.

comments.author: TimEvens

If the order violates the protocol spec, it's the job of the ingress relay to enforce that.  If the order passes the ingress relay, then the order is maintained to all active subscribers, which includes via interconnected relays. If we have to support anything else, it will result in playback from cache for subscribes, which is overly complicated and will introduced delays with real-time delivery.

issues.title: Handling subgroup discontinuity at a relay
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
This came from the comments on #587 

The context is that a track has a subgroup with only even numbered objects, eg: 2, 4, 6, 8.

> sending 2, 4, 8 = illegal (in order, but with an omitted object in the middle.)

If a relay gets a subgroup with objects `2, 4, 6, 8`, I expect it can send one of the following

```
Nothing
2
2, 4
2, 4, 6
2, 4, 6, 8
```

However, consider this case:

```
          /--- relay 1 ---\
Publisher                  relay3 ---> Subscriber 
          \--- relay 2 ---/
```

For a particular track/group/subgroup (eg: group=77, subgroup=11) relay3 gets the following from relay1:

```
Control Stream: <GOAWAY>
Subgroup Stream: 2, 4<RELIABLE_RESET>
```
as well as a new ANNOUNCE from relay2.  

relay3 starts making a new subscription to relay2, but doesn't close anything downstream.  

relay3 issues SUBSCRIBE(latest object) to relay2, and gets a stream with just `8` for group=77 subgroup=11.
If it gets any non-sequential object (even 6) it has no idea if it missed any objects.

Would the relay be allowed to send `2, 4, 8` on the subgroup stream downstream?  If not, then what is it supposed to do?

* FETCH to fill in the gap?  
* Reset all the downstream subgroup streams?
  * If so, can it open a new subgroup stream containing just `8` or stop trying to forward this subgroup?
* Something else?

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
Your scenario is pretty specific on the mobility/resume use-case where the publisher moves from relay 1 to relay 2. Is that correct? 

Mobility/resume/reuse does need to be handled, which I don't see in the current MoQT draft.  Effort is needed to define how to resume and properly handle GOAWAY to migrate/transition existing  tracks from one to another. 

Regarding peering between relays, such as relay 1 and relay 2 to relay 3... fetch should not be used by relays unless the subscriber requested it.  IMO, fetch should be focused on subscriber specific uses  and not be used to globally sync/replicate caches. If we want to define a cache sync protocol, then that's a different discussion... for example, we really need to look at distributed centralized caches that support relays that are behind load balancers and anycast (load balancers). 

As I would implement the above, the following would happen:

1. Publisher would make a new connection to relay 2
2. Publisher would undergo the normal connect/subscribe/announce states for the tracks. 
3. If publisher does not disconnect (unsubscribe, unannounce) from relay 1, it will result in the publisher appearing as two publishers for the same track(s). In other words, multiple publisher scenario. 
4. Assuming the publisher is not sending duplicate data to both relay 1 and relay 2, publisher would send only new data to relay 2. In this sense, resume, and the group would start at the next sequence.
5. Assuming peering is established between relay 2 and relay 3, the data would be forwarded based on FIFO (publisher in to peer out) order. In this case, publisher wouldn't start over with old data, it would simply pick up where it left off, so subgroup 12. 

Upon new subscription and publicacation, as in this scenario, to relay 2, the publisher is required to start the stream as it normally would for start of group/subgroup. While the publisher could pickup where it left off in group 11, it really should have started on subgroup 12 or group 78.  If it didn't, it would still work, but would be a bit messy till next group/subgroup. 

Lossless methods for transitions/migration between relays of existing/live tracks is possible, but it requires specific handling that is not defined in MoQT to facilitate it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Discussed in Denver.  I think we  could use some text on using a Fetch to retrieve any Objects between two subscriptions to avoid there being a gap of Objects in a Subgroup, which would likely make the tail of the Subgroup unplayable.

As a related point, we might want to clarify the 'not dropping Objects' statement in the text to be more specific.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Maybe we can say something like:

The relay can only forward object X on a subgroup stream if it knows it's not missing anything since the previous object sent (X-1).  It can know because:

1) Object X and X-1 have sequential object IDs
2) Object X and X-1 arrived sequentially on the same subgroup stream
3) All object IDs between Object X and Object X - 1 have been observed in other subgroup streams
4) A FETCH has confirmed the non-existence of any other objects in this subgroup between X and X-1

Otherwise, the relay MUST close the downstream subgroup stream with X-1 and open a new one to forward X.  If there is a gap, the application will have to detect it and FETCH it.

issues.title: Support wildcard/pattern subscribes
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body:
There are many use-cases where we would like to subscribe to a namespace tuple prefix to receive existing and new tracks that match that subscribe prefix.  In these use-cases, the publisher knows the available tracks and does not need to rely on the subscribe full track information to choose which track to send. Instead, there is a controlled set of tracks that the publisher would send based on the subscribe match. 

> Example:

Subscribe to namespace tuple `<meeting id>/participants/primary audio/*` , name is null. 

The relay would: 
1. lookup existing published tracks that matches the subscribe, such as `1234/participants/primary audio/endpointId=456`  and start forwarding to the subscriber this content. The track alias would reflect the full track name. The subscriber would be notified via control channel of what the full track name is for the given track alias.  
2. Upon new announcement, relay would forward to publisher the subscribe prefix requested. The publisher would then choose which tracks to transmit. The publisher would send to the relay (aka subscriber) the track full name information via the control channel with a track alias along with data objects that include the track alias. The original subscriber would receive the new track alias via data objects and associate it to the control channel full name information that was sent upon initial match.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
There was a previous issue #253 for "wildcard subscribe" that got closed when SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES was landed #498.  Perhaps the difference is that you expect only a single track to be forwarded per SUBSCRIBE?

Your proposal conflicts with the current design where the subscriber is in control of the Track Alias space - if the publisher or relay chooses one, it could be taken by an in-flight SUBSCRIBE.  It also suffers from the HoL blocking problem where the objects with an unknown alias arrive at the subscriber before the control message linking them.

I'm curious what you mean by "controlled tracks" - are these fixed or will the publisher choose one of several based on some application logic.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
> There was a previous issue #253 for "wildcard subscribe" that got closed when SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES was landed #498. Perhaps the difference is that you expect only a single track to be forwarded per SUBSCRIBE?

It's not about finding the announces to subscribe because as defined announces only contain namespace, sans name. Thus, the announce doesn't contain the full track name/alias. In the wildcard use case, the subscribe would result in receiving multiple track aliases (full track names) that matched a prefix for the subscribe. This is kind of a problem with MoQT design that has subscriber providing the track alias. In this case, it's the publisher needing to provide the track alias.   Therefore, this doesn't really work with wildcard subscribes where the subscriber will have no idea of what the track alias will be.  

The nice thing about track alias in data objects header is that it does allow for us to distinguish the different sources (aka tracks that matched) but it doesn't provide us the opaque details of the namespace tuple/name.  Even if we subscribe announce, it would not help unless publisher announced full track names with alias. Even if we do announce full track names, I'm not sure subscribe announce is the right approach to get information on matching wildcard (or pattern/regex based) subscribes, which is really a transaction.  A possible improved approach is to directly feedback to the subscriber the matching tracks with associated information (e.g., the namespace tuple and name opaque data). This would be a good use-case for subscribe ID.  The subscription will have to be updated based on new announces that happen post subscribe... hence there is a need to update the information... until unsubscribe. Again, subscribe ID is a good use-case here to support the transaction/state. 
 
> Your proposal conflicts with the current design where the subscriber is in control of the Track Alias space - if the publisher or relay chooses one, it could be taken by an in-flight SUBSCRIBE. 

Exactly, which is mentioned above.... it's a fundamental problem with MoQT design that has subscribers defining the track alias. IMO, it needs to change. 

> It also suffers from the HoL blocking problem where the objects with an unknown alias arrive at the subscriber before the control message linking them.

Not sure I follow your HoL issue here. Can you elaborate on why your implementation would HoL?.? An unknown track alias received that references a **known** subscribe ID will be dropped (metrics will count how many times this happens) in most cases till track alias information is known.  Track alias information on matching subscribes would be sent via control messaging, which is over the control stream that has the highest priority. There are race conditions, which can be mitigated with short buffering of these unknown track aliases data objects... which does not result in HoL. 

> I'm curious what you mean by "controlled tracks" - are these fixed or will the publisher choose one of several based on some application logic.

Probably bad wording, but what I meant by "controlled tracks" is that we know them ahead of time via the catalog service. They are **provisioned tracks**, often conveyed via catalog service. Problem is that we have no idea what the track alias will be for these tracks. While each subscriber could subscribe to the 1 million tracks, **the intent for this issue is to ask/callout that we find it inefficient to be required to subscribe to a million tracks when a simple wildcard/pattern subscribe could have sufficed.**

There are discussions that we should be using a global track alias, which would help to mitigate the track alias issue, but that only works with an internal/custom implementation, which breaks interoperability...  unless the draft is updated to handle this scenario.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> announces only contain namespace, sans name

This is true, though there's nothing stopping an application from defining a namespace that is sufficiently unique and either a blank or otherwise fixed track name.  See [MoQ Chat](https://github.com/afrind/draft-frindell-moq-chat/blob/main/draft-frindell-moq-chat.md).  Would this meet your use case?

> Exactly, which is mentioned above.... it's a fundamental problem with MoQT design that has subscribers defining the track alias. IMO, it needs to change.

[Chair Hat on]: 

The working group has established consensus on this issue based on discussions in 2023.  This was prior to the introduction of Subscribe ID, so the Track Alias served both to identify the subscription and as a compressed identifier for the track name.  To meet the requirement that all downstream subscriptions *could* use the same identifier, we added the Retry Track Alias error code to Subscribe Error.  I'll note there was skepticism that this single identifier would make a meaningful performance difference, compared to say, QUIC stream IDs and per-hop encryption.  I'm individually curious to see a benchmark comparison.

There are other issues with discussion of Track Alias now that show others are also unhappy with it, but in a different way, see #597.

[Chair Hat off]:

> An unknown track alias received that references a known subscribe ID will be dropped

It's not clear to me how that works, since Objects only contain Track Alias and not the Subscribe ID in the current version of the draft.

> Can you elaborate on why your implementation would HoL?

> The publisher would send to the relay (aka subscriber) the track full name information via the control channel with a track alias along with data objects that include the track alias. 

The objects containing the new Track Alias will race this control message.  If the objects arrive first, they are likely not usable until the control message arrives and have to be buffered.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: After discussing this more, I think this makes more sense in the context of publisher speaks first, because wildcard is not a subscription to a track, it's a subscription to a set of tracks, somewhat like SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES is a subscription to a set of ANNOUNCEs

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - the direction of the publish PR is likely to resolve this.

issues.title: Can we replace FETCH_CANCEL with STOP_SENDING?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
> A subscriber issues a FETCH_CANCEL message to a publisher indicating it is no longer interested in receiving Objects for the fetch specified by 'Subscribe ID'. The publisher SHOULD close the unidirectional stream as soon as possible.

One reason I can see for FETCH_CANCEL to be separate is so it can be issued before receiving the FETCH stream.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
One thing i liked about fetch_cancel is , it provides an nice application API. 
Curious to understand what might be the downside of having it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> One thing i liked about fetch_cancel is , it provides an nice application API.

Nothing really changes about your application API if we change the wire signal from FETCH_CANCEL to STOP_SENDING.

> Curious to understand what might be the downside of having it.

The downside is there are edge cases with FETCH_CANCEL that don't exist with STOP_SENDING - 

1) cancelling a fetch with an invalid subscribe ID
2) fetch already closed
3) cancelling a fetch before the fetch OK -- though as mentioned in the OP, this problem moves to the client side.

Victor suggested using a bidi stream for FETCH and its response on #632 which mitigates these, but would introduce (solvable) problems with control message ordering.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: There are a number of ways to do this and I don't have a strong opinion.  Putting FETCH on a single bidi stream seems sensible, and I'm unsure if there are any downsides?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment

>  I'm unsure if there are any downsides?

The primary downside is that it can create ordering problems, for example see #638 where the FETCH needs to follow 
the SUBSCRIBE.  I recall this was discussed in Boston.  This is tractable but does need to be addressed.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Another reason to prefer bidirectional streams is that the sender of the FETCH is guaranteed to have an allocated return path for the data.  If we use control+unidirectional stream, there's a case where the publisher is out of stream credit to reply.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Relatedly, do we need FETCH_DONE in case the publisher wants to terminate it before the stream exists (perhaps due to a lack of stream credit?) Or is FETCH_OK a commitment to open the stream?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm now inclined to leave this as is, maybe with editorial clarification around the edge cases.  Once the data stream is open, I would expect FETCH_CANCEL and STOP_SENDING to be handled equivalently by the publisher, so sending both is redundant, but basically free.

I don't think moving FETCH to a bidi stream is solving more problems than it creates, and FETCH_CANCEL is basically fine.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Related question - does a publisher need to send FETCH_ERROR if it receives a FETCH_CANCEL or STOP_SENDING before sending FETCH_OK/_ERROR?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @afrind has decided the status quo is fine.

issues.title: What is the purpose of FETCH_CANCEL?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: Surely, a STOP_SENDING is both necessary and sufficient?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: dup with #630

issues.title: What happens when FETCH_HEADER is lost?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
I have the following test case where the publisher makes an API error and publishes an object on a fetch stream with the wrong length:

C->S: FETCH
S->C: FETCH_OK
S->C: open fetch stream (2), 
S->C: write FETCH_HEADER (2, delayed/lost)
S: API error, RESET_STREAM (2)

The client is expecting a fetch stream that will never come.  

The client needs to have a timer on the arrival of the FETCH_HEADER in any case, because a malicious or buggy server might never send one on purpose.  We should add text to this effect.

We can also short circuit the timer in cases like the above by using RESET_STREAM_AT (always deliver the FETCH_HEADER).

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: I feel like between this and the other issue you filed, this makes a good case for switching fetches to bidi streams.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I was thinking a bit about N control streams.  The main argument against it has been ordering would not be guaranteed for important sequences of operations, but I think that could be handled with a control message sequence number.  I guess that opens a new flow control problem though.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: I'm not sure what N control streams would do to help the state tracking problem.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Sorry, that was a tangent -- FETCH is a control message, so putting it on a bidi stream implicitly makes N control streams.  Once we do that, it's tempting to put, say, SUBSCRIBE/SUBSCRIBE_OK/SUBSCRIBE_ERROR/SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE for a given Subscribe ID also on a bidi stream, as well as other message groups (ANNOUNCE*, SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES*).

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: That is one possible direction, though I'm not sure that it makes much sense to me.  A fetch is well-suited for this since everything can happen on a single stream; subscribes span multiple streams, making the advantage of simplifying the state management much less appealing.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I agree with Victor that the case for FETCH on a single stream is much cleaner than SUBSCRIBE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment: 

If I recall the design principles of FETCH from Boston, I believe it was intentional to allow an intermediary to begin sending objects before sending FETCH_OK.  This is because FETCH_OK contains information about liveness of the track/live head, which may require an RTT upstream.  If we move FETCH to a bidi-stream, how would this change?  

1. Keep FETCH_OK on control stream but FETCH and Objects go on the bidi stream
2. Put FETCH, FETCH_OK and Objects on the bidi stream, but make the wire format flexible so FETCH_OK can appear mid-stream.
3. Put FETCH, FETCH_OK and Objects on the bidi stream, but require the FETCH_OK to come first

issues.title: Can we relax the error when SUBSCRIBE start group/object is in the past?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The subscriber likely has no idea where the live head is before issuing a Subscribe, so sending any Subscribe with a start point is risky, even if your intention is to filter in the future.

My proposal is that as long as Subscribe will return at least one object it's not an error.

Subscribe OK already tells you the start point.  So if you Subscribe(0, 0) and Get Subscribe OK (10, 0), it should be fine.

Fetch doesn't error when End Group/Object is in the future, so relaxing this constraint makes them symmetric.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: That seems sensible to me.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This was fixed in draft-08

issues.title: Synchronized complementary tracks of non-traditional media
issues.author: ac-freeman
issues.body:
This is my first time jumping in on the MoQ working group, so please forgive my ignorance if I'm missing something in the draft or existing issues.

I'm working on a streaming system for non-traditional media known as [event-based video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_camera). It has a very high (and highly variable) data rate, and no image frames; pixels have independent, asynchronous samples that are sparse in time. 

Since the pixel samples are independent, I've explored splitting them up across several tracks. The client can then recombine the samples from any tracks that it's subscribed to. Since the samples are independent, this process doesn't rely on certain data to be decoded first, as with SVC. For a given segment of time, each track that we publish any data to will have roughly the _same_ amount of data. However, some tracks might not have _any_ data for that time segment, in the case that the overall data rate from the camera drops.

For low-latency applications, it's vital that the tracks are synchronized, so that each subscription for a given client is getting the latest data possible. If there's congestion when subscribing to a new track, however, the first group received from that track may be older than what the other tracks are sending. What mechanisms are there currently to avoid such a problem?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Welcome to MoQ and thanks for your interest.  #475 describes a similar problem.  There was a presentation at the last IETF meeting in November about potentially using timestamps for cross-track synchronization.

It's also possible to use subgroups to organize independent data within a single track.  The main differences between multiple tracks and a single track with multiple subgroups are:

1. A subscriber can independently subscribe and unsubscribe from tracks, but not subgroups
2. All objects in the same track share an ID space regardless of subgroup, but multiple tracks have independent ID spaces (though they can be theoretically coordinated).

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
Thank you for the information. I definitely need to stick with a multiple-track approach, since the receiver performs rate-based adaptation through (un)subscribing to additional tracks. Timestamp-based synchronization would help, I think, but I suppose the use case is different than what's been discussed in that issue.

In this case, the client may have knowledge about the end-to-end latency, assuming some send timestamp is encoded in the object payload. The latency is below the target threshold, so it can receive more data. The client subscribes to one more track, but there's congestion at the relay then, so the subscription takes a while. Now the second track is out of sync. The congestion dies down, and the client issues a subscribe update to get things back in check.

In isolation, this isn't a big deal. But for my use case, tracks may be added and dropped with high frequency. This is for machine vision applications, though, so there's no concept of human QoE.

Another strategy may be to issue new SUBSCRIBEs with an AbsoluteStart set for some object in the future that hasn't been sent yet. But there would be no guarantee that the congestion will have recovered by then to the point that the tracks are resynchronized. It's also not clear to me if the protocol currently does or should define the behavior for requesting group/object IDs that are later than the newest data.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
> 2. All objects in the same track share an ID space regardless of subgroup

To confirm, does this mean that you cannot have two objects with the same ID in the same group, but different subgroups?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> It's also not clear to me if the protocol currently does or should define the behavior for requesting group/object IDs that are later than the newest data.

It does.  You can send a SUBSCRIBE with a start group/object in the future.

> To confirm, does this mean that you cannot have two objects with the same ID in the same group, but different subgroups?

Correct.  Track+Group+ID uniquely identifies an object.

On your overall problem, what does it mean for tracks to be out of sync?  Is it that track A is delivering data at time T and track B is delivering data from T - delta?  One way to help address this in MOQT is to set a delivery timeout in your subscription.  If the track B data is too old is will be skipped or reset, and the system should converge on delivering data that is approximately the same age, +/- the timeout value.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
> One way to help address this in MOQT is to set a delivery timeout in your subscription

Yes, that was the idea I had over the weekend. I'm thinking that for my purposes it might work with the subgroup approach plus the delivery timeout. Then you wouldn't have the overhead of (un)subscribing to several tracks when the bandwidth for the relay-client connection changes--just update the timeout delivery for the one track subscription.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @ac-freeman : is there a change to the draft you are seeking via this issue or is it ok to close now?  As I recall you were able to make things work via delivery timeouts.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body: I think it's okay to close this issue.

issues.title: When can a relay send SUBSCRIBE_DONE with status SUBSCRIPTION_ENDED?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
1. Relay has a single client subscribed to a single track with no end group specified
2. A second client joins with a fixed end group (N)

Here the relay is responsible for generating the SUBSCRIBE_DONE towards client 2, but when?

A triggering event could be a) receiving an END_OF_GROUP status or b) seeing an object with group > N.

The relay could send it immediately when it sees a triggering event, but if it does so, it has to pick the Stream Count at that time, and cannot open any new subgroup streams for late arriving objects in groups <= N.

It could start a timer when it sees the triggering event, and send SUBSCRIBE_DONE with a final stream count when the timer expires.

It would be nice to have a short circuit in this case, but it requires the original publisher include a Stream Count with END_OF_GROUP status.  This is also a per-hop value due to DELIVERY_TIMEOUTs that may have expired, which is a little weird, since otherwise object status and content is end-to-end.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: If it's delivered (a) the last group in the SUBSCRIBE or (b) the EndOfTrack object, and it's closed all streams it's going to open.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> and it's closed all streams it's going to open.
 
The relay cannot know this without knowing how many streams the upstream is sending in the last group in SUBSCRIBE. 

eg, say subscribe ends at group 2

S->R: G2, SG0, O1
S->R: G2, SG10, O3
S->R, G2, SG20, EOG
S->R: G3, SG0, O1

Are there more subgroups in G2?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: it's not super clean, but at some point it's going to decide to stop, and then it can send DONE.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
It seems like there are a few exacerbating factors here to determine if you've received (and therefore sent) all the Objects in a group.

An End Of Group can help, but only if you've received all the Objects.  If you haven't, you don't know if there's a gap in Object IDs or if there are one or more subgroups you haven't received yet.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> An End Of Group can help, but only if you've received all the Objects. If you haven't, you don't know if there's a gap in Object IDs or if there are one or more subgroups you haven't received yet.

You can solve this with stream counting like with do for SUBSCRIBE_DONE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'd like to add an option to include a Stream Count with End Of Group.  I see two mechanisms:

1) Define a special extension header - the problem with this is that the current extension design doesn't work with 'hop-by-hop' headers, because the default is to forward unknown headers and this would be wrong.  We'd have to make this header mandatory to understand (at least to not forward), or tweak the extension design.

2) Add an optional field in Object that's only present when status=End Of Group.  This feels a little clunky.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I don't object to a stream count here, but I think SUBSCRIBE_DONE with SUBSCRIPTION_ENDED only gets sent if the original publisher sends it first.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> I think SUBSCRIBE_DONE with SUBSCRIPTION_ENDED only gets sent if the original publisher sends it first.

From the draft (new in #833)

> Subscription Ended - The publisher reached the end of an associated Subscribe filter.

Subscribe filters are likely only going to the first hop relay (See #815), so relays need to send SUBSCRIPTION_ENDED sometimes.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Good point, Absolute filters will need this

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Thinking about this more, particularly in light of Group Order = Descending and other reordering, I don't think a _relay_ can _ever_ send confidently send SUBSCRIBE_DONE + SUBSCRIPTION_ENDED for a subscription with an EndGroup set, unless the relay has some kind of scoreboard and knows that every object in the requested range has been delivered.  The subscriber will have to UNSUBSCRIBE when it has what it was looking for or times out locally.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I think the most sensible behavior would be to keep the subscription open until either subscriber unsubscribes, and the upstream is gone with all of the data either delivered or expired.  If you think of SUBSCRIBE as "deliver all newly generated 
 objects", and of EndGroup as a filter on it, there is no reason EndGroup should affect SUBSCRIBE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> keep the subscription open until either subscriber unsubscribes, and the upstream is gone with all of the data either delivered or expired.

This seems reasonable.  I think we could use some editorial text, probably in the relay section?

issues.title: Clarify non-terminal error codes for FETCH and ANNOUNCE
issues.author: englishm
issues.body:
Discovered while writing https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/638

- FETCH_ERROR
- ~SUBSCRIBE_ERROR~
- ANNOUNCE_ERROR

Each of these messages has a field for an error code, but we don't currently appear to have any specific error codes defined other than reasons for terminating the entire session: https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-termination

Edit to add: I found the table for `SUBSCRIBE_ERROR`:
https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-5.1-8

Also, we do have [this](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-6.7-10) text for Fetch:

issues.title: How do relays set upstream DELIVERY_TIMEOUT?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Does the upstream timeout need to be at least the MAX of the current downstream subscribers, or is ok for it to be smaller?  Does that mean relays SHOULD/MUST issue SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE upstream when downstream subscribers with the largest timeout join/leave the subscription?

Note we already specify that the publisher can optionally set its own DELIVERY_TIMEOUT and the relay uses the min of the pub and sub values.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
I don't think MOQT should specify any normative guidance on relays aggregating dissimilar upstream timeouts. While taking the MAX seems the intuitive answer, there are other factors driving distribution systems (cache capacity, CPU, economics, SLAs etc) that might cause a relay to want to make a different decision. And it should be allowed to. We could add an informative note with some suggested relay behaviors. 

> Note we already specify that the publisher can optionally set its own DELIVERY_TIMEOUT and the relay uses the min of the pub and sub values.

But what of the use case where a publisher sets a 1s timeout (because it believes the majority of end-clients want low latency), but then there is one archive client that has a much higher tolerance for delivery latency and would like to archive that low latency stream with a 10s timeout. By taking the MIN of the two the relay is preventing the archive use-case. Shouldn't the relay take the MAX of the two? Under that scenario the low latency clients would also set 1s timeout and get their low latency while the archive client would get its 10s timeout.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I'm inclined toward some considerations and discussion, but no normative text here.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: +1 on not defining what happens within the relay network. we do have different strategies that we are playing with and having flexibility is important.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: Agree on leaving it open spec-wise. Private relays serving a homogenous traffic type are going to make different decisions to public relays serving heterogenous content. It would be wrong for us to impose normative constraints on how they should handle DELIVERY-TIMEOUT.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Note that this text exists for publisher specified timeouts:

>  The publisher SHOULD always specify the value received from an upstream subscription when there is one, and nothing otherwise.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Also this:

> When sent by a subscriber, this parameter is intended to be specific to a subscription, so it SHOULD NOT be forwarded upstream by a relay that intends to serve multiple subscriptions for the same track.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: There's already text describing this, which seems fine.  Closing.  Someone can file a PR if they want more description.

issues.title: Relays should never use EndGroup with a SUBSCRIBE
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
If a relay is subscribing on behalf of clients that used an EndGroup, it should ignore those EndGroups and make the subscribe open-ended.

This is because if a SUBSCRIBE is up to Group 3, and then another client asks for up to Group 4, the relay can't have multiple SUBSCRIBEs for one track and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE can't extend the EndGroup. so the relay's only choice would be to UNSUBSCRIBE and then SUBSCRIBE again right away, which may involve a FETCH to cover gaps, etc.

At the very least, the relay section should provide this advice.

Or maybe we need to re-think the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE rules?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE can't extend the EndGroup. 

But according to the current draft, it can ...


```
SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE Message {
  Type (i) = 0x2,
  Length (i),
  Subscribe ID (i),
  StartGroup (i),
  StartObject (i),
  EndGroup (i),
  Subscriber Priority (8),
  Number of Parameters (i),
  Subscribe Parameters (..) ...
}
```


For ALL the parameters of SUBSCRIBE _UPDATE, we have a time of flight problem. Imagine the relay is 150ms RTT from the origin and groups are 25ms apart ( for whatever reason). If you set StartGroup at 100 and then 100ms later set it to 105, the Groups 100-104 may already be on the wire. This is true for all the parameters (  StartGroup, StartObject, EndGroup, Subscriber Priority (etc) that can be changed. We should add an informative note to the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE section indicating that the client may still receive objects that don't comply with the update, or have gaps in objects sequences as a consequence of the update.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Read the text above that:

> The start Object MUST NOT decrease and when it increases, there is no guarantee that a publisher will not have already sent Objects before the new start Object. The end Object MUST NOT increase and when it decreases, there is no guarantee that a publisher will not have already sent Objects after the new end Object.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The reason I added those restrictions to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is because of what Will is pointing out about it being racy.

One big reason to not allow multiple SUBSCRIBEs was because of track alias.  If we included Subscribe ID instead, there wouldn't be ambiguity.

The most straightforward change I can think of is to relax the one subscription rule to "MUST NOT have two overlapping SUBCRIBEs and the peer MAY close the session if you do."?  Or we could say SHOULD NOT because it's wasteful to have overlapping SUBSCRIBEs and assume people won't want to waste the resources?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: The simplest change, IMO, is just to tell relays not to do that. Always do an open-ended subscribe and just kill it if the one downstream client goes away

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: So as soon as the relay has received all the Objects necessary to fulfill the final subscription, it cancels the SUBSCRIBE upstream?  That does waste some bandwidth with useless Objects, but it's doable.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I wrote #653 to fix a different issue, but it's somewhat related to this one.  I'm increasingly thinking that the restriction of only one SUBSCRIBE per track is potentially really limiting.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: We should allow subscribers to make as many concurrent SUBSCRIBES and FETCHES for the same track as they like. There is going to be tremendous complexity in how relays aggregating and propagate dissimilar requests from downstream clients. They can be clever and try to munge all downstream requests into one constantly updating upstream request, or they can maintain multiple upstream requests with duplicate data over the wire. The optimum balance will have economic, hardware, cache and network constraints and the core protocol should give them the flexibility to seek those optima.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> We should allow subscribers to make as many concurrent SUBSCRIBES and FETCHES for the same track as they like. There is going to be tremendous complexity in how relays aggregating and propagate dissimilar requests from downstream clients. They can be clever and try to munge all downstream requests into one constantly updating upstream request, or they can maintain multiple upstream requests with duplicate data over the wire. The optimum balance will have economic, hardware, cache and network constraints and the core protocol should give them the flexibility to seek those optima.

That is certainly another way to resolve this problem. I don't have a strong opinion on how to resolve this, but issuing guidance to relays seems like the least disruptive change.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I think restricting to one live subscription per track has been extremely helpful in simplifying the concepts and implementations -- particularly around ensuring that live objects are never duplicated in a session. I can live with the fallout of "relays make open-ended subscriptions upstream".

> We should allow subscribers to make as many concurrent SUBSCRIBES and FETCHES for the same track as they like. 

FETCH - yes.  SUBSCRIBE - why?  We know the live objects will be the same.  The things that can be different are:  

Start/End - the receiver should be able to manage these filters
Priority - It doesn't make sense to prioritize two subscriptions to the same track - the data is only sent once
Group Order - This for priority inputs, so same as above
Parameters:
  Delivery Timeout - if the object is only sent once then multiple delivery timeouts don't make sense.
  Auth - we may want/need an optional verb that delegates auth of a subscription to upstream without initiating a new flow of objects.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
> We should allow subscribers to make as many concurrent SUBSCRIBES and FETCHES for the same track as they like.

All of those SUBSCRIBEs will be eventually routed to the original publisher, and in many scenarios the original publisher barely has enough bandwidth to publish even a single copy of the track in question, so I don't think allowing duplication here is practically viable.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Group Order - This for priority inputs, so same as above

@afrind Can you clarify how conflicting Group order can be resolved with a single subscribe? Imagine a relay has two subscribers, both requesting the same track, but one in ascending and the other in descending group order. What single forward subscription does the relay make? Whichever choice it makes screws one of the downstream receivers. Group order is different to the other parameters (priority, start/end, timeout) in that there is no inclusive value which can satisfy all subscribers (as I can go forward with the highest priority, the earliest start, the longest timeout etc).

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> All of those SUBSCRIBEs will be eventually routed to the original publisher, and in many scenarios the original publisher barely has enough bandwidth to publish even a single copy of the track in question, so I don't think allowing duplication here is practically viable.

That statement is true if you frame the original publisher as an individual producing UGC content on their mobile phone. However the origin might also be a sports broadcast hosted on a cloud provider, in which case it might happily produce multiple variants.  To accommodate all permutations of original publisher and distribution network options, we should not prohibit subscription duplication by design.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> @afrind Can you clarify how conflicting Group order can be resolved with a single subscribe?

You are correct here, if there is one subscriber with ascending preference and another with descending, then subscription upstream needs to pick one.  However, allowing a second subscription upstream with the inverse preference that would trigger duplicate objects all the time doesn't seem like it will help.  The preference is used to choose what to send when you can't send everything, and doubling the number of objects on the link will make that more likely.  #636 is one proposal.  Or if we retain it, the relay can choose a preference that suits the majority.  Ultimately I don't think relay-upstream-subscribe-group-order will have much impact on delivery.

comments.body: I will say that the "no duplicates" rule does mean I MUST have a third data structure that keeps track of outgoing SUBSCRIBES by track name, in addition to structures that index by track_alias and subscribe_id, to prevent the application from doing something that is illegal. issues.title: Fetch Object serialization isn't efficient
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Objects in a Fetch stream have to be in increasing Group and Object ID.

Currently it's:
```
{
  Group ID (i),
  Subgroup ID (i),
  Object ID (i),
  Publisher Priority (8),
  Object Payload Length (i),

issues.title: DELIVERY_TIMEOUT is unimplementable
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 7.1.1.2:

> If an object in a subgroup exceeds the delivery timeout, the publisher MUST reset the underlying transport stream

To properly implement this, there should (conceptually) be a timer on every object in the stream. Unfortunately, since the Webtransport API does not inform the application when data is acknowledged, and there are no object ACKs, there is not way for MoQT to identify if a given object was delivered within the timeout.

Furthermore, even with full knowledge of ACKs, a lost ACK (at QUIC or MoQT layer) could cause a spurious reset. Putting some responsibility on the receiver to send STOP_SENDING could solve many of these problems, though the spec solely makes demands of the publisher, and the receiver does not know the original arrival time.

When implementing, I approximated it as follows:

1) Record the time of every object arrival in the queue.

2) When trying to send an object to the QUIC layer, reset the stream if delivery_timeout is already expired.

3) Set a timer when FIN is sent; reset the stream if still open when the timer fires.

This approach seems tractable, but does not cover the case where objects not sent with FIN are sent on time, but retransmissions cause delivery to exceed the timeout.

I don't have a specific proposal to solve this, although @vasilvv does.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Waiting for ACK to cancel the delivery timeout timer seems too late, since that will have at least 1/2 RTT additional delay. 
 However, the QUIC stack should be allowed to retransmit the object as long as the timeout has not expired.  Can we request a new parameter to the WebTransport send API meaning "stop retransmitting the bytes in this range after this time, and reset if loss in this range is detected afterwards".

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: We discussed this at may 7 interim and it did not sound like this was a problem. There is no requirement to  remove it from a QUIC transport once it has been sent.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> We discussed this at may 7 interim and it did not sound like this was a problem. There is no requirement to remove it from a QUIC transport once it has been sent.

I disagree. "MUST reset the transport stream" is a requirement to remove it from the transport.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think what was said is that when an implementation considers an object "delivered" for the purpose of stopping the delivery timeout timer is implementation specific.  In JavaScript, this probably means "it was written handed to WebTransport".  You only need to reset the stream if your object became useless before you were able to hand it off.  Since JS is likely only the original publisher of any track, this is probably fine.  Delivery timeout is mostly for downstream relays.

If you are writing a relay, hopefully you have a transport interface that will help you get more useful timeout functionality from your QUIC stack (though as of this writing I do not - but I plan to!).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - Victor has the action to bring a proposal to the table for consideration.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> In JavaScript, this probably means "it was written handed to WebTransport". You only need to reset the stream if your object became useless before you were able to hand it off.

Doesn't this defeat the whole purpose of delivery timeout?

I see delivery timeout as a way to ensure bounded latencies in real time streaming where we can afford to loose data, correct me if that is not the intent.

If we decide to push it to WebTransport and believe our commitment to achieving real time latencies is done, there is a good chance we are not achieving the desired latencies, if WebTransport is buffering the object for some non (atleast approximately) deterministic amount of time isn't the purpose lost? Either we need some control over the time WebTransport is buffering the object before sending it or hand it off to WebTransport only when we can confidently say it won't be buffered for too long.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I'm trying to think about this from first principles.

1) The authoritative source to know if something is late is the receiving application. The ultimate backstop has to be liberal use of STOP_SENDING. This does not even need a DELIVERY_TIMEOUT parameter to function. If an object arrives late, STOP_SENDING the stream.

2) The limitation of STOP_SENDING is that potentially quite a bit of data will be delivered in the ~0.5 RTTs it takes the frame to propagate as far up the chain as appropriate.

DELIVERY_TIMEOUT is therefore an optimization. Because of imperfect information, some objects will be sent even though they are too late.

3) The following rules are possible. Here, "sent" refers to the lowest layer of control MoQT has -- in some implementations, it will be delivery to the transport; in others, it will be objects sent on the wire. Obviously, the latter will reduce the number of useless objects.

For each object, record the time of arrival (relays) or time of creation (original publishers). Start the notional timer for DELIVERY TIMEOUT.  When the timer expires for an object:

(a) if the object is not "sent", reset its stream.

(b) any stream that has an un-"sent" object in that group with a lower object ID can also be reset, even if it arrived later.

(c) any stream carrying objects for an earlier group (for any definition of earlier) can be reset, even if they arrived later. Future streams for that group need never be opened.

(d) if the last object in a stream, that stream can be reset regardless of what has been sent.

(e) if an EndOfGroup status object, all streams can be reset in that group.

(f) If MoQT has access to loss detection, and the transport declares a packet containing all or part of the object lost, its stream can be reset.

4) Timing from object arrival at the relay carries some risk. The end subscriber is measuring from the arrival of the first object in the subscription; if that was abnormally delayed, other objects could sit at the relay for longer than DELIVERY_TIMEOUT and still be on time.

For example, say DELIVERY_TIMEOUT is 300ms, implying a receiver buffer of that size. The first object, (0,0) takes 250ms seconds on each of its three hops, and so arrives 750ms after it was created. A much later object, (5, 0), blows through the first two hops in essentially no time. The final relay actually has ~750ms to deliver (5,0) but will reset it after only 300.

5) While I'm not advocating for this, we could gain higher precision if all objects were timestamped by the original publisher relative to the first object. The relay could record the timestamp of the first object in the subscription and the time it sent it downstream. If the gap between creation and sending increases by more than DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, then more streams could be reset instead of waiting for STOP_SENDING.

The logic is relatively simple: if the sender does not FIN a subgroup, it means it likely intends to send more data on it.  This only applies for subgroups, since datagrams work fine as-is.

(the practical scenario here is an SVC model where there is a "base layer" subgroup that lasts seconds, and "enhancement layer" is just a bunch of one-object subgroups that we do want to actively time out while the base layer is still alive)

comments.body:
I wonder if our failover logic and multi-publisher rules effectively require this though.  eg: 

```
C1 -> R:  PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (foo)
R -> C1: GOAWAY
```
C1 starts connecting to a new relay

```
C2 -> R: SUBSCRIBE foo/bar
```
Doesn't R have to send SUBSCRIBE foo/bar to C1?

Eventually, C1 gets a new connection to R', then sends
```
C1 -> R: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE
```

I'm inclined to say nothing. The sender of the GOAWAY can continue to send requests until the peer sends GOAWAY, or closes.

issues.title: Rethink (remove?) per-object extension fields
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Having just reviewed an implementation of per-object extension fields, I am now of the opinion that they add a considerable amount of implementation complexity, while the value they add remains fairly nebulous to me.  We should probably rethink how we're doing them, and possibly remove them altogether.

The use cases that were originally proposed here were 5G XR, tracing, and LOC.  My observations with respect to those use cases are:

1. I'm not sure I understand why 5G XR needs those (I tried reading the explanation twice, and got lost in the 3GPP jargon every time), but from what I can gather, they want to apply some routing policies depending on the object payload.  This seems to be a reasonable goal for a per-subgroup extension mechanism (though it's not clear to me if the same can't be achieved with existing MoQT mechanisms), but I don't see what it adds on per-object basis (since we don't forward subgroups differently).
2. I don't understand the benefits of tracing on granularity higher than a subscription, given that within the scope of the same subscription, the publisher and the subscriber remain the same.
3. As discussed before, nothing LOC does requires relays inspecting LOC headers, thus those should not be using extensions.

As a separate point, I find it odd that by default, the relay is supposed to forward extensions it does not understand.  Given that extensions are not needed in direct publisher-subscriber sessions, and relay-to-relay sessions are out of scope for MoQT, the only case where extensions are relevant are end-user-to-relay sessions.  End users can't do anything with extensions they don't understand, so there is no point for them in sending or receiving those.

@ chairs -- this is my formal objection to consensus on #433 / #502, please let me know if you also need me to send an email to the mailing list.

vasilvv
comments.body: Parsing extension headers within the object payload is much easier for us, since we only parse payload once we receive the entire object (similar to how control frames currently work).  For extension headers, we have to deal with reading partially available data at any point.

I think it's something like:

issues.title: Use of square brackets  to indicate optional groups of things is pushing the convention
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The document gives a non-normative summary of the RFC 9000 notation it imports, which omits details. In RFC 9000 the notation is defined as

> Packet and frame diagrams in this document use a custom format. The purpose of this format is to summarize, not define, protocol elements. Prose defines the complete semantics and details of structures.Complex fields are named and then followed by a list of fields surrounded by a pair of matching braces. Each field in this list is separated by commas.Individual fields include length information, plus indications about fixed value, optionality, or repetitions. Individual fields use the following notational conventions, with all lengths in bits:

Whereas MoQT does things like:


```
FETCH Message {
  Type (i) = 0x16,
  Length (i),
  Subscribe ID (i),
  Subscriber Priority (8),
  Group Order (8),
  Fetch Type (i),
  [Track Namespace (tuple),
   Track Name Length (i),
   Track Name (..),
   StartGroup (i),
   StartObject (i),
   EndGroup (i),
   EndObject (i),]
  [Joining Subscribe ID (i),
   Preceding Group Offset (i),]
  Number of Parameters (i),
  Parameters (..) ...
}
```

where there are two optional groups of things. 

Possible ways to improve the situation:

1. Explicity extend the convention - state what it means to put square brackets around a set of fields. Including whether the last element should have a trailing comma inside the brackets or not. 
2. Convert these groups into structure. For instance, the QUIC ACK frame has an optional `ECN Counts` field, a structure https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#figure-25.
3. Convert each individual field into being option. This seems like the worst possible approach since it would be easy to get confused what field belongs to what logical group.

issues.title: Resource attacks via Track Name(space)
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
I didn't put much thought into this but it seems like the following aspects of the protocol design put it at risk of attacks:

* Track names can be up to 2^62 - 1 bytes long.
* Track namespace (prefix) tuple fields can each be up to 2^62 -1 bytes long
* Track namespace can hold up to 32 entries
* Track namespace prefix can hold up to 32 entries. 
* IIUC Track namespace prefix is used to match against N (what is limit?) namespaces (based on my reading of https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#section-7.13, where it states "f the publisher is a relay that has received ANNOUNCE messages for namespaces ("example.com", "meeting=123", "participant=100") and ("example.com", "meeting=123", "participant=200"), a SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES for ("example.com", "meeting=123") would match both."

For example, I could simply announce N huge track namespaces of 32 * 2^62 - 1 to consume memory. Or I could send N namepsaces with carefully selected tuple fields, and then throw a worst case track namespace prefix to trigger CPU consumption on the receiver as it attempts to do matching. 

I tried looking for bounds on this data but didn't see any. I didn't see any security considerations. 

Do we _really_ need to support such humungous byte sequences? Other protocols (or their implementations) tend to apply finite limits to mitigate such problems. If we don't say anything in the document, we risk interoperability problems when implementations add their own hardening. For example, this sort of thing has affected HTTP headers for a long time and shows little sign of going away (see examples in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#fields.limits and https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html#section-7.2.4.1-2.2.1)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See also #473

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
+1 for limiting the size of track Names and Namespace tuples. They are intended to be an addressing scheme. To that end, here are two options for rational upper limits:

1. The upper end of addressability might be to insert a GUID into each Namespace field and into the name. A GUID (Globally Unique Identifier) is typically represented as a 128-bit (16-byte) value, commonly formatted as a 36-character string, including hyphens. Encoding with UTF-8 would take 36 bytes, raw binary would be less as its just a 128-bit number. That gives us a max size of (32 + 1)*36 = 1188 bytes. 

2.An alternate addressing scheme would be to use URLS, as we know work on the internet today for HTTP routing. If we set a maximum URL length of 2048 characters (Namespace + name), and encode to UTF-8, then this would require between 2048 bytes (all ASCII) and 8192 bytes (all 4-byte characters) depending on the character set. 

Taking the max of these two, I would propose a 8kB limit on the size of Namespace + Name.

issues.author: martinduke

Say a relay has observed objects 1 and 3 and cached them. It then receives a FETCH for 1 to 3. It sends Object 1 and tries to FETCH and receives FETCH_ERROR. What then? Does it Reset the data stream?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> I don't see a problem with removing the "Largest Group ID" and "Largest Object ID" from FETCH_OK. Apps can use track status to get that.

I remembered why these are needed.  All gaps between the last object delivered in fetch to the end of the range are "NOT_EXISTS".  If the live head is *before* the end of the range, we need the FETCH_OK values so we don't mark future objects NOT_EXISTS by mistake.

I think that means for tracks not currently live at the relay, one can send the FETCH_OK immediately if the end is smaller than the largest cached object.  However if the end is {10,10} and the largest cached is {8,7}, the relay must delay the FETCH_OK until it gets an upstream FETCH that covers {10,10}, or updates the live head to something between {8,7} and {10,10}.

If I start serving objects from my cache from the beginning of the range while the upstream fetch is happening, I may get a FETCH_ERROR from upstream, but the current rules prohibit sending either FETCH_OK or FETCH_ERROR.

I can see a couple ways out:

1) allow FETCH_ERROR to come after we start serving FETCH objects, it's weird but not sure there's harm?
2) remove the values from FETCH_OK and add a new Object Status like "Largest Known" that can be the last object in a Fetch response

I think for now (v1 of MOQT) we should not create a registry and identity scheme for token types. The reasons are:
1. There is a high cardinality of token schemes that can be used now and going forward with moqt
