issues.title: Resolving FETCH for distributed publishers of the same track
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
If not all publishers who ANNOUNCE are authoritative for the entire track, relays need to send FETCH to all publishers.  However, that creates problems:

1. No single upstream FETCH response is authoritative.  The upstream responses must be merged to correctly populate the cache and produce a correct downstream response.
2. If one of the publishers is temporarily disconnected from the relay when a FETCH arrives, groups it produced will be marked NOT_EXISTS, and the response is incorrect.

Saying applications with distributed publishers won't use FETCH is problematic
1.  This is the same as saying "Don't use a cache", since only FETCH retrieves from a cache
2. Joining Fetch is a potentially common operation
3. Nothing stops a malicious/buggy client from sending a FETCH

It might be better to prohibit distributed publishing on a single track.

There are many degrees of freedom currently in MoQT - is there an example of an application that cannot replace distributed publishing on the same track with each publisher publishing a single track (perhaps in a common namespace), or another MoQT feature (eg: SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES)?

This is what was discussed in Denver.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

First, let me state my opinion that distributed publishing different groups on the same track is a hack and a bad idea in moqt.  I don't see what's being accomplished that can't be accomplished by having each publisher publish their own track in the same namespace.  Or if there is, say what it is and we'll see what we can do.  This question keeps going unanswered in writing, eg, in the original post:

> There are many degrees of freedom currently in MoQT - **is there an example of an application** that cannot replace distributed publishing on the same track with each publisher publishing a single track (perhaps in a common namespace), or another MoQT feature (eg: SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES)?

---
Now, based on discussions in Denver that occurred after I wrote this issue, I see how this hack *can* work without placing any burdens on relays.

Let me invent some terminology just for discussion:

I'll call a publisher FETCHY if it can return via FETCH every object that exists or will exist in the track from {0, 0} to {maxint, maxint}.  

Distributed publishers where one publisher only publishes evens and another publishes odds are NOT FETCHY.  
Distributed publishers where one publisher publishes group 12345 and another publishes 54321 are NOT FETCHY.
Distributed publishers that are publishing the exact same data (eg for redundancy) are FETCHY.
Distributed publishers that have some way of coordinating (shared cache/database) are FETCHY.
A single relay connected to one or more NOT FETCHY publishers for a track is implicitly NOT FETCHY for that track

Adding a rule that NOT FETCHY publishers return FETCH_ERROR for unknown objects makes the hack work. This limits what the subscriber can do, but that may be fine. In the OP example, range requests to the relay fan out to currently connected publishers, and NOT FETCHY publishers return FETCH_ERROR for unsatisfiable ranges. The relay then returns FETCH_ERROR to the subscriber, leaving the cache state unchanged.

Very high value content would warrant subscribing to both, but that'd be the exception, not the rule.

As long as all authoritative sources of a Track would return the same Object payloads as any other, I think things are ok.

If there are multiple non-coordinated publishers, then something like Wildcard Subscribe #615 with different Track names makes more sense.

issues.title: How to populate Largest Group/Object in FETCH_OK
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The text says it 'largest available' and I recall from our discussion in Boston that these values were supposed to be set to the live head.  But what happens when the track is not live, and not yet ended either?  My first implementation of a fetch cache sends FETCH_OK

1) immediately if the track has a active upstream subscription
2) after the first gap-filling upstream FETCH returns with a new value of largest
3) after I've served the entire range from cache, which is weird.

Am I doing it wrong?  It seems like it would be better to get the FETCH_OK fired off as soon as possible.  Maybe these values in FETCH_OK are obsolete with joining FETCH?

If I delay FETCH_OK, it introduces a hazard where I've sent cached objects but hit an error, and sort of have to send an FETCH_ERROR, but this is prohibited here:

> Objects MUST NOT be sent for requests that end with an error.

issues.title: Have each Group have a pointer to the prior Group ID to assist with intentionally sparse IDs
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
[Proposed by Zafer Gurel] For publishers publishing sparse Group IDs, it would assist relays in knowing that a gap has been intentionally created, since relays are required to attempt to fill such gaps when responding to a FETCH request. 

Consider a relay receiving groups 1,2,3,5. It caches those groups. A later FETCH then requests the range 1..5.

If the relay has no information about the gap, it must make an upstream FETCH (4).

If however Group 5 carried a header indicating that the prior Group was 4, then the relay does not need to make any upstream FETCH as it knows the gap is intentional. 

This efficiency gain may seem trivial for one missing object, if however a publisher has produced 10,000 sparse gaps then this efficiency gain becomes meaningful for a relay operator. 

This indicator of the prior group need only exist in the stream header so it will not materially effect wire size.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
From a functional perspective, I believe this is equivalent to Missing Group in Object Status: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-08.html#section-8.1.1.1

issues.title: Computing Object Uniqueness to support Caching of Objects
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body:
How are we to compute object uniqueness of objects when considering extensions headers being appended or mutated inflight? Object uniqueness as defined in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-08#name-objects 

> [Section 2.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-08#model-group) An object is uniquely identified by its track namespace, track name, group ID, and object ID, and must be an identical sequence of bytes regardless of how or where it is retrieved. An Object can become unavailable, but its contents MUST NOT change over time.


If a relay decides to add extension headers, such as relay ID, region id (geo info), trace Id, trace of relay hops, telemetry, ... the extension headers will be relative to the path and relay that the subscriber received the object. In this sense, some of the extension headers are relative to point in time transmission in forwarding.  

If we replay the data, such as suggested by https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-jennings-moq-file-00, we would contaminate the extension header metadata. 

If caching uniqueness is computed based on extension header + payload, the object of same `group-id` and `object-id` will appear to be different, resulting in the same track alias, group-id, and object-id being cached more than once. Is that what we want? 

If caching is only based on group-id/object-id, then regardless of extension headers and payload, the data will appear to be duplicated, resulting in discards. Is that what we want? 

Is `track-alias` and `group-id` and `object-id` only used to determine uniqueness, ignoring extension headers and content that can be mutated hop-by-hop and have point in time relavance? If so, a replay of a cached file, such as via  https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-jennings-moq-file-00, would not result in an update to cache causing replay data to be discarded due to same data already seen.  This would have the net effect of NO or partial replay The updated extension headers with maybe new application timing, would not take effect.  For example, if extension headers include application real-time timestamps, those values in stored cache/files would become stale and would need to be updated on replay.  If replay results in discards because of duplicate group-id/object-id, the updated timestamps would never take effect. 

Careful though is needed in caching as we could result in caches on different relays being completely different based on extension header mutations. 

Maybe extension headers are non-transitive and are not cached.  Much of this complexity goes away if we do that.  The problem is that folks are using extension headers as application payload headers, assuming that they will be transitive.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

This is a great question and I believe we discussed it during one of the virtual interims when discussing extensions. I believe the answer was that extensions are not part of the cache key and are not subject to immutability requirements.  If you receive a second copy of an object with different extensions, you can either ignore or update your cache.

Do we need a normative behavior for relays?  If nothing else we need more text describing the expected behavior.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body: We definitely need more clarity around how a relay handles extensions in terms of mutating (adding to, changing, removing, ...) and how it pertains to caching of objects.  I suspect the desire is that object cache store does not include extension headers, but then fetch suffers from application encoded extensions headers that were needed to be updated. Does cache store only the first seen set of extension headers or does cache update extension headers on duplicate entry indexed by `track_alias->group-id->subgroup_id->object_id`?

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: A related thing that came up is if they are mutated, and they get bigger, that can push a datagram over MTU size

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> A related thing that came up is if they are mutated, and they get bigger, that can push a datagram over MTU size

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Cache management of extension header could be based on the same principles as HTTP headers. In short, some extension headers are about caching of the Object (the Cache-Control), some extension headers are supposed to be cached (Content-Type, Cache-Control, Last-Modified, Content-Encoding, ...) while some others are supposed to not be cached (Set-Cookie, Authorization, Date, Transfer-Encoding, ...)

Note that the case where an object is in cache and nonetheless the Relay receives a new "version" of the object with the same ids but different headers is not supposed to happen. If the Object is in cache, then the Relay has no reason to receive the Object unless it is an error.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I am strongly on point of view that cache key is *only* tuple of namespace, track name, group ID, object ID.  That is what the data model clearly says. The headers are cached and delivered on fetch.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
The more i think about , I agree with @fluffy  and @afrind point on 
  - Cache Key = ( Track Namespace, Track Name, GroupID, Object ID )
  - Cache Value includes headers and payload
  - If a relay receives multiple objects for the same cache key, relay does what the draft says today
I don't see a need to define normatively the relay behavior either

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: The data model section is very clear about what is immutable "A relay MUST NOT combine, split, or otherwise modify object payloads."

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
When reconciling with replicated caches, the caches will not be same at the ext+payload level if extensions are included. Relays that initially cache will have a different view of "content" than other relays. This is because other relays add their own or change/mutate existing extensions.  Why would we replicate a cache? well maybe because we need to prime a new relay or support a distributed cache where there is fast access cache in the region/AZ for relays that are scaled up behind a load balancer, which could include anycast. 

@fluffy, considering the track alias is ephemeral per session, the cache **must** take into account the full track namespace (full array) and name, along with `group-id` and `object-id` . The original thought of using track alias is very problematic, especially with interop and the way MoQT has defined track alias being ephemeral at the session scope.  This results in the unique key constraint for caching to be `track namespace array of items, track name, group-id, object-id`. 

While a unique key constraint can exclude extensions and payload information, the object payload (extensions + actual payload of data) will be different by relay cache when considering extension headers. 

This is the root of why I opened this issue.  Should we be caching extension headers? Should we have extension headers that are candidates for cache (aka transitive headers) vs non-transitive headers? 

If extension headers are mutable, includes changing existing ones that would be duplicated, adding new, and even removing... it results in caches of the same object by unique key constraint being different relay by relay.  

Attempting to prime a newly created relay with a cache or using a distributed cache (e.g., redis cache of content in the local AZ) will be challenging when considering extension headers and the impact of those.  Which ones should be changed? Which ones should be left untouched? Does order matter, ...

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
> A related thing that came up is if they are mutated, and they get bigger, that can push a datagram over MTU size

For streams, increasing or decreasing the size should not be an issue. For datagram, increasing the size could result in loss. Major problem IMO.

issues.title: Clarify interaction of extension headers and caching
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body:
Related to #741.... 

The topic has come up that we need to cache fetch streams of data objects in addition to the live stream of data objects based on subscribes. 

Our original thought was that a cache is populated upon subscribed objects being received... Now that fetches may exist outside of a subscribe...  A new requirement has come up that we cache fetched data objects.   This introduces some complexities on reconciling cache within the relay (as well as any replication or distributed cache).


The unique key constraint of `<track namespace array/tuples>, <track name>, <group-id>, <object-id>` being used by both live subscribed data and fetch response data may differ in extension headers. 

It's assumed that the relay would service the fetch request from local cache if it has the data...  but that may not be the case if the range is out side of the local cache store . Fetch would then possibly fill those gaps of data with objects, but now the extension headers are possibly different because the data objects are from a fetch and not live stream of data.  For example, extension headers may have updated headers based on the fetch request, such as timestamps to be relative to the time of the fetch, etc...

If the fetch request is for a range of 200 - 300 group-ids and the local cache only has 250-300, the missing gaps are fetched upstream toward the original publisher to get 200-249.. Those objets returned by the fetch now may have headers that don't jive with the headers 250-300. The next fetch request comes in for the same range of 200-300, which now comes from local cache, but the headers for 200-249 are in conflict with the original headers from the live stream that was cached for 250-300. 

How is this supposed to be handled?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the same condition can occur without FETCH --eg: if the relay has redundant publishers for the same track, which are following different relay paths and therefore different headers.  I'm retitling the issue to address the generic relationship between headers and caching.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: agree needs clarification but I think the solution would be very easy to just say when an object is written to cache, then the headers that were with it are also written to cache. And when an object is read from cache, so are the headers with it. If a relay receives a 2nd copy of a object that is already in cache, the new copy is discarded and cache remains the same.

comments.author: afrind
suhasHere
comments.body: I will be in support for caching header extensions and those getting served when retrieved from the cache.  It might be more useful to say relays SHOULD drop if there is a duplicate entry for a object key.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
I believe the answer to this challenge is to indicate in the extension header if it's mutable or immutable.  Immutable **MUST** not change or be removed (aka transitive), so we can safely cache it, while immutable means we do not cache it and it may mutate (remove or update) anywhere long the forwarding plane.  For example, replace operation of ext immutable header to identify the origin relay that received the object. 

Mutable vs Immutable is a flag that could be encoded as a single bit in a flags byte (8).   Even vs Odd on type to indicate if the value will be only a var-int or if it'll be a var-in followed by bytes of that size could be just an another flag bit instead of the cryptic usage of odd vs even types. 

Extension headers would benefit from having the following change:

```
Extension Header {
  Header Type (i)
  Header Flags(8),  <--- This is new to add up to 8 flags to indicate header value encoding, transitive/non-transitive, ...
  Header Value(..)
}
```

`Header Value(..)` is relative to the type and flags. 

Type could be used, such as with [QUIC stream type](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#frame-stream) but that is a bit of a cryptic use of combining flags + type to be just type.   

Possible option to be clear would be:

```
Extension Header {
  Header Type (6), 
  Header ValueAsBytes(1), // 1 indicates if value is encoded as var-int followed
                          //  by array of bytes of var-int size. 0 indicates value is only a var-int
  Header Mutable(1), // 0 indicates that the value cannot change and must be forwarded, 1 can change and can be dropped
  Header Value(..)
}
```

comments.body:
Am I correct in my read that this and #741 are describing the same issue:

comments.body:
> As we were discussing at the interim, I think text about how a FETCH shouldn't generate more than one upstream FETCH is likely important, though.

A single FETCH will likely generate one upstream FETCH per gap in the cached range.  Otherwise the cache will have to pull objects it already has in cache.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> we are going to want a RELAY to be able to tell a [FETCH] the range requested was too large

+1 Ian, I don't think we need an error code that like range too large.  Servers gonna do.  If they have implementation specific limits, they can use INTERNAL_ERROR.

>  also give information about what sort of range would work.

We can add advisory parameters for this kind of thing in SETUP (eg: MAX_FETCH_GROUPS=<number of groups>).  Does that work?  An implementation can use that to break a large FETCH API request into N fetches of publisher-allowed sizes.

> I think text about how a FETCH shouldn't generate more than one upstream FETCH is likely important, though.

I filed #899 to track that.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I haven't been able to come up with a resource exhaustion or attack issue with a large number of groups.  I'd like to better understand the problem we're trying to fix before adding a mechnaism.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in Madrid:

The sentiment in the room was it's fine to add a specific error code.  Because Groups and Objects are variable in size, there wasn't a clear proposal what to advertise as a maximum in setup, so we're not planning to add that for now.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: Let me make a clear proposal that we specify the limit in bytes.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Unfortunately, a limit in bytes is not that useful.  As a Relay, I would need to scan my cache for the requested range to compute it's size before sending any objects.  If the cache has gaps, the Relay also needs to fill them before determining this.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Further, a limit in bytes doesn't achieve the aim of telling the subscriber how they can change their request to get it to succeed, since the subscriber doesn't know the size of the groups/objects they are requesting.  For that, the only thing that really makes sense to me would be a limit expressed in Groups and/or Objects.

Following up on Ian's earlier comment here:

>  I'd like to better understand the problem we're trying to fix before adding a mechanism.

I agree with this.  Serving a large number of bytes from cache is not really a problem that relays need to protect themselves against.  An HTTP cache is basically on the hook to serve the largest resource it has cached. MoQ tracks could be much larger than "typical" files served via HTTP (though LLM models or mega git-repos are probably pushing that).  Having some kind of limit that forces the subscriber to use smaller ranges could be beneficial -- especially as fetching large quantities have an impact on server availability and reliability, as shutting down with active requests causes errors.

I'd be fine with expressing fetch range limits as SETUP params.  I think the simplest is just MAX_FETCH_GROUPS, and Relays are on the hook to serve at least 1 group per FETCH.  A group can be arbitrarily large, but so can a single object.  Note that because of Joining FETCH, 1 group is the implicit minimum already.

The advantage of advertising at SETUP is that you won't fail and have to retry in the first place.  This could be used by a non-relay endpoint to disable FETCH (by setting MAX_FETCH_GROUPS=0) -- see #1107.  Setting the limit in terms of objects can be done but is annoying and I wonder if it's necessary.

I also wonder if there's an intersection between what's being asked here and #1057 -- that the FETCH may be asking for something too far in the past that is not available, and being able to serve what is available rather than failing?  I think we can add range trimming in fetch responses to address that.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
Many relays will not implement this error as they would not want to compute anything, they will just pass on the fetch, that is fine. But if a relay wants to implement this error, it is going to be checking something.

So how do I implement this? We need to say how this is implemented. I don't care if it is a limit on bytes, objects, or groups but we need to be specific because what the client does next relies on knowing what was exceeded and what the threshold is. We could allow communication of limits on all three, I don't care. But an error that says "bring me rock, I won't tell you what rock I want" seems like a bad design.

comments.body:
Copying @fluffy comments from [761](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/761#issuecomment-2746866438) here:
---
So here is requirements and then I will describe solution stolen from WebRTC>

Requirements when using E2E Encryptions (note many things will not use E2E Encryption):

the whole payload is E2E encrypted - no more, no less. This makes it easier to reason about security proofs.

by default, MoQ headers extensions are not part of the E2E "extra authenticated data"

There is a header extension called "start of authenticated headers". All the headers extension after that header are including in the E2E "extra authenticated data"

Relays can not modify, or remove headers that follow this one but they can add, change, remove header extensions before the "start of authenticated headers".

issues.title: LatestObject Subscribe filter is ambiguous.
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Individual comment:

Sec 8.6 says:

> Specifies an open-ended subscription beginning from the current object of the current group. If no content has been delivered yet, the subscription starts with the first published or received group.

@fluffy says this can be interpreted two ways:

1) Objects will be forwarded if the sequence number exceeds (Largest Group ID, Largest Object ID) as reported in SUBSCRIBE_OK. I would expect a relay to just send the largest object ID it's observed on a track when composing SUBSCRIBE_OK.

2) Objects will be forwarded if they arrive after the moment of Subscribe, regardless of ID. Largest ID might be (5, 0), but if (4, 25) arrives later due to prioritization/loss/etc, the publisher will send that along too.

Some points:
- I strongly believe that we should clarify this: subscribers should have a solid expectation of what they get when they send SUBSCRIBE. 
 
- For the "regular" use case where group IDs are increasing, interpretation (2) is wasteful. In general, (4, 25) is not going to be decodable without other objects that the publisher is never going to deliver. Furthermore, corresponding Fetch streams are hard to reason about if some pre-largest-ID objects are delivered via Subscribe streams. So I definitely think we need to express "send only higher sequence numbers", alternative (1), in the SUBSCRIBE message somehow.

- It wouldn't be a ton of code to have a new filter that expresses (2). This would accommodate the random Group ID use case we talked about in Denver. It gets us away from "random group ID is something that just happens to work" to "random Group ID is a thing we are explicitly supporting with protocol codepoints." I personally would not add this complication for what I see as a marginal use case, but if we have consensus to do it, I won't lie down in the road over it.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> * For the "regular" use case where group IDs are increasing, interpretation (2) is wasteful. In general, (4, 25) is not going to be decodable without other objects that the publisher is never going to deliver. Furthermore, corresponding Fetch streams are hard to reason about if some pre-largest-ID objects are delivered via Subscribe streams. So I definitely think we need to express "send only higher sequence numbers", alternative (1), in the SUBSCRIBE message somehow.


I want to explore a possibility where groupIds are still sequential and relay can still receive  4,25 after 5,0. this would be the case of descending group order subscription, where under congestion, a upstream relay decided to send 5,0 before sending 4,25.  When this happens, the relay would forward 4,25 to the end subscriber even it reported 5,0  in the SubscribeOk , since 5,0 was the last one it observed when the Subscribe message happened.

So even in the normal temporally increasing group behavior, this is totally a possible outcome. Unless we remove Dsc group order for subscription, you are bound to recieve out of order groups.

The more i think if it, it feels like what is reported in SubscirbeOK is a hint and end subscribers needs to handle changes. May be we need to clarify this behavior for Dsc Group Order and explain for the Asc Group order the latest object means Current Object (even it is not fully received)

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Of course it's possible for objects to arrive out of order. The whole point of the subscribe filter is to indicate what the subscriber wants.

Say I subscribe to HighestObject when Group IDs increase with time, and Largest ID is (5,2). I can't actually decode (5,2) without (5,0) , so I send a joining FETCH that goes back 0 groups.

Say (4,12) arrives late. I don't want this object! I'm never going to be able to decode it.

Say (5,0) arrives late because of a retransmission, or whatever. This object is useful to me, but I already requested it via Joining FETCH. So is it delivered via Fetch, via Subscribe, or both? If I'm trying to decode Group 5, I shouldn't rely on earlier objects in the group straggling in late due to reordering. Instead, I'll just do a Joining Fetch.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> Say (4,12) arrives late. I don't want this object! I'm never going to be able to decode it.

You already have received 4,0 - 4,11 and yes you can decode 4,12. The only reason 4,12 came after 5,0 is because of DCS order.  Caches that was to store 2-3 recent groups, will make use of this data too.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> > Say (4,12) arrives late. I don't want this object! I'm never going to be able to decode it.
> 
> You already have received 4,0 - 4,11 and yes you can decode 4,12. The only reason 4,12 came after 5,0 is because of DCS order. Caches that was to store 2-3 recent groups, will make use of this data too.

issues.title: How does a relay honor opposite DeliveryOrder requests?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Individual (implementer) comment:

Section 6.1 says

> The publisher communicates its group order in the SUBSCRIBE_OK message; the subscriber can override it in its SUBSCRIBE message. The group order of an existing subscription cannot be changed.

Sec 8.6:

> A subscriber MUST NOT make multiple active subscriptions for a track within a single session and publishers SHOULD treat this as a protocol violation.

Say I'm a relay. Subscriber A asks for "Foo" in ascending order. Subscriber B asks for "Foo" in descending order. By 6.1, these preferences override publisher priority. I'm not allowed to make two upstream subscriptions.

So if the relay subscribes ascending, it's really going to struggle to deliver objects in anything but ascending order, or vice versa, without a huge amount of buffering and delay. "Relays gonna do", I guess: priority is not enforceable, so B is going to get it in descending whether it likes it or not. This is not a great state of affairs!

Some possible remedies.
1) The group order in SUBSCRIBE_OK is definitive; that's how you're going to get it. The publisher SHOULD do it in the requested order if it can. That way, the client can UNSUBSCRIBE if it can't live with the result. This is kinda what 8.7 says but I don't know what 6.1 means if it's the current standard.
2) allow two subscriptions to a track if one is ascending and the other is descending
3)  SUBSCRIBE_ERROR if the relay just isn't going to do that group order for whatever reason

There should be some advice in the document.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I think good advice is to send "Default" as the subscribe group order preference when going upstream from the relay.

Also, remember it's just a priority signal in subscribe, so it only really matters during congestion.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> allow two subscriptions to a track if one is ascending and the other is descending


Allow the relay to make a choice in optimizing the downstream traffic by making two upstream subscriptions with differing group order. There may be some relay networks which are willing to double their midgress traffic in order to optimize for the last mile. As a consequence, the relay must introduce group order into its key of "do I already have this subscription". As Alan mentioned, relay networks should have less of a problem with congestion than the last mile, but we should allow them the choice of making two upstream requests for the same track.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
Subscribe_Ok tells the publisher preference of the group order and what it can support for a given subscriber. It is totally possible for the same relay to deliver groups in ascending order to one subscriber and descending order to another subscriber. In many cases it can do so even by not sending 2 upstream subscriptions.

Delivery order is an input to "what to pick next" when there are objects from multiple groups available that are not yet sent ( some kind of backlog going on) .. Since it is per subscriber specific choice made by the publisher, a relay can support both the options.

I am with Will to also have relay making a choice on what it does upstream.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Subscribing twice upstream to express different preferences seems counterproductive - it increases the likelihood of congestion.  Doesn't the current draft precludes multiple subscriptions to the same track?  I'm ok letting the relay choose any of the orders, but "Default" still seems like the best to me.

issues.title: Should we merge Track Namespace and Track Name?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The system design leverages the separation in these places today:

1. ANNOUNCE only announces namespaces
2. Relay routing is done only on namespace matching
3. By including a track name in SUBSCRIBE and FETCH, it's clear you can only use those verbs to operate on a single track per message (eg: no wildcards).

I think we could merge the two fields together if we think that makes sense and consider changing the other design elements separately.  That would constrain this largely to a wire-format and editorial change.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Considerations:

1. Without wildcard subscribe, which we still have at least mechanical issues with, SUBSCRIBE <namespace> has to always error.  Keeping them separate prevents it from even being encoded, assuming you think an empty track name is still a track name.

2. As pointed out in #766, merging the namespace and names implicitly allows `ANNOUNCE <Full Track Name>`.

comments.author: Sy0307
comments.body:
There might be two issues to consider:
 
1. Compatibility. This merge will involve many fields in the control messages, which will be a significant change. Once we agree to this merge, we may need to consider how to handle the client messages from previous draft versions.

2. Regarding representing this track after the merge, do you expect us to use a tuple or a string? Theoretically, I think they are similar. However, if possible, I recommend using a string. Parsing tuples can be quite troublesome (considering that sometimes messages might be truncated and sent in multiple complete parts). I can still process strings quickly. This can be achieved by using a trie and specifying a maximum length.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  we may need to consider how to handle the client messages from previous draft versions.

Up until now, the working group has not put much thought into draft-to-draft compatibility. I think this should be a secondary, but not a primary concern -- eg: we should make decisions based on what we agree will be best for "V1" before considering backward impact with intermediate drafts.

> Regarding representing this track after the merge, do you expect us to use a tuple or a string? 

Collapsing namespace into a string can create ambiguities.  eg: ("a", "b") and ("ab") are two completely disjoint namespaces.  If there were a character that were not legal in a namespace, you could use that as an unambiguous separator (maybe \0?), but so far the group consensus is that namespace tuple fields and track names have no restrictions - they are just bytes.

comments.author: Sy0307
comments.body: I mean what type we will use for the "New track" if we merge track namespace and track. String or tuple?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Almost certainly tuple.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - we're not inclined to merge these based on the direction of PUBLISH.

comments.body: I'm confused as to how those two things are related.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
@vasilvv I think you stepped out when we talked about this.  The summary is:

SUBSCRIBE and PUBLISH -- only operate on Full Track
SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES and ANNOUNCE -- only operate on namespace

There was also discussion about merging verbs, and the feeling in the room was "don't", though someone suggested making the names symmetric like:

SUBSCRIBE_TRACK, PUBLISH_TRACK
SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, PUBLISH_NAMESPACE

I suppose if I squint we could allow the "SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES" action to take a full track name (I'm waiting for this track only); this makes things a bit messy.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
(just wanted to add a note here, we touched on this during the last meeting, and there were at least three people who expressed sentiment along the lines of "why are those split")

@afrind I don't understand how splitting/not splitting this is related.

In a world where those are merged:
- If you say `PUBLISH ("foo", "bar")`, you publish a track with full name `("foo", "bar")`
- If you say `ANNOUNCE ("foo", "bar")`, you announce that you have all tracks of form `("foo", "bar", ...)`.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Let's assume that we merged them.  Now:

`SUBSCRIBE namespace` and `PUBLISH namespace` are possible, but have no meaning.
`ANNOUNCE full-track-name` and `PUBLISH full-track-name, forward=0` are two ways of doing extremely similar things.
etc
`SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES full-track-name` sort of makes sense?

I don't know if the minutes from Stockholm captured more of the discussion, or we need to rewatch the video, or we need to just bring this up again.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
> `SUBSCRIBE namespace` and `PUBLISH namespace` are possible, but have no meaning.

They aren't possible in the proposal that I just posted above though?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> They aren't possible in the proposal that I just posted above though?

Oh I see. Then you have sort of weird logic where relays take `SUBSCRIBE ftn` and match `ftn[:-1]` against ANNOUNCE'd ns and `ftn` against PUBLISH'd tracks.  `SUBSCRIBE namespace` still seems like an error.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
We can remove ANNOUNCE entirely, along with SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES. 

If you are a publisher, you would use `PUBLISH  ("foo","bar" forward=0)` to 'announce' a FTN.

1. Original publisher does `PUBLISH ("foo","bar", forward=0) `to relay#1. Nothing else moves across the wire, but relay#1 now knows that publisher is the source of "foo","bar". 
2. A subscriber connects to relay#2 and `SUBSCRIBE ("foo","bar", forward=1)`
3. Relay#2 issues a `SUBSCRIBE ("foo","bar", forward=1)` against relay#1
4. Relay#1 issues a `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE ("foo","bar", forward=1)` to the original publisher, and traffic starts flowing. 

We should also enable wildcard subscriptions, with the restriction that the wildcard MUST be the last tuple element. 

For example, If I want all the streams produced by "foo", I could `SUBSCRIBE ("foo", *, forward=1)`
This would get me `"foo","bar"` , `"foo","any","thing","else"` etc 

Getting rid of ANNOUNCE and SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES would simplify the spec. They never seemd a natural fit with the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH symmetry.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
See slides 14 / 15 from the Stockholm discussion, which also covers merging the verbs.

https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/interim-2025-moq-09/materials/slides-interim-2025-moq-09-sessa-moqt-issue-burndown-part-1-00

I wrote a PR that merges the verbs while I was writing PUBLISH but didn't put it up.  At least one problem I found is the text ends up describing two different behaviors - one SUBSCRIBE'ing to a single track and another SUBSCRIBE'ing to wildcards, and it got quite awkward, at least editorially.

See this contemporaneous comment: https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/764#issuecomment-2857428036

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Here's one option:

* Redefine Full Track Name to be a 1..32 tuple.  The last tuple field is the "name" and anything before that is the "namespace"
* Change SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH from Namespace+Name to Full Track Name
* Leave SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE/ANNOUNCE (eg: SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE/PUBLISH_NAMESPACE) with Track Namespace

The reasoning to keep the verbs separate is that SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH establish a subscription (eg: makes things happen in the data plane) but SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE/PUBLISH_NAMESPACE do not.

Suggested Definition:

```
Full Track Name is an ordered tuple of bytes sequences with 1 to 32 fields. The
last field is designated as the Track Name, and the preceding fields form the
Track Namespace.
 
The total number of fields in the Full Track Name MUST NOT exceed 32. If an
endpoint receives a Full Track Name with 33 or more fields, or a Track Namespace
with 32 or more fields, it MUST close the session with a Protocol Violation.
```

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
I implemented a merged namespace/name. It's cool that tracks were announced, but it's redundant given the catalog already provides that functionality and more (at the cost of 1 RTT). The downside was that you needed a way to group tracks into a broadcast, ie. this audio track and this video track go together because they share the same prefix of length n-k. 

I decided that it just increased the number of announcements and complicated the code so I reverted it.

And there is actually an upside to not announcing track names: they can be unguessable. Namespaces are public but track names are private. It's kind of like DNS names versus HTTP paths (I guess).

comments.body: Asked on list for input here: https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/moq/oNQnXJawgSNWGmnf662spzVL-Yk/

issues.title: Should we revisit relay routing on exact namespace match?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The current design is:

1. Publishers ANNOUNCE individual namespaces to the relay
2. SUBSCRIBE/FETCH has a namespace field
3. The relay compares these field and routes to sessions that match exactly

An alternate design is prefix match on either the namespace only, or the namespace and the name.  We previously decided not to prefix match because there was no safe way to do this before we tupleized namespace.

See related #764

comments.body: +1 on revisiting this. Relays need to implement prefix match for  Authz purposes.

> Relays need to implement prefix match for Authz purposes.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
For authorization, the claim in the token will typically be a prefix of the actual namespace or ftn that will be provided in the corresponding control message ( for ex: slide 2 in https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/interim-2025-moq-01/materials/slides-interim-2025-moq-01-sessa-authorization-in-moq-00)

Relays will do prefix match to see if the announced namespace is covered by the claim, for example

comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> Relays will do prefix match to see if the announced namespace is covered by the claim, for example

I think what the relay does is separable into two steps:

1) check if the user authorized is for the action+track
2) routing upstream SUBSCRIBE/FETCH if needed, based on matching logic 

We could decide to use prefix matching in auth but exact matching for routing.  I'm not trying to argue against prefix based routing, but I don't think it's a hard dependency.

issues.title: Should a publisher be able to ANNOUNCE individual tracks?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Today ANNOUNCE is for a namespace only and not individual tracks.  One of the reasons was that the name alone wouldn't tell you enough to consume the track without out-of-band knowledge.

If we allow individual track announcements, perhaps it could be a list inside the ANNOUNCE message if they share other params (eg: auth).

See also #764 and #765

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
If we merge Namespace and Name, then you can't tell whether what you are announcing is a namespace prefix or a full track name. The knowledge of that division resides with the application and the relays don't need to know about it. 

Relay receives announces for 

```
example.com/conference1234/bob
example.com/conference1234/carol
example.com/conference1234/ted
example.com/conference1234/alice
```

It would behave the same in terms of routing subscriptions if it received these announces which are actually the full track names.

```
example.com/conference1234/bob/video
example.com/conference1234/bob/audio
example.com/conference1234/carol/video
example.com/conference1234/carol/audio
example.com/conference1234/ted/video
example.com/conference1234/ted/audio
example.com/conference1234/alice/video
example.com/conference1234/alice/audio
```

There is a difference in the size of the table the relay needs to store announces between the two cases. For efficiency, the guidance should be that a publisher SHOULD announce the smallest (merged) NAME prefix that uniquely identifies its traffic.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - No need for ANNOUNCE to do if PUBLISH (#995) does that.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: PUBLISH with forward=0 can be used to "announce" a single track.

issues.title: Does SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCEs belong in the transport?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body: An alternate design is to create a separate draft that defines a well known track name for relays - for example (".well_known", "announce").  The objects in this track would be the encoded ANNOUNCE and UNANNOUNCE messages.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Two questions on this approach:

1. Assume there are thousands of tracks being announced. Right now SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES allows you to set a filter against the NAMESPACE prefix you want to listen to. How would this work with the track version? if I want to get all the announces for "example.com/conference/1234" would I subscribe to the track ".well_known.announce.example.com/conference/1234"? A relay would have to automatically accept such a subscription even if it didn't have any current matches. When a new ANNOUNCE comes in, it must look through its list of well_known.announce. subscriptions, find those for whom the prefix matches and then publish an object with the update.

2. Assume a relay has 4 prior annoucements which are still active (they have not unannounced or timed out)
```
example.com/conference/1234/bob
example.com/conference/1234/carol
example.com/conference/1234/ted
example.com/conference/1234/alice
```
A track subscription comes in for ".well_known.announce.example.com/conference/1234". If it only sends future data on the subscription, the client will not know about all the prior subscriptions. To be consistent with track semantics, then client should FETCH the announces from the past. But how far back does it know to go? It has no catalog. We could say it should FETCH from group 0, but the relay can only make one group 0 and where does it draw that line in the sand?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I think your points are excellent reasons to keep this in the transport for now.  There are perhaps ways to work around all these problems, but then the transport solution will look much cleaner.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - PUBLISH (#995) uses this mechanism to solicit PUBLISH messages, so we do think this will stay in the transport.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Closing with no action

issues.title: Allow widening a subscription in SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Currently, you can SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, but only narrow the subscription.  This is to avoid raciness, since in the worst case you receive a few Objects that you no longer want, but otherwise the behavior is not racy.

Multiple subscriptions are not allowed, but there needs to be some way to say "Actually, I want one more group from this track" when doing ABR switches, because if the next quality up takes longer to arrive for whatever reason, you'll want to stay on the current track.  There are likely other use cases when this is very useful.

Cancelling a subscription and re-subscribing in sequence has even more raciness issues than trying to do SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE.

The easiest solution is to allow multiple subscriptions to the same track.  If we wanted to be restrictive, we could say that subscribers SHOULD not have multiple subscriptions that overlap.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
@wilaw and I have spent some time brainstorming about ABR switch in the recent months. We will document our conclusions in the coming weeks (a WARP draft?). 

Let's say you play a track UHD at group 34 and you want to switch to track SD. In the algorithm we discussed during Denver interim, you need to select a target group ID in the future for the transition. Let's say you choose to switch at group 37. The switching algo is:
1- SUBSCRIBE SD low-priority
2- Absolute_Joining_FETCH SD 37 high-priority
3- wait for the first SD object **ahead of playtime**
4- SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE UHD end=first SD object ahead of playtime
5- SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE SD high-priority

Overall, this 5-step algorithm is less clean than a unique SWITCH as initially suggested, but it does the job. Note that the situation you described cannot happen because you stop UHD only when you are sure you can play SD. 

Yet, there is a risk at step 3. Indeed, between step 2 and step 3, you continued playing track UHD. When you receive the group 37 from the SD track, it is possible that you are already playing UHD group 39 (for example because a long RTT). In the event that you selected a transition ID that was too optimistic (the choice for 37 here), then you need to wait for the Absolute_Joining_FETCH track to catch up. Hopefully, it should happen but it is not sure because three tracks are concurrently competing: 1/ the old SUBSCRIBE UHD since you cannot transition yet, 2/ the high-priority Absolute_Joining_FETCH SD which is doing the transition, and 3/ the low-priority SUBSCRIBE SD. It is a lot of data for a client who wants to down-switch due to congestion.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I am confused by this proposal.  If I have a subscribe for groups `<= N`, but I ask to extend it to `<= N+1`, the risk is that `N+1` will arrive to the relay before it receives a subscribe update; allowing multiple subscriptions does nothing to mitigate the fundamental race at hand.

I am also skeptical of the overall scenario as a whole.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - we're going to keep the restriction on one subscription per track, but change SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE to allow widening the end and add an OK/ERROR response from the publisher.

issues.title: FETCH_ERROR "No Objects" clarification
issues.author: RichLogan
issues.body:
There are a couple of references to a "No Objects" `FETCH_ERROR` code, but it isn't currently defined in the `FETCH_ERROR` code table. There is however "Invalid Range". Should there be a new code for "No Objects (0x6)", or would the declared "Invalid Range" work and we update the text to reflect that? Happy to throw up a PR but wanted to check the intention. 

[8.12. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html#section-8.12)[FETCH](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html#name-fetch)
> If StartGroup/StartObject is greater than the latest published Object group, the publisher MUST return FETCH_ERROR with error code 'No Objects'.

[8.12.1 Calculating the Range of a Joining Fetch](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html#name-calculating-the-range-of-a-)

issues.title: Reconsider object IDs
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We currently identify tracks via a tuple of `(full track name, group ID, object ID)`.  I think we should consider making object IDs track-global, i.e. the publisher will assign every object on the track sequential IDs (first object is 0, then 1, then 2, 3, 4) regardless of what group or subgroup they're in.  This results in every object being uniquely identified by `(full track name, object sequence ID)`, which is a simplification.  It also makes it easier to reason about ranges and offsets, since there would be no 2D index.

We discussed this during Oct 2024 interim in Cambridge, and there was a certain lack of interest in this proposal, some people saying that the current 2D index "is closer to how media naturally works".  I think we should consider this again, for the following reasons:

- With subgroups, object IDs no longer have the desirable sequential properties they used to have.
- Given how much we spent discussing group and object IDs after Cambridge, we clearly should have considered this more seriously, given that this might be an answer to the disagreements that the working group has regarding group ID gaps and ordering.

Of course, a lot of this depends on specifics; I'll try to prepare a PR or some other form of detailed write-up to have a solid idea of how this is supposed to work.

comments.author: englishm
comments.body: One downside of a flattened object ID space is that it would limit the ability to use objects within groups as a way of encoding additional meaning for targeted Fetch and Subscribe applications. e.g. currently object 0 for many uses cases is likely to represent an I-Frame or similar non-delta-encoded object.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: True, which is why I still need to make a more specific proposal that makes that possible (e.g. by marking start of the group explicitly).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

Given the current loose restrictions on group IDs and object IDs, you can already do this in your application protocol running on top of MoQT.

You can use an Object Header Extension to tag IDR objects.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: For audio, where each object is a new group, this would impact bandwidth usage

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
> Given the current loose restrictions on group IDs and object IDs, you can already do this in your application protocol running on top of MoQT.

The goal here is to simplify caches and relays, so I'm not sure how that helps?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The goal here is to simplify caches and relays, so I'm not sure how that helps?

Can you explain in more detail how the flat identifier scheme helps caches and relays?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: We discussed this at Stockholm; the conclusion appears to be that this does not seem to have enough upsides to be worth pursuing further.  Closing with no action.

issues.title: No AUTHORITY parameter
issues.author: bemasc
issues.body:
MoQT has a PATH parameter, but AFAICT it doesn't have an AUTHORITY parameter.  That means the server doesn't know who the client thinks it's talking to.  This sort of thing turns out to be important for virtual-hosting, which is why HTTP/1.1 had to add a "Host" header.

I recommend adding an AUTHORITY parameter.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: Is that really necessary given that a raw MoQT connection has access to SNI?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I find that there are a lot of situations where the TLS SNI is not convenient for application usage.  Applications often sit atop a high-level API that doesn't expose this information, or behind a TLS-terminating load-balancer that loses it.

The TLS working group tends to view the SNI as an implementation detail of certificate selection in the handshake, not a signaling path for application logic.  Its presence is optional (if not explicitly mandated by some application profile), and even in modern browsers it is sometimes omitted (e.g. when the authority is an IP address).

issues.title: When can a FETCH be served from Objects retrieved via SUBSCRIBE?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
This was briefly discussed in Denver and I believe in some other issues, and is related to #715.

There are cases when Groups will arrive out of order, even if they were created in order.  One example I have in mind is an original publisher who wants to keep within a certain boundary of live, and may have to delay sending some Groups of a higher bitrate stream until later when it has more bandwidth.

Assuming there is no Delivery Timeout, the Groups will eventually be sent from the Original Publisher, but may be quite delayed.  For cases when one wants the VoD copy to have the highest fidelity possible (ie: a video call being recorded), this seems useful.

This example is quite a bit worse than the 'this group was slightly delayed due to packet loss' example we've discussed before, but they're instances of the same issue.

I think the answer is that you can't answer the Fetch entirely from cache if there are any gaps in the Group ID space, because you don't know if you just haven't received the Group yet unless an explicit Group Does Not Exist was published and cached.

A related concern is that all of these Fetches might need to go all the way back to the original publisher unless we're careful about Fetch/request coalescing.  If that does happen, does the Fetch hang indefinitely for the Groups the Original Publisher hasn't had the bandwidth to send?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I've been implementing a fetch cache.  In the case where the cache has no information about an object, it issues a FETCH upstream.  The reply will be definitive (present or missing) and this is always cached to prevent future upstream lookups.  The subscriber's FETCH is blocked while the upstream FETCH resolves, even if subsequent objects are available.  I have request coalescing implemented so that no object will ever be FETCH'd more than once, ASSUMING the upstream returns a FETCH_OK and an object >= to the requested one.  If I go upstream and hit a FETCH_ERROR or early reset, the waiting client will issue its own FETCH.

The logic is non-trivial but seems doable so far.  I strongly recommend everyone who wants to talk about FETCH write or sketch out an implementation of the cache, or review an implementation.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Thinking about this, I wonder if we should add an Object/Group status of "Not Yet Available", which indicates it exists, but can't be delivered at the moment.  This would likely need a TTL for when one can attempt to Fetch it again.

issues.title: Video ingestion has extra latency and is awkward
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
I believe the intended flow for ingestion today is a client connects, then sends an ANNOUNCE for the namespace it wants to publish to, then the server sends a SUBSCRIBE for a track.

This takes an extra RTT at best over the client just beginning to publish once it connects.

How does the server know which track name(s) to subscribe to?

It seems like a simpler model would be similar to HTTP POST, where the client connects and starts publishing whenever it wants to, and the server can cancel the PUBLISH at any time if it doesn't want to receive the data.

As implied, this requires a new verb, ie: PUBLISH to allow the publisher to initiate publication of a Track.

comments.body:
Individual Comment:

The awkwardness of "publisher speaks first" is not limited to video ingestion either.  We are investigating moqt to carry existing relay-to-relay realtime traffic and would likely use something like PUBLISH if it existed.

issues.title: MoQT lacks support for track level object extension

MoQT is not very specific about whether a object extensions are session level or track level, however, only allows extension to be negotiated as the session setup. This means the object extensions are applicable for the whole session.

However, all extensions such as metadata about tracks is not necessarily a uniform session-level property. There can be several kinds of metadata that may be needed in one track and not in another. One example is the "rendered pose" in a split rendering scenario, i.e. the server signals ( say in an RTP header extension) the pose used to render the video frame carried. Another example is the audio level header extension [RFC 6464], which indicates the audio level of the audio sample carried in the RTP packet.
 
It is unclear how such per track level object extension can be negotiated.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think audio level might be a poor example, if it's something that can change as the track moves along. I think better examples might be something that only needs to be communicated once and doesn't change -- maybe like an init segment?  See https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-cenzano-moq-media-interop-02.html#section-2.4.3 for something that could probably benefit?

>  Is the expectation that, this is set by the OP and gets sent all the way to end subscriber ?
