issues.title: Enabling Low Latency Adaptive Bitrate Live Streaming of Scalable Video Encoding (SVC) encoded media using MOQT
issues.author: Johan511
issues.body:
# Motivation

I have been working on implementing the MOQT draft version 7 and creating an application which simulates Adaptive Bitrate Live Streaming with a focus on achieving low latency (in order of 100ms)


During the process, I came across multiple scenarios where the MOQT implementation had to deviate from the draft and am raising this issue with the intent to reach out to the community and get their opinion on how such an application should be implemented using MOQT; debate the pros of my approach and possibly suggest enhancements to the draft

# Setup

## Object Model

Following elaborates the video encoding model

```
Video_Stream/
│── small independent chunk (media length is around few hundred milliseconds)
│   ├── Base Layer (SVC splits each video chunk into multiple base and enhancement layers)
│   ├── Multiple possible base layers (for video, audio, subtitles, ...)
│   ├── Enhancement Layer 1
│   ├── Enhancement Layer 2
│   ├── ... (multiple enhancement layers)
│── ... (multiple such small independent chunks)
```

A live stream is represented by one and only one Track (Track Namespace + Track Name)

Each Group in the track represents a Base/Enhancement Layer

Each Object in the Group represents an independent chunk of video

**Example**: 
Group 0 -> Base Layer (480p)

Group 1 -> Enhancement Layer 1

Each chunk represents 250ms of media

If we receive 
1. Group 0 - Object 0 (G0-O0) we play a 250ms chunk of video at 480p
2. G0-O0 + G1-O0 we play the 250ms chunk of video at 1080p (we have received Base + Enhancement Layer)
3. G0-O0 + G0-O1 we play 250ms + 250ms of video at 480p
4. G1-O0 only, G0-O0 is not received, we can't play any video because enhancement layers build upon base layers

Each group has a Publisher priority with base layers having the highest priority and enhancement layers having monotonically decreasing priorities.

NOTE: we repeatedly use 250ms as the media chunk size, this is not a specific number we are proposing. It is simply the number we use in our application and believe mentioning the window duration helps the reader get better context rather than a verbose mention of "an independent media chunk of corresponding to a few hundred milliseconds"

## Live Streaming Model

The subscription first starts out by sending the latest object (greatest object id) to the subscriber, every time a new object is received by the Publisher for a particular group, it aborts the send of the previous object in that group and sends the new object which has been received.

NOTE: In our case, each subgroup has only one object; so when we mention "abort" we are aborting the data stream with the corresponding `STREAM_HEADER_SUBGROUP` header

To enable this in our implementation, we set the objects contained in the group to range from 0 to (maximum number of objects in a group which is approx. UINT62_MAX)

We also have a concept of ethereal and concrete objects
- **concrete**: object can be requested, it is available and will be immediately served
- **ethereal**: object can be requested, but it is not available yet, the publisher will publish it at some future point of time

Initially all the objects in the group are ethereal and become concrete as the publisher receives them.

*TODO*: Check if the concept of ethereal and concrete objects make sense for relays to adopt, currently this is an internal implementation detail which we are not proposing

In our application, we receive a new object every 250ms in all groups simultaneously; we send whatever latest objects (in each group) we can in the 250ms window before the next set of objects arrive at which point the objects currently queued to be sent are aborted. The subscriber stitches together whatever base and enhancement layer chunks have been received and displays the media of the corresponding bitrate.

To prevent the case where no objects are received due to continuous aborts when even delivering the base layer takes longer than 250ms, we introduce a `MUST_SEND` field which is true for base layers. Objects which are tagged with the `MUST_SEND` priority must be delivered and their delivery will not be aborted.

## Why prefer this stateful model?

Why to use this stateful model over the Request-Response model which has popularized by protocols such as HLS and DASH? 

Answer: **Low Latency**

I roughly view the server and client as 2 units of execution attempting to communicate between each other, similar to 2 threads communicating within a process; except there is a significantly higher overhead for communication/synchronization between the units of execution.

This overhead of communication between the 2 units of execution (publisher and subscriber) depends on the network conditions.

To improve latency, it makes sense to minimize the communication (or synchronization) between the client and server. A stateful setup where the publisher keeps a very lightweight state of what is to be sent next and sends it when preempted by an event on the Publisher side (which in this case is the arrival of a newer object in the group) helps achieve a lower latency.

In a Request-Response model, would require much better network conditions to achieve the same latency as we need to send a request and receive the response within 250ms as opposed to simply receiving the object from the publisher in our proposed model.

The stateful model described is also very reactive to unstable network conditions and scenarios with bursts of packet drops (such as wireless networks), the number of enhancement layers received in every 250ms window is almost independent of the other such windows. If there was a brief hiccup in network conditions (lasting 1-2 seconds), neither the publisher nor subscriber needs to do anything about it at an application level; the QUIC transport layer takes care of it by limiting the send rate and aborts the objects it is unable to send within the window.

We only need to wait for the transport layer congestion control mechanism to adapt to the changes in the network conditions and start streaming more enhancement layers objects.

# Suggestions to the MOQT draft

## A Must Send priority

Consider very bad network scenarios where even objects of the base layer can not be sent within the 250ms time window, in such cases if the application were to abort the send; the user would never receive any objects. This is not ideal, to solve this issue we never abort the send of base layer objects.

Hence, to solve this problem we propose that MOQT has an idea of which objects are base layer and which ones are enhancement layer objects. More specifically, we need some flag to identify if the object is `MUST_SEND` or not. Base layer objects would be `MUST_SEND` while enhancement layer objects are not.

NOTE: We consider higher number to mean higher priority that is, should be sent first. The draft seems to have the opposite idea for Subscriber Priorities and does not comment on Publisher Priorities

We propose that the most significant bit of Subscriber/Publisher Priority denote this.

(Publisher Priority & 0x80) denotes if the publisher believes the object should be `MUST_SEND`

(Subscriber Priority & 0x80) denotes if the subscriber subscribes with a `MUST_SEND` filter

*TODO*: How do relays handle the `MUST_SEND`? 


## Subscribe messages are not exhaustive

This section points out some issues initially faced while implementing subscriptions for the application, it does not need any changes in the draft and there exist solutions which involve updating our object model but we would like to highlight the fact that the existing SUBSCRIBE message is not exhaustive enough to fulfill all the possible use cases which might be faced in the semi-distant future. 

The draft seems to suggest the use of [different tracks for each resolution](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html#section-2), We did not choose this object model for the following reason

- This requires the Subscriber to first send an "SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE" to get information of all tracks in the namespace and then send multiple subscribe messages to the tracks, this introduces 1-RTT latency which we aim of avoid. Whilst this issue can be solved by pattern matching based subscription, the draft is yet to comment on support for pattern matching based subscriptions.

Currently there is no SUBSCRIBE filter type which subscribes to latest objects of all groups in a track. 

This can not be achieved using existing filter types either
**WHY?**
1. *Latest Group (0x1) and Latest Object (0x2)* only subscribe to the "Current Group" which introduces sequentiality between groups, we want to send all objects in all groups concurrently

2. *AbsoluteStart (0x3) and AbsoluteRange (0x4)* can send groups concurrently but require a "Start Group" and "Start Object", this is clearly inefficient because it requires some sort of "Track Manifest" to first be received by the Subscriber before actually subscribing to the media. Existing solutions to receive "Track Manifest" such as the TRACK_STATUS message do not fulfill the requirement either.

We do not propose a new `SUBSCRIBE*` format in this issue firstly for the sake of brevity, and secondly because we are unsure if the community sees this as a requirement worth considering.


# Cons of the Above Mentioned Streaming Model

The above mentioned streaming model has some cons which I am still looking into for solutions

1. Because of aborted sends, a significant fraction of the network bandwidth is used to send data which ends up getting discarded by the subscriber, this is in the order of 20-30%. One solution we have is a client side abort of the data stream if it starts sending packets very late in the 250ms window.

2. In very bad network conditions, we need to send a subscribe update to stop the streaming of enhancement layers until we are certain that base layer objects can be streamed consistently within the 250ms window. We do this because otherwise the publisher would be attempting to send G1-O20 while the subscriber is still receiving G0-O1, that is we need some application enforced synchronization between base layers and enhancement layers. Thought, this problem has a solution in the form of SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE followed by another SUBSCRIBE (if network conditions get better) we are looking into better solutions.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Thanks for your interest in MoQT and sharing your application experience here.  Some comments, as an individual

> A live stream is represented by one and only one Track (Track Namespace + Track Name)

> Each Group in the track represents a Base/Enhancement Layer

I'm curious why you chose these particular mappings.  A couple other models you might consider:

* One track for video, another for audio, another for subtitles, etc.  Have your application synchronize the group numbers across these tracks such that group=N represents roughly the same point in time across tracks.
* For SVC video, either use a different _subgroup_ for each layer or use a different track for each layer, but with coordinated object IDs.

The temporal nature of groups was the subject of much debate at the last interim.  In general the protocol operates best when group IDs increment with time for a particular track.  The working group does not forbid non-temporal groups, but we expect the use cases for those to be more on the fringe than mainstream.

> concrete vs ethereal

I think I see where you are going, but in my implementation at least, this is more an implicit concept (every object might exist until either you receive it, or you learn (via FETCH) that it doesn't exist.

> Why to use this stateful model over the Request-Response model which has popularized by protocols such as HLS and DASH?
> Answer: Low Latency

100%

> Subscribe messages are not exhaustive

You are describing problems of track discovery here.  MoQT tries to offer some discovery mechanisms, and they continue to evolve.  Note that discovery can also be handled out-of-band, and SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES can be effective to discover tracks if you given them sufficiently unique namespaces, see also #766. Further, there was a proposal during Monday's session for how to issue a "wildcard subscribe" which is similar to what you suggest.  The feedback in the room was  somewhat mixed, but the proponents plan to write a PR in the coming weeks.

> One solution we have is a client side abort of the data stream if it starts sending packets very late in the 250ms window.

Have you looked into the DELIVERY_TIMEOUT features of MoQT and are they able to help address this?

> we need to send a subscribe update to stop the streaming of enhancement layers until we are certain that base layer objects can be streamed consistently within the 250ms window.

In MoQT, you cannot unsubscribe from a group or a subgroup, only a track.  If delivery timeout is not viable, I suggest trying the multi-track approach.  I wonder if the new "forward" flag in subscribe could help as well in that case #743.

> We do this because otherwise the publisher would be attempting to send G1-O20 while the subscriber is still receiving G0-O1, that is we need some application enforced synchronization between base layers and enhancement layers

#475 describes a similar synchronization problem, I think, though I believe the intention is to use a combination of priority, delivery timeouts to get "close enough"

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> One track for video, another for audio, another for subtitles, etc. Have your application synchronize the group numbers across these tracks such that group=N represents roughly the same point in time across tracks.

Yes, this approach is something I agree with. The drawback to it as pointed out in the "Subscribe messages are not exhaustive" section is that it requires pattern matching based subscribe messages or multiple subscribe messages to be sent which I was trying to avoid in my implementation.

> For SVC video, either use a different subgroup for each layer or use a different track for each layer, but with coordinated object IDs.

Different tracks is makes sense, and would be great if pattern matching based subscription would be introduced. Is there any discussion in the mailing list / github where pattern matching has been debated upon?

---

As for using a different subgroup for each layer; in my implementation, subgroups are not part of the object hierarchy and **only serve as hints** as to which objects can be sent on the same stream and which objects should not be.

Example:
Group 0 has 100 objects with objects ids ranging from [0, 100), contiguous ranges of objects are tagged with a subgroup id which do not serve any purpose in identifying the object within the hierarchy but only as a way of clustering them together

- [0, 25) -> Subgroup 0
- [25, 50) -> Subgroup 1
- [50, 100) -> Subgroup 2


In case of a live stream, we create couple group (representing number of layers) with `UINT62_MAX` number (ethereal) objects because we have no idea how many objects are going to be published.

I believe, what you are suggesting is that each 250ms chunk is one group, and each layer of the 250ms chunk is one subgroup; have UINT62_MAX number of groups to represent all the chunks and couple subgroups per group to represent the layers.

**Let us say the user wants to throttle the the layers they receive (despite having very good network conditions).**
I do not see how the user can subscribe only to certain subgroups in a group

As elaborated previously, subgroups are not part of my object hierarchy so the subscribe message can not be modified to include subgroup id. Personally, I do not like the idea of bringing subgroups into the object hierarchy; there are going to be use cases for a deeper and deeper hierarchy and we can't keep prefixing `sub-` everywhere. Variable length track namespaces is a sufficient solution in my humble opinion.

Each layer in a track is a much better solution to the problem, except for the possible initial delay introduced due to track discovery.

A very naive suggestion I have for avoiding track discovery is to make the Track Name field optional, if it does not exist, you are requesting for all tracks within the namespace. Which is pretty much in the lines of pattern matching based subscriptions.

```
SUBSCRIBE Message {
  Type (i) = 0x3,
  Length (i),
  Subscribe ID (i),
  Track Alias (i),
  Track Namespace (tuple),
  Track Name Length (i),
  [ Track Name (..) ],            // <-- Change, Track Name does not exist if Track Name Length is 0
  Subscriber Priority (8),
  Group Order (8),
  Filter Type (i),
  [StartGroup (i),              
   StartObject (i)],
  [EndGroup (i),                 
  EndObject (i)],
  Number of Parameters (i),
  Subscribe Parameters (..) ...
}
```
---

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> Have you looked into the DELIVERY_TIMEOUT features of MoQT and are they able to help address this?

I don't think delivery timeout is the solution I am looking for, it has the same problem I had mentioned

> If an object in a subgroup exceeds the delivery timeout, the publisher MUST reset the underlying transport stream

Excerpt from [v10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html) of the draft

Let us say a some subgroups keep being reset every time they are attempted to be sent because the delivery timeout guarantee can not be fulfilled, these packets are effectively discarded by the client and are only hogging up resources on the publisher side and the network.

Currently, my implementation uses the arrival of a new set of objects in the base/enhancement layers as the "event" to abort the send of subgroups currently in transit, the delivery timeout is a replacement to it that is, every 250ms the data streams will be reset serving the subscription will be reset. 

This approach can also do away with the `MUST_SEND` flag proposed as base layer objects will not have a delivery timeout parameter in their subscription

One apprehension I have on the top of my head about this approach is the overhead timer infrastructure required to manage the delivery timeouts. This is the reason we used the "event" to abort the send to be the arrival of a new set of objects instead of a timer event.

Correct me if I am wrong in overestimating the weight of managing multiple independent timeouts.

Consider the scenario where we want to be maintain a 20ms accuracy for the delivery timeouts, that is we abort the stream no later than 20ms after the timeout has triggered.

In that case, every 20ms you have this stop the world event where your server starts aborting all the streams which have timed out, even if it makes no logical sense to abort those streams.

We call this as stop the world because the underlying QUIC transport is busy processing all the aborts, which can be many in case of a server meant specifically for live streaming.

If the subscriber has requested that latest objects of a group/track be delivered, I believe we can deduce that they once a newer object is available; the send of the current object should be aborted (unless it is qualified with the `MUST_SEND` flag)

There still are going to be interrupts associated with the publisher receiving the objects, but none associate with timer events.

I am not against the idea of delivery timeouts, I simply believe there might be a more light weight (and scalable) solution

The reason I am in favour of the client aborting the stream is because the client would not need to manage multiple such timeouts. I have not fully thought of this from the relay perspective, but I would assume relays would make sure all their subscriptions/fetches are `MUST_SEND` qualified.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  Is there any discussion in the mailing list / github where pattern matching has been debated upon?

#615 - I recommend reviewing the slides and possibly video from Monday's MoQ session also as this was presented and discussed.

> I do not see how the user can subscribe only to certain subgroups in a group

That is currently true, and one of the reasons why you might want track-per-layer instead of subgroup per layer.  It's unclear how #441 will be resolved but it could be an option.

> A very naive suggestion I have for avoiding track discovery is to make the Track Name field optional, if it does not exist, you are requesting for all tracks within the namespace.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

> Let us say a some subgroups keep being reset every time they are attempted to be sent because the delivery timeout guarantee can not be fulfilled, these packets are effectively discarded by the client and are only hogging up resources on the publisher side and the network.

The delivery timeout is supposed to be applied by the publisher, not the subscriber, to prevent using bandwidth for stale data.  Generally, the timeout is meant to help with temporary problems rather than persistent ones (eg after a few datagrams / subgroups are discarded, congestion should ease, or the subscriber should ask for less data).

> Currently, my implementation uses the arrival of a new set of objects in the base/enhancement layers as the "event" to abort the send of subgroups currently in transit

@vasilvv proposed something similar during the hybrid interim in Denver - that is DELIVERY_TIMEOUT would not have a significant effect unless newer data is available to send.

> Correct me if I am wrong in overestimating the weight of managing multiple independent timeouts.

moxygen uses a construct called a [Hashed Hierarchical Wheel Timer](https://github.com/facebook/folly/blob/main/folly/io/async/HHWheelTimer.h) to manage many concurrent timeouts in an efficient way so I'm not overly concerned, though we have not implemented delivery timeout yet.

> MUST_SEND

I like the concept of a subscription that is fully rather than partially reliable, and draft-08 [introduced text](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/blob/main/draft-ietf-moq-transport.md?plain=1#L1142-L1146) that for subscriptions with no DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, the publisher/relay cannot reset streams within the subscription.  Instead it delivers everything, but if the client lags too far behind, the subscription is terminated.  There was an objection (#715) and the working group needs to discuss this more.

issues.title: Object Extension Types should not rob the bottom bit for even/odd games
issues.author: mzanaty
issues.body:
The current design robs the least significant bit of the object extension type to signal whether the following varint is the value or a length followed by the value. The goal is wire efficiency to avoid the extra byte of length for a simple extension. However, this actually harms wire efficiency since it reduces the efficient code point space from 64 (0-63 all) to 32 (0-62 even) possible small extensions. If an extension requires a length because it can't fit in the largest varint, that means it is over 8 bytes, hence it should not be a candidate to use the small space for small extensions.

If folks agree, I will create a PR to remove the even/odd shenanigans, and define all extension types 0-63 as varint values for small extensions, and all extension types 64-maxvarint as followed by varint length followed by value for larger extensions.

But I agree if #549 lands any changes, that would impact the range we reserve here. To be clear, I want to drop the odd/even design no matter what #549 does.

issues.title: Correlation of control messages
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
So the subscribe and fetch message control messages are all correlated using subscription ID. However, the ANNOUNCE and SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE related are correlated based on track name space. To me this indicates that we might end up with uncertainties about messages. If an endpoint would send two messages before they receive the response message there could be uncertainty to which message the response belongs to. I think there are hidden assumptions here, maybe based on in-order delivery, but are we certain that all implementation may not have different processing. For example receiving a SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES request, forward that upstream before responding, and then getting a second one with an error in, then the response to the error one could be delivered first.

I also get the impression that forcing strict order between request and responses will delay control messages unnecessary. 

So my ask wouldn't a request ID be a clearer handling of this, or do other believe using  track name space is sufficient robust?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: TRACK_STATUS has the same issue as ANNOUNCE FYI

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: I think this applies to all messages that aren't SUBSCRIBE or FETC.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: We could also put these on their own streams, as we've discussed before, particularly for FETCH.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
As noted, SUBSCRIBE and FETCH have ids to correlate already.  That leaves

ANNOUNCE family
SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES family
TRACK_STATUS family

It's easy enough to add a control message identifier to correlate, say, ANNOUNCE_OK with the ANNOUNCE.  I don't think we should allow more than one concurrent announcement per namespace though.  eg:

P->S: ANNOUNCE x
S->P: ANNOUNCE_OK x
P->S: ANNOUNCE x  // this replaces/updates the first announce.

In other words UNANNOUNCE and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL would still use namespace rather than an ID.

The same should be true for SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES, eg: UNSUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES only references the namespace.

issues.title: Timeout behavior for publisher with no subscribers
issues.author: DanielFay22
issues.body:
In the scenario where a publisher joins a relay and announces one or more tracks, but there are no subscribers for those tracks, the relay will likely not issue its own subscribe to the original publisher. In this case, the publisher cannot send objects to the relay until someone comes along to subscribe, and if no one comes within the publishers or the relays idle timeout window then the connection will be closed.

In moxygen we handle this issue by having the server repeatedly announce/unannounce a track called “ping”, however this seems like an inefficient way to accomplish this heartbeat type of connection (and since “ping” is not actually a reserved track its entirely possible someone else could announce and/or subscribe to it, causing churn at the relay). Do we need some kind of keep-alive type message, which would have the same effect without requiring the relay to actually process the announce/unannounce?

With the introduction of publish, I believe a publisher could initiate the connection to the relay and solve this issue (dependent on how that ends up being defined), so this may be a moot point.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I hope this will be solved with Publish, and I agree that the current approaches, like your "ping" approach are quite awkward.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
In moxygen we're planning to add the keep-alives at the QUIC layer, to defeat the idle timeouts and get rid of ping. 

Regarding PUBLISH: I think we should incorporate the `forward` flag, and a PUBLISH with forward=0 won't send any objects until a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, which will have the same problem.  I suppose PUBLISH with forward=0 is isomorphic to ANNOUNCE with a full track name.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I don't think publish solves the timeout problem - the publisher -> relay connection can still go idle and get closed.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm inclined to say this is implementation specific.  There are mechanism at the transport layer (eg: QUIC ping) or even MoQT (useless control messages, eventually grease) that will keep the underlying connection alive.  Publisher-clients that get dropped by a relay for lack of activity need to handle reconnecting and/or keep-alives.  Do we need editorial text for this?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Let's write some editorial text

issues.title: Clarify behavior for pending subscribes
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
there are use-cases where relays might receive subscribes before publisher announcing a track. This is common on meeting scenarios where users join the meeting  before broadcast starts or host joins in.

Subscribing clients can apply some logic of retries to see if one the the subscription works. However, It would be nice to allow relays to pend on subscribes and possibly timeout and send subscribe error.  This can be achieved with SubscribeOk as defined today which includes expiry timeout.

Proposal here is to clarify and allow this behavior in relays.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> This can be achieved with SubscribeOk as defined today which includes expiry timeout.

Can you explain this interaction a bit more?

Are you looking for something like:

SUBSCRIBE track=t, wait up to x milliseconds for ANNOUNCE before returning SUBSCRIBE_ERROR?

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> > This can be achieved with SubscribeOk as defined today which includes expiry timeout.
> 
> Can you explain this interaction a bit more?
> 
> Are you looking for something like:
> 
> SUBSCRIBE track=t, wait up to x milliseconds for ANNOUNCE before returning SUBSCRIBE_ERROR?


I was thinking more like, 
S -> R: Subscribe
R -> S: Subscribe Ok ( expires = 30s)
...
No Announce Received 
R -> S: Subscribe End ( ErrorCode = XYZ)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> R -> S: Subscribe Ok ( expires = 30s)

Is this what the `expires` field is for?  I thought it meant something completely different.

Sending the SUBSCRIBE_OK before the subscription exists is dicey.  There are fields in the message that cannot be populated, like Group Order, Largest and parameters.

There's also this:

> The relay will have to send an upstream SUBSCRIBE and/or FETCH if it does not have all the objects in the FETCH, or is not currently subscribed to the full requested range. In this case, it SHOULD withhold sending its own SUBSCRIBE_OK until receiving one from upstream.

1) this can be accomplished today without pending subscribes:

When a client joins, it sends

ANNOUNCE namespace/me/mytrack
SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES namespace

Then it will SUBSCRIBE in response to ANNOUNCEs it receives.

2) this may all be changing if we are going the PUBLISH route, so it might be best to park this issue and revisit once that is sorted.

3) If we still require this feature in the publish universe, I'd want the subscriber to opt in via a parameter, and would prefer we add a SUBSCRIBE_PENDING intermediate status message.  So the flow would be:

S->R: SUBSCRIBE track=t, {waitUpTo=30s}
R->S: SUBSCRIBE_PENDING

later either
R->S: SUBSCRIBE_OK
or
R->S: SUBSCRIBE_ERROR

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Parking this pending the outcome of PUBLISH / Wildcard Subscribe, which may address the underlying use case.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - plan is to recommend using PUBLISH + SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES to handle "pending subscribe" behavior.  Relays will have to wait for SUBSCRIBE_OK upstream before sending SUBSCRIBE_OK. No special pending handling is necessary.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Publish has landed.  Draft now reads:

> The relay MUST have an established upstream subscription before sending SUBSCRIBE_OK in response to a downstream SUBSCRIBE.

Closing for now but please reopen if we missed something.

issues.title: Clarify restrictions on object IDs
issues.author: DanielFay22
issues.body:
In [section 9.1.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-10.html#name-canonical-object-fields), objects IDs are defined as:

> The order of the object within the group. The IDs starts at 0, increasing sequentially for each object within the group.

From discussion in slack and #772 it seems people are treating it as more relaxed than this, something more along the lines of IDs increase over time, but are not required to either start at 0 or be sequential, so we should clarify in the text (and probably move this definition to the object model section as well).

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body: Group ID has the same issue and needs to be clarified, especially how joining fetch offset will work when groups are not sequentially incrementing by 1 from the previous. For example, group could increment by time, where the start of the next group is the current time in microseconds. In this case, current group - previous group will likely not be 1.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Oops this shouldn't have been closed by moving the sentence to the model section.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> especially how joining fetch offset will work when groups are not sequentially incrementing by 1 from the previous. For example, group could increment by time, where the start of the next group is the current time in microseconds. In this case, current group - previous group will likely not be 1.

See: #358 for group discussion.  There's no efficient way for a relay to know what the "previous group" is if the application has arbitrary gaps between groups.  Applications need to understand their group structure and set the Previous Group Offset to something sensible for Fetch, or use Absolute Joining Fetch.  All the relay can do is subtract the offset from the current group.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> > especially how joining fetch offset will work when groups are not sequentially incrementing by 1 from the previous. For example, group could increment by time, where the start of the next group is the current time in microseconds. In this case, current group - previous group will likely not be 1.
> 
> See: [#358](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/358) for group discussion. There's no efficient way for a relay to know what the "previous group" is if the application has arbitrary gaps between groups. Applications need to understand their group structure and set the Previous Group Offset to something sensible for Fetch, or use Absolute Joining Fetch. All the relay can do is subtract the offset from the current group.

+1 on applications being aware of group structure and setting the appropriate group offset.  This was discussed extensively and my preference would be to keep it that way.

issues.title: Max_cache_duration is an confusing name for things that don't cache
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
the idea behind "max_cache_duration" was a publisher picked time for object's lifetime, more in the lines of TTL for an object. 

I wonder if we should instead call it as Object_TTL instead ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The current definition of MAX_CACHE_DURATION seems to intersect with DELIVERY_TIMEOUT.  In my head (which is not what's in the draft) is MAX_CACHE_DURATION is something that only impacts a FETCH cache, and is precisely what's on the tin - the maximum amount of time to keep an object in a FETCH cache.

Does that definition work better than the current one, which doesn't even mention caching?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: 891 clarified the meaning rather than changing the name.  Feel free to reopen this if you still want a name change, or open a new issue if there's some more fundamental problem with MAX_CACHE_DURATION.

issues.title: Why are Control Messages TLV if they can't be ignored?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
The reason to use a TLV format is that Messages can be skipped if they aren't known to the receiver.  But it seems like we don't want to skip over control messages, at least for all the existing messages.  Given that, TV seems to make more sense.

This also makes #709 obvious.

Inspired by #830

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: We had TV and moved to TLV so we didn't need trial parsing of control messages.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I think the WG came to consensus after much discussion on what Alan said above.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Closing this one since we did debate it and I don't think we should reopen it #474.  We want implementations to negotiate extension frames (eg: using SETUP, or new versions) rather than silently ignore them, but we also don't want to trial parse control messages or implement progressive parsing state machines for every message.

issues.title: Use consistent terminology for the application
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: We define "streaming formats" in Section 1 and then never use those.  We probably should use something like "application" and make sure we are consistent throughout the draft.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I added a definition of application and replaced one usage of Streaming Format.  I think it's ok to mention streaming formats in the intro, since that is part of the overall picture of how we expect MoQT to work.  However, I think it's better to have "the application" be the actor MoQ vs Streaming Format

issues.title: Elaborate on the role of the original publisher
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: Section 1 defines "original publisher" and "end subscriber", but it doesn't really explain what they are and what properties we expect from them.  Notably, we to some extent assume that the original publisher is unique (or at least is able to coordinate itself to appear as such, otherwise you will end up publishing conflicting objects).

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: In Section 2.1 we say original publisher is "solely responsible for the content of the object payload", but I am not sure what that actually means.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: FWIW ... I don't read that to mean much other than things other than the original publisher can not change the object payload.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
In Toronto:

Parking in hopes that Mo's proposal around SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE filters allows us to make it clear that uncoordinated original publishers are not designed to be well supported in MoQ.

issues.title: ALPN versioning
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> The ALPN value [[RFC7301](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#RFC7301)] used by the protocol is moq-00.

I assume this is meant to be `moq-NN`, where `NN` is the version of the draft?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See #499, which adds that text.  We were holding it waiting for WebTransport to actually support this feature.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I was confused with too. Perhaps it might be worth writing what text in the draft will say then adding a note that says until blah blah, implementations should use moq-00.

issues.title: Can an implementation close a session on Data Stream Timeout?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> Data Stream Timeout: The session was closed because the peer took too long to send data expected on an open Data Stream [Section 9](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#data-streams). This includes fields of a stream header or an object header within a data stream. If an endpoint times out waiting for a new object header on an open subgroup stream, it MAY send a STOP_SENDING on that stream, terminate the subscription, or close the session with an error.

I think it's extremely odd for this to cause a fatal connection error?  Especially given that this is can easily occur naturally with due to the publisher being flow control blocked.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: In HTTP/3 I think there's language that basically says any stream error can be elevated to a session error by an implementation if it feels like it.  Maybe we should add a comment to that effect, but remove the mention of session error here.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
From RFC 9114:

> An endpoint MAY choose to treat a stream error as a connection error under certain circumstances, closing the entire connection in response to a condition on a single stream. Implementations need to consider the impact on outstanding requests before making this choice.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Yes. IMO Implementations have the right to close anything, at any time, for any reason. The H3 text is pretty decent at articulating that.

issues.title: Do we need "Unauthorized" session error code?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> Unauthorized: The endpoint breached an agreement, which MAY have been pre-negotiated by the application.

I do not understand what this error code does, nor what the normative MAY is supposed to imply here.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm tempted to remove this session error code, now that each message has its own Unauthorized code.  Unless we think we will include an auth parameter in CLIENT_SETUP. 

Maybe related to #721 

CC: Auth guru @wilaw

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - see #721 - you send Unauthorized if your application requires a token to establish a connection and the endpoint did not present valid auth.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm going to fold this into #721

issues.title: ANNOUNCE is not routing
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> An ANNOUNCE indicates to the subscriber where to route a SUBSCRIBE or FETCH for that namespace.

I think we should not use the word "route" anywhere, since MoQT does not do any routing.  An ANNOUNCE indicates that the sender has tracks for the specified namespace available; what the peer does with it is application-specific, unless the recipient is a relay.

issues.title: Namespace Discovery section needs editing
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Going point by point:

- The way it uses terms "subscriber" and "publisher" is extremely confusing.  In MoQT, publisher sends objects, and subscriber receives them, but nothing in this section is about exchanging MoQT objects.
- The section talks about publishers being "authoritative", but we never define that term.
- It mentions "upload or chat applications" (I have no idea what those are, especially the first one).
- "If it has accepted an ANNOUNCE with a namespace that exactly matches the namespace for that track, it SHOULD only request it from the senders of those ANNOUNCE messages."  I re-read this twice, and I am still not sure what this requirement does, or why do we have it.
- The section probably needs more text about how the workflow looks from the publisher side (especially the preamble).

issues.title: SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES name is confusing
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We define SUBSCRIBE as something that only lets you get objects in the future, but SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES requests both current, and the future subscriptions.

(is doing this actually a good idea?)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES requests both current, and the future subscriptions.

current and future ANNOUNCEs, do you want to call it SUBSCRIBE_AND_JOINING_FETCH_ANNOUNCES?

> (is doing this actually a good idea?)

See also #767 

It has to work this way in order to do what we want it to do -- see how moq-chat uses this message https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-frindell-moq-chat-00.html#section-3.4.  Can you elaborate why you are concerned?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Well we changed it back to SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.  Are we willing to live with the awkwardness that SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE solicits existing ANNOUNCE/PUBLISH and not just future ones like SUBSCRIBE?

I recommend we close with no action.  @vasilvv ?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: SGTM

issues.title: ANNOUNCE via SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES vs ANNOUNCE by itself
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: I feel like we should distinguish those two.  If I'm a publisher and I send an ANNOUNCE, I should get an OK or ERROR in response.  If I am a client who asks relay to SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES, I should not have to OK/ERROR everything relay sends to me.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
Thinking more about it, if I want to SUBSCRIBE to a track, the SUBSCRIBE_OK from the relay probably should not be head-of-line blocked by notifications of tracks existing that are in front of it.

Also, since implementations always read control messages proactively, this means that incoming announces are effectively not flow controlled.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES now forwards PUBLISH also -- those clearly need OK/ERROR.  Should ANNOUNCE be different?

> Thinking more about it, if I want to SUBSCRIBE to a track, the SUBSCRIBE_OK from the relay probably should not be head-of-line blocked by notifications of tracks existing that are in front of it.

Are you suggesting we change our control-stream model so control messages do not HoL block?  This would be a fairly fundamental change at this point.

> Also, since implementations always read control messages proactively, this means that incoming announces are effectively not flow controlled.

All Control Messages that create state now require Request ID, which is flow controlled by the receiver, so I think we're good there.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @kixelated solved this with `ANNOUNCE_INIT` that conveys current state vs ANNOUNCE for new.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body: IMO every ANNOUNCE should have a corresponding SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES. Unsolicited ANNOUNCE is weird, how do you know the peer even wants them?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> IMO every ANNOUNCE should have a corresponding SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES. Unsolicited ANNOUNCE is weird, how do you know the peer even wants them?

I agree a Relay should never send unsolicited ANNOUNCE (PUBLISH_NAMESPACE).  A relay _client_ **can** send unsolicited PUBLISH_NAMESPACE to the relay to advertise its ability serve tracks under that namespace.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: After re-reading this, I do think ANNOUNCE by itself is different from one in response to SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES, including Victor's point about how those in response to SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES shouldn't need OK/ERROR or CANCEL.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in 10/20 virtual interim:

Group would like to see a PR that divides the current responsibilities of SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE into two different operations:

1) wildcard subscribe

The publisher sends PUBLISH messages to establish subscriptions under the namespace, but doesn't send any PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages.  The filter design team's "top N" filter would apply here.

2) discovery

The publisher sends the names of available nested namespaces and tracks, and deltas to this set.  The response is not on the control stream.  The response entries do not consume request IDs and do not solicit an OK/ERROR response.

We discussed unsolicited PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (announce) and agreed that is still a valid use case, largely for client publisher -> relay where the client has many or unenumerable tracks.

issues.title: Improve discussion of caching
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We mention caching multiple times, but never elaborate how it works, and in what context.  We should probably have a dedicated section for that.

From my understanding, SUBSCRIBE and FETCH can both cache-fill, but only FETCH uses cache.  Is that correct?

We assert that once in the cache, the object never changes, but we also talk about how relays MAY "update the cache", which does not appear to be consistent with immutability.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> SUBSCRIBE and FETCH can both cache-fill, but only FETCH uses cache. Is that correct?

This is my interpretation.

> MAY "update the cache", which does not appear to be consistent with immutability.

I created a caching section that talks about what can be updated in #826 .

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> > SUBSCRIBE and FETCH can both cache-fill, but only FETCH uses cache. Is that correct?
> 
> This is my interpretation.

If, among multiple concurrent SUBSCRIBEs, one of them is far behind live, then the Relay can use cached Objects to serve the late SUBSCRIBE. 

For SUBSCRIBE at Relay side, I see two designs:
- either the Relay stores the Object it receives from Publisher in a memory until this Object has been sent to _all_ Subscribers (including the late ones). Let's call it a "Subscribe_memory". 
- or the Relay stores the Objects it receives from Publisher directly in the cache. It then serves all "late" Subscribers from the cache.

In the first case, the Relay needs to create two copies of the Object: one in the "Subscribe_memory" and one in the Cache for future FETCH. The second option may be quicker (it depends on the I/O of the cache vs I/O of the "Subscribe_memory").

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
In my implementation, all object payloads are refcounted so there's no difference between memory in the cache and memory queued for transmission, but I get that not all implementations are like that.

I'm trying to envision how to implement SUBSCRIBE as pulling from a cache - do you queue the group ID/object ID for transmission, and do a cache lookup when it's time to send it?  What happens if the cache has evicted that item?

issues.title: Can relays guarantee Object deduplication?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> The relay will drop duplicate objects received on both subscriptions.

We do say that relays are allowed to drop objects if they already have one in cache, but it is certainly not guaranteed that a relay will deduplicate objects, since the memory it uses to remember past objects is limited.

We should have text explicitly stating that if a publisher sends duplicate objects to the relay, there is non-determinism about how many exactly will be forwarded past the first one.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
Would something like this text work for you?

"Given a relays will not keep state about all the objects they have received in the past, there is guarantee that a relay will not forward and object it has previously forwarded."

issues.title: Do we need End of Group at the transport layer?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We define it, but we don't really use it anywhere.  I do remember writing code that relied on it heavily in the past, but apparently it is all gone now, so that makes me thing that the need of it has been overcome by events (especially the introduction of subgroups).

(it is certainly plausible that the application might want to know when a group ends, but if the transport does not need to know, the application should take care of that itself)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I have a use case is in #641.  It's also handy for caching - if you have an END_OF_GROUP marker, you don't need to go upstream for downstream FETCHes that cover objects larger than the END_OF_GROUP.  eg:  if you have G1, O0-10 and G2, O0 in cache, and you get a FETCH for G1/0 to G2/0, you have to go upstream to find out if there are any objects in G1 larger than 10.  If you had G1/11=END_OF_GROUP, you can serve it entirely from cache.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - yes we need this signal because it can save an upstream FETCH for origins.  However, the group would like a more compact way to express this (eg: it can either be a flag on an existing object, or a separate object)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: #1009 Tracks the compact encoding, closing this issue.

issues.title: Intermediaries that are not relays
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: We should have some discussions about intermediaries that are not relays and _do_ modify tracks (transmuxers, etc): we both need to acknowledge those exist, and give practical considerations as to how those should be done (e.g. what to do with the track names).

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I don't think there is anything to say about them other than they must meet all the rules of a publisher and subscriber. They will tend to subscribe to some tracks and publish some new tracks. What else would we say about them ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Maybe acknowledging their existence and clarifying that if they are changing track data they MUST change the track name, group ID or object ID also, because MoQT objects are immutable.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I added a definition of "intermediary" in #1107 but didn't add extra text explaining that something like a transmuxer needs to publish on new tracks. I didn't mark it as closing this issue in case folks still want some explanatory text.

issues.title: Should we remove Network Switchover guidance in favor of QUIC connection migration?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Draft says:

> This section describes behavior that a publisher MAY choose to implement to allow for a better users experience when switching between networks, such as WiFi to Cellular or vice versa.

This feels like a situation that is better suited for QUIC connection migration.  The latter paragraph discusses an endpoint that "does not have QUIC connection migration available", but it seems to me like this is the wrong direction -- the solution for the discussed problem is connection migration, and if the client has access to two network interfaces at the same time, it is more than capable of performing it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Presumably MoQT will have a TCP fallback at some point, and not all stacks have QUIC connection migration implemented and deployed (ours does not).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think this is editorial, since the algorithms described use MoQT features we plan to ship regardless, right?

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: QUIC connection migration would not work for the case where the wifi uses a relay in the wifi AP and the 5G uses a relay in 5G edge.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: Sure, but in that case, this is just a relay switchover?

issues.title: Original Publisher crashes
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We should add a discussion on how MoQT publishers should handle crashes.

If one runs a video conferencing website, it is tempting to have track naming scheme like (`example.com`, `my_videoconference`, `username`, `video`).  The problem is, if the client crashes and has to reconnect, it can no longer use that name, since it does not remember the state of the track at the publication point, so the track should have some unique random number (or maybe the client startup time or something) to distinguish those.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See your own previous issue where I left you a comment: #335.

issues.title: Does the Object Extension Header Type space need to be global?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
It seems like some extensions might apply to any kind of track (eg: relay tracing information, or timestamps), but other information might be specific to the format of the track (eg: moq-mi has Video metadata and Audio metadata).  It seems like we could get more use out of the 1 byte space if we reserved _some_ points for track-format-specific extensions, and allowed the same code point to have a context-dependent meaning.

The downside is that relays don't know the track format, so could never interpret or modify these values without out-of-band information.  That might be a good thing?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Stockholm - recommendation is to park this for now and be stingy with 1 byte space, revisit closer to WGLC.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Turns out this just bit moq-mi, as draft-02 had selected 0x0B as an extension code point that moqt took back in draft-14.  We will need to make it clear to applications how to safely select code points that won't be taken in future transport revs.  https://github.com/afrind/draft-cenzano-media-interop/pull/15

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Unparking for Boulder extensibility discussions

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I can see the benefits, but is there a proposed approach?  Object Extension Headers are not hop-by-hop, so we can't negotiate support for them.

Similar to the authenticated headers, one can imagine a meta-header that encapsulates all the moq-mi headers in a more compact form?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Similar to the authenticated headers, one can imagine a meta-header that encapsulates all the moq-mi headers in a more compact form?

This is viable.  Add one MOQT extension which is "application extensions" which contains k/v pairs with similar encoding as MOQT but the code points are entirely application defined.  The publisher and subscriber know what to do with these.

An alternative is to define a range of MOQT extension code points as "application range" (eg: #1268).  MOQT will never use these points.  A relay can log them, but not assign any semantic meaning to them, unless it understands the application through out of band means.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
We encode Extension Headers and Parameters with a delta-encoding, so there's minimal cost to giving an extension higher codepoints as long as the codepoints are close to each other (ie: within 128 codepoints).

Given this, I'd suggest we provide guidance to this effect and setup the IANA registry to reflect it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> so there's minimal cost to giving an extension higher codepoints as long as the codepoints are close to each other (ie: within 128 codepoints).

This is true for Track extensions but not Object extensions, where the "base" extension value could be repeated in every object.

issues.title: Are Groups really join points anymore / SUBSCRIBE start on group boundaries
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In 2.3 and elsewhere, it mentions that a Group is a join point.

It does make intuitive sense for a Group to be a join point, as starting at Object 0 gives you the key frame.

However, the protocol doesn't really elevate the group as an important join point anymore. LatestObject (and its potential descendants) don't care about Groups. AbsoluteStart, AbsoluteRange, and regular FETCH don't privilege Object 0 at all.

We're just left with Joining FETCH that uses groups as a join point.

What I'd propose is that AbsoluteStart and AbsoluteRange simply have a start group rather than a start group and object. Is there a use case for a SUBSCRIBE to a future group starting mid-group? It sounds nonsensical.

Alternately, we could change the text to make less sweeping claims about join points.

yes mid-group joins are totally fine and end applications that have joined and looses connection for a short bit can subscribe to latest obect and back fill couple of seconds of missed objects. For groups that run longer, having to pull in all the objects from the beginning of the group shall not work or is pretty wasteful.

Groups as the data model as sync points are still true and clients can depend on it to re-sync ( as we do in all IDR refreshes today)

1) If it's a group in the future, I have trouble imagining a use case for requesting mid-group. Can someone articulate one?

2) If it's a current or past group, the new filter semantics mean that only reordered objects (or objects with unordered groups) will be delivered. Again, I struggle to see why one would need to restrict this to nonzero object IDs.

issues.title: Flow Control and Priorities
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
The priority algorithm in 6.2 may be suboptimal given certain receiver flow control states. For example:

- Streams might have different flow control credit, allowing send on a lower priority stream but not a higher one. This is most likely to happen if a frame granting stream credit is lost, or if the available data in a subgroup exceeds the initial flow control credit.

- Connection flow control might shut down delivery over streams, but cannot limit sending of datagrams.

- There may be no stream creation credit for a high-priority stream, but we can keep delivering on the low-priority one.

If we actually want low-priority stuff to be blocked in this case, then the current language is fine. Otherwise, this has to be rewritten a bit. It may be easiest to update to the definition of schedulable object in 6.1, and then the rest would be unchanged.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> If we actually want low-priority stuff to be blocked in this case

This is the important question: if I have a high pri stream that's FC blocked and a low pri one that is not, do I send *nothing*?

I've also wondered if we need a moq specific level of flow control that is per subscription.  Per-stream is too fine and Per-connection is too coarse.

You essentially never want the sender to run out of stream credit, unless you can partition it per subscription.

issues.title: Difficult to limit resource consumption of a Subscription
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
For FETCH, flow control on the stream can limit the resource consumption.

For Subscribe, there's no limit to the number of Subgroups that a publisher can publish to simultaneously, which could allow one Track to consume a huge number of streams, potentially starving resources from other subscriptions.

A simple solution would be to add a Parameter to SUBSCRIBE that allows limiting the number of simultaneous unidirectional streams for the subscription.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> limiting the number of simultaneous unidirectional streams for the subscription

The problem is that the sender and receiver can have different views of this number, and definitions like this are subject to rapid-reset style attacks.  The "QUIC way" would be to have a "MAX_CUMULATIVE_SUBGROUPS" parameter and the subscriber needs to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE periodically to grant more.

We may need to take a step back and examine what we want to protect against.  What would happen if we recommended that MoQT implementations set the stream limit to infinity?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I suspect we are a potential major application of WebTransport. Would it make sense for the WG to formulate a list of feature requests for Webtrans?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
WebTransport does have stream limits. The WT_MAX_STREAMS capsule ([Section 5.6.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-12.html#name-limiting-the-number-of-stre)) establishes a limit on the
   number of streams within a WebTransport session. The client supports an initial limit (W3C spec recommends 100) which is then negotiated higher. The web application can give a hint as to how many streams it needs via the [anticipatedconcurrentincomingbidirectionalstreams](https://w3c.github.io/webtransport/#dom-webtransportoptions-anticipatedconcurrentincomingbidirectionalstreams) method. Yup, that's the worlds longest method name :)

comments.body:
> > limiting the number of simultaneous unidirectional streams for the subscription
> 
> The problem is that the sender and receiver can have different views of this number, and definitions like this are subject to rapid-reset style attacks. The "QUIC way" would be to have a "MAX_CUMULATIVE_SUBGROUPS" parameter and the subscriber needs to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE periodically to grant more.

Agreed, that suggestion is racy, but the MAX_CUMULATIVE_SUBGROUPS approach is very chatty, so?

> 
> We may need to take a step back and examine what we want to protect against. What would happen if we recommended that MoQT implementations set the stream limit to infinity?

Allowing an infinite number of Streams allows the peer to consume an unlimited amount of memory by opening a huge number of streams and not closing them.  Sending data that isn't at offset 0 would probably be even more costly for most implementations, and it wouldn't be deliverable to the application.  Implementations could have somewhat arbitrary limits that they use to close Subscriptions or Sessions they believe to be malicious, but it'd be nice if it wasn't a heuristic.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
It may be sufficient to just specify a hard limit on the maximum number of Subgroups in MOQT, as the MOQT means to control the number of streams. Although there is no hard constraint on how Objects are assigned to to Subgroups, the only example in the draft is assigning each temporal sublayer in a temporal scalable bitstream to a Subgroup, which does make a lot of sense. Video coding standards H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, and H.266/VVC use 3 bits for the temporal_id (and HEVC and VVC make it temporal_id_plus1) allow up to 8 or 7 temporal sublayers. Even considering bitstreams with multiple full layers (e.g., of different resolutions or different views) and each full layer is temporally scalable, specifying a hard limit on the maximum number of Subgroups in MOQT to be something like 64 or 128 is good enough. Such a hard limit is also aligned with hard limit of up to 256 different priority values (considering that it is possible for different tracks to have different priorities).

Therefore, as a strawman, and food for thought, it is suggested to specify, in MOQT, a hard limit on the maximum number of Subgroups in a Group to be 128.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Some uses of MOQT may use a subgroup/stream per object, so I don't know that 128 will be sufficiently large.

Even if we limit the number of subgroups per group, the number of groups isn't limited, so the number of streams is still relatively unbounded.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> Some uses of MOQT may use a subgroup/stream per object, so I don't know that 128 will be sufficiently large.
> 

Could you give an example of such use? I am trying to understand whether there is really a practical case for that use to make sense.

> Even if we limit the number of subgroups per group, the number of groups isn't limited, so the number of streams is still relatively unbounded.

Group ID increases with media time. If a stream is used for a subgroup of a group, then typically when the next group is being received and processed, the previous group has already been processed and the streams are done. They can be some rare occasions wherein two or even three continuous groups might be processed at the same time , but those are really rare.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
We previously discussed _merging_ priority and subgroup ID, and one reason we decided against it is it would either require expanding priority to larger than its current 8 bits or restricting the number of subgroups per group to 256.

MoQT is also for non-media use cases -- eg logs, metrics, etc and different types of cameras, eg: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.15003v1.  I don't think we want to be overly prescriptive in the MOQT layer unless we think we derive a real benefit. Strictly limiting the number of subgroups per group does not limit the number of subgroups a publisher can open concurrently for a subscription, even if in practice it would be rare.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I realized that Flow Control in MoQT could mean something different from HTTP when reading #1316 again.

If there was a way (ie: a 'PauseAt' param) for the subscriber to keep bumping out the largest Group to be delivered, and when the publisher hits that PauseAtGroup, it pauses for some period of time (15s or 30s) in the expectation the subscriber may want to unpause to get more Groups.

This could in theory apply to the past (ie: SUBSCRIBE in the past). By the time flow control is a problem for Subscriptions as they stand today, the Objects causing the problem are inherently in the past anyway, so it's more a matter of where you start.

I was thinking Group Granularity, but it could be (MaxNumSubgroups, GroupID) if we think subgroups granularity flow control is useful for those Object per stream Tracks?  In the most conservative case, you could grant flow control one Subgroup at once, which approximates an in-order stream of bytes.

The nice part about this is it works in the domain that MoQT does, with Group ID and Object ID increasing over time.

So I'm not sure how else to deal with that than allow one to specify a Max Subgroup ID as well.  It's not particularly difficult to add and there could be some use cases where it's valuable.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I also tried to design approaches that used stream or byte limits. All would greatly benefit from moving Subscriptions to their own Bidi control stream (ie: #1389).

All approaches below use a MAX_SUB_STREAMS and/or MAX_SUB_BYTES Parameter sent by the Subscriber in SUBSCRIBE or PUBLISH_OK to set initial limits and then increase those limits in REQUEST_UPDATE.

The **Initial** design I came up with was:

For **stream limits** to work, I believe you need the RESET_STREAM_AT feature to ensure the peer receives at least the header.

For **byte limits** to work, I believe you also need to expose the final offset from QUIC's RESET_STREAM (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-19.4), which is not exposed by WebTransport or likely most other applications.

But we don't require support of RESET_STREAM_AT (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/blob/main/draft-ietf-moq-transport.md#session-establishment-session-establishment) today.

An **alternate** and probably better approach I considered that does not rely on RESET_STREAM_AT is to have the Publisher say "I sent you X bytes for Subgroup S in Group G and then RESET it".  It's impractical to expose the QUIC Stream ID, because WebTransport and some QUIC implementations don't expose it, but we can use Group ID and Subgroup ID.  For Streams that aren't RESET, no extra metadata would be required.


All of these have a potential issue that you can consume the limits with future data and then the application might not want to use that data, and you end up deadlocked.  Though possibly that can be avoided with some cautionary text about not using up the last streams or bytes to send Objects that are unlikely to be consumed immediately?

I am favoring the approach I wrote up in #1404 but I can write up one of these in a PR if people think they'd be a lot better?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
One other approach I've considered is limiting the number of Streams a Publisher can open per Group.

For example, setting it to 1 would cause the Publisher to deliver all Subgroups over a single stream, which would be relatively easy to flow control, but wouldn't introduce the larger-scale HoL blocking problems FETCH has.

This would require a change to allow sending multiple Subgroups on a single QUIC Stream when needed by this feature or potentially because the Publisher is very low on available unidirectional Streams, but that seems like a simple framing change.

comments.body:
> One other approach I've considered is limiting the number of Streams a Publisher can open per Group.

>

I guess so?  But it seems relatively easy, so I wanted to list it as a potential option.  I wrote up the option I prefer.

issues.title: Section 7 Minor Issues
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 7.1:
- The first paragraph doesn't mention FETCH, and should.

- "it SHOULD withhold its own SUBSCRIBE_OK until receiving one from upstream."  This really ought to be a MUST. First of all, if there is no upstream SUBSCRIBE, sending SUBSCRIBE_OK immediately is irresponsible. If there is a partial upstream SUBSCRIBE, behavior when the upstream sends SUBSCRIBE_ERROR is undefined. We could say SHOULD in this very narrow edge case, but would have to define that behavior. Better to just say MUST.

- "dependent on the congestion response". What does this mean? I think it means "send it as fast as congestion & flow control allow" but that is a condition on literally all things sent in the protocol.

- Re: Cache poisoning. Add an informative reference to RFC 9111?

Sec 7.2
- This section doesn't mention FETCH at all, and should

- The namespace=foobar example is not very helpful, because it doesn't illustrate a non-exact match.

- Mention of track_alias needs to be updated?

- "Relays MUST forward objects to matching subscribers in accordance to each subscription's priority, group order, and delivery timeout". s/in accordance to/in accordance with. Also, shouldn't this be SHOULD? All that stuff is best effort, no? In Sec 7.3 it says relays SHOULD respect priority, so one of these has to change.

- "If an upstream session is closed due to an unknown or invalid control message or Object, the relay MUST NOT continue to propagate that message or Object downstream, because it would enable a single session to close unrelated sessions." This only applies if there are multiple upstreams.

Sec 7.3
- "To mitigate this, a relay MAY read and write stream data out of order subject to flow control limits. See section 2.2 in [[QUIC](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#QUIC)]." What does this mean? It seems to conflict with a lot the assumptions that underlie the FIN/RESET strategy

Relay has 1 upstream subscription for a track with 100 downstream sessions subscribed
Upstream publisher commits a session-level error of some kind, resulting in upstream session closure

The goal is to not repeat the session-level error on all 100 downstream sessions (though probably a subscription-level error needs to be sent).

See section 2.2 in [[QUIC](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#QUIC)]." What does this mean? issues.title: What if the subscriber needs an immediate SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
I cannot send SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE for a LatestObject subscription if I haven't received SUBSCRIBE_OK because I don't know what to put in the Start field to avoid a protocol error. It's possible to immediately send UNSUBSCRIBE and then another SUBSCRIBE if there are enough IDs, I suppose.

The most likely reason is a sudden change in priority. Waiting an RTT for this seems wrong, especially if the message goes all the way back to the original publisher.

Relatedly, this is super-pedantic, but it is legal to send a SUBSCRIBE with AbsoluteRange and EndGroup 2^62-1, even though it is equivalent to AbsoluteStart with no end. It is impossible to update other properties of this subscription without accidentally shortening it, unless the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE EndGroup field is zero. Code should be smart enough to detect the case and not report it as a widening of the window.

There are many spelling changes that can fix this, but one clean way would be to make Start and EndGroup be diff encoded. This also eliminates most error cases -- no way to expand the window.

I'm also fine with diff encoding. What's positive about that is it makes it impossible to express widening of the window.

issues.title: remove RESET_STREAM_AT
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body:
The RESET_STREAM_AT add considerable more stuff and it is not clear how it will help in deployments. I would like to remove it from the draft for now until we can see a concrete use case for adding it. 

None of the NPU vendors I am aware of have it on their roadmap to add to QUIC stacks - I can imagine it will get there over time.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I wouldn't say this is considerable more stuff.

The benefit is in allowing abrupt termination of streams while delivery some key critical data. Without that you'll resort to timeouts or other things as described in the spec.

WebTransport over HTTP/3 already mandates RESET_STREAM_AT for its needs. So MOQT over WebTransport not using it is pointless subletting.

Rather than bifurcation of the spec, implementations should implement extensions that are useful.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
The problem is you have to do the timeouts anyway so this just adds extra. I was also under the perhaps mistake impression that some QUIC stacks don't implement this.  I'm certainly not promoting bifurcation the spec but I note that this is not part of the core QUIC spec. 

I think the core part I am stumbling on here is the "what is critical data" that we can deliver with this and how does that help us. Perhaps I am just not understanding the value proposition of using this. Right now it has the feel of there is a feature in QUIC we have not yet used so we must find a way to use it. If feel like a tweek we could add a year from now if we had data that showed it helped.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
In this case, my understanding is that the SUBGROUP_HEADER object is the critical element. I'll let others more familiar with MoQ weigh in on the relation with SUBSCRIBE_DONE  that is noted in the draft.

The RESET_STREAM_AT work was adopted primarily to support WebTransport. The design is complete and we are awaiting more implementing until progressing the draft to IESG. I expect that concrete use cases like WebTransport coming to fruition will motivate QUIC stacks to add support for this lightweight extension. The ability to deliver data reliably is already a core feature of QUIC (i.e. when a stream is FIN'd). The extension merely adds a mode to allow abrupt termination to also benefit.

There are real benefits to resetting streams vs. closing them with FIN. Unfortunately the core design makes it all or nothing, which can impacts application (speaking in the general sense, not specifically to MoQ). 

The situation is not dissimilar to the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. It was widely implemented once there was a popular use case of MASQUE. 

QUIC is designed to be extensible. I don't think we should be worried about core vs extension split argument. MoQT already levies DATAGRAM to be mandatory. 

It might be possible to design out the use of RESET_STREAM_AT. However, that might require a design that can't use RESET_STREAM at all (I genuinely don't know, again deferring yo MoQT experts to answer that). What I'm concerned about is pushing complexity up the stack in the name of avoiding implementing a simple QUIC extension.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
My understanding is that one does not need to use RESET_STREAM_AT in MoQ, but using it allows for cleaner SUSCRIBE_DONE properties in some cases. @afrind 

I'd prefer to keep it as optional if we can, but I don't think it needs to be removed entirely.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Individual comment:

@ianswett is correct - it is optional, and will not prevent MoQ adoption.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This was also discussed in Denver, and on the mailing list here: https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/moq/qGWs5MJ6XVir6C1BwJ2Gx8zUm2A/

RESET_STREAM_AT is completely optional in QUIC and MOQT, and we should keep it that way.  It doesn't harm anyone to explain where it can be useful.

>  my understanding is that the SUBGROUP_HEADER object is the critical element. I'll let others more familiar with MoQ weigh in on the relation with SUBSCRIBE_DONE that is noted in the draft.

SUBGROUP_HEADER is useful for SUBSCRIBE_DONE.  It does not remove the need for a timer, but it short-circuits the timer in the common case.

It is also helpful when needing to reset a data stream to ensure the subscriber or relay doesn't get a partial object that is effectively useless.  Let's say my objects are large (500kb) and a relay has transmitted all of object 37, but the upstream disappears.  It needs to reset the downstream data stream, and that reset can race the last byte of the object.  If the relay ends up with 499999 bytes, it's the same as having 0, because there is no way to request less than a full object the next time.  RESET_STREAM_AT ensures the existing work won't be wasted.

+1 to keep as is
