issues.title: Editorial issues in draft-ietf-moq-transport-10, section 2
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 2 of draft-ietf-moq-transport-10 includes the following paragraph:

To give an example of how an application might use this data model, consider an application sending high and low resolution video using a codec with temporal scalability. Each resolution is sent as a separate track to allow the subscriber to pick the appropriate resolution given the display environment and available bandwidth. Each "group of pictures" in a video is sent as a group because the first frame is needed to decode later frames. This allows the client to join at the logical points where they can get the information to start decoding the stream. The temporal layers are sent as separate sub groups to allow the priority mechanism to favor the base layer when there is not enough bandwidth to send both the base and enhancement layers. Each frame of video on a given layer is sent as a single object.

I can see the following issues:
1) The term "group of pictures" is a loose term that can have different interpretations. The intent of the term herein appears to mean "independently coded sequence of pictures".
2) Both "picture" and "frame" are used. It'd be better to consistently use only one of them. Using "picture" would be better, as in video coding standards a picture can be either a progressive frame or a (top or bottom) field picture. 
3) The reasoning "because the first frame is needed to decode later frames" can use some improvement, as the real reason herein is that the first picture in an "independently coded sequence of pictures" can be used as a random access point.
4) The phrase "send both the base and enhancement layers" can also use some improvement, as the current wording gives an impression that there are only two scenarios: send only the base layer or send both the base and enhancement layers, while actually there can be as many scenarios as the number of layers.
5) Both "subgroup" and "sub group" are used. Better to consistently use "subgroup".

For resolving all the issues above (and some other minor issues not mentioned), it is suggested to update the paragraph to be as follows:

To give an example of how an application might use this data model, consider an application sending high and low resolution video using a codec with temporal scalability. Each resolution is sent as a separate track to allow the subscriber to pick the appropriate resolution given the display environment and available bandwidth. Each independently coded sequence of pictures in a resolution is sent as a group because the first picture can be used as a random access point. This allows the client to join at the logical points where decoding of the stream can start without needing information before the join points. The temporal layers are sent as separate subgroups to allow the priority mechanism to favor lower temporal layers when there is not enough bandwidth to send all temporal layers. Each picture is sent as a single object.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: The comment also applies to draft-ietf-moq-transport-11.

issues.title: Editorial: "consistent with sharing a stream" -> "consistent within a stream"?
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
In Section 2.2, the following sentence: 

Objects in a subgroup have a dependency and priority relationship _consistent with sharing a stream_ and are sent on a single stream whenever possible. 

The phrase "consistent with sharing a stream" seems having some editorial issue. Should be "consistent within a stream" instead?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think the text is as intended.  Data that shares a stream has some dependency and priority relationship --

Nearly all QUIC implementations deliver stream data in order, meaning they HoL block on loss.  So putting data B into stream after data A means: B depends on A and/or is not higher priority than A.

CC: @martinduke who penned the line if I recall.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Yes, the wording is intended. A stream implies that later bytes are dependent on earlier bytes, and are therefore lower priority. So the placement of two objects in a stream should be consistent *with* that.

However, this a pretty subtle bit of English and I'm happy to accept a rewording that makes it clearer. But "consistent within" isn't it, IMO.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: @afrind @martinduke Thanks for the clarification! Got it. I thought a bit more and could not figure out a better wording. Thus I am going to close this issue soon.

issues.title: On assigning Objects to Subgroups
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
The last paragraph in Section 2.2 is as follows:

An example strategy for using stream properties follows. If object B is dependent on object A, then delivery of B can follow A, i.e. A and B can be usefully delivered over a single stream. Furthermore, in this example:
- If an object is dependent on all previous objects in a Subgroup, it is added to that Subgroup.
- If an object is not dependent on all of the objects in a Subgroup, it goes in a different Subgroup.
- There are often many ways to compose Subgroups that meet these criteria. Where possible, choose the composition that results in the fewest Subgroups in a group to minimize the number of streams used.

I can see the following issues:

1) "delivery of B can follow A" is not equivalent to "A and B can be usefully delivered over a single stream", thus using "i.e." therein does not seem to be the best wording.

2) The third bullet item is not about the example strategy, but rather a general guideline. Thus, if to have the sentence at all, it should be in a separate paraph instead.

3) The criteria for the example strategy described by the first two bullet items are hard to understand, e.g., based on the example of temporal layers each in its own subgroup described in the 2nd paragraph in Section 2. For one example, a picture in a particular temporal layer does not necessarily depends on all previous pictures in the same temporal layer, and if so, then according to the criterion described in the 2nd bullet item, the picture should go in a different subgroup than some of the previous pictures in the same temporal layer. For another example, a picture in a particular temporal layer may depend on all previous pictures in a different temporal layer, and then according to the criterion described in the 1st bullet item, the picture should go in the same subgroup as the previous pictures in a different temporal layer.

The biggest issue is the third one. Unless I am misunderstanding something herein and before that is clarified, the best suggestion I have now is to replace the paragraph with something simple like the following:

When assigning Objects to different Subgroups, a reasonable tradeoff should be considered between having a good number of Subgroups (hence a good number of different priorities) in a group and minimizing the number of streams used.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: The comment also applies to draft-ietf-moq-transport-11.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think we still want to retain some of the original text, because subgroups are delivered consistent with the properties of a QUIC stream.

If an object _does_ depend on all the objects in subgroup A, then it should probably also be in subgroup A, and if it depends on _none_ of the objects in subgroup A, it probably shouldn't be in subgroup A.  But it should be quite general or exemplary in nature, since an application may decided to break either rule for its own reasons.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
OK. The wording should be as soft/non-binding as possible.

I just feel that it is a bit weird that the only specified example rule on assigning Objects within a Group to Subgroups is not consistent with the only example use of Subgroups in the entire document, which is assigning each temporal layer within a Group to its own Subgroup. It might be good to add an example use that is consistent with the specified example rule.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
@yekuiwang Ok you raise a very good point.  Perhaps the idea of mapping temporal layers to subgroups is what's wrong?  I'm not a video encoding expert, but if the dependencies are like this:

```
Base: 0 <- 2 <- 4 <- 6
      |    |    |    |
Enh:  1    3    5    7
```

Then one subgroup for base and one _per enhancement frame_ would be a more apt mapping, though it might not be as performant, as there is some additional wire overhead and processing required for each stream/subgroup.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
When temporal scalability is use, assigning each (temporal) sublayer to its own subgroup is pretty good, as it makes perfect sense to assigning each sublayer a particular priority, the lower the sublayer, the higher the priority.

For temporal layering, there can be many coding structures but the following three are typical.

1) Hierarchical coding structure, highest coding efficiency, but also highest coding delay

In one example, the bitstream order (i.e., decoding order) of the pictures (assuming GOP size 8) would be 0 8 4 2 6 1 3 5 7, pictures 0 and 8 (and all other pictures with an index value of 8*n with n being any non-negative integer) belong to sublayer 0, pic 4 (and all other pictures with an index value of 4*m with m being a positive odd-valued integer) belongs to sublayer 1, pics 2 and 6 (and all other pictures with an index value of 2*k with k being a positive odd-valued integer) belongs to sublayer  2, and pics 1, 3, 5, and 7 (and all other pictures with an odd-valued index) belong to sublayer 3. 

In one example, any picture in sublayer 0 (except the first picture in sublayer 0, which is intra-coded and coded as a random access point) refers the previous picture in sublayer 0 in decoding order for inter prediction reference (e.g., pic 8 refers to pic 0 for inter prediction), and any picture in sublayer s with s > 0 refers to the two closest pictures (in picture index value, i.e., in output order) that are in the same or lower sublayers (e.g., pic 4 refers to 0 and 8, pic 2 refers to 0 and 4, pic 6 refers to 8 and 4, pic 1 refers to 0 and 2, pic 3 refers to 2 and 4, pic 5 refers to 4 and 6, and pic 7 refers to 6 and 8).

2) 1-picture coding delay

The bitstream order (i.e., decoding order) of the pictures would be 0 2 1 4 3 6 5 8 7, pictures with even-valued index (0 2 4 6 8) belong to sublayer 0, other pictures belong to sublayer 1. 

Picture 2n refers to pic 2n-2 for inter prediction, picture 2n+1 refers to pics 2n and 2n+2.

3) No coding delay

The bitstream order (i.e., decoding order) of the pictures would be the same as their output order, i.e., 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8, pictures with even-valued index (0 2 4 6 8) belong to sublayer 0, other pictures belong to sublayer 1. 

Picture 2n refers to pic 2n-2 for inter prediction, picture 2n+1 refers to pics 2n.

@afrind This one is the same as you drew above, I think.


For all the above coding structures with temporal scalability enabled, including the third, I think it makes perfect sense to assign each sublayer to its own subgroup. IMHO, for the third coding structure, assigning each sublayer to its own subgroup is better than assigning sublayer 0 to its own subgroup but assigning each sublayer 1 picture to its own subgroup. For example, if the bitstream/track contains 1 hour video of 30 frame per second, assigning each sublayer 1 picture to its own subgroup would need 54K subgroups/streams.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
BTW, although some of the above example coding structures with temporal scalability enabled look complicated, they are really simplified versions what video encoders can do. The only necessary rule of temporal scalability is that any picture of a particular sublayer cannot use another picture of a higher sublayer for inter prediction reference. That means, whenever the encoder finds out that for encoding any picture when using inter prediction from an earlier coded picture of the same or a lower sublayer can improve coding efficiency, the encoder may likely use it (within the limit of the maximum buffering of decoded pictures). 

Therefore, for the third coding structure above, it is always possible that the encoder may code picture 2n+1 referring to pic 2n-1 or any other picture earlier than picture 2n for inter prediction. Therefore, unless the bitstream is pre-encoded and fully inspected, the sender won't know that picture 2n+1 for any value of n only refers to pic 2n.

issues.title: Auth Token Error Handling
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
I find this annoying to implement (parsing the parameter requires reporting two levels of error) and it follows inconsistent principles about what is session-level and what is request-level.

AFAICT there are six error outcomes:
1. Auth Token Cache Overflow. This is a hard session error, which makes sense. Even a stupid subscriber shouldn't do this.
2. Duplicate Auth Token Alias. Ditto, this is a protocol violation.
3. Expired Auth Token. The text is vague* on this, but I strongly suspect this is a request-level error. Failing the session seems harsh if expiration is not always detectable?
4. Unknown Auth Token Alias. The spec says this fails the request, not the session. Why?
5. Malformed Auth Token due to a mangled serialization. This is a request-level error.  I don't know why. Any requesting relay can detect if the parameter framework is correct.
6. Malformed Auth Token due to a value that doesn't match the token type. It's a request level error, which makes sense because some requesters can't verify the token internal structure.

* Yes, I can go to the individual message descriptions to find out it's a request-level error code, but that's a pain.

Editorially, this text is hard to read because all of the error codes are buried in prose. Some are session-level, and some are request-level. 

I would recommend the following changes:
a) Organize the text to separate session-level and request-level errors. Maybe have a  table?
b) Split Malformed Auth Token into Malformed Auth Token Parameter (Session error) and Malformed Auth Token Payload (Request-level). Probably rename to something less horrible than what I just proposed.
c) Clarify Expired Auth Token as Request-level
d) Change Unknown Auth Token Alias to Session level.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Put another way  -- expired tokens and tokens that are internally Malformed are not violating MoQT, they are violating a different layer, and should be request-level errors.

everything else -- a screwed-up parameter formats, alias table errors -- are violations of MoQT, and should kill the session.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Unknown Auth Token Alias. The spec says this fails the request, not the session. Why?

I was trying to not blow up the session the sender pipelined two requests (REGISTER, USE_ALIAS) and registration failed.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> > Unknown Auth Token Alias. The spec says this fails the request, not the session. Why?
> 
> I was trying to not blow up the session the sender pipelined two requests (REGISTER, USE_ALIAS) and registration failed.

OK, that makes sense on some level, but I'd like to drill down on how we get to that state.

I think registrations only fail if they violate the MoQT spec (e.g. the alias is too large). If the token fails because of the signature or whatever, that's not an Unknown Alias, that's an bad token, which is rejected just as if it was USE_VALUE and it didn't work.

This cleanly separates things the parser rejects from things the authenticator rejects.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Can you use Key-Value Formatting Error if the token structure is malformed, or you think we need a new session error specific to token?

I think I agree with your logic that all the reasons registration fails can be session errors, so invalid alias can be a session error too.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I don't have a strong opinion on how many errors you create here, but...

it is a layer of formatting below the key-value pair. If we are not going to create a bunch of structured parameter values, this special flower should get its own error code. If we are, then maybe not?

How many errors this needs also depends on how buggy it's going to be, for which I'd completely defer to your experience with QPACK.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Malformed token cases that should be a session error are

1) if the Key-Value-Pair's length field for AUTH_TOKEN is longer than the enclosing control message length
2) one of the internal length specified fields in token (varint or token length) extends beyond the Key-Value-Pair's length field.  
3) the token structure don't consume the entire Key-Value-Pair's length

These all seem like Key-Value Formatting error.

Are there any other malformed cases?

issues.title: Are Authorization Aliases unidirectional?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 8.2.1.1 sayeth:

> The TOKEN value is a structured object containing an optional session-specific alias. The Alias allows the client to reference a previously transmitted TOKEN in future messages. 

and later

> The Token Alias MUST be unique within the Session.

But 'client' is neither here nor there. A client can be a subscriber or a publisher, or both. Even if single-role, subscribers use tokens for SUBSCRIBE, FETCH, AND TRACK_STATUS_REQUEST. Publishers use it for ANNOUNCE. So clearly, both endpoints can use tags.

So either
1) the tables are separate for each direction. This certainly allows asymmetric tag cache sizes to coexist easily.
2) the tables are common to both directions. In which case, I think the tag IDs need even/odd separation to avoid collisions in-flight, and the cache size has to be min(client, server)

I think I prefer (1) but don't really care.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: My understanding is that they were separate for each direction (1).  This makes sense for all the auth situations I can think of.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: There are other references to 'client' in the section, which should be replaced as well.

issues.title: Signatures for Control Messages containing Authorization Token
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
The Auth Token structure, as defined today, doesn't provide a way to sign and attach the signature.  This goes back to dpop-token idea that was discussed during the interim (https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/12gPovk09BOKqof_OuaD000CLizh9gotq-DatILPUR-k/edit?slide=id.g339295cd5e3_0_89#slide=id.g339295cd5e3_0_89) 

This is very important when traversing to untrusted/proxy relays , to preserve the token misuse.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Since there is no format specified for Token Value, a token with a signature could define a structure like

```
Token Length (i)
Token (..)
Sig Length (i)
Signature (..)
```

Is there value in having this structure in MoQT, or is it sufficient to defer to the specs that define the tokens?

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
I was thinking something along the lines of 
```
TOKEN {
  Alias Type (i),
  Signature(...),
  [Token Alias (i),]
  [Token Type (i),]
  [Token Value (..)]
}
```


The signature field needs to be in the moq transport and what does the signature cover can be in individualized authz specification. If we push it inside Token Value, we will end up having certain tokens with no signatures and it opens up token reuse issues.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
MOQT does not need to define how to sign tokens. There are many token formats, all of which already specify a signing mechanism. With CAT for example, the signature is built into the token. It already has support for DPoP. If we force the signature to be in a MOQT-defined serialization, then we can't use off the shelf tokens, which would be a step back for MOQT in terms of interop with the existing media industry.

If you want the serialization suggested above, you caould create a separate RFC to define the token structure, give it a name and make your own token. 

But the core MOQT specification should only provision for an opaque byte array.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: I am fine with saying we don't need new serialization. I feel if we don't mandate formats that supports signed token, we are opening up for security vulnerabilities, especially when the path can have untrusted moq-relays acting as proxy

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
@wilaw What @suhasHere is talking about is not how to sign tokens.  It's about the security of bearer tokens in a system with untrusted intermediaries.

Given the presence of untrusted intermediaries in MOQ, any token system in which tokens are not sender-constrained is not secure.  An intermediate relay can observe a token being used for one purpose, and use it for any other purpose allowed by the token.

The basic solution here is to make sure that the token cannot be used in any context other than the one in which it is legitimately used.  You can create this property either by creating single-use tokens (think Google Docs sharing URLs) or multi-use tokens that "sender-constrained" so that they can only be redeemed by the legitimate user of the token (think certificates or [DPoP tokens](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html)).  The latter property is called 

What we should do in MOQT is make the protocol friendly to the latter, safer approach, as a way of helping guide applications in that direction.  There are two technical things you need to implement that approach: (1) a token scheme that binds public keys to tokens, and (2) a way to sign protocol actions.  Protocol support is important for the latter half.  If you look at DPoP as an example, they had to invent a way to sign HTTP requests (sadly, they were just ahead of [RFC 9421](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html)), which introduced both a bunch of complexity and a bunch of risk.  We have the opportunity to do better here because we know the need exists.

What I would propose here is:

* Add security considerations basically capturing the dichotomy I mention above.
* Whenever a protocol message includes a token, it should also have a field for a signature over that message.
* MOQT should define a representation of the message that the token scheme should use to sign it.
* The format of the token and the signature can remain opaque.

That way, if a token scheme doesn't implement a sender-constraint mechanism, they can just leave the signature blank.  But if it does, writing the MOQT integration will be straightforward and secure.  And either way, the application will be on notice that they need to have an authorization system that accounts for untrusted intermediaries.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Whenever a protocol message includes a token, it should also have a field for a signature over that message.

All messages that can carry an Auth Token already have a flexible parameter set similar to HTTP headers.  I assume it should be sufficient to define an optional parameter like "Signature", which would parallel RFC 9421?

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: Since the signature is tied to token mechanism in effect, i wonder why don't we add it as optional field on the Token itself ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Since the signature is tied to token mechanism in effect, i wonder why don't we add it as optional field on the Token itself ?

That could work too, although it makes a bit of combinatorial explosion of Alias Type -- eg: register, use_alias and use_token all have two values, one with signature and one without.  Either way seems to work though.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Since the signature is tied to token mechanism in effect, i wonder why don't we add it as optional field on the Token itself ?

The tokens we would likely use with MOQ ( CAT, JWT etc) already have signatures built into their serialization. Signatures are a key part of modern tokens and are already contained within the token value. We have a token 'type' field which informs the receiver how to extract the signature from the token 'value' field. 

A reasonable way forward would be to:
1. Add language to the security section of the MOQT draft emphasizing the importance of signatures and proof-of-possession when using tokens to protect access and constrain behavior across untrusted MOQT networks. 
2. Add language that any token registered in the IANA "MOQT Auth Token Type" table SHOULD contain a signature as part of its serialization.

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
@wilaw you're conflating two types of signatures here.  Yes, tokens are signed.  That's fine to be part of an opaque token format.  We're talking about a second signature, which binds the token to an individual protocol message.  The first signature is by the issuer of the token, over the information in the token; the second signature is by the subject of the token, over the protocol message.

I think @afrind is more on the right track here.  Following the high-level outlines of RFC 9421 seems like a good idea, in the sense of defining a signature inputs and where to put it.  Couple of friendly amendments:

* I would probably be more prescriptive than RFC 9421 about what goes in the signature, since I think this protocol has a clearer demarcation of which fields are logically E2E and which are relay-controllable.  

* Syntactically, I like @suhasHere's suggestion of having a signature field associated to the token.  I would **not** make it optional, so that you could write spec text like "you MUST verify the signature field according to the token scheme in use"-- while syntactically allowing the field to be empty, so that a token scheme could choose not to use it.

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
I like associating it to the token because (a) authorization is a specific, core use case and (b) this avoids conflict with other potential uses of signatures.

It may also be good to have a more general RFC 9421-like mechanism, but that would be for another issue.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> We're talking about a second signature, which binds the token to an individual protocol message. 

@bifurcation  - thanks for the clarification. That certainly changes the conversation and consequently I'd support the proposal of https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/968#issuecomment-2841929892

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Just for the sake of understanding the requirement.

> An intermediate relay can observe a token being used for one purpose, and use it for any other purpose allowed by the token.

Can you give an example here? 
Do you mean an intermediate relay that processes the signed token (so it is a trusted entity) but nonetheless it misuses this token to perform some other actions?
Or a relay that cannot read the token, but randomly try to do actions just in case (while avoiding any "Protocol Violation")? 
I am not sure to understand what actions are under consideration in the MoQ pub-sub scheme. And what are the consequences.

> Following the high-level outlines of RFC 9421 seems like a good idea

The main motivation behind 9421 is that "_HTTP permits, and sometimes requires, intermediaries to transform messages in a variety of ways. This can result in a recipient receiving a message that is not bitwise-equivalent to the message that was originally sent._" As far as I understand, MoQ does not grant relay such transformation. What high-level outlines of RFC 9421 do you refer to?

> * I would probably be more prescriptive than RFC 9421 about what goes in the signature, since I think this protocol has a clearer demarcation of which fields are logically E2E and which are relay-controllable.

Which "fields" are relay-controllable in MoQ? Do you mean actions?

> * Syntactically, I like [@suhasHere](https://github.com/suhasHere)'s suggestion of having a signature field associated to the token.  I would **not** make it optional, so that you could write spec text like "you MUST verify the signature field according to the token scheme in use"-- while syntactically allowing the field to be empty, so that a token scheme could choose not to use it.

I don't think that adding a MUST in a spec is a " friendly amendment".

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
> > An intermediate relay can observe a token being used for one purpose, and use it for any other purpose allowed by the token.
> 
> Can you give an example here? Do you mean an intermediate relay that processes the signed token (so it is a trusted entity) but nonetheless it misuses this token to perform some other actions? Or a relay that cannot read the token, but randomly try to do actions just in case (while avoiding any "Protocol Violation")? I am not sure to understand what actions are under consideration in the MoQ pub-sub scheme. And what are the consequences.

The concern here is something like:

* ExampleTube gives me a token that says, "this is Richard", which gives me permission to subscribe to a bunch of private streams on ExampleTube
* I can connect to ExampleTube via a relay I discover dynamically, say one on the airport WiFi
* I use such a relay to stream a single video while I'm in the airport
* The relay now has my token, and can use it to download any private stream I have access to

So specifically, the concern is relays that are trusted **for a specific MoQ interaction** (pub/sub), but not more broadly, re-using tokens to get access to content that they are not supposed to have access to.
 
> > Following the high-level outlines of RFC 9421 seems like a good idea
> 
> The main motivation behind 9421 is that "_HTTP permits, and sometimes requires, intermediaries to transform messages in a variety of ways. This can result in a recipient receiving a message that is not bitwise-equivalent to the message that was originally sent._" As far as I understand, MoQ does not grant relay such transformation. What high-level outlines of RFC 9421 do you refer to?

My understanding does not match yours.  MOQT absolutely allows information to change between relays in multi-hop scenarios.  For example, the "track alias" in the SUBSCRIBE message is only meaningful between a specific pair of peers.  The parameters of course can carry arbitrary data, with no rules on when it can be changed.

By "high-level outlines", I mean what I said -- specifying how a signature over a protocol message should be computed, and where to put the signature.

> > * I would probably be more prescriptive than RFC 9421 about what goes in the signature, since I think this protocol has a clearer demarcation of which fields are logically E2E and which are relay-controllable.
> 
> Which "fields" are relay-controllable in MoQ? Do you mean actions?

See above.

> > * Syntactically, I like [@suhasHere](https://github.com/suhasHere)'s suggestion of having a signature field associated to the token.  I would **not** make it optional, so that you could write spec text like "you MUST verify the signature field according to the token scheme in use"-- while syntactically allowing the field to be empty, so that a token scheme could choose not to use it.
> 
> I don't think that adding a MUST in a spec is a " friendly amendment".

I meant a "friendly amendment" to @afrind's proposal.  And making sure the MUSTs are right is the whole point of editing a spec -- especially when it comes to security -- which is the whole point of this GitHub repo.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
1. We should disambiguate the terms here:
- _native_ signature of a token, which guarantees its integrity (native in the sense that it is typically present in modern token format e.g. CAT)
- _proof-of-possession_ signatures (such as DPoP), which guarantees that a token has been generated for the entity presenting the token (to prevent reuse of the token from misbehaving relays and/or pirates)

For the sake of clarity, we should find another terminology than the generic term “signature” to avoid confusion.

2. I would suggest the "PoP signatures" in MoQ to be **optional**. And, if present, the PoP verification MUST be performed. Three cases could then cause token rejection:
- a PoP signature and a token that does not have the relevant PoP claims to perform the verification e.g. the PoP key thumbprint
- a token that has PoP claims but no PoP signature
- a token and a PoP signature that do not match.
 
3. If the above is agreeable, MoQT shall “only” specify a relevant vehicle to transport the "PoP signature" (if in use) next to the token. As far as I understand DPoP RFC, PoP signatures cannot be part of the token itself.

comments.author: bifurcation
comments.body:
> 1. We should disambiguate the terms here:
> 
> 
>     * _native_ signature of a token, which guarantees its integrity (native in the sense that it is typically present in modern token format e.g. CAT)
> 
>     * _proof-of-possession_ signatures (such as DPoP), which guarantees that a token has been generated for the entity presenting the token (to prevent reuse of the token from misbehaving relays and/or pirates)

Yep, this is the distinction I have tried to make several times in this thread.  Couple of nits:

* Instead of "native" signatures, I would use "token" signatures, since the structure of PoP signatures is also defined by the token scheme.
* Tokens do not have to be signed; they can be [opaque](https://www.ory.sh/docs/oauth2-oidc/jwt-access-token/) and often are.  Since tokens are always opaque to MOQT, though, "native" signatures in your taxonomy are not visible to MOQT; the spec should say nothing about them.
* MOQT _does_ need to say something about PoP signatures, since they are intended to bind the token to a protocol message.

>     2. I would suggest the "PoP signatures" in MoQ to be **optional**. And, if present, the PoP verification MUST be performed.

I would frame this differently.  I would require that any token scheme defined for use with MOQT MUST define a PoP mechanism and verifiers MUST verify PoP as defined by the token scheme.  But a token scheme's PoP mechanism MAY be optional or null, with warnings in the spec about the consequences of omitting PoP.  This accommodates the same cases your framing does, but it guides toward implementations that do have real PoP.

> Three cases could then cause token rejection:
>
>     * a PoP signature and a token that does not have the relevant PoP claims to perform the verification e.g. the PoP key thumbprint
> 
>     * a token that has PoP claims but no PoP signature
> 
>     * a token and a PoP signature that do not match.

Since MOQT doesn't know anything about the internals of tokens, talking about "claims" isn't meaningful.  These failure cases would be internal to the token scheme, in the sense that the token scheme needs to provide an algorithm `verify(token, moqtMessage, signature)`, which would have those three failure modes among possibly others.

>     3. If the above is agreeable, MoQT shall “only” specify a relevant vehicle to transport the "PoP signature" (if in use) next to the token. As far as I understand DPoP RFC, PoP signatures cannot be part of the token itself.

Yes, though in line with the above, I would make the PoP signature field non-optional.  For example, as a field in the AUTHORIZATION TOKEN parameter.

You are correct that PoP signatures cannot be part of the token, because they are generated after token issuance, and tokens cannot be modified by the holder.

issues.author: suhasHere

I am coming around to think about the utility of Alias to begin with , after my chat with Richard Barnes.


Why can't the server retrieve the token from the context ? 
   Let's say Subscribe used Token X and got Ok. Now when I do SubscribeUpdate, i can retrieve token from the subscription context. Otoh, if we need to update the token (say due to expiry), the senders needs to include a new Token anyways. Same can be said about connection level token too.

CC: @wilaw

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Alan has already answered, but there are multiple uses cases where an alias is useful
1. When doing ABR switching via SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE across different tracks. The tuple would be different and hence there is no fixed context  across each switch
2. When using the same token for CONNECT as well as SUBSCRIBE, FETCH, ANNOUNCE etc

Extensions originally used NumExtensions, but at the time someone (me) wanted to just take them as a blob and pass them up without parsing. We are starting to come up with extensions that are useful to relays, so maybe that's been overcome by events.

issues.title: Announce upstream delivery timeouts
issues.author: ac-freeman
issues.body:
The current draft specifies that a a delivery timeout `is the duration in milliseconds the relay SHOULD continue to
   attempt forwarding Objects after they have been received.`

If data is traveling through **multiple relays**, however, you may want to communicate the _cumulative_ timeout at each stage. For example, the end subscriber may want to have a guarantee that the end-to-end latency is < 1 second (give or take a bit of handoff latency). If a relay in the middle has a delivery timeout of 5 seconds, there's currently no way for our subscriber to know that. You may want to choose a different track subscription if certain latency guarantees are crucial.

This could be partially addressed with a new parameter, like `DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_CUMULATIVE` that could be included in `TRACK_STATUS` requests/responses.

Problems with this solution:

- For the responses to be accurate, upstream relays must have already issued a request for this cumulative timeout parameter
- If an upstream timeout changes, how do we notify downstream subscribers?

Perhaps, if a client initiates a `TRACK_STATUS` with the cumulative timeout parameter, it should initiate a chain of upstream requests to get the most up-to-date cumulative timeout. This would increase the time taken to initiate a subscription, but wouldn't slow down subscribers that don't care about the cumulative timeout.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Do you have use cases where the delivery timeout of a track from the publisher's perspective changes over the life of the track?

See also #648 which is related, but has been closed.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
Not necessarily from the original publisher's perspective, but subscribers (including those that function as relays) in video analysis systems may frequently change their timeouts in response to higher-level requirements. 

The draft text `The publisher SHOULD
   always specify the value received from an upstream subscription when
   there is one, and nothing otherwise` confuses me. Suppose we have a topology of `A -> B -> C -> D`, where `B` and `C` are relays. If `B` follows this recommendation, what good does it do to set the same delivery timeout for its published track to `C` as its received track from `A`? If its subscription timeout to `A` is 1 second, and if `C` receives that track from `B` with its own timeout of 1 second, then the end-to-end delivery timeout `A -> D` is effectively 2 seconds.

My point with this issue is simply that subscriber `D` would not _know_ that its true timeout is higher than what it asks for, because it doesn't know anything about the network topology. This could be bad for latency-critical applications. Maybe this is best left for a draft spec outside the transport protocol, but it could be worth discussing anyway.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the cumulative timeout for objects across multi-hop relay networks probably is important for realtime use cases.  @fluffy @suhasHere any thoughts?

comments.body: Parking this until we have more experience with delivery timeout and resolve existing issues.

issues.title: UNANNOUNCE and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL should use request Id
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body: Announce and related messages have been changed in draft 11 to add **Request Id**, making announce stateful by this new Id. Previously, the namespace was used to id the original announce. Request Id replaces the need for namespace in these subsequent messages that relate to the original announce.  `UNANNOUNCE ` and `ANNOUNCE_CANCEL` was missed.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Introducing Request ID wasn't intended to make ANNOUNCE any more stateful than it already was, but a more direct way of correlating the OK/ERROR with the original request.

Invoking UNANNOUNCE or ANNOUNCE_CANCEL by Name rather than request ID should be functionally ok, I think?  Note UNSUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES also uses Track Namespace Prefix rather than the Request ID of the original SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES.  That said, it's asymmetric with SUBSCRIBE, which uses Request ID.

I'm somewhat neutral.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
> Introducing Request ID wasn't intended to make ANNOUNCE any more stateful than it already was, but a more direct way of correlating the OK/ERROR with the original request.

It wouldn't introduce any more state if `UNANNOUNCE` and `ANNOUNCE_CANCEL` also use request Id.  It would be a net zero change to switch from track namespace (exact) matching for state to request id.  

Correct me if I'm wrong, but as I read the draft the below defines the message state handling, which always starts with the announce state first being created/considered... otherwise the subsequent ones are invalid. 

```
ANNOUNCE - Creates the state of announce.. subsequent messages change the state of this announce
   \/
    |-- ANNOUNCE_OK - Sent by producer; Announce state is active and allowed
    |-- ANNOUNCE_ERROR - Sent by subscriber=relay/server; announce state ends
    |-- ANNOUNCE_CANCEL - Sent by subscriber=relay/server; announce state ends, but may linger
    |-- UNANNOUNCE - Sent by producer; announce state ends
```

> Invoking UNANNOUNCE or ANNOUNCE_CANCEL by Name rather than request ID should be functionally ok, I think?

Yes, but it requires additional state to track by full namespace (all tuples) matching as we do/did `<` draft-11 long with the new state tracking by request id.  

The tuple track namespace in announce is only used for subscribe and subscribe announces prefix matching.  Prefix matching is not performed for subsequent message handling of announce.  In other words, we would have never prefixed matched an `UNANNOUNCE` to one or more `ANNOUNCE`s.  IMO, request Id is a better way to handle the state so that we don't get ourselves into sticky situations where the same namespace (either by prefix match or not) matches more than one request-id.  Request ID also allows us to better mitigate DoS attempts by quickly invalidating the message instead of loosely matching the message to a state object. 

> Note UNSUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES also uses Track Namespace Prefix rather than the Request ID of the original SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES. That said, it's asymmetric with SUBSCRIBE, which uses Request ID.

This issue/PR is only for announce.  `UNSUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES`, IMO, should be updated as well to use request id. There does seem to be value here where you might want to take advantage of unsubscribing to announces for a more specific  to the SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES sent, but it gets a bit complex to support that.  For example, say you do a subscribe announces for `{a, b}`, which then matches tuples a and b of all announces.  Say you decide that you want to filter/block noise caused by `{a,b,X}`. You could simply send an unsubscribe announces for `{a,b,X}`, which in effect acts as a filter.  While this works, it does get complicated to support this type of filtering.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in Stockholm - the logic is an application could ANNOUNCE multiple times (maybe updating an auth token), but UNANNOUNCE would revoke any/all ANNOUNCEs previously sent.

Afterwards, I thought ANNOUNCE_CANCEL might make more sense with Request ID - the use case for the message is (eg: ANNOUNCE credentials expired).  If the subscriber detects this, and sends CANCEL and the publisher detects this and sends a new ANNOUNCE - we don't want the CANCEL to be ambiguous.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
As an individual, I'd rather just remove ANNOUNCE_CANCEL.  All it says to the publisher is "I won't send subscriptions for this namespace to you".  Except actually it still can if it wants to.

I opened an issue for this, but #802 has what is likely the best description of the intent, which is largely around auth expiring.  But then it's basically the same as ERROR, it's just there might be a case one sends ANNOUNCE_OK and then ANNOUNCE_ERROR later?

I was thinking we'd remove ANNOUNCE entirely, but if we're going to keep it, it'd be nice to clean it up some.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the use case of ANNOUNCE_CANCEL is clear enough.  We don't allow any other _ERROR message after _OK, though maybe we can now with Request ID.  Technically SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES might have the same use case for a publisher side, post _OK cancellation though.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think this issue can be closed with no action.

Per my previous [comment](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/978#issuecomment-2858821203), I don't think ANNOUNCE_CANCEL with namespace is ambiguous, because in that flow, the new ANNOUNCE needs an _OK or _ERROR before anything happens.  eg:


```
P->S: ANNOUNCE (ns=foo, id=1)
S->P: ANNOUNCE_OK(id=1)
... time passes, publisher and subscriber simultaneously realize auth expiry...
S->P: ANNOUNCE_CANCEL(ns=foo)  | P->S: ANNOUNCE (ns=foo, id=2)
```
The publisher can ignore or process the cancellation, the new announcement will get an OK or ERROR soon enough.

  Type (i) = 0x16,

issues.title: Motivation needs addressing
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
`The speed at which a protocol can detect and respond to congestion determines the overall latency. TCP-based protocols are simple but are slow to detect congestion and suffer from head-of-line blocking. Protocols utilizing UDP directly can avoid queuing, but the application is then responsible for the complexity of fragmentation, congestion control, retransmissions, receiver feedback, reassembly, and more.`

The above part of the section is filled with factual errors. For example, UDP can't avoid in network queuing. A particular byte of an object may have reduced latency at the arriving end-point. 

The response to congestion control when comparing QUIC and TCP is all depending on what is implemented. 

So I think a rewrite here is needed. 

I still think some motivation around what aspects MOQT tries to address in regards to latency is needed. But can we please be more correct in how it attempts to provide benefits. It is all around scheduling of data, transmission order prioritizations, and being able to cancel receiving data when falling to far behind.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See also #913, which suggested removing the section entirely, moving some info to an appendix and some to the relay section.

issues.title: On Considerations for Setting Priorities
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
The first paragraph in Section 6.3 is as follows:

Relays SHOULD respect the subscriber and original publisher's priorities. Relays can receive subscriptions with conflicting subscriber priorities or Group Order preferences. Relays SHOULD NOT directly use Subscriber Priority or Group Order from incoming subscriptions for upstream subscriptions. Relays use of these fields for upstream subscriptions can be based on factors specific to it, such as the popularity of the content or policy, or relays can specify the same value for all upstream subscriptions.

The first sentence (Relays SHOULD respect the subscriber and original publisher's priorities.) and the third sentence (Relays SHOULD NOT directly use Subscriber Priority or Group Order from incoming subscriptions for upstream subscriptions.) appear, to me, a little contradicting with each other. Is it possible to rephrase to avoid such seemingly contradiction, or it is totally fine with everyone (thus my feeling is simply not correct)?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: The first sentence talks about the priorities on the downstream connection, the third one talks about the upstream connection.  We should probably make this clearer.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
@vasilvv Thanks! What about changing the first sentence to something like the following?

**For downstream subscriptions, r**elays SHOULD respect the subscriber and original publisher's priorities.

issues.title: Problems with the Max Auth Token Cache Size description
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 8.2.1.1.

> Any message carrying an AUTHORIZATION TOKEN with Alias Type REGISTER that does not result in Malformed Auth Token MUST effect the token registration, even if the message fails for other reasons, including Unauthorized. This allows senders to pipeline messages that refer to previously registered tokens.

first of all, s/effect/affect.

<incorrect issue deleted>

I don't know what it means to register a token you won't honor (i.e. do I have to store the value?). 

I would not be sad if we decided this was too much to take on and punted MOQPACK to a protocol extension.

See below for other minor issues.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Furthermore, if we're counting bytes, then it should be 8B for the alias + 8B for the token_type + token size, not token_size + 8

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Oof:
Sec 8.3.2.3:

> The token size is calculated as 8 bytes + the size of the Token value (see [Figure 4](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-11.html#moq-token)).

If I go to Figure 4, it describes a structure in which one field is "Token Value", but the *title* of the figure is also 'Figure 4. AUTHORIZATION TOKEN value]. I assume you mean the length of the field, not the struct, but the nomenclature could stand to be cleaned up here.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I withdraw the original core of the issue, because overflow became a session error and so storing it doesn't matter. But the other notes apply.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> first of all, s/effect/affect.

The intent was to use effect as a verb "meaning to cause something to happen or to bring about a result", but the subject of the sentence is the token, which doesn't effect anything. Editors will address.

> I don't know what it means to register a token you won't honor (i.e. do I have to store the value?).

The intent that so long as the registration is not a session error, then a subsequent message using the alias is also not a session error.  Yes, you have to store the value.  The key example is eg: an expired token, a token with an invalid signature, or a token that does not authorize the operation carrying it.  Yes, MoQT needs to store such tokens until deleted by the sender.

> I would not be sad if we decided this was too much to take on and punted MOQPACK to a protocol extension.

@wilaw who was a primary advocate.  Note that it is already _entirely optional_ both for the sender and receiver.  The sender can use `USE_VALUE` and the receiver can set the max size to 0.

> Furthermore, if we're counting bytes, then it should be 8B for the alias + 8B for the token_type + token size, not token_size + 8

Seems legit, so size+16.

>  I assume you mean the length of the field, not the struct, but the nomenclature could stand to be cleaned up here.

Yes, I meant the length of the field, not the entire structure.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Everything here is editorial, except changing the size allowance to +16 instead of +8, unless of course there's a strong push to remove MOQPACK.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: The more I think about this, the more I think having a token received in an request that got an error response be added to the token cache is going to be a bad idea.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The more I think about this, the more I think having a token received in an request that got an error response be added to the token cache is going to be a bad idea.

Here's why it's necessary.  Say I have a token that says I can SUBSCRIBE track A until 7:00pm, and SUBSCRIBE track B until 8:00pm.  At 6:59:59, I send SUBSCRIBE to A and B.  A registers the token and B uses the token alias for it.  The publisher fails the track A subscribe because it got processed at 7:00:00.  If it did not register the token in the cache, SUBSCRIBE B becomes a session error, even though it should succeed.

issues.title: Inconsistency on relay modifying extension headers in different sections
issues.author: yekuiwang

Sec. 9.1.1.2 contains the following sentence: "If supported by the relay and subject to the processing rules specified in the definition of the extension, Extension Headers MAY be modified, added, removed, and/or cached by relays."

However, in Sec. 7.4, it is said that "A relay MUST NOT modify Object properties when forwarding.", while in Sec. 9.1.1 (titled Object Properties), one of the listed Object properties is Object Extensions, which is defined as a sequence of Object Extension Headers. 

Therefore, some changes need to be made to avoid this inconsistency. Sorry that I am not familiar with all involved aspects enough to confidently suggest a modification, thus I am just reporting the issue without a suggestion to resolve it.

issues.title: On future extensibility for control messages
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Sec. 8 (Control Messages) contains the following sentence: "An endpoint that receives an unknown message type MUST close the session."

That implies that future extensibility for control messages is disallowed, i.e., there is no way to specify any new types of control messages in a future version of MOQT. Is this understanding correct? Has this aspect been discussed before and has it been concluded that lacking of future extensibility for control messages in the design is acceptable?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The extensibility model is to negotiate the extensions either 1

1) moqt protocol version (in SETUP today, or in ALPN and its WebTransport equivalent soon)
2) negotiating specific moqt extensions in the SETUP message exchange

The base protocol allows extensions to individual objects, and likely also extensions to tracks via parameters, see #781.

Are these mechanisms sufficient, or do you think additional mechanisms are necessary?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: @afrind Thanks! I see; the version negotiation would allow a future version to have new types of control messages (and of course other stuff) specified and allow both the client and the server agree on working based on that future version. It just does not allow a client and a server working based on different MOQT versions. Many other standards allow so-called backward compatible extensions, where senders/encoders/servers and receivers/decoders/clients implemented based on different versions of a standard could interoperate. The design model herein regarding extensibility for new types of control messages is different than those. But on the other hand, this is also a fine design choice.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: It doesn't seem there is a compelling reason to change at this time. Closing.

issues.title: A bunch of minor and seemingly obvious editorial improvements
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
As I continue reading the draft, I have gathered a bunch of minor and seemingly obvious editorial improvements, and counting. Following @afrind's suggestion, I could directly file a PR for each of these editorial improvements. However, it'd be much easier and more convenient to bundle these collectively in one PR. Thus, I am posting what I have so far below, just in case someone objects to one or more of them, then those that are not agreeable can be excluded from the PR. Any opinion on any of the suggestions is appreciated.

Here is the list of my minor and seemingly obvious editorial improvements so far. The changed parts are highlighted in **bold fonts**.

a.	2.1: "All objects belong to a group, indicating ordering and potential dependencies. Section 2.3" -> "All objects belong to a group, indicating ordering and potential dependencies **(see Section 2.3)**."

b.	3.1.3: "The syntax of the Connection URL and the associated connection setup procedures are specific to the underlying transport protocol usage Section 3." -> "The syntax of the Connection URL and the associated connection setup procedures are specific to the underlying transport protocol usage **(see Section 3)**."

c.	3.2: "It also includes the union of all Setup Parameters Section 8.2.2 required for a handshake by any of those versions." -> "It also includes the union of all Setup Parameters **(see Section 8.2.2)** required for a handshake by any of those versions."

d.	3.4: "The application MAY use any error message and SHOULD use a relevant code, as defined below:" -> "**When terminating the Transport Session, t**he application MAY use any error message and SHOULD use a relevant code, as defined below:"

e.	3.4, 8.4: "equal or larger than" -> "**equal to** or larger than".

f.	3.4: "The session was closed because the peer took too long to send data expected on an open Data Stream Section 9." -> "The session was closed because the peer took too long to send data expected on an open Data Stream **(Section 9)**."

g.	6.2: "If two objects have a different subscriber priority associated with them, the one with the highest subscriber priority is sent first." -> "If two objects have **different subscriber priorities** associated with them, the one with the highest subscriber priority is sent first."

h.	6.2: "If two objects have the same subscriber priority, but a different publisher priority, the one with the highest publisher priority is sent first." -> "If two objects have the same subscriber priority, but **different publisher priorities**, the one with the highest publisher priority is sent first."

i.	6.3: "Relays use of these fields for upstream subscriptions can be ..." -> "**Relays' use** of these fields for upstream subscriptions can be ..."

j.	7.3.1: "This section describes behavior that a publisher MAY choose to implement to allow for a better users experience when switching between networks, such as WiFi to Cellular or vice versa." -> "This section describes **a behavior** that a publisher MAY choose to implement to allow for a better **user experience** when switching between networks, such as WiFi to Cellular or vice versa."

k.	7.3.1: "Once the subscriptions have migrated over to session on the new network, the publisher can stop publishing objects on the old network." -> "Once the subscriptions have migrated over to **the session** on the new network, the publisher can stop publishing objects on the old network."

l.	7.3.2: "This section describes behavior that a publisher MAY choose to implement to allow for a better user experience when a relay sends them a GOAWAY." -> " This section describes **a behavior** that a publisher MAY choose to implement to allow for a better user experience when a relay sends them a GOAWAY."

m.	8.2: "Some messages include a Parameters field that encode optional message elements." -> "Some messages include a Parameters field that **encodes** optional message elements."

n.	8.2: "The number of parameters in a message is not specifically limited, but the total length of a control message is limited to 2^16-1." -> "The number of parameters in a message is not specifically limited, but the total length of a control message is limited to **2^16-1 bytes**."

issues.title: Fetch Header doesn't start with Type
issues.author: zafergurel
issues.body:
The Fetch Header starts with a Request  ID (9.4.4).
Subgroup Header starts with a Type (9.4.2). 

It's not possible to understand a stream starts with a Fetch header or Subgroup Header.

FETCH_HEADER{

Sec. 8.2.1.1 includes the following:

> The AUTHORIZATION TOKEN parameter MAY be repeated within a message.

>   Alias Type (i),
>   [Token Alias (i),]
>   [Token Type (i),]
>   [Token Value (..)]
> }

>   Alias Type (i),
>   [Token Alias (i),]
>   [Token Type (i),]
>   [Token Value (..)]
> }
> Figure 4: AUTHORIZATION TOKEN value

The second sentence has some issues. Was the intention to have the sentence to say something as follows?

> If the peer receives a PATH parameter from the server, or when WebTransport is used, it MUST close the session with Invalid Path.

issues.title: No way to know if/how a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE was processed
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Originally, SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE was designed to always succeed.  However, there are things like DELIVERY_TIMEOUT that the publisher might not be willing to honor.

Additionally, one can't tell if a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE was processed before or after sending the SUBSCRIBE_DONE, which is potentially annoying.

My strawman proposal is a PUBLISH_UPDATE, which would allow the publisher to ACK the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE and would also allow the publisher to unilaterally change things like track priority (if it existed).

Additionally, if a peer is going away, it might want to tell the subscriber that it's going to end the subscription early at a group in the near future, so the subscriber would know what Group to start subscribing at from a different publisher.

Under what circumstances would the original SUBSCRIBE have been accepted but the UPDATE is some new level of privilege. Works for single-object streams and single-stream-groups.  If you are using multiple subgroups-per-group and multiple objects-per-subgroup, you just have to send a full EOG object. comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Related to #877, so not too late

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I think there are at least two use cases that are important here. 

The first is when the publishers will know the object is the last and the other is when it does not know. 

last object known case: For example, when doing audio with 1 object per group, the publisher knows the object it is sending is the last one. I think it has to be able to indicate this in a bit efficient way to make low bitrate audio work. 

last object not known case: For example, when going stream per I-frame, a video encoder outputs blocks of bits and they get sent as object, but after they are sent, the video codec starts a new i-frame that starts a new group. The last object in the previous group has already been sent. There has to be some way to send some additionally info that indicates what the last object in the group was even though that will likely arrive later than the last object in the group. 

I think there are many ways that we could solve both the above. The property I want in a solution is that it can work for datagrams not just streams ( will be unreliable of course ), will be in the data plane not the control plane because there will be lots of these and want to minimize impact on relay performance, and finally will keep the bitrate low particularly for low bitrate audio.

issues.title: In publish, need equivalent of subscribe expires
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body: When A sends a publish to a relay, there needs to be a way for relay to say when A needs to redo the auth for the Publish. ( and there needs to be a way to do that like PUBLISH_UPDATE )

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The requirement is to notify the sender of an authentication token an idea of how long they have to renew the auth before the subscription is terminated.  Since auth is carried in SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH then the expires needs to go in SUBSCRIBE_OK and PUBLISH_OK, and also why we need PUBLISH_UPDATE.

See also #879, I think `expires` is a good candidate for a parameter.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Is it correct to say that ANNOUNCE_OK and SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES_OK should also have expires?  It seems like it's relevant to all of them.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
I am a bit surprised by this issue. 

If I understand correctly: The sender of an auth token sends a token (that it got from a third party), and the server processes the token, extracts the expiration time, and includes the expiration time in the confirmation. Am I correct?

It seems odd: One of the reasons tokens are encrypted is that the issuer does not want anyone on the path to know the claims.

It is annoying in practice: When a CDN edge server acts as Relay, the token validation system usually runs in a separate module. The criteria to analyze the token are out of the Relay's knowledge. We would need to create APIs between Relay and "token validation module" to collect some information from the token claims. 

Why would we restrict this mechanism (token information sharing) to the "expiration" claim, which is only one of the claims in the token?

Note that, in CAT, "_catr_" is a claim that allows a token validation system to trigger some actions when a token is close to expire. It runs at the server-side (in the module that processes the token), which is the natural behavior. Possible actions includes the generation of a new token or re-routing this client to the token issuer. Rather than an "expires" parameter of OK messages, I would consider embedding some MOQT actions in the catr's claim of CAT.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think the utility is to give the client a hint about when to ask the third party for a new token and update an existing subscription before it expires.  It is optional (if we make it a param) if it is too challenging or a security problem for the relay to set this.

However for PUBLISH (client -> relay) one problem is that the relay will simply UNSUBSCRIBE when the token expires, which doesn't contain a code indicating why.  Is that a clear enough signal to the publisher, or does UNSUBSCRIBE need a code?

issues.title: Discussion on Delivery Timeout
issues.author: Johan511
issues.body:
Delivery Timeout is defined as 
>  It is the duration in milliseconds the relay SHOULD continue to attempt forwarding Objects after they have been received ... There is no explicit signal that an Object was not sent because the delivery timeout was exceeded.

Consider the following scenario 

We try to publish 1MB every 250ms, 32KB + 64KB + 128KB + 256KB + 512KB each corresponds to a different enhancement layer and put in a different track. With decreasing priorities (512KB object is sent only after the 32KB object is sent). A DELIVERY_TIMEOUT of 250ms makes sense

Consider we are on a 64KBps connection, ideally we want to send the 32KB chunk and not any of the other chunks as there is no way they will be received in the 250ms window

But if the Congestion Control Window is 100KB, The transport layer puts the 32KB and 64KB chunk on wire

Resetting the stream carrying the 64KB chunk does not serve any purpose as the bytes are now on wire where they will block the send of the future 32KB chunks

The draft mentions that 
> Publishers SHOULD consider whether the entire Object is likely to be delivered before sending any data for that Object, taking into account priorities, congestion control, and any other relevant information.

Is there any suggestion by MOQ (in works or already exists) on how this should be done or is it left open to the implementer?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Is there any suggestion by MOQ (in works or already exists) on how this should be done or is it left open to the implementer?

moxygen hasn't implemented delivery timeout yet, and I believe @martinduke and @vasilvv were struggling because of webtransport API constraints (see #667).

If you had a bandwidth estimate X, you could subtract off what you've already committed (32kb) and divide the remainder by the next object size (64kb) and compare the result to the delivery timeout.  I'm not sure what else you can do.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> If you had a bandwidth estimate X, you could subtract off what you've already committed (32kb) and divide the remainder by the next object size (64kb) and compare the result to the delivery timeout. I'm not sure what else you can do.


This seems like we are only ever thinking about an ideal case scenario. 

Let us assume we have the right bandwidth estimate (from BBR)

Now I need to run this check of { can I send this object? } when the stream starts sending the object (starts writing bytes into wire). 

The QUIC implementation I use does not signal this event (object has started being written into wire), this also seems like a very vague event to signal. 

What if the stream is halted because a higher priority stream now has been opened and needs to send a object, should there be a signal every time the stream is the highest priority stream? or should there be a signal every time the stream writes a data frame into into wire, this sounds like it will hamper the performance of the transport layer?

If the idea is to decide whether queue the object to be sent based on bandwidth predication this means when I am deciding whether to send the object, I need a API which tells me the objects with higher priority already queued and objects with higher priority which will be queued in the near future. The latter would make this approach unnecessarily complicated.  


One idea I considered exploring was waiting for the ACK of the "stream subgroup header" to figure out when QUIC has started putting the subgroup on wire, but this would have atleast 1RTT delay which sounds like it could be significant. Any opinions on it? This still does not solve the problem of another higher priority stream showing up and blocking this send after the subgroup header has been ACKd.

Looking forward to @vasilvv ideas on this.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
On a side note, has there been any opinion on forcing upstream relays to ignore any delivery timeout by the Publisher? 
Possibly by setting subscriber delivery timeout to 0, currently I would never see someone attempting to that as it'd mean that the stream is reset as soon as the object is queued onto it. 

Why would this be useful?

I believe it would allow the subscriber to very smoothly tradeoff latency for receiving more data.

If delivery timeout exists -> we have a bounded latency but would loose objects which are not delivered within that time

If delivery timeout is ignored -> latency numbers would be higher, but we the data we requested for

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Now I need to run this check of { can I send this object? } when the stream starts sending the object (starts writing bytes into wire).

That's a good point. Some QUIC implementations buffer application writes internally, and use the stream priority to determine what goes out on the wire.  Others, however, (picoquic is an example, I think) don't track priority or buffer internally.  Instead they upcall to the application to fill a packet based on priority.  In some cases (eg: webtransport) it's computationally infeasible to have that kind of design.

> The QUIC implementation I use does not signal this event (object has started being written into wire), this also seems like a very vague event to signal.

mvfst provides an option to receive a signal when a particular stream offset was first transmitted (or acked).  It's not exactly what you are asking for since it's retroactive -- eg the stream has already written at least that offset and possibly more.

Do you have running code implementing the draft that can demonstrate problems?  I think that would help drive the conversation.  I can imagine it being bad -- eg: committing the first 64kb causes the second 32kb to miss its delivery timeout and both streams get reset?  I guess you would set longer timeouts on the more important streams?

QUIC stacks and APIs may need to evolve to suit MoQ needs - we shouldn't view them as unchangeable.

> On a side note, has there been any opinion on forcing upstream relays to ignore any delivery timeout by the Publisher?

The spec doesn't have exactly that, but if neither the publisher nor subscriber have timeouts then the relay has to deliver everything.  Is that sufficient?  See #715 and #1014.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> Do you have running code implementing the draft that can demonstrate problems? I think that would help drive the conversation. I can imagine it being bad -- eg: committing the first 64kb causes the second 32kb to miss its delivery timeout

Yes, this issue was raised after collecting analytical results, the setup is identical to what is mentioned in the issue.
With 0% packet loss (congestion control window blown up due to CUBIC congestion algorithm) we observed very high latencies, upto 5s (with very high variance, with BBR we observed latencies of 800ms which is far from ideal too) as the wire was overflowed which came down to closer to the expected value of 250ms when the packet loss was raised to 10% (because the congestion window is now much lower and the wire is not overflown with packets).

Only difference is that we do not use delivery timeouts, rather we use a `MUST_SEND` flag as described in #792, where every time a greater object is received the object being delivered is aborted and we generate monotonically increasing objects on each track every 250ms so it acting identically to delivery timeout.

In sight of this issue, we are moving to a delivery timeout based implementation so MOQ is aware of the deadline placed on it and can estimate delivery accordingly. 

> eg: committing the first 64kb causes the second 32kb to miss its delivery timeout and both streams get reset?

Streams being reset end up having no effect as QUIC has already dumped all the bytes onto wire (because the congestion window allows it) and is just waiting for ACKs now, resetting the stream does not prevent the lower priority bytes on wire blocking the higher priority bytes published later on. 

 > I guess you would set longer timeouts on the more important streams?

No, I send whatever data I can within the 250ms window, so all streams carrying enhancement layer objects have the same 250ms DELIVERY_TIMEOUT
Streams carrying base layer objects do not have any DELIVERY_TIMEOUT

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> The spec doesn't have exactly that, but if neither the publisher nor subscriber have timeouts then the relay has to deliver everything. ...

My vision is the sort of the opposite

Delivery timeout is set by the Publisher, but the Subscriber sends some flag or parameter upstream to the relays (and the publisher) which tells them, ignore any DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, I need this object even if you believe it has expired and should not be sent, that is never reset the stream because a delivery timeout occurred.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
I could be missing something, but might we be overcomplicating things? If the CC window is small, but still greater than the actual bandwidth, we may indeed oversaturate the connection by sending too much data. But the CC window would shrink in response, preventing us from immediately sending the next object of the same size. So there will be a delay, and by the time we can send the next object, the delivery timeout may be exceeded (and we drop it).

You have a slight delay in being able to detect the increased latency (congestion) and actually enforce the delivery timeout, but we see such behavior all throughout the network stack. It's up to the developer to make the objects small enough that this initial delay is within the requirements of the application, and ensuring that objects are sent with semi-regular timings. For media applications, both of these should be doable.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
@ac-freeman 
> If the CC window is small, but still greater than the actual bandwidth,

CC window and bandwidth are different units so they can't be compared, I assume you suggesting comparing ccwnd and (bandwidth * delivery_timeout). Delivery_timeout in my case is around 100ms, but what I observed is that ccwnd is often many times greater than (bandwidth * delivery_timeout). Consider 0% packet loss, in case of CUBIC, the ccwnd just explodes to a very high value.

With the following netem rules `delay 25ms 2ms rate 2Mbit loss random 0%` I had observed a 300KB ccwnd (BBR). The bandwidth of 2MBit should allow only 32KB chunks, so ideally we want a congestion control window of 32KB but that is not the case. And it does make sense too, CC algorithms are designed to be generic, not tuned towards LL / real time transport.  

> But the CC window would shrink in response, preventing us from immediately sending the next object of the same size.

Why would this necessarily happen?  CC window would decrease in response to congestion, not in response to us aborting streams.

Also, if I had a high priority track without any DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, the delays on it would keep compounding.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Also, if I had a high priority track without any DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, the delays on it would keep compounding.

If you have a high priority track with no delivery timeout, it's going to effectively starve everything else.  Use sparingly -- eg: catalog updates.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> If you have a high priority track with no delivery timeout, it's going to effectively starve everything else. Use sparingly -- eg: catalog updates.

I have my base layer to be high priority with no delivery timeout. The idea behind it is that if network conditions are bad, the application protocol allows you to still live stream albeit with slightly higher latency.

This makes sense for the (last relay) - (subscriber) link

For (publisher-relay) or (relay-relay) link, I believe what you said does make sense. I have not been involved in building CDN and was under the assumption CDN-CDN communication is often not congested and there's always enough bandwidth for communication.

comments.author: ac-freeman
comments.body:
>Why would this necessarily happen? CC window would decrease in response to congestion, not in response to us aborting streams.

I'm saying that if you _do_ send too much data, it would cause congestion. The system should sort itself out if the object sizes and delivery timeouts are reasonable.

I have an implementation of delivery timeouts that I'll be evaluating soon under various latency requirement scenarios, so hopefully I can get some empirical results to back this up.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
> I have an implementation of delivery timeouts that I'll be evaluating soon under various latency requirement scenarios, so hopefully I can get some empirical results to back this up.

Looking forward to it, I would much rather prefer knowing that I am wrong than reaching a consensus that we need to add deadline awareness at the QUIC layer or another congestion control algorithm at the application layer.

Please do try to obtain results in scenarios where bandwidth is very low (barely enough to send the objects within the deadline) and so are other factors like latency and packet loss. 

My [initial attempts](https://raven-presentation.vercel.app/#/22) at evaluating performance scaled bandwidth inversely with packet loss (that is, lower bandwidth scenarios always had higher packet loss) and it hid this issue being discussed.
