issues.title: Semantics of Request ID in the MAX_REQUEST_ID message
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Sorry if this has already been discussed and concluded.

In Sec. 8.5, the semantics of Request ID in the MAX_REQUEST_ID message is as follows:

> Request ID: The new Maximum Request ID for the session. If a Request ID equal or larger than this is received by the endpoint that sent the MAX_REQUEST_ID in any request message (ANNOUNCE, FETCH, SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES or TRACK_STATUS_REQUEST), the endpoint MUST close the session with an error of 'Too Many Requests'.

The first sentence says that this is the maximum Request ID, i.e., the maximum value is allowed. However, the second sentence says that the maximum value is not allowed, Therefore, the two sentences are not entire consistent with each other.

Either the first sentence and probably also the name of the message should be changed to be aligned with the sentence. Or, the second sentence is changed to be as follows (changing the sentence is probably simpler from the text point of view):

> If a **Request ID larger than this** is received by the endpoint that sent the MAX_REQUEST_ID in any request message (ANNOUNCE, FETCH, SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES or TRACK_STATUS_REQUEST), the endpoint MUST close the session with an error of 'Too Many Requests'.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Since 0 means "you can't send a request", so MAX_REQUEST_ID actually contains the smallest request ID you _can't_ send.  Or maybe another way to express it is 

>  The new Maximum Request ID for the session, plus one.

issues.title: Subgroups and DELIVERY_TIMEOUT can result in pathological FETCH
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Consider this setup:

Publisher -> Ingest Relay -> Egress Relay -> Subscribers

The Publisher has one track, with two subgroups: base (id=0) and enhancement (id=1).  The base layer is higher priority.  The object IDs are in decode order, such that sg=0 has even objects and sg=1 has odd objects.  There is a DELIVERY_TIMEOUT between the ingest relay and the Publisher for this track.

During congestion, there is sufficient bandwidth such that sg=0 makes it to the ingest relay, but sg=1 gets reset.

As a result, the egress relay cache contains only even objects for this track (0, 2, 4, ...)

A new subscriber joins this track and issues a Joining FETCH for this track.

This causes the relay to make a FETCH request to the original publisher either:

1) one request for every odd object
2) a request for the entire group up to the current object

As #945 describes, the original publisher may not even have sufficient bandwidth to handle any FETCH requests in parallel with current live data.  If the relay can't get object 1, it can't serve object 2 either.

I think the fundamental problem is the interleaving of mixed priority/reliability data in the FETCH response (eg: does the Joining FETCH need all subgroups in order to start playing?).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Brainstorming a few options:

1. Do nothing - applications with this structure and usage pattern will cause upstream roundtrips and higher join latency.

2. Recommend different usage - applications like this can use multiple tracks instead of multiple subgroups - keeping the even object IDs in one track and odds in the other, and include object ID gap markers.  Then there are 2 independent joining fetches, one that succeeds immediately and one that may have to go back to origin.

3. Add a different kind of FETCH - maybe joining FETCH can filter only for subgroup=0?  Caches need some additional logic to record if two objects in the subgroup with an ID gap came on the same stream with no interruption.

4. Disallow caching when DELIVERY_TIMEOUT is present (suggested by @mzanaty).  This means a Joining FETCH will go back to the original publisher.

5. Require contiguous object IDs _in a subgroup_ - Object ID is no longer the exact decode order, but the decode order can be computed from a combination of object ID, subgroup ID, and the publisher's maximum number of objects per-subgroup.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
@afrind 
Can you also mention what is the ideal case scenario you would like to see in the given setup?

If relays are not able to receive the track fully because of constant DELIVERY_TIMEOUTs, I see the best we can hope to do being receiving the higher priority objects.

> This causes the relay to make a FETCH request to the original publisher either:
one request for every odd object 
a request for the entire group up to the current object

Is this the major concern?
Because, I do remember a previous draft of MOQ mentioning that objects (should / need) not be sent more than once over a single connection. Won't such a restriction be useful to solve this problem?


On a side note, as an implementer/performance-tester I am curious, is it common for inter-CDN communication to be bandwidth bound? We do provide a very inexpensive (in performance terms) way to scale horizontally.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Can you also mention what is the ideal case scenario you would like to see in the given setup?

The player is using joining fetch to start playback ASAP, and presumably needs only subgroup=0 to start playing the base layer.  If the relay has subgroup 0 cached, I'd like to see all of subgroup 0 delivered without blocking on an upstream fetch.  As a bonus, I'd like to reduce the total number of upstream fetches required but it's less important.

> Because, I do remember a previous draft of MOQ mentioning that objects (should / need) not be sent more than once over a single connection. Won't such a restriction be useful to solve this problem?

That is true for subscribe, but not for FETCH.  FETCH always returns the objects even if they have been sent in the same session in a previous SUBSCRIBE or FETCH.

>  is it common for inter-CDN communication to be bandwidth bound?

In my example, the bandwidth constrained relay is from the original publisher, who could be a live streamer on a mobile device.

comments.author: Johan511
comments.body:
Publisher -> Ingest Relay -> Egress Relay -> Subscribers

(Subscriber A) sent a subscribe request and now sends a joining FETCH to the Egress Relay to fill it's playback buffer

Did I get it right?

Just an idea dump

Ideally we do not want any duplicate objects to be received, so we need to decompose the request into sub requests which I believe is not possible because you can't decompose sub group requests (option 2 should solve the problem), this is the reason I have been in favour of having different tracks for each layer. 

> Disallow caching when DELIVERY_TIMEOUT is present (suggested by @mzanaty). This means a Joining FETCH will go back to the original publisher.

I do not understand how this solves the problem, I only see it causing more issues. The publisher is already congested, how can it handle sending the latest Base Layer Objects along with the Base Layer objects we expect from the fetch?

Coming to the major issue you are facing, which I believe can be summed up as cached delivery being blocked because one object in between hasn't been cached and the delivery of that object is starved.

A wild idea, but won't a group order of type WILD (I can't think of a good name at the moment) workout here, which basically mentions that there is no group order. I just  need this range of information deliver it any jumbled fashion which suits you. 

**EDIT**: Right now {group order} orders based on <Group Id, Object Id> tuple, ordering based on <Publisher Priority, Group Id, Object Id> tuple (basically scheduler priority) might also make sense in this case.

> Add a different kind of FETCH - maybe joining FETCH can filter only for subgroup=0? Caches need some additional logic to record if two objects in the subgroup with an ID gap came on the same stream with no interruption.

If you want to filter over subgroups, isn't that taking steps towards bringing subgroups into the object model, further deepening it?

I believe in Stockholm @vasilvv had proposed making filters into [parameters](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/interim-2025-moq-10/materials/slides-interim-2025-moq-10-sessa-subscribe-filters-00.pdf) which I was really hoping to see. If the usecase is very specific, I hope it'd now allow for implementation extensions to filters which might make sense.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
Like to point out that subscribe could do FETCH 1, FETCH 3, FETCH 5, etc - I suspect for some use cases a join will only want to get the lowest layer for old stuff. 

I also assumed we would eventually define filters that were usable in FETCH / SUB that allowed filtering in some form by layer. That could be stream id, object patterns, or priority levels. For example fetch me group 3 to 50 but only the object with a publish priority more important than 7.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think filters and/or application design are going to make this better.  Parking for now.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I feel like FILL_TIMEOUT and forthcoming ability to filter subgroups for joining specifically address my concern here.

issues.title: Proposed new requirements for expires
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Comments on #1012 that are actually new proposed requirements to draft-10:
 
* Client has to renew before the expiry time
* After the time is exceeded, relay can just remove the subscribe state with no signaling to the subscriber. 
* Make expires mandatory not advisory
* We need to talk about how much before and randomness so they don't all happen at the same time.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I very much oppose "After the time is exceeded, relay can just remove the subscribe state with no signaling to the subscriber."  That's just bound to cause problems.

What does "renew" mean in this context?  Is it auth, or something else?

MoQ is already going over a reliable QUIC connection, so I don't think there's any need for a signal that one wants to continue receiving the subscription, as WebRTC requires (if I remember correctly?).

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: This really comes into the we need to figure out the security design and then this probably be easier to figure out what bits we need where.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: WebRTC needed consent at stun level so if new device got IP addess of old machine, the packets for old machine would stop. I don't think we have any problems like that here given it is all in a QUIC connection that takes care of that issue for us.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I think there are two design direction we could go

1) server tells client to reauth and gives it some time to do it.

2) client does reauth before old auth expires. 

I lean towards 2 as it pushes the timers onto client not server.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
It occurred to me that `expires` has a use outside of auth.  If a subscriber uses a filter that produces no objects for some period of time, I think the relay will need to reap that subscription.  eg:

For example, if the track is currently at group=1000 and I subscribe with an Absolute Start=1000000.  I'm forcing the relay to maintain state indefinitely.  The expires field is still advisory, but perhaps useful?  The relay can send SUBSCRIBE_DONE + EXPIRED.  If that's the case, any SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, even one that changes nothing, should probably extend the life of the subscription?

I think this relay "idle" termination is required in a case where the the subscription has an End Group.  Unless the track is trivial, the relay can't possibly know that no more objects are coming that will match the filter, so the relay needs to be able to terminate the subscription.  See #641.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
I think there a several solutions to this problem, which differ based on the characteristics of the original publisher:

For low latency sports broadcasts, the current semantics would allow the original publisher to produce a dedicated tack of dense i-frames. Participants would subscribe to this only when joining (or switching down). These would be cached at relays and would work at scale (millions of joins over a few seconds). This approach is used by HESP and L3DASH today and works well in practice, because the original publisher is a well-connected and powerful encoder and packager.  

For web conferencing and UGC use-cases,  in which the original publisher can be poorly connected and under-powered, we would not want to burden them with having to constantly produce new i-frames (groups). In this case, the suggestion of Suhas to enable the sparse-triggering of new groups is a sensible one. There are three options here:

1. The trigger inserts a new group into the track such that all current subscribers also receive that group. This is bit-inefficient, as only the new joiner needs the new group, but it is a simpler approach. 
2. There is a separate track established for the purpose of providing "joining groups". This track would hold sparse data  - basically adding a new group only when someone joined. The end of each sparse group would be aligned with the beginning of a group in the bit-efficient track, so the client would switch from this starting group to the efficient track after starting. 
3. We create a message called GENERATE_GROUP(trackname). As its name suggests, it returns via GENERATE_GROUP_OK a payload which is a single group from that track. This message would get relayed to the original publisher who would synthesize the group and time-synch it with the group boundaries they are already producing. I like this approach because a) it doesn't push a new group to existing subscribers b) Is cacheable if we define a TTL for the response c) We don't need a duplicate joining track for each primary track. d) It's not media specific.

 The current proposal is on the lines of 3  and is influenced by some techniques done in large scale conferences today and mapped to moq.  A draft PR in progress and the plan is to  submit soon to collect early feedback on the same

If there's already a subscription at a relay for the latest Group, then it'd naturally wait for the previous upstream subscription to generate a Group, which is a nice property if you have many participants coming, going and up/down switching.

I find adding a new verb for this potentially awkward, because we have SUBSCRIBE and FETCH and JOINING Fetch, all of which are oriented around getting Objects and Groups around the live head.  It feels to me like those verbs should be enough because really what we're saying is "Get me either a new or recent Group that allows me to join this other Track."

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Based on today's discussion, I'd recommend the following:

1.  Make it a param in SUBSCRIBE/SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE (NEW_GROUP_REQUEST, value=largest group)

The reason is it's less new machinery than a new message type.

2. The OP needs to opt-in to this on a per track basis - include a param indicating support in PUBLISH and/or SUBSCRIBE_OK.  

This prevents subscribers and relays from forwarding messages towards the OP when it's not willing/able to handle them. 

3. Add a publisher param for the minimum interval between new group requests

OPs that support dynamic groups should have a throttle anyways, communicating the throttle to the relay saves additional work.  This could be the same param as 2), eg sending a non-zero min interval means you support it.

Then the MTI bit for relays is:

a) if there's no active subscription, it's ok to send new group request upstream in a SUBSCRIBE
b) if there is an active subscription, send a SUBSCRIBE_UDPATE upstream with NEW_GROUP_REQUEST when receiving a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST param via PUBLISH_OK, SUBSCRIBE or SUBSCRIBE_UDPATE AND:
1. Track supports NGR
2. No pending NGR
3. NGR.Largest Group == Largest Group
4. now > largest group update time + MIN_NGR_INTERVAL

Clear the pending NGR when receiving an object with a group >= NGR.Largest Group

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
Having multiple ways of doing the same thing in a standard is always not a good thing, unless there is significant benefits of doing that.

Having multiple ways of doing the same thing in a standard, and then specifying one as an error and the other not as an error is kind of sick.

Therefore, I am for removing one of the two. As for which one to remove, no strong opinion, but I tend to think that it is more straightforward to keep "FETCH_ERROR + No Objects" and forbid FETCH_OK + an empty data stream, and this is also more consistent with other cases of "no content for your request" like `TRACK_DOES_NOT_EXIST`, `TRACK_ENDED` (or `DOES_NOT_EXIST` in PR #1159 ).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in Madrid:

We've talked about a few multi-publisher use cases:

1. Make-before-break
2. Crash and restart
3. Redundant ingest (active/active and active/passive)
4. Distributed Publishers producing different portions of the same track

The plan is to change this language to MUST subscribe to all publishers, as that is required for some if not all of these use cases.  @ianswett will separately make a proposal for the indication described above, which could limit the scenarios in which a relay MUST subscribe.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Here's how I interpret those use cases in terms of protocol messages:

Make before break (moving between paths without connection migration):

```
C->S (path1): ANNOUNCE
S->C : ANN_OK/SUBSCRIBE
C->S: OK, data ...
...
C->S (path2): establish session, ANNOUNCE/OK
```
--> Relay now has two publishers for this track, it's cue to stop publishing on path1 is when it gets a SUBSCRIBE on path2

Crash and Restart:

```
C->S: ANNOUNCE
S->C : ANN_OK/SUBSCRIBE
C->S: OK, data ...
...
crash + restart
C->S: ANNOUNCE
```
--> Relay now has two publishers for this track, since it hasn't detected the old connection is dead yet

Redundant Ingest, active/active:

```
C1->S: ANNOUNCE
S->C1 : ANN_OK/SUBSCRIBE
C1->S: OK, data ...
C2->S: ANNOUNCE
S->C2 : ANN_OK/SUBSCRIBE
```
--> Relay now has two publishers, has to subscribe to both in order to switch immediately in case one fails

issues.title: Simplifying joining at the latest available join point.
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
Groups conceptually represent join points in tracks, so there are many use-cases in which we want to join the track at the latest available point. 
One media use case is retrieving the latest version of the catalog. Since we moved the ability to start a SUBSCRIBE at the largest group (only latest object is now supported) , the current API structure would require us to use two messages 

SUBSCRIBE catalog – latest object
FETCH relative joining 0

This is dual message requirement for what should be a core & efficient behavior of a pub/sub protocol - joining at the latest available join point. 

**The proposal is to add back a SUBSCRIBE filter option for "largest group start".** A relay which has caching ability would return content starting from that point and continuing into the future.  Relays which have no cache ability can return a SUBSCRIBE_ERROR with reason code 0x13 - Largest group start unavailable.

This removes complexity for the client in stitching together a FETCH and SUBSCRIBE and simplifies a core operation of the protocol.

comments.author: tobbee
comments.body: I support this idea. It will simplify this basic use case, and lower the barrier for making MoQ used.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
To what degree is this an API concern rather than a protocol concern?  eg: SUBSCRIBE + joining FETCH gives you the exact data that you want.  moxygen defines ["join"](https://github.com/facebookexperimental/moxygen/blob/main/moxygen/MoQSession.h#L166) which translates to this message sequence under the hood.

> The proposal is to add back a SUBSCRIBE filter option for "largest group start". 

Given how filters are defined in draft-11, a subscribe filter for "largest group start" would have a different meaning -- eg: setting the filter start location to {Largest Group, 0}, but not delivering already seen objects between that and {Largest Group, Largest Object}.

comments.author: tobbee
comments.body:
I'm far behind others on the implementation side, but when I am trying to implement this, it is quite complex.

On the client subscriber side I can send a SUBSCRIBE and a JOINING FETCH and make sure to write them right after each other.
On the publisher side, I will see a SUBSCRIBE message first, but while parsing it, I have no idea that it is part of combo with a later JOINING_FETCH. Should I for every SUBSCRIBE wait a while to see if there is a JOINING_FETCH coming? In that case, for how long?

Sending the SUBSCRIBE stream corresponding to the last part of the group in parallel with the FETCH stream from the beginning of the stream is not good if there is some bandwidth limitation. Sending the FETCH stream before sending the final group objects as part of the SUBSCRIPTION is what I would aim for, and it seems to be what @vasilvv  does as well.

Ideally, I would like to have one command and one stream for the full group. That is conceptually easy to understand and the client implementation would be quite simple.

If this is not possible due to complex filtering rules, or some grand scheme, I wonder if we at least could have a flag in SUBSCRIBE to tell that it is part of a combo with  a JOINING_FETCH which is coming right after it so that I can get the publisher parser and dispatcher into  the proper state? Of course, we may then need some timeout for the JOINIING_FETCH part of the combo,  but I think that is still better than the current implicit combo.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Should I for every SUBSCRIBE wait a while to see if there is a JOINING_FETCH coming? In that case, for how long?

This isn't necessary.  In my code, SUBSCRIBE only adds the subscriber to a forwarding table, and can be processed immediately regardless if a Joining FETCH is coming or not.  The additional piece of state required to support a future Joining FETCH is to remember the Largest used to start the subscription.  If a Joining FETCH comes later, I can still compute the correct Absolute range for it, even if new objects have been published that pass the filter.  This obviates the need for a timeout.

> Sending the SUBSCRIBE stream corresponding to the last part of the group in parallel with the FETCH stream from the beginning of the stream is not good if there is some bandwidth limitation. 

If catching up to the group is important, you can set the priority of the FETCH to be higher than the priority of the SUBSCRIBE.  In the common case (the publisher has the current group cached) you will get all the FETCH objects first.

>  it seems to be what vasilvv does as well.

Actually I think Victor's code delivers the objects as they arrive, but using the same callbacks that subscribe uses.

comments.body:
I'm outspoken on this of course.

99% of the time, a consumer wants a subscription to start at a group boundary. Groups were intended to be join points for tracks that use delta encoding, like video codecs or JSON patch. The decision to start subscriptions at non-join points is baffling from an API design.

The convoluted dance between SUBSCRIBE + FETCH + joining FETCH exists because of misguided philosophical principles. This would be okay if it simplified the message protocol but it doesn't. I 100% agree with @martinduke that the combined SUBSCRIBE+FETCH was an overall better API.

At the very least, SUBSCRIBE should start at the latest group, not object. Tracks that don't use delta encoding can use a group per frame to more-or-less get the current behavior.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
Re-reading the original issue, I don't think it brings up any new points we did not originally consider when we decided to split SUBSCRIBE and FETCH.

> The proposal is to add back a SUBSCRIBE filter option for "largest group start". A relay which has caching ability would return content starting from that point and continuing into the future. Relays which have no cache ability can return a SUBSCRIBE_ERROR with reason code 0x13 - Largest group start unavailable.

What happens if the client does receive 0x13?  Does it have to wait for the current group to finish?  If so, that can add a lot of join latency.  Does it have to send FETCH?  In that case, I don't see how this is an improvement over the status quo.

1. Don't confuse API and wire format.  Having decomposed primitives does not prevent any implementation from having a `join` API.
2. The current design seems functional even if it won't win any beauty contests.  Reopening this will take months and likely not change anything.

issues.title: Flow control with SVC
issues.author: Alexd067
issues.body:
The problem discussed in #867 shows an issue where the stream with higher priority is blocked and other streams with lower priorities are not. The problem seems to be solved in Stockholm by not treating an object in a flow control blocked subgroup as schedulable. 

However, this approach may introduce a new problem: subgroups are not always independent(As #929 points out). In the case of layered codec like SVC, the layers are dependent. If the base layer is blocked, transmitting extra enhancement layers is meaningless, because they all rely on the base layer to be decoded. In this scenario, head-of-line blocking remains unaddressed.

Am I correct here? Or are there any other solutions for this issue?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think you are correct.

The only solution I can think of is to grant enough stream flow control to base layer subgroup streams to prevent them from becoming blocked, but not too high to open the subscriber to memory DoS attacks.  I agree with the 867 resolution - sending data that you _can_ send is better than sending nothing and hoping something better happens.

Let's consider the happy case: the tracks being published fit in the pipe between publisher and subscriber, and the subscriber is consuming the data (and releasing flow control) at the same rate the publisher is publishing it.  The subscriber set the limits to something approximating BDP.  Flow control should never block here.  So how does flow control block?  

1) The subscriber set the limits too low
2) The subscriber isn't consuming the data as fast as it's being produced (better unsubscribe, you are not live anymore)
3) The publisher is producing at a rate higher than the bandwidth (better unsubscribe)
4) Data was lost at the head of a stream, preventing the subscriber from consuming it and releasing flow control

So 4 is the case to consider.  Loss happens so the flow control needs to be set higher to allow the sender to keep sending new data on the stream without blocking while it is being repaired.  If you are regularly getting flow-control blocked, especially in a base layer, your real-time pub-sub system is going to have a bad time.

issues.title: Is knowing no Objects in a Fetch are Unknown practical?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Currently we say:
> If an Original Publisher receives a FETCH with a range that includes an object with
> unknown status, it MUST return FETCH_ERROR with code Unknown Status in Range.

If I issue a Fetch for 1 million Objects, I have to be sure the status isn't unknown before returning FETCH_OK, because I can't return FETCH_OK and then FETCH_ERROR.

Is this really practical?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The use case for UNKNOWN_STATUS_IN_RANGE is for distributed publishers.  It's expected that a given publisher will instantly know that a requested range covers groups that it is not responsible for.  See also #1117.

Consider a relatively straightforward example - a publishing client (C), a long term storage system (S) and a single relay (R) and a fetch client (F).  

```
S->R: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (foo)
S->R: SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (foo)
C->R: PUBLISH (foo, name=x)
R->S: PUBLISH (foo, name=x)
C->R: Objects starting from Group ID = [start time]
Objects go to both R and S (and downstream clients)

Client crashes and restarts
C->R: PUBLISH (foo, name=x)
R->S: PUBLISH (foo, name=x)
C->R: Objects starting from Group ID = [new start time]
...
F->R: FETCH start=A, end=B // where R < new start time
R->C: FETCH start=A, end=B
C->R: FETCH_ERROR, UNKNOWN_STATUS_IN_RANGE
R->S: FETCH start=A, end=B
S->R: FETCH_OK
```

I'm not saying this is a great architecture for ingest/storage, but it's at least plausible.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I thought the other use case is when I recover after the crash, and I know that I can only serve group starting with a certain group ID?  In that case, this does seem practical.

I am not sure this is a good idea, though?  Mostly because if I start at time 100, and the subscriber requests [50, 150], I think they'd much rather get the [100, 150] range than an error.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
#728 notes mention that there's interest in trimming the range to what is known by the publisher, rather than failing outright.  I could be ok with that, however, FETCH is already quite complicated so adding more mechanisms, particularly when not many people have implemented the ones we have, gives me pause.

Also, @vasilvv what is your proposed normative relay handling when I have the above scenario -- two publishers with different answers for FETCH [50, 150]?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I mean, if we assume that there is only one original publisher active at a time, this is really simple -- you just forward FETCH to that publisher (over any of the upstream connections available).

If we allow multiple publishers with disjoint state knowledge, there will be in fact a lot of complexity (you'd have to know who knows what, or do the `O(n)` search).

issues.title: Enforcing Ascending Group Order at Relays
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
In Ascending order subscription mode, relays are required to send all objects from Group N before any from Group N+1. However, if a relay forwards objects directly to the QUIC layer, high-priority objects from Group N+1 may be emitted before lower-priority ones from Group N due to QUIC’s internal scheduling.

For example, if a relay receives objects (20,0)...(20,29) and then (21,0), and if the object (21,0) belongs to a high-priority subgroup while some of Group 20’s objects are low-priority, then QUIC would schedule (21,0) first. It violates the group order.

I'm curious: how do current implementations handle this requirement?

One possible solution is to implement a MoQT-level buffer at the relay that holds back all objects from Group 21 until it is certain that all of Group 20 have been emitted. However, it may increase latency and introduce head-of-line blocking.

Should we relax the group order requirement at Relay side?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: Group order only applies after subscriber and publisher priorities, see https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport#name-scheduling-algorithm

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
As Victor said, group order is a tie-breaker within a track when objects from different groups have otherwise _equal_ priority.  So your example, where 21 has higher publisher priority than 20 means that delivering 21 first is by design.

@gwendalsimon is that workable?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Yes, it is. I missed this section of the draft. I'll close it.

For your information, the background of this issue is the ABR switch, say from track A to track B starting at group 21. We would like to use priorities to make sure that the Relay streams track A until group 20, and then streams track B from group 21. Two problems can happen: (a) some objects of Track B from group 20 are received, (b) some objects of Track A from group 21 are also to be delivered. We would like to skip these useless objects by using priorities and group order.

issues.title: Outside-in compression: scaling MOQT for high capacity ingest
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
Forgive the Pied Piper Reference. The purpose of this issue is to initiate a design discussion around making MOQT efficient for many-to-one distribution. 

Much of the preceding design of MOQT assumes either few-to-few (e.g. video conferencing) or one-to-many (live sports) distribution. We can leverage caching to enable scalable egress, combined with a fan-out architecture for non-cacheable real-time content. 

But what about the use-case of "fan-in" - millions of sensors providing real-time telemetry to a single monitoring point? In this case, caching does no good from a scale perspective, as the content is only ever going to one subscriber. The fan-out architecture works in reverse to collapse all upstream data onto downstream pipes. 

What features do we need in MOQT to make high capacity ingest efficient?:
1. We want a way for a publisher to signal to all relays that a track should not be cached. Currently the MAX CACHE DURATION Parameter can only be present in a SUBSCRIBE_OK, FETCH_OK or TRACK_STATUS message. It cannot be sent by a publisher. Setting the DELIVERY TIMEOUT Parameter to zero is not equivalent to do-not-cache. 
2. Keep-alives for long running sessions. Imagine a security camera that sends sparse data once every 5min. We can rely on application level pings to keep the connection alive, or should web build in a mechanism into the protocol to keep connections alive (with auth protection so untrusted clients cannot keep connections open forever). 
3. Can the central collectors use the relays as configurable filters? What if we do want to leverage the cache to "batch" the collection of telemetry? For example, sensors output temperature data every second, but the collector only wants to retrieve the last 5mi of data every 5min. We could create a FORWARD_FILTER Parameter which the subscriber can send during subscription, which specifies a key parameter and a threshold value. For example, I subscribe only to objects for which the "foo" parameter is > 10. 
4. Much telemetry data is timeline-based. Can we have a standard mode in which a track is identified as a timeline and make sure that works efficiently for our major actions (SUBSCRIBE, FETCH etc). Is setting each group number to be a millisecond epoch timestamp sufficiently robust? 
5. Publisher authentication and authorization: is our current token scheme sufficient for high-capacity ingest?
6. End-to-end encryption: we allow the payload to be encrypted, but is this sufficient for sensitive IoT data at city-wide scale?

What else might be important for high-capacity ingest that we can address now before we fail at scale? 

Cheers
Will

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
For 2, my own experiences on keep alive in various shapes would lean towards doing nothing in the protocol itself and leave this for the application layer to drive it (or alternatively, implementation-defined choices)

QUIC negotaties connection idle times and silent close for various reasons, including saving batteries. Even in cases where there are NATS, the nature of QUIC lends itself to "quiet" connections. 

Furthermore, session resumption and possibly 0-RTT is a general solution to avoid needing to keep active state. I don't know off hand how well that works for WebTransport and MoQ given all the bootstrapping needed. comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
In general, I'd like to push as much of this as possible to either applications of moqt or extensions, rather than the base protocol.

1) - MAX_CACHE_DURATION should be allowed in PUBLISH, see #1071
2) See #805, which is related.  I'm mostly inclined to +1 Lucas and let applications solve timeouts at the QUIC layer, though I wonder if that works for browsers.
3) Relays can only filter or batch objects on moqt metadata - group ID, object ID, etc.  Maybe filter/batch are a good extension candidates; if you don't understand the extension, it doesn't _break_ it's just less performant.
4) I don't think any changes are required to moqt for applications that want to use timestamps as group IDs?
5) I'm not an auth expert - do you foresee challenges with the current scheme?
6) I'm not sure what you are driving at -- do you want to preclude e2e encryption for these cases to get more relay functionality?  If so, then it sounds like you are designing a republisher rather than a relay, since the opacity of payloads to relays is fundamental to moqt.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
So for [3] I propose a new FILTER parameter on SUBSCRIBE. It works numerically, because the majority of filter operations are either natively numeric, or can be cast to be  numeric. It takes 3 arguments
1. The operator : one of >, >=, <, <=, =, !=o
2. The operand: one of groupID, object ID, or a extension header ID.
3. The threshold value 

The extension ID must point at an extension header with an even type i.e one with a single integer value. It allows applications to supply custom data in an extension header and then filter on that.

Examples:
1. Only forward me the first object in every group
FILTER ( =, object ID, 0 )

2. Only forward me Group IDs larger than 1752138462
FILTER ( >, group ID, 1752138462)

3. Only forward me security camera groups where the activity level is greater than or equal to 25%. The activity level is added to each object as the custom extension with a type of 400.
FILTER (>=, extension 400, 25)

4. Only forward me temperature data from zip code 94925. The zip code is stored as the custom extension header 1444.
FILTER (=, extension 1444, 94925)

5. Only forward me log data from the media player with subscriber ID 847362511. The subscriber ID is sent in extension header  768 by the media player. 
FILTER (=, extension 768, 847362511)

One detail to work out is where the filtering happens. Ideally we want it to happen at the edge, to prevent unwanted traffic from moving through the network. One consequence of this is that the subscriptions with different filters MUST NOT be aggregated. Imagine a publisher producing  a track and three subscribers on the other side of the network, issuing subscriptions with filters, one for groups < 1000, the other for groups > 1000 and the third for groups > 2000.  The edge relay will receive 3 subscriptions for the same track. The first two are mutually exclusive, however the second two, for groups numbers > 2000, result in duplicate traffic being forwarded. This duplication is acceptable, as attempting to decide which subscriptions are children of others would be fragile and unstable if a parent subscription suddenly disappears. Additionally in practice subscribers within a real-world application would likely apply non-overlapping filters.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> @wilaw is this proposal different from https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/441


Hmm, forgot I wrote #441 :). So yes, #441 proposes only an Object filter (which I still think is valuable). This current proposal allows you to filter on object IDs, but also on groups IDs as well as extension headers, which I think has greater utility. To combine the two, we could use the range convention in place of the threshold value and also remove the operand, as its implicit in how we define our range.

So FILTERv2 has two arguments

1. The operand: one of groupID, object ID, or a extension header ID.
2. An array of values, with the following meaning

[0] - only send items with a value of 0
[0,5] - only send items with an value of 0 or 5.
[0..5] - only send items  in the range 0 to 5 inclusive.
[0..2, 16..20] - only send items in the range 0 to 5 inclusive, or 16..20 inclusive.
[5..] - only send items >= 5
[..5]  - only send items <= 5

1. Only forward me the first object in every group
FILTER ( object ID, [0] )

2. Only forward me Group IDs larger than 1752138462
FILTER ( group ID, [1752138462..])

3. Only forward me security camera groups where the activity level is greater than or equal to 25%. The activity level is added to each object as the custom extension with a type of 400.
FILTER (extension 400, [25..])

4. Only forward me temperature data from zip codes 94925 and 23554. The zip codes are stored as the custom extension header 1444.
FILTER (extension 1444, [94925,23554])

5. Only forward me log data from the media player with subscriber ID 847362511, 657372 and 8251132 The subscriber ID is sent in extension header 768 by the media player.

issues.title: Why not use request ID in UNANNOUNCE and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Indexing ANNOUNCE_OK and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL by request ID means that I need to keep a map of outgoing ANNOUNCEs by request ID.

If UNANNOUNCE and ANNOUNCE_CANCEL still use Track Namespace, then I have to also keep a map by namespace.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: This is especially annoying if UNANNOUNCE comes immediately after ANNOUNCE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Previously discussed in #978 

The reasoning is that UNANNOUNCE would withdraw all announcements for a given namespace.  eg: 

ANNOUNCE a, id=1
ANNOUNCE a, id=2
UNANNOUNCE a

should leave you in a state with no announcements, especially since there is no ANNOUNCE_UPDATE and the second ANNOUNCE may be refreshing auth?

I went back and forth on ANNOUNCE_CANCEL, but ultimately decided the same reasoning applied.

P->S: ANNOUNCE a, id=1
S->P: ANNOUNCE_OK
P->S: ANNOUNCE a, id=2
S->P: ANNOUNCE_CANCEL a

If I squint there's a case that the second ANNOUNCE and the CANCEL are racing, and then the subscriber sends ANNOUNCE_OK id=2.  The publisher may be left in an awkward state.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: OK, SGTM

issues.title: Is it a protocol error to get ANNOUNCE_CANCEL before ANNOUNCE_OK/ANNOUNCE_ERROR?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
A well-behaved subscriber should not do this.

allowing ANNOUNCE_CANCEL first makes the state machine more complicated.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
A scenario where a publisher is re-announcing at the same time the subscriber is cancelling looks like this - eg:

```
P: ANNOUNCE ns=a, id=1
S: ANNOUCE_OK id=1
...
P: ANNOUNCE ns=a, id=3   and S: ANNOUNCE_CANCEL ns=a
```

I think we can say that the subscriber must also ANNOUNCE_OK or ERROR id=3 (we probably already say this), so in effect, the cancel doesn't apply to pending ANNOUNCE.

So to answer your question, if there are no _established_ ANNOUNCE's, then ANNOUNCE_CANCEL can be a protocol violation.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I guess the bigger question is whether there's any limitation on duplicate PUBLISH_NAMESPACE besides the request ID. Is there a use case to send PUBLISH_NAMESPACE for the same namespaces once a second, without ever sending PN_DONE?

And similarly, should the same overlap rules from SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE apply? Can I publish a, a/b, and a/b/c without withdrawing any of those?

And if the answer is they can overlap, then what does PN_CANCEL a/b do in the above example?

I don't have a use-case driven answer to these questions, though as an implementer it's easier to reason about if the namespace tree always has the same restrictions, which means only one PN can be outstanding for a namespace at one time.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I was going to write a PR, but I don't know what to write. Is this really "Needs PR?"

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
So in my above example, the publisher sent another PN for the same namespace while there was one open, to refresh the auth.  I don't know if that's real or not.  I suppose it could PN_DONE/PN, but that would cause downstream churn.  Do we need PN_UPDATE (please say no)?

> And similarly, should the same overlap rules from SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE apply? Can I publish a, a/b, and a/b/c without withdrawing any of those?

The overlapping rules are there to prevent duplicate PN being forwarded to the same subscriber, though I guess that could be resolved through other means.  So I don't think we need to prevent overlapping PNs.

> And if the answer is they can overlap, then what does PN_CANCEL a/b do in the above example?

I think CANCEL is an exact match (cancel a does not cancel a/b or a/b/c).

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Don't we still have the duplicate PN problem? If PNs arrive at the relay from multiple upstreams, or even a single upstream sends several of them for the same namespace.

Maybe I don't understand the duplicate PN restriction.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
From Toronto:

Yes, this type of thing would be a protocol error for SUBSCRIBE, and it's preventable, so it should be a protocol error for ANNOUNCE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
```mermaid

stateDiagram-v2 
    [*] --> Idle: Initial state
    Idle --> Pending: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (pub)
    Pending --> Established: REQUEST_OK (sub)
    Pending --> Terminated: REQUEST_ERROR (sub)
    Pending --> Terminated: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE (pub)
    Established --> Terminated: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_CANCEL (sub)
    Established --> Terminated: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE (pub)
```

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This is also tied to #1267

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: See #1329.  If merged, the answer be YES it's a protocol error to give CANCEL before OK/ERROR.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: If we're going the #1389 way, this will become moot.  Parking pending resolution there.

issues.title: EndOfTrack is unenforceable
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
9.2.1.1 says

> 0x4 := Indicates end of Track. GroupID is either the largest group produced in this track and the ObjectID is one greater than the largest object produced in that group, or GroupID is one greater than the largest group produced in this track and the ObjectID is zero. This status also indicates the last group has ended. An object with this status that has a Group ID less than any other GroupID, or an ObjectID less than or equal to the largest in the specified group, is a protocol error, and the receiver MUST terminate the session. This SHOULD be cached.

The problem is, of course, that there is no assured way to know the largest group produced in the track in non-FETCH situations. I think it would be better to say original publishers SHOULD do that, and receivers MUST throw an error if its Location is lower than any location observed.

If Group IDs are not increasing, that's also an issue.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think we can say publishers MUST NOT publish objects with Locations past end of track.  The subscriber handling here may already be covered in malformed tracks, which is just a track error not a protocol / session terminating error.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Agreed

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Except that in the random Group ID case, I don't know that it's even true. 

If it were me, I'd forbid EndOfTrack objects when group IDs are not increasing. But there are other ways to handle this?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm not sure how you ever use END_OF_TRACK in multi-publisher without some out-of-band coordination.  I think we can add the MUST in there and let the multi-publisher endpoints figure out how to comply.

issues.title: Omitting Extension Header Length is a subtle API change
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
If the subgroup ID is zero, or the first object ID, the relevant bits of the subgroup stream type can be determined on the fly for each hop.

However, to omit the extension header lengths from a stream, I have to know that all objects in the stream will not have extension headers. AFAICT consistent presence of extensions in a subgroup is not a requirement in the object model.

So either:
1) Relay MOQT framers ~never omit the extension header length in a subgroup;
2) There is a new sending API parameter "will never use extensions" when delivering an object for a new subgroup.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Yes, in order to take advantage of the compression, your `beginSubgroup` API needs a flag indicating if you plan to use extensions in that subgroup.  If you are unsure, pass true.

Is there a change you are asking for in the document?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
This is a subtle thing for relay design -- part of the stream type has to be carried over from inbound to outbound. It might be good to explicitly say so in the relay section.

Architecturally, it's a bit odd for the application to be this involved in a compression decision, but it's where we are.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Something like:

If a relay receives a subgroup header indicating no extensions are present, it really ought to preserve this when forwarding downstream, assuming it doesn't add its own extensions.

Is it worth it?

issues.title: Disallow USE_ALIAS and DELETE auth token ops in CLIENT_SETUP
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
USE_ALIAS doesn't make sense, since there can't be any previous aliases, except those earlier in the same message.

DELETE doesn't make sense either, since you can only have just registered this alias in the same message.  Since the client can send REGISTER without knowing the server's size, allowing DELETE makes it complicated for the client reconcile the cache state is, for example:

Server's cache size=100
```
REGISTER x, size=100 -> registered
REGISTER y, size=100 -> converted to USE_VALUE
DELETE x
REGISTER z, size=100 -> success
```

Without DELETE, the client can just set the known size and evict based on LIFO.

Another option is to make the rule more generic - disallow USE_ALIAS or DELETE in the same parameter set that REGISTERs an alias.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Another option is to make the rule more generic - disallow USE_ALIAS or DELETE in the same parameter set that REGISTERs an alias.

This is tricky to verify in non-setup without keeping a bunch of state, because some patterns are ok, eg:

```
SUBSCRIBE:
Auth Token: Use Alias=1
Auth Token: Delete Alias=1
Auth Token: Register Alias=1, Token=y
```

I think the simplest call is forbid USE_ALIAS and DELETE in CLIENT_SETUP only.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
In Toronto:

Agree that it's wise to forbid USE_ALIAS and DELETE in CLIENT_SETUP.

issues.title: How to Achieve Low-Latency Subscriptions for Pre-Configured Tracks?
issues.author: Sy0307
issues.body:
## Background

In our production environment, we have a strong requirement for extremely low-latency media delivery using MOQT.

Our previous implementation, based on an earlier draft (`draft-04`/`draft-05`), was very efficient. The client could specify a `track_alias` within the `SUBSCRIBE` message itself. This allowed the client to begin sending media data immediately after sending the `SUBSCRIBE` request, without waiting for a response. The flow was:

1.  `Client -> Server: SUBSCRIBE (with client-defined track_alias)`
2.  `Client -> Server: Media Data (starts immediately)`

Edited: this flow has a little mistake.

The right flow should be:

```
Client -> Server: PUBLISH (with client-defined track_alias)
Client <- Server: Media Data (Server starts to push media data immediately)
```

However, in the more recent drafts, the `track_alias` has been removed from the `SUBSCRIBE` message. It is now assigned by the server and returned in the `SUBSCRIBE_OK` message.

---

## The Core Problem: Mandatory RTT for SUBSCRIBE_OK

The fundamental issue is that the client **must now wait for the `SUBSCRIBE_OK` message** before it can send any media data. This is because the client needs to learn the `track_alias` that the server has assigned for the track.

This requirement introduces a full round-trip time (RTT) of latency that did not exist in the previous flow. For low-latency applications, this additional RTT is a significant performance bottleneck.

The new flow is:

1.  `Client -> Server: SUBSCRIBE`
2.  *(Client must wait...)*
3.  `Server -> Client: SUBSCRIBE_OK (with server-assigned track_alias)`
4.  `Client -> Server: Media Data (can only start now)`

---

## Our Use Case

In our specific use case, the available tracks are **fixed and known in advance** by both the client and the server. We do not require the flexibility of dynamic track announcements at connection time. We are willing to trade this flexibility for lower setup latency.

---

## Question for the MOQ Working Group

Given this context, we would like to ask for guidance on the recommended best practice for achieving the lowest possible subscription latency:

1.  Is there a mechanism in the current specification to accommodate use cases with pre-configured tracks to avoid the mandatory `SUBSCRIBE_OK` wait?
2.  Could a client, in a scenario with known tracks, start sending data immediately after the `SUBSCRIBE` message, perhaps using a pre-agreed `track_alias` or another identifier?
3.  Are there any other established patterns or best practices for minimizing this initial setup RTT that we might be overlooking?

Thank you for your time and consideration.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
```
Client -> Server: SUBSCRIBE (with client-defined track_alias)
Client -> Server: Media Data (starts immediately)
```

This flow is not correct.  The entity sending SUBSCRIBE should be _receiving_ the media, not sending it.  What you want here is PUBLISH, which has a publisher defined Track Alias.

So the low-latency flow is:

```
Client -> Server: PUBLISH (with client-defined track_alias)
Client -> Server: Media Data (starts immediately)
```

comments.author: Sy0307
comments.body:
Sorry, there's an error pointed to by the arrow. It should actually be like this.

```
Client -> Server: PUBLISH (with client-defined track_alias)
Client <- Server: Media Data (Server starts to push media data immediately)
```

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Ah, in that case, the client still uses SUBSCRIBE and the server sends SUBSCRIBE_OK and begins publishing. Because the control stream has higher priority, the Track Alias will be known at the client before data arrives unless there is packet loss. The client needs to buffer unknown alias streams/datagrams for a “brief period” to allow QUIC to repair losses.

If your application has a fixed set of tracks, you can also use fixed Track Alias values to avoid buffering.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @Sy0307 does the above work for you?

comments.body: It seems to work for me. I need to put it into practice later. But you can close this issue now. Thank you :D

issues.title: End of Group flag in Subgroup/Datagram Header creates new ways to malform a track
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Header indicates Contains End of Group and

1) subgroup contains no objects and ends with a FIN -- cannot determine EOG Object ID
2) subgroup/datagram ends with an object with status = Object Does Not Exist

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: How would people feel about changing the end-of-group flag in the header to mean there's an implicit END_OF_GROUP object with ID = <last object id> + 1?  That at least fixes the second malformed case above, and allows for more symmetric APIs with cases where the EOG is explicitly vs implicitly sent.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
The current design creates unfetchable objects and adds unacceptable latency to implementations. IMO changing the definition to mean there is an additional object with ID + 1 and EndOfGroup is imperative.

1) There is no way to express an object with non-normal status and a payload in a FETCH stream, so these objects cannot be delivered by FETCH.

2) The current design adds latency.  On a subgroup stream that contains EndOfGroup, a receiver cannot deliver an object to the upper layer until it either receives a byte from the next object header, or a FIN, because until then it doesn't know the status of the received object.

issues.title: Unlimited ANNOUNCE spam prevention?
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body: From my reading of the spec, it looks like an endpoint could send ANNOUNCEs for any number of namespaces. Relays would be required to store the mappings, possibly forever. A flood of bogus namespaces could bloat data structures on a relay that store namespace tables. Are there any protections in the spec against this?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: The number of announces is limited to the maximum request ID sent by the relay

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
The maximum total length of a Full Track Name is 4096 bytes, so the maximum amount of additional memory an endpoint could exert on a relay due to announces would be on the order of (available_request_ids * 4096) bytes. Do we want a separate limit for the per-session sum of lengths of announced namespaces, or do we just want a relay to protect against this by appropriately setting the MAX_REQUEST_ID that they advertise at any point of time?

Is there potentially a case where a relay may want to set a large MAX_REQUEST_ID to allow for a large flight of initial requests, but at the same time protect against a peer using all of those request ids to just announce a bunch of bogus namespaces?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
ANNOUNCE is also supposed to carry authorization credentials which the relay will validate.  I imagine relays could also have application specific policies (eg: rate limits or other resource limits).

We should at least mention this in the security considerations.

We could also add a MoQT specific prevention - a limit on the number of active announcements, or announcement related data.  Note this also applies to PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, but not SUBSCRIBE or TRACK_STATUS.

issues.title: Relay security consideration: SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE with a short prefix
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body:
If an entity sends a relay a SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE message with a short prefix, it can cause the relay to send a lot of ANNOUNCE messages. As churn continues in the tree of prefixes being announced/unannounced, the relay would have to continue to send ANNOUNCE/UNANNOUNCE messages to the entity that had sent the SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.

I was thinking of adding some text in the "Security Considerations" section in order to encourage Relay implementations to have protections in place for this. For instance, by only allowing SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE messages to more specific prefixes. Thoughts?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think authorization is key here - subscribing to something close to the root of a large tree is bad.  I think production relays might have namespaces like 

conference.com / meetings / <id> / participants / <id> / …

The relay would set authorization rules such that SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE would only succeed under a particular meeting or lower. No one can SN to all meetings.


Some security consideration text is warranted.

issues.title: Prefix matching under specified
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
The current draft states:

> Prefix matching is used to determine which publishers receive a SUBSCRIBE or which subscribers receive a PUBLISH. For example, a SUBSCRIBE namespace=(foo,bar), track=x message will be forwarded to the sessions that sent ANNOUNCE namespace=(foo) and ANNOUNCE namespace=(foo, bar) respectively, but not one that sent ANNOUNCE namespace=(foobar).

This does not indicate if a match can be achieved where the prefix is not a contiguous tuple field . This seems to be an assumption of the draft but it is not explicitly stated.  Traditional prefix matching allows a left-side match but has no requirement that what is being matched is a complete tuple field. 

For example, if there is an ANNOUNCE namespace=(firstfield,secondfield), then do the following subscriptions match?

SUBSCRIBE namespace=(firstfield)
SUBSCRIBE namespace=(first)
SUBSCRIBE namespace=(firstfield,second)
SUBSCRIBE namespace=(first,second)
SUBSCRIBE namespace=(f,s)

When we say "prefix matching" do we instead mean that there must be an "exact match" for each tuple field, starting from the left?

issues.title: Track switching at the live edge using MOQT's current messages?
issues.author: tobbee
issues.body:
Here I  want to raise the question how one can possibly make a clean switch between two synchronized
tracks with MOQT's present (draft-13) means using SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, possibly
enhanced with priorities between tracks.

What I want to achieve is a seamless switch between track A and track B without gaps or parallel 
sending of objects representing the same media content, in particular at the live edge; 
a typical ABR case, but it could also be a switch between audio languages at the same bitrate.

I know that there are som open issues about ABR and collaboration between server and client (#44, #259).

When discussing the track switch process with Gwendal Simon and Will Law,  we found issues and tried to solve
them with track priorities. However, we arrived at opposite priorities. The reason was that we looked at
two different problematic cases.

Our current understanding is therefore that there is something lacking. The purpose of this issue
is to start a discussion and possibly confirm the issue, before discussing possible additions to
arrive at a good solution..


## Base case: Switching in the future at specified group start

Switching at a future group boundary should in general be problem-free.

If we know that group X+1 starts in the future, there should be no problem to send 
`SUBSCRIBE B absolute start location={X+1,0}`, and `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A range end_group=X+1`
(sending up to the end of group X) at the same time. Ideally, the client should also have sent a 
`SUBSCRIBE B forward=0` to warm up the relay beforehand (the same is true for the cases discussed below as well.
Subscribing to multiple tracks for switching was also discussed in #259.

## Switching at the live edge

However, switching at the live edge may be problematic.

At the live edge, the subscriber cannot know the optimal start group value, and to switch "immediately" we think it is best that
 the subscriber sends `SUBSCRIBE B next_group` and uses the returned `SUBSCRIBE_OK largest_location group=X+1`
to send a  `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A range end_group=X+1` to stop the subscription of track A at the end of group X.

The outcome may go one of three ways, listed below, and with sequence diagrams further down:

1. *Good case*: With very short RTT, and no congestion, this type of track switch normally works well. 
    I have that up and running in my code.
2. *Late update case*: If the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE arrives late, the relay starts sending group X+1 of 
      both track A and B. For this group, track B is more important, so to improve the case, 
      track B should be prioritzed (lower priority value)
3. *Congestion case*: If instead the relay is slow in sending track A (e.g. due to congestion), it may still 
     be sending "track A group X" at the same time as it receives the SUBSCRIBE B request and starts
     sending "track B group X+1". To improve the situation and finish sendiing group X track A, before 
    "track B group X+1", track A should be prioritized.

Thus to make the parallel sending of track A and B as problemfree as possible we need opposite priorities in case 2 and 3.
In general, this overlap should be transient, so after that, the priority of the new track should be changed to the same
as the previous track in order to avoid an accumulated staircase of monontonically changing priorities.
It thus seems like changing priorities is neither helpful, nor desired.

Below are the same three cases as sequence diagrams.

### Sequence Diagrams

#### Good Case: Optimal Switching

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Subscriber
    participant Relay
    participant TrackA
    participant TrackB

    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Track A is delivering group X

    TrackA->>Relay: Group X objects
    Relay->>Subscriber: Group X objects (Track A)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE B next_group
    Relay->>Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE_OK B (largest_location: group=X+1)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A (end_group=X+1)
    
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Clean handoff - no overlap or gap
    
    TrackB->>Relay: Group X+1 objects
    Relay->>Subscriber: Group X+1 objects (Track B)
```

#### Bad Case 1: Late SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE

Here SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A arrives after the Relay should
have stopped sending track A.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Subscriber
    participant Relay
    participant TrackA
    participant TrackB

    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Track A delivering group X

    TrackA->>Relay: Group X objects
    Relay->>Subscriber: Group X objects (Track A)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE B next_group
    Relay->>Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE_OK B (largest_location: group=X+1)
    
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A end_group=X+1 arrives late
    
    par Both tracks start group X+1
        TrackA->>Relay: Group X+1 objects
        Relay->>Subscriber: Group X+1 objects (Track A)
    and
        TrackB->>Relay: Group X+1 objects  
        Relay->>Subscriber: Group X+1 objects (Track B)
    end
    
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: PROBLEM: Duplicate content sent
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Improvement: Track B should have higher priority (lower value)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A (end_group=X+1)
```

#### Bad Case 2: Slow Track A Delivery

Here track A is delayed, likely due to congestion or bandwidth limitation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Subscriber
    participant Relay
    participant TrackA
    participant TrackB

    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Track A slow/congested, still sending group X

    TrackA->>Relay: Group X objects
    Note over Relay: Queue: Group X Track A (congested)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE B next_group
    Relay->>Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE_OK B (largest_location: group=X+1)
    
    Subscriber->>Relay: SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE A (end_group=X+1)
    
    
    par Overlap: Different groups
        Relay->>Subscriber: Group X objects (Track A - from queue)
        TrackA->>Relay: Group X+1 objects
    and
        TrackB->>Relay: Group X+1 objects
        Relay->>Subscriber: Group X+1 objects (Track B)
    end
    
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: Want Track A group X objects sent before Track B group X+1 objects
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: PROBLEM: Track A group X interleaved with Track B group X+1
    Note over Subscriber, TrackB: SOLUTION: Track A should have higher priority (lower value)

```

## Solutions?

In summary, we have not found a reliable consistent way of switching between two tracks at the live edge.

Priorities is as far as we have found, not enough to remedy these issues.

It should be possible to achieve an experimental setup to verify that the tricky cases above can really happen,
and possibly experiment with extensions to solve this.

However, if there already is a solution to how to achieve a consistent track switch, I am very much interested
in learning that first?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:

Assuming Group IDs are aligned (ie: WARP), you can send the SUBSCRIBE+SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE at the same time with an explicit Group ID in the future.  In this case, you can always prioritize the existing Subscription (A) over the new one. I do think Server-side ABR is an interesting topic and there are opportunities to improve that, but I believe this issue was filed with Client Side ABR in mind?

issues.title: Delivery timeout, Datagrams, and Caching
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
The draft is quite clear that even if the forwarding preference is Datagram, the Delivery Timeout applies:
> "The start time for the timeout is based on when the beginning of the Object is received, and does not depend upon the forwarding preference."

So if I have no delivery timeout, I expect to get all the Objects.  But then there's text about how a datagram might be dropped along the path if a hop doesn't have sufficient MTU.  Of course publishers will try to avoid that, but this feels like a "You'll get all the Objects, except you might not and you'll never know what."

I expect this to create challenges for caches, unless publishers are very good at indicating all Object ID gaps, Group ID gaps, and end of Group.

I'll note this also means I can have (almost) fully reliable Datagram subscriptions and fully unreliable Subgroup subscriptions.  Both are quite implementable, but if that's the case, why have a Datagram forwarding preference at all?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm not sure exactly what change you are asking for in this issue, and how it relates to the title.

A "fully reliable datagram subscription" would require a QUIC stack that supports retransmission of datagrams, which is rare, and I don't think we want to make this a requirement (yes, I know Google's can do this).

I think it's known that with DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, subgroups can be dropped or reset, but when it's not present, the intention is that you will get everything or your subscription will be dropped with TOO_FAR_BEHIND.  Don't use datagrams or delivery timeout if you want to get everything.

> why have a Datagram forwarding preference at all?

I think folks have made it clear that the three properties of a datagram (< MTU, not flow controlled, not retransmitted) are ideal for audio, which is part of the core MOQT use case.  That said, I've started to wonder why we still disallow mixing and matching subgroups and datagrams within a single Track.  My implementation does not enforce this requirement on the sender or receiver.  In MOQT the currency is Objects, and as long as you respect the per-object Forwarding Preference at Relays, nothing will break.  Someone approached me in Madrid asking specifically for relaxing this restriction (Huawei?). 

Does anyone have a strong reason to disallow mixing and matching?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: In discussion, there was also disagreement about whether Datagrams are ever retransmitted at any point in the path, particularly if there's a long or no delivery timeout.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> I think folks have made it clear that the three properties of a datagram (< MTU, not flow controlled, not retransmitted) are ideal for audio, which is part of the core MOQT use case. That said, I've started to wonder why we still disallow mixing and matching subgroups and datagrams within a single Track. My implementation does not enforce this requirement on the sender or receiver. In MOQT the currency is Objects, and as long as you respect the per-object Forwarding Preference at Relays, nothing will break. Someone approached me in Madrid asking specifically for relaxing this restriction (Huawei?).
> 
> Does anyone have a strong reason to disallow mixing and matching?

Currently, Forwarding Preference is a track-level, always-implicitly-derived property, determined by the Original Publisher. To allow mixing and matching per-object, then it needs to be changed to be an object-level, explicitly-signalled property. On the other hand, even to allow mixing and matching, is it needed to be as fine-grained as object-level, as switching the object transport modes between Subgroup Streams and Datagrams might be heavy in that case; it is probably sufficient to be at group-level.

No, it can continue to be implicitly signaled on a per-object basis -- you send it like you received it, except FETCH obviously.

> it is probably sufficient to be at group-level.

issues.title: Clarify hop-by-hop nature of track_alias when going through a relay
issues.author: lminiero
issues.body:
While implementing the changes for draft -12 and -13 to add support for `PUBLISH` and publisher-originated values for `track_alias` in both `PUBLISH` and `SUBSCRIBE`, I got confused on how to handle the case of a subscriber subscribing to different tracks of different publishers where both might decide to use the same `track_alias` value. Intuitively I understood this meant that, through a relay, `track_alias` was meant to be a hop-by-hop property (meaning that whatever `track_alias` the publisher chooses, it might not be the one a subscriber may actually see), but the draft is currently silent on that. The only reference to what a relay is supposed to do with `track_alias` is in section 7.3:

> Relays use the Track Alias ([Section 9.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13#track-alias)) of an incoming Object to identify its track and find the active subscribers. Relays MUST forward Objects to matching subscribers in accordance to each subscription's priority, group order, and delivery timeout.

but that only addresses how to handle incoming objects from a publisher from a demultiplexing perspective, and not what happens to `track_alias` when negotiating subscriptions. Discussing this on the MoQ slack channel, it looks like text existed to clarify that but was then removed as part of #977.

IMHO some text should be added back, since as it is the draft is silent, if not ambiguous, on this, which makes the spec incomplete for those interested in implementing a relay. I got confused as a developer, and good chances are others will too, meaning that some text, even if minimal, to address the potential hop-by-hop nature of the property should be there, otherwise the RFC won't be enough for people to implement the spec, as they'd need to dig up external resources to be aware of caveats (which is probably not what we want).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Text from an earlier version of the PR to consider:

```
Though a Track Alias is only required to be unique within a single session,
Publishers MAY set Track Alias to a more unique (possibly globally unique)
identifier for the Track.  Relays SHOULD assign the Track Alias received in an
upstream SUBSCRIBE_OK to downstream subscriptions for the same track. Since
subscribers can request Tracks from uncoordinated publishers through a single
relay session, it is not always possible to reuse the upstream Track Alias.
```

issues.title: What are the rules for overlapping prefixes in UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE is very clear that overlapping prefixes are prohibited.

UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE is not as carefully described.

Say a node is subscribed to namespaces a/b/c and a/b/d.

1) Clearly, it can send UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE for a/b/c and/or a/b/d.

2) Can it send UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE for a/b and remove both?

3) Can it send UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE a/b/c/e and thus retain a subscription for a/b/c except for a/b/c/e.  I would guess not!

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
From section 5.1: An UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE withdraws a previous SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.

The wording is “withdraws **a previous** SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE”, i.e. it is meant to cancel one specific, already-existing subscription. Because overlaps are disallowed at subscription time, the set of active namespace subscriptions on a connection is a set of disjoint prefixes.

Applying this to your examples,
- It can't send UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE for a/b, because there is no active subscription for exactly a/b
- It can't send UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE for a/b/c/e because no active namespace subscription has the exact prefix a/b/c/e

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: I think it would be better to clearly spell that out that overlapping prefixes are also prohibited for UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, in similar wording as for SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
From Toronto:

People felt that the UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE should be paired with the SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE via request ID, so if you want to end two SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACEs, you need to send two UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACEs.

> Objects within a Group are ordered numerically by their Object ID.

comments.body:
> I guess the intent was to say "ordered numerically, ascending and without gaps, by their Object ID values". 

That is not the intent. The intent is to say that, within a group, Object IDs can be compared numerically to determine an ordering.  Object IDs are compared numerically when matching filters, assembling FETCH responses and as a priority tiebreaker for datagrams.

I could not figure out what the final part, i.e., "or a more generic set including that namespace" means in the context. Any clarification would be appreciated. And whatever the clarification is, it might be good to have the clarification done in the text in the next version of the draft.
