issues.title: Clarifications likely needed for "SHOULD report this to the application" in Section 5.2
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 5.2 incudes the following two paragraphs:

> An endpoint SHOULD NOT, however, send an ANNOUNCE advertising a namespace that exactly matches a namespace for which the peer sent an earlier ANNOUNCE (i.e. an ANNOUNCE ought not to be echoed back to its sender).
> 
> The receiver of an ANNOUNCE_OK or ANNOUNCE_ERROR SHOULD report this to the application to inform the search for additional subscribers for a namespace, or abandoning the attempt to publish under this namespace. This might be especially useful in upload or chat applications. A subscriber MUST send exactly one ANNOUNCE_OK or ANNOUNCE_ERROR in response to an ANNOUNCE. The publisher SHOULD close the session with a protocol error if it receives more than one.

There are two possible minor issues herein:

1. Is the word "this" in "SHOULD report this to the application ..." in the 2nd paragraph referring to that an ANNOUNCE was echoed back to its sender? In any case, it might be better to clarify in the text.
2. It seems that "abandoning" in "or abandoning the attempt to publish under this namespace" in the 2nd paragraph should be "abandon".

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
In that sentence, “this” refers to the outcome conveyed by the message that was just received — i.e.:
• If an ANNOUNCE_OK was received, “this” is the fact that the announce operation for that namespace succeeded.
• If an ANNOUNCE_ERROR was received, “this” is the fact that the announce operation for that namespace failed and the accompanying error information.
So the implementation should pass that success-or-failure result (along with any associated details such as error code or reason) up to the application layer, enabling the application either to look for other potential subscribers (after success) or to give up/try a different strategy (after failure).

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
Thanks @sharmafb! I see. It should be better to make it clearer, e.g., by changing "this" to "the reception", or changing the entire sentence to be like the following:

An endpoint SHOULD report the reception of an ANNOUNCE_OK or ANNOUNCE_ERROR to the application to inform the search for additional subscribers for a namespace, or to abandon the attempt to publish under this namespace.

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body: Yeah, that would work. You could submit a PR.

issues.title: Possible issues in handling of objects when subscriber priority is changed
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 6.2 includes the following:

> When subscriber priority is changed, a best effort SHOULD be made to apply the change to all objects that have not been sent, but it is implementation dependent what happens to objects that have already been received and possibly scheduled.

The first half of the sentence talks about handling of objects that have not been **sent**, but the second half of the sentence talks about object that have already been "received" and possibly scheduled. Was the word "received" intended to be "sent"? Also, the second half including "possibly scheduled" seems a bit inconsistent with the first half.

Would it be an improvement to change the entire sentence to be as follows?
> When subscriber priority is changed, a best effort SHOULD be made to apply the change to all objects that have not been sent **and have not been scheduled**, but it is implementation dependent what happens to objects that have already been sent **or scheduled**.

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
I believe that “Received” is intentional.

At the moment the subscriber changes its priority, the node can be dealing with three classes of objects:

1. Objects it has not yet obtained at all (they have not been “received” by this node). Those obviously have not been sent either. For them the node can trivially apply the new priority.
2. Objects it has already obtained/​ingested (“received”) from upstream or from the application, but that it has not yet put on the wire toward the subscriber. Some of these may already sit in the QUIC library’s send buffers or be in the node’s local scheduling queue (“possibly scheduled”).
3. Objects that have already left the node and are on their way to – or have arrived at – the subscriber. Those are beyond the node’s control.

The first half of the sentence talks about class 1 (objects “not been sent” yet); the second half talks about class 2 (objects the node has received and may already have placed in its own scheduler). Whether a particular implementation is willing or able to reshuffle that already-queued traffic is left open (“implementation dependent”).

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
@sharmafb Thanks!

A clarification question on item 1: For objects the (receiving) node has not yet received, how could it apply the new priority? Isn't (the first half of) the sentence talking about the sending node applying the new priority to those objects the sending node has not yet sent out thus it can apply the new priority?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think the use of "received" is a little awkward because it's considering a relay or proxy (eg the objects being set are ones received from elsewhere) rather than a generic publisher.  Since the entire section is about _scheduling_ objects to be sent, I think it should be:

>  but it is implementation dependent what happens to objects that have already been _scheduled_.

We might benefit from some ancillary cleanup related to what it means to be scheduled and reconcile that with language in the next section (algorithm) that instead talks about "sent first" -- I think we intend these to be synonymous.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
Making two aspects clearer would probably be greatly helpful, as the confusion came from therein:
1. Make it clear that this is talking about a relay or proxy.
2. Make sure the word "sent", "received", or "scheduled", whenever used, is used to describe something done by the relay or proxy.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: To be clear, I'd like to remove any references to proxies/relays in the priority section, since that applies to any publisher.

issues.body:
Section 8.2.1.2 (DELIVERY TIMEOUT Parameter) includes the following sentence: 

> However, if **neither the subscriber or publisher specify** DELIVERY TIMEOUT, all Objects in the track matching the subscription filter are delivered as indicated by their Group Order and Priority.

Should "neither the subscriber or publisher specify" be changed to "neither the subscriber nor publisher specifies"?

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body: Yes, that would be grammatically better.

issues.title: An Object been delivered before sending any data of that Object
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 8.2.1.2 (DELIVERY TIMEOUT Parameter) includes the following sentence:

> Publishers SHOULD consider whether the entire Object is likely to be delivered before sending any data for that Object, taking into account priorities, congestion control, and any other relevant information.

The first half of the sentence reads weird to me, as before sending any data for an Object, that Object won't be delivered in any case, right? Was "data" intended to be something like "metadata"?

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
In this context “before sending any data for that Object” simply means “before you put the first byte of the Object on the wire.”
The guidance is: think ahead. If, given the current priorities, congestion-control state, delivery-timeout value, etc., you judge that you probably will not be able to transmit the whole Object before the timeout fires, you ought to refrain from starting to transmit it at all.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
@sharmafb Got you. Thanks! With that understanding, it seems that it would be much clearer to change the sentence to be something like the following:

   Publishers SHOULD consider whether the entire Object can likely be successfully delivered within the timeout period before sending any data for that Object, taking into account priorities, congestion control, and any other relevant information.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Your suggestion looks good.

issues.title: Inconsistent descriptions of Version Specific Parameters
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 8.2.1 and the beginning of Section 8.2.2 are as follows:

> [8.2.1. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#section-8.2.1)[Version Specific Parameters](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#name-version-specific-parameters)
> Each version-specific parameter definition indicates the message types in which it can appear. If it appears in some other type of message, it MUST be ignored. Note that since Setup parameters use a separate namespace, it is impossible for these parameters to appear in Setup messages.
> 
> [8.2.1.1. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#section-8.2.1.1)[AUTHORIZATION TOKEN](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#name-authorization-token)
> The AUTHORIZATION TOKEN parameter (Parameter Type 0x03) MAY appear in a CLIENT_SETUP, SERVER_SETUP, SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, ANNOUNCE, TRACK_STATUS or FETCH message. This parameter conveys information to authorize the sender to perform the operation carrying the parameter.
> 

I got confused by the last sentence in Section 8.2.1, which says: "Note that since Setup parameters use a separate namespace, it is impossible for these parameters to appear in Setup messages."

In that sentence, "these parameters" seem to mean Version Specific Parameters. Is that understanding correct? Because the meaning cannot be "Setup parameters" as Setup parameters by definition can appear in Setup messages.

On the other hand, if "these parameters" do mean Version Specific Parameters, then for AUTHORIZATION TOKEN, specified in Section 8.2.1.1 thus seeming to be a Version Specific Parameter, the first sentence in Section 8.2.1.1 indicates that the AUTHORIZATION TOKEN parameter MAY appear in a CLIENT_SETUP or SERVER_SETUP message.

Something seems to be wrong here. Is there a problem to simply remove this sentence?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think we're planning to overhaul a lot of this when version negotiation moves to ALPN in #499.  We will already know the version before sending any parameters, so they don't need to be version specific.

issues.title: Potential typo: "URL" -> "URI" in Section 8.4

issues.body:
Section 8.4 includes the following sentences: 

> If the URI is zero bytes long, the current URI is reused instead. The new session URI SHOULD use the same scheme as the current URL to ensure compatibility.

The first sentence uses "the current URI", while the second sentence uses "the current URL".

Shouldn't "the current URL" in the second sentence be changed to "the current URI"?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I _think_ we want URL.  At the very least we should be consistent.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> I _think_ we want URL. At the very least we should be consistent.

Do you mean to use "URL" to replace all instances of "URI" in Section 8.4 (GOAWAY), including in the message field names New Session URI Length and New Session URI?

issues.title: Increase MAX_REQUEST_ID to keep the number of available subscriptions roughly consistent
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 8.5 includes the following sentence: 

> For example, implementations might choose to increase MAX_REQUEST_ID as subscriptions close to keep the number of subscriptions available roughly consistent.

Three aspects:
 
1. Was "as subscriptions close" intended to be "as subscriptions are closed"?
2. Why "increase MAX_REQUEST_ID as subscriptions close" can keep the number of available subscriptions roughly consistent?
3. It seems slightly better to change "the number of subscriptions available" to "the number of  available subscriptions".

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Was "as subscriptions close" intended to be "as subscriptions are closed"?

Sure, that works.

> Why "increase MAX_REQUEST_ID as subscriptions close" can keep the number of available subscriptions roughly consistent?

The language should be updated because now request ID applies to all requests including possibly SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE - #1106.  The general idea is if you want to allow you peer to make up to 100 requests without additional credit, you can increase MAX_REQUEST_ID as requests complete.

> It seems slightly better to change "the number of subscriptions available" to "the number of available subscriptions".

Yes, but per the above, all the language may need a refresh.

issues.title: Possibly incorrect cross referencing for Request ID

> Maximum Request ID: The Maximum Request ID for the session on which the endpoint is blocked. More on Request ID in [Section 8.7](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#message-subscribe-req).

If no content has been delivered yet, the filter Start Location is {0, 0}. There is no End Group - the subscription is open ended. For scenarios where the subscriber intends to start more than one group in the future, it can use an AbsoluteStart filter instead.

issues.title: Semantics of SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
> The Start Location MUST NOT decrease, and if it increases, there is no guarantee that the publisher has not already sent Objects with Locations smaller than the new Start Location. Similarly, the End Group MUST NOT increase, and if it decreases, there is no guarantee that the publisher has not already sent Objects with Locations larger than the new End Location.

I can understand the second sentence above, as it talks about that there is no guarantee that the publisher's operation is within the new range. However, I cannot figure out what the first sentence is talking about.

Was the phrase "no guarantee that the publisher has not already sent Objects with Locations smaller than the new Start Location" in the first sentence intended to be "no guarantee that the publisher has already sent all Objects with Locations smaller than the new Start Location", such that the first sentence would also talk about that there is no guarantee that the publisher's operation is within the new range?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
It's supposed to communicate:

Old Start Location = x
New Start Location = y

Publisher might have sent an object with `x < location  < y` between when the subscriber sends UPDATE and when the publisher receives it.

Maybe we can just say narrowing the subscription is subject to race conditions that might cause the subscriber to receive objects outside its currently specified filter.

Also, I think there was consensus to allow widening the filter and @ianswett was going to make that change?

issues.title: Difference in semantics of End Group for SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
There is a key difference in the semantics of End Group for SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, as follows:

    For SUBSCRIBE: The end Group ID, inclusive. 
    For SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE: The end Group ID, plus 1.

Is that difference of 1 for the value on the wire intentional? If yes, why?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I was hoping the Parameter discussion would resolve.  If we make END_GROUP a param, then it will be the same for both messages.  They should probably be the same in any case.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: I think they should be the same, too. Which one is better? I guess probably just saying "The end Group ID." for both,  with neither "inclusive" nor "plus 1", seems the best.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Sure, that seems fine.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Sorry, I was wrong.  In SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE the End Group field is currently required, and uses 'plus 1' so 0 can mean "none".  We need to resolve this along with #872.

issues.title: Is TRACK_STATUS_OK with track_alias > 0 an error?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: There is no normative language here, so it's unclear if anything can be enforced.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: If we keep this "set it to 0" logic then it should probably be normative.  I think there might be some value in communicating a real Track Alias - particularly for publisher/subscriber systems that use fixed Track Alias.  I'm not sure how critical it is.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I have no opinion about this except that the spec be explicit. We can say "the publisher puts whatever it wants here" and have no enforcement, or require it is zero and kill the session, or say the publisher SHOULD put in the actual track alias if it has one.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: Saying "the publisher SHOULD put in the actual track alias if it has one" seems making a lot of sense; even MUST seems good.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Might as well make it MUST if we care at all.

issues.title: Semantics of the End Location field in FETCH
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
> End Location: The end Location, plus 1 Object ID. An Object ID value of 0 means the entire group is requested.

What does the first sentence of the semantics (i.e., "The end Location, plus 1 Object ID.") mean exactly?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This looks like a bad line wrap or mismerge.  I think it should read something like:

> End Location: The end Location, plus 1.  A Location.Object value of 0 means the entire group is requested.

issues.title: All Error message formats are the same
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
TRACK_STATUS was changed to be exactly like SUBSCRIBE, so the section for each message just refers to the original format.

However, all the REQUEST_ERROR messages are identical. They could all use the same language. Better yet, let's collapse it all into a single REQUEST_ERROR message and use the request ID to disambiguate what it means.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: If we did this, I could eliminate a lot of code by having a function for general request correctness checking (is the request ID correct, did I send/receive GOAWAY, does the track exist etc) and just send REQUEST_ERROR if any of that fails.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I hadn't thought about making a single REQUEST_ERROR message, but I had thought about sharing a parser/serializer for all error messages.

If we shared a single message, would you collapse the error code spaces (eg: < 100=common errors 100=subscribe errors, 200=publish errors, etc)?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Error codes don't really matter that much, but I'd have as many codes as possible be common. Certain numbers would mean different things for different types of request. This is pretty much how it is with the current numbering, and in fact I use a single set of constants for request error codes.

issues.title: Semantics of the End Location field in FETCH_OK
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
> If the relay is subscribed to the track, it uses its knowledge of the largest {Group, Object} to set End Location. If if is not subscribed and the requested End Location exceeds its cached data, the relay makes an upstream request to complete the FETCH, and uses the upstream response to set End Location.
> 
> If End is smaller than the Start Location in the corresponding FETCH the receiver MUST close the session with Protocol Violation

Four issues herein:
1. "If if" -> "If it"
2. After the above change, the first part of the second sentence (i.e., "If it is not subscribed and the requested End Location exceeds its cached data") is still not easy to understand: If the relay is not subscribed to a track, how the relay has cached data for the track? In this case the relay should not have any cached data for the track, right?
3. "If End is smaller than" -> "If End Location is smaller than"
4. Add the missing '.' to the end of the last sentence.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
1, 3, 4 all look like fine editorial corrections.

> After the above change, the first part of the second sentence (i.e., "If it is not subscribed and the requested End Location exceeds its cached data") is still not easy to understand: If the relay is not subscribed to a track, how the relay has cached data for the track? In this case the relay should not have any cached data for the track, right?

This is a scenario where the relay was perhaps previously subscribed to the track and unsubscribed, or the cache was pre-populated with some data out of band.

issues.title: Is there an intent for stream type values and datagram type values to share the same value space?
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Table 10 provides stream type values 0x05 and 0x08-0x0D, and Table 11 provides datagram type values 0x00-0x05. From the type values in the two tables, it can be seen that, except for one common value (0x05), stream type values and datagram type values share the same value space.

So the question is: Is there an intent for stream type values and datagram type values to share the same value space? If not, why overlapping values are largely avoided? If yes, is that one common value an overlook?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Is there an intent for stream type values and datagram type values to share the same value space? 

No.  The datagram type and subgroup type spaces are disjoint - they arrive via different contexts and aren't easily swappable.

> If not, why overlapping values are largely avoided? 

The types are selected so an implementation can use bit-masks to determine which fields will be present.

issues.author: yekuiwang

"terminate the session" -> "the session SHOULD be terminated"

comments.body:
9.3.1

> OBJECT_DATAGRAM {
>   Type (i) = 0x0-0x4,
>   Track Alias (i),
>   Group ID (i),
>   Object ID (i),

"0x0-0x4" -> "0x0-0x3"

comments.body:

Already fixed in the main branch

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
9.3.1

> If an endpoint receives a datagram with Type 0x01 and Extension Headers Length is 0, it MUST close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

Change "with Type 0x01" to "with Type & 0x01 equal to 1", as the same should apply for Type values 0x01, 0x03, 0x05, and 0x07.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
9.3.2

In -13:

> If an endpoint receives a datagram with Type 0x03 and Extension Headers Length is 0, it MUST close the session with Protocol Violation.

In editor's draft (https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-datagrams):
> If an endpoint receives a datagram with Type 0x05 and Extension Headers Length is 0, it MUST close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

Per the the editor's draft, "with Type 0x05" should be changed to "with Type 0x21".

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
9.4

> If a stream ends gracefully in the middle of a serialized Object, the session SHOULD be terminated with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

It seems better to remove "gracefully", as having it gives an impression to readers that it is OK if a stream ends ungracefully in the middle of a serialized Object, whatever "ends gracefully" mean even if it is defined.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: In all Tables in Section 9, some of the table column names span in to the second row when displayed, but those words (e.g., "Present" in "Extensions Present") are not in bold/black fonts, while those words remain in the first row (e.g., "Extensions" in "Extensions Present") when displayed are in bold/black fonts.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
9.4.3

- A relay knows that an Object is the next Object in the Subgroup if at least one of the following is true: * the Object ID is one greater than the previous Object sent on this Subgroup stream. * the Object was received on the same upstream Subgroup stream as the previously sent Object on the downstream Subgroup stream, with no other Objects in between. * it knows all Object IDs between the current and previous Object IDs on the Subgroup stream belong to different Subgroups or do not exist.

The items should be made as bullet items (currently they are just prefixed with a '*' in a long paragraph).

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
9.4.3

> A relay might immediately reset the corresponding downstream stream, or it might attempt to recover the missing Objects in an effort send all the objects in the subgroups and the FIN. 

"in an effort send" -> "in an effort to send"

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
10.1

> If an endpoint receives an Object with a Group ID within a previously communicated gap it also treats the track as malformed (see [Section 2.5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-13.html#malformed-tracks).

Missing ')' in the end.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> It seems better to remove "gracefully", as having it gives an impression to readers that it is OK if a stream ends ungracefully in the middle of a serialized Object, whatever "ends gracefully" mean even if it is defined.

This has a specific meaning - which is that the stream terminates with a FIN rather than a RST.  Terminating with a FIN in the middle of an object is a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION (eg session error) but terminating with a RST is not even necessarily an error - it could happen because a delivery timeout elapsed or an upstream publisher went away, etc.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: Got it; thanks! Is the specific meaning obvious or would it be helpful to clarify it a bit e.g., by adding some of what you said above?

issues.title: OBJECT_DATAGRAM_STATUS Type field values

issues.title: Whenever objects are sent on streams, the stream begins with a Subgroup Header?
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Section 9.4 starts with the following sentence:

> When objects are sent on streams, the stream begins with a Subgroup Header and is followed by one or more sets of serialized object fields. 

However, objects can also be sent on a fetch stream.

Is it good enough to just change the sentence to be as follows?

> When objects are sent on streams, the stream begins with a Subgroup Header or a Fetch Header and is followed by one or more sets of serialized object fields.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Sure, Subgroup or Fetch header is fine.

issues.title: Fetch header format and semantics
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
9.4.4 (Fetch Header)

> Each object sent on a fetch stream after the FETCH_HEADER has the following format:
> 
> {
>   Group ID (i),
>   Subgroup ID (i),
>   Object ID (i),
>   Publisher Priority (8),
>   Extension Headers Length (i),
>   [Extension headers (...)],
>   Object Payload Length (i),
>   [Object Status (i)],
>   Object Payload (..),
> }
> [Figure 36](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#figure-36): [MOQT Fetch Object Fields](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-moqt-fetch-object-fields)
> The Object Status field is only sent if the Object Payload Length is zero.
> 
> The Subgroup ID field of an object with a Forwarding Preference of "Datagram" (see [Section 9.2.1](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#object-properties)) is set to the Object ID.

Two questions:

1. Section 9.4 is about MOQT streams, thus the semantics above about the Subgroup ID field is about an Object in a (fetch) stream. Since the semantics only mention the case of an object with a Forwarding Preference of "Datagram", so does that imply that a) Fetch streams can only be used when Forwarding Preference is "Datagram", i.e., when subgroups are used (which can only be used when Forwarding Preference is not "Datagram") FETCH control messages cannot be used?
2. If the Subgroup ID field is always set to the Object ID, then the values of the second and third fields, i.e., Subgroup ID and Object ID, are always the same, then why not omit one of the two?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  Since the semantics only mention the case of an object with a Forwarding Preference of "Datagram", so does that imply that a) Fetch streams can only be used when Forwarding Preference is "Datagram"

No, FETCH can be used for any Track, regardless of preference, but Datagram Objects have no logical subgroup ID to serialize, hence that sentence is there (set to Object ID).

> If the Subgroup ID field is always set to the Object ID, then the values of the second and third fields, i.e., Subgroup ID and Object ID, are always the same, then why not omit one of the two?

See this PR #949

issues.title: Cacheability of MALFORMED_TRACK
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: Not just FETCH_ERROR.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I don't see how you can get a MALFORMED_TRACK From TRACK_STATUS, unless the relay has cached the malformity?

Somewhat the same with SUBSCRIBE_ERROR - either you cached the bad status or the upstream malformed it before you returned ok?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Why not? The relay previously served Track A, and now knows that A is malformed. Further requests for Track A should be rejected for that reason.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I guess it's fine to include it.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
Uh, I don't care about this but .... 

If a relay gets a malformed track, the draft says it needs to unsubscribe to upstream and presumably end the downstreams.  If it later gets a new subscribe for the same track, I don't think it should reject that track, it should send the subscribe upstream and see if can get a non malformed track. 

Without that, an attacker can poison the namespace and no one can ever subscribe to it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Maybe we should repurpose this issue to discuss cacheability of malformed tracks?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm repurposing this issue to discuss cacheability of malformed tracks.

In the HTTP caching world, if you detect something like this, the object does not become permanently unretrievable.  Usually, you purge the minimal amount of state (up to the entire object), and a subsequent GET might be able to retrieve it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
MALFORMED_TRACK is weird because I'd expect you to find out the track is malformed after you have started to send Objects to the subscriber, so I can't see when you'd be able to send it in response to a SUBSCRIBE_OK or FETCH_OK.

I agree that purging the malformed Objects and re-fetching is a more sensible approach.

Would it make sense to talk about Malformed Objects, Malformed Groups, and Malformed Tracks as separate types of misformatting?  If so, that might be the natural granularity on which to purge the cache and re-fetch?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Also, wouldn't it make sense for a subscriber to be able to send this when it receives an invalid Object/Group/etc?  Presumably the publisher shouldn't be forwarding these along?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  so I can't see when you'd be able to send it in response to a SUBSCRIBE_OK or FETCH_OK.

You can send it in FETCH_ERROR because you can start serving objects from a cache and then get a malformed piece from upstream.  That said, maybe this is best in the data plane (eg: in SUBSCRIBE_DONE and as a fetch stream reset error code only)?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
In Toronto:

There was agreement that you shouldn't cache the Object(s) that cause the Track to be invalid, in addition to unsubscribing.

Christian was concerned that if we don't tear down the session, the peer might not realize that they did something invalid.  Putting an error in UNSUBSCRIBE might be one option?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: It's hard to tell what objects caused the track to be invalid. If the EndOfGroup object comes before  a normal object, which one is the violating one?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think we don't know enough to be overly specific here, but I think it's reasonable to say that if a new Object comes in that makes the track malformed, don't cache that Object, even if the real issue might be something else.  In the case of EndOfGroup, re-fetching the entire Group might make sense, but I'm hesitant to say that for sure.

issues.title: Should we remove INTERNAL_ERROR?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
See this comment: https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1159#discussion_r2288261228

> INTERNAL_ERROR

> I'd like to remove this error. It it completely unspecified what the device receiving this error does when it gets it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Specs that have this error:

QUIC: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-20.1
HTTP/2: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#name-error-codes
HTTP/3: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#name-http-3-error-codes

AI also thinks XMPP and even DNS (ServFail) have similar errors.

Endpoints will fail for reasons not listed in the spec.  Trying to enumerate them all is not possible, so you have to have a catch all.  If you don't, then endpoints will either 1) make their own, non-standard catch all code or 2) use a defined code incorrectly, both of which are worse outcomes.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The comment https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1159#discussion_r2288261228 seems to have the presumption that endpoints do anything with regards to receiving specific values of error codes.

That is a pattern we don't follow in QUIC or HTTP/3. 

I agree with Alan here that there is valueing i signalling that a failure happened for some internal non-protocol reason, precisely because the protocol may have no way to react to that other than give up and fall the problem to humans to go investigate out of band.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
As an implementer, Internal Error is just the default error I sent when something wrong went on my side (disk I/O error or something).

> It it completely unspecified what the device receiving this error does when it gets it.

The answer for 95% of error scenarios is "fail the operation and optionally propagate the error message to the end user".

comments.author: fluffy

If sending an internal error also always closes the connection at the same time, then this makes sense. But if it is something like a disk read on a fetch failed and the user should try again in 2 seconds the the error should be fetch failed with information to retry after 2 seconds.

comments.author: ianswett

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The issue is, at this point the everything is in a pretty unknown state of what can happen next. If sending an internal error also always closes the connection at the same time, then this makes sense. But if it is something like a disk read on a fetch failed and the user should try again in 2 seconds the the error should be fetch failed with information to retry after 2 seconds.

There's nowhere we currently recommend ending something with INTERNAL_ERROR.  I generally agree that if you want to enable some specific behavior by the receiver of the error (eg retry this), we should define specific error codes for that.  Maybe we could split INTERNAL_ERROR into retryable and non-retryable variants? I'll note that HTTP has structure semantics (Retry-After) that could be useful.

issues.title: Remove Request ID from SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE (back out #1106)
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
As an individual:

If a subscriber wants to change everything about a SUBSCRIBE, it can UNSUBSCRIBE and then re-SUBSCRIBE.

SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE has a much more limited use case -- it is a time-delay unsubscribe. "I will not be interested after group 10, so please stop then". There are a few other parameters like flipping the forward bit. I am skeptical there is a DoS vector here, any more than there is a MAX_REQUEST_ID DoS vector,  and would want to see data (or at least a more detailed argument) to that effect.

From an implementation perspective, I have to add two new message types and testing for them, a state machine, and have to remap the request from one ID to another.

If we run out of request IDs, there are unfortunate edge cases like requesting forward=0 and being unable to turn the flow on, etc.

This quite a bit of churn to make things worse, IMO.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I assume you are referring to adding a Request ID to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE #1106.

> I am skeptical there is a DoS vector here, any more than there is a MAX_REQUEST_ID DoS vector

I am fairly confident there's a DoS vector.  I don't think we want to give endpoints the ability to send unlimited SUBSCRIBE_UPADTE messages without additional credit.  The messages can be quite small, so I can send thousands of these fairly cheaply. Even flipping the forward bit or updating the priority can result in expending publisher resources, especially if some streams have been created but not given credit to send.

CC: @LPardue who likes to talk about things like rapid reset.

> If we run out of request IDs, there are unfortunate edge cases like requesting forward=0 and being unable to turn the flow on, etc.

This may be real, since some Request IDs create long-lasting state (SUBSCRIBE, FETCH) while others are more ephemeral (the others).  I suppose it's possible if I create too many subscriptions then I can't update them.  This problem already exists with the other messages, I can file a separate issue.  I _really_ don't want two types of "MAX IDs" though?  I suppose QUIC does with unidirectional and bidirectional streams.

> From an implementation perspective, I have to add two new message types and testing for them, a state machine, and have to remap the request from one ID to another.

I'm not sure why this is such an implementation burden?  We didn't introduce new message types here, or change the subscribe state machine.  "I already implemented the last draft" is not a compelling reason to not make changes.

issues.title: Ephemeral vs Long-lived Request IDs
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
All requests have a request ID that is used as a correlator between the request its response.  SUBSCRIBE and FETCH also use this Request ID for subsequent purposes (SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, PUBLISH_DONE, FETCH_CANCEL) and it has a longer lifetime.  This means it's possible to consume all Request IDs with subscriptions and not have any credit left to send other messages like FETCH, TRACK_STATUS or PUBLISH_NAMESPACE.  This is exacerbated by #1106 which means you might not even be able to update subscriptions you created.

We could

1) Leave this as is
2) Split the ID space
3) Something else?

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body: I'm not sure that I see why this is an issue. If the peer updates the MAX_REQUEST_ID appropriately (as it should), then this won't be a problem, right?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: My feeling is that option 1 ( leave this as is) is likely the best. The value space of Request ID can be as large as 2^62, thus careful implementations should be able to handle Request IDs in a workable fashion, noting that there is the mechanism to increase max Request ID already specified through the MAX_REQUEST_ID message. Also note that to do option 2 (Split the ID space) would not only require implementations to have separable tables to track different types of Request IDs, but also the MAX_REQUEST_ID message need to be updated to add request types. Another consideration is that splitting the ID space does not seem save anything, on bits-on-the-wire efficiency or implementation complexities. Just my two cents.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> I'm not sure that I see why this is an issue. If the peer updates the MAX_REQUEST_ID appropriately (as it should), then this won't be a problem, right?

The root of the issue is that Request ID is solving two problems:

1.  Limiting the number of requests the peer can send without more credit
2. Limiting the amount of state the receiver is committing to

For example, our implementation only releases request ID's taken by a SUBSCRIBE when the subscription completes.  If say, MAX_REQUEST_ID is 10 and the peer makes 10 open-ended subscriptions, we won't grant more requests unless they UNSUBSCRIBE.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I'm understand why we might want to limit the number of outstanding subscribe, publish, fetch etc but each of these should probably be it's own limit not merged together. Trying to limit the number of request_id seems the wrong way to do this. 

Overall, I very skeptical that these limits actually help with the ways a system can DDOS MoQ and we should have a serious design discussion about DOS attacks, what things can be billed for by relays, and how to deal with this.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Overall, I very skeptical that these limits actually help with the ways a system can DDOS MoQ

Please read up on rapid reset, made you reset, and other modern attacks on HTTP for why credit based request IDs are essential to prevention.  Those of use who've had to deal with it will be hard to convince that this should be removed.

> and we should have a serious design discussion about DOS attacks

#374 is the place to add any color.

> what things can be billed for by relays

I have no idea what the intersection is with billing.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: The current system is not perfect but I tend to think that a more complicated solution will also have problems and be more complicated.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in 10/8 Interim - @englishm to lead a design team agreeing on the potential threats.  Parking this pending design team output.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: The more I've thought about this, I think it's annoying for SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, but likely unacceptably bad for PUBLISH_NAMESPACE.  For example, if I only want 20 subscriptions at once, and then I do SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, I could easily get more than 20 PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages in response, which might be fine, but they would use up all the Request IDs I've given to the peer until I grant more.  The cost of processing a PUBLISH_NAMESPACE will be be vastly less than that of a PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE or FETCH.  One is inserting an entry into a data structure and the other creating more state and consuming memory and bandwidth.

issues.title: Editorial and Other Draft-13 Notes
issues.author: sgodin

https://github.com/sgodin/moq-rs/commits/sgodin-update-messaging-to-draft-13/

- Section 2.5: I found the placement of the Malformed Tracks section a little odd -  seems a little too detailed for this part of the doc, might be better later in the doc?  This section also contains an instance of 'MoQT' vs 'MOQT' - there are 1 or 2 more of these throughout the doc as well.  Just listing this as I saw an effort was made to change most references.

Hope to meet some of you in September.

Scott Godin
SIP Spectrum, Inc.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Does this read better?

### Object Datagram {#object-datagram}

An OBJECT_DATAGRAM carries a single Object in a datagram. The presence of a
status or payload depends on the `Type` field.

~~~
OBJECT_DATAGRAM {
  Type (i) = 0x0-0x7, 0x20-21,
  Track Alias (i),
  Group ID (i),
  [Object ID (i),]
  Publisher Priority (8),
  [Extension Headers Length (i),
  Extension headers (...)],
  [Object Status (i),]
  [Object Payload (..),]
}
~~~
{: #object-datagram-format title="MOQT OBJECT\_DATAGRAM"}

The `Type` value determines which fields are present in the `OBJECT_DATAGRAM`.

|------|---------------|------------|-----------|------------------|
| Type | End Of Group  | Extensions | Object ID | Status / Payload |
|      |               | Present    | Present   |                  |
| 0x00 | No | No | Yes | Payload |
| 0x01 | No | Yes | Yes | Payload |
| 0x02 | Yes | No | Yes | Payload |
| 0x03 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Payload |
| 0x04 | No | No | No | Payload |
| 0x05 | No | Yes | No | Payload |
| 0x06 | Yes | No | No | Payload |
| 0x07 | Yes | Yes | No | Payload |
| 0x20 | No | No | Yes | Status |
| 0x21 | No | Yes | Yes | Status |

  * End of Group: For `Type` values where End of Group is "Yes," the Object is
    the last Object in the Group. Status Objects MUST NOT be the end of a
    Group, use END_OF_GROUP Status instead.

  * Object ID: The `Object ID` field is present for all status types. For other
    types, its presence is determined by the `Object ID Present` column. If an
    `Object ID` is not present, its value is 0.

  * Extensions: If `Extensions Present` is "Yes," the `Extension Headers Length`
    and `Extension headers` fields are included. If an endpoint receives a
    datagram with `Extensions Present` as "Yes" and a `Extension Headers Length`
    of 0, it MUST close the session with `PROTOCOL_VIOLATION`.

  * Payload and Status: The `Object Status` field and `Object Payload` are
    mutually exclusive.
      * For `Type` values 0x20 and 0x21, the `Object Status` field is present
      and there is no `Object Payload`.
      * For `Type` values 0x00** through 0x07, the `Object Payload` is present
      and the `Object Status` field is omitted.

There is no explicit length field for the `Object Payload`. The entirety of the
transport datagram following `Publisher Priority` contains the payload.

issues.title: Incorrect Calculation for End of a Joining FETCH
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Originally raised by @martinduke in #876 [here](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/876#issuecomment-3214432964):

This is the end of 9.16.1. Calculating the Range of a Relative Joining Fetch

> Fetch End Location: Subscribe Largest Location

> A Fetch End Location.Object of 0 requests the entire group, but Fetch will not retrieve Objects that have not yet been published, so 1 is subtracted from the Fetch End Location.Group if Fetch End Location.Object is 0.

This is confusing to talk about because the encoding of Fetch End Location is one more than the abstract End Location.

Subscribe Largest Location is the highest Location that the SUBSCRIBE will not deliver, so it is the inclusive end of the FETCH range. So if Largest Location is (7, 0), the actual fetch end is (7, 0) but the wire encoding in FETCH_OK will be (7, 1). I don't know what to do with the text about subtracting one from the group; I don't see where that arises.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Here's the case we were discussion at the time:

The caller wants one full group before the current group (pgo=1), and Largest is {7,0}.

With the text saying End = Largest, that would mean FETCH _all_ of group 7, which would be wrong, so we added the "-1 group" logic.  However, I wonder if we were confusing ourselves?

The FETCH in this case needs to deliver all of Group 6 _and_ (7,0), because we decided that SUBSCRIBE will not get (7,0) if that is Largest.  The correct _encoded_ End Location is (7,1), and (7,1) will be the first object delivered via SUBSCRIBE.

So I think the text should read:

> * Fetch End Location: {Subscribe Largest Location.Group, Subscribe Largest Location.Object + 1} 
>
> This is the encoded Fetch End Location as described in the preceding section.  The last Object requested by the Joining FETCH is Subscribe Largest Location.

and remove the -1 group stuff.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: Let me propose something worthing thinking about. Say var int supported negative numbers, or we had a SignedVarInt. In that case would the design here be different and less confusing. We could trivially add a SignedVarInt.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Let me propose something worthing thinking about. Say var int supported negative numbers, or we had a SignedVarInt. In that case would the design here be different and less confusing. We could trivially add a SignedVarInt.

There are some places where I can see how Signed Varints could be helpful, but I don't see how it helps _here_?  Maybe you suggesting standalone fetch would use End.Object ID=`-1` to mean "the whole group" and the end is always inclusive?  I'll note there's another simple encoding, that doesn't require negative varints, which is to make the End always _exclusive_, and to request all of group 7, send End={8,0}.

issues.title: Handling of non-defined error codes
issues.author: michalhosna
issues.body:
Hi,

The draft says an application “SHOULD use a relevant error/status code as defined below” in several places.

- Are implementations allowed to send an error/status code that is not specified in the draft?
- What is the expected behavior if an implementation receives such a non-defined code (e.g., treat as generic failure, ignore)? 
- Do we want to allow implementation-specific error codes with some kind of reserved range?

Sorry if this was already discussed — I wasn’t able to find a prior thread in issues, PRs, or the mailing list.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Responding as an individual and error code enthusiast

> Are implementations allowed to send an error/status code that is not specified in the draft?

Yes they should be. Error codes are an extension point of the protocol

> What is the expected behavior if an implementation receives such a non-defined code (e.g., treat as generic failure, ignore)?

We can turn the question around and ask what does a receiver do with an error code it knows? The answer is basically the same - deal with the fact something errored independent of the code, then possibly log the code and present to user 

> Do we want to allow implementation-specific error codes with some kind of reserved range?

I would advise us not to reserve any special range apriori. The space is large any way. At the point some custom error codes might be useful, you'd probably be better off with application-level mecahnsim to exchange information (i.e. something on top of moqt). You'd probably implementations to be aware if they are speaking to each other, a shared reserved range doesn't address that itself and would seem to be likely to increase the chance of collisions. Better to negotiate the use of custom things via an extension if really needed. The process for requesting moqt extension codepoints should be clear and simple enough to encourage people to do it this way.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
+1 to everything @LPardue said

Since there's now effectively a "User-Agent" setting, you can use the combo of that and the non-standard code to figure out what happened.

comments.author: michalhosna
comments.body:
I agree that sending non-specified errors should be allowed and properly handled. If we agree on this, I think the spec should state it explicitly.

(In the wild: [streaming-university/moqtail errors out on unknown error codes](https://github.com/streaming-university/moqtail/blob/73860deb323e64fe32154210e0975569991da6ea/libs/moqtail-rs/src/model/control/constant.rs#L247-L250))

> We can turn the question around and ask what does a receiver do with an error code it knows? The answer is basically the same - deal with the fact something errored independent of the code, then possibly log the code and present to user

I’d argue error handling can be error-code-dependent today. At least in the current draft, some error codes could be handled gracefully or retried (e.g., EXPIRED_AUTH_TOKEN), and some may not even be “errors” for an application depending on semantics (e.g., NO_OBJECTS in FETCH_ERROR, see #1036).

As long as the specification explicitly defines error types, implementations may have type-specific handling. Otherwise, why define specific error types?

Therefore, I think that if non-defined error codes are allowed, we also need to specify or at least recommend how implementations receiving such codes should handle it. 

Also, what does error propagation mean for relays, and how should that be handled? Can applications expect specific relay behavior regarding error handling? Should all errors be propagated? Should the origin of the error be indicated? This seems underspecified today. But that's probably for another issue.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Error codes are a best effort thing. Bring overly prescriptive on how to react to them will cause a fragile design because experience shows the generator sometimes can't or won't use a specific error code.

Agree the spec would benefit from more text to capture some of the point in this discussion. For example, there's a long-open task to add greasing to this extension point, that would need to state what happens when an unknown error code is received.

comments.author: michalhosna
comments.body:
> Error codes are a best effort thing.

There are several places in the draft that use language like “MUST respond with a specific error code” or “…MUST close the session with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.”

I (an IETF novice) would read “MUST” as much more prescriptive than “best effort”, as something that implementations can rely upon.

I am not advocating whether errors should be best effort or strictly defined, but in my view the current wording of the document leans toward explicit error handling.

Examples:
> 9.16 Fetch: “…MUST respond with a Fetch Error with code INVALID_JOINING_REQUEST_ID.”

> 9.16.1: “…the publisher MUST respond with a FETCH_ERROR with error code INVALID_RANGE.”

> 9.28 SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE: “…MUST respond with SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE_ERROR, with error code NAMESPACE_PREFIX_OVERLAP.”

And there are other places without explicit MUST (or any other BCP 14 keyword) that also read as quite prescriptive in my opinion.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Yeah, the text in this draft needs to be updated to clarify that these statements are to be interpreted as "MUST error and, as a best effort, send error code FOO". Not that specific text but the intent. The reason being that there may be good reason someone rejecting something doesn't want to provide the specifics.

The proscribed behaviour we need to avoid is misleading a receiver into thinking that their peer will will always generate an expected code and how to deal with that.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  the text in this draft needs to be updated to clarify that these statements are to be interpreted as "MUST error and, as a best effort, send error code FOO"

I'll note that HTTP/3 does nothing of the sort.  Everything is "MUST treat as a connection error of type X".  I'd like to keep it simple here.

While I was there I found this text, which MoQT should take more or less as is:

> Because new error codes can be defined without negotiation [...], use of an error code in an unexpected context or receipt of an unknown error code MUST be treated as equivalent to XXX.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I think this the wrong design. There should be no undefined error codes for a given version of the protocol. Later version of a protocol can add new error codes but for a given version, it should be clear what the element receiving the error code needs to do based on the error.  Everywhere the spec says "send some random error" should be replaced with a specfic error to send. 

This needs to be covered in the extensibility design.

comments.body: I don't think this is ready for a PR - I think this is a basic design issue that needs discution

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
See also https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-11

> An endpoint that detects an error SHOULD signal the existence of that error to its peer. Both transport-level and application-level errors can affect an entire connection; see Section 11.1. Only application-level errors can be isolated to a single stream; see Section 11.2.

> The most appropriate error code (Section 20) SHOULD be included in the frame that signals the error. Where this specification identifies error conditions, it also identifies the error code that is used; though these are worded as requirements, different implementation strategies might lead to different errors being reported. In particular, an endpoint MAY use any applicable error code when it detects an error condition; a generic error code (such as PROTOCOL_VIOLATION or INTERNAL_ERROR) can always be used in place of specific error codes.

martinduke

issues.title: Need a way to pause/resume a track in the data plane
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
The protocol lacks an **"efficient"** way for publishers to indicate that the track data will be paused. Common use-cases is user pauses the broadcast or muting audio/video track in a conference.

There are few ways to address the general requirement 
1. Have a centralized server that subscribes to pause events and distributes it to all the subscribers --> This will not scale even for medium sized population of publishers and subscribers.
2. Have a separate track that carries the state of media. This would generally work but with challenges of synchronization between the media tracks and meta tracks and also needing to deal with additional complexity of managing across tracks multiplcity.
3.  Have publisher send empty objects whenver the user wishes to pause media on a given track.  This ends up wasting bandwidth and also contention when shared with other things on the connections

My rough proposal is to extend Object Status to have a new "Paused State" and  define the following
1. On pause , publisher shall start a new group and send a single object with Object Status of Paused
2. On resume, publisher starts a new group and starts sending the objects as usual. However, the publisher shall use the GroupID gap extension to specify the last group ( if there was a jump)

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Not clear at all that we need this at the protocol level. If the publisher wants to "pause", just don't send anything. Our connection timeouts may kick-in if you pause too long, but that is easily and flexibly countered with application level keep-alives. The relays don't care about gaps between objects.

"Pausing a broadcast" is an application construct and as such could be a feature that you propose for WARP. Similarly, muting a track is an application signal and you could easily be achieved by creating a application control channel to communicate that and other application-specific behaviors.

comments.author: vasilvv

In that case, the action by userA should not affect interactions between other users, right? For example, when userA pauses/mutes, userB as a publisher would still publishes Objects (through relays) to userC.

If that is the case (which seems so), then userA's pausing/muting operations should just be an implementation issue, and consequently there is no need to change MOQT or WARP.

Sorry if I am missing something, and if so, appreciate if you could let me know.

For example, when userA pauses/mutes, userB as a publisher would still publishes Objects (through relays) to userC.
> 
> If that is the case (which seems so), then userA's pausing/muting operations should just be an implementation issue, and consequently there is no need to change MOQT or WARP.
> 
> Sorry if I am missing something, and if so, appreciate if you could let me know.

Oh, I get it, the use case is that one user (userA) pauses its own outgoing data as a publisher.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The protocol lacks an "efficient" way for publishers to indicate that the track data will be paused. Common use-cases is user pauses the broadcast or muting audio/video track in a conference.

I'm also confused about what the problem is - why does the subscriber need to know the track is "paused" vs just not receiving any objects on it.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
I think pause / resume terminology might be a bit confusing here. I think of the scenario more like this. 

A twitch stream is live streaming their video camera over UDP. Bunch of people are subscribed. The person live streaming turns off their camera for a bit for some privacy. It might be nice if they could periodically send something that indicated they were "not transmitting but still here". That would allow all the subscribers to know to do something like display a gray video frame to indicate their was no video being sent vs try to recover the video or display that video was broken. It allows the receiver of UDP packets to differentate between send stoped sending and 100% packet loss.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I have very mixed feelings about if this needs to be at the MoQT level or defined by the applications above MoQT that defines wha goes in the object.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I tend to think this should be at a higher later than MoQT.

Live video has the idea of commercial indicators where advertisers replace the video (or lack thereof) with commercials for some period of time.  This feels similar to that problem, which is best solved at a higher layer.

comments.author: mzanaty
comments.body:
The key question for MOQT is whether this impacts relays (I think not) or applies generally to all types of tracks/objects (I think so) not only some specific applications. But maybe we don't need any wire changes with a new object status, just clarify that zero-length zero-status (Null Normal) objects can be used to indicate a pause or keepalive when the publisher has nothing to send for this Location.

[Proposed additions] to Section 10.2.1.1 Object Status:
Status can have [the] following values:
0x0 := Normal object. This status is implicit for any non-zero length object. Zero-length objects explicitly encode the Normal status [which MAY be used to indicate a pause or keepalive when the publisher has nothing to send for this Location].

LOC could strengthen this to say audio/video tracks SHOULD use Null Normal objects when muted/paused.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I wonder if an application defined extension on a NORMAL object is a more clear way for the app to communicate a pause.

>  [which MAY be used to indicate a pause or keepalive when the publisher has nothing to send for this Location]

This is not explicitly prohibited in any text today, so I wonder if we need to add an explicit MAY?  A publisher can send an empty Normal object for any reason at any time.

I think when we discuss and resolve expires (see #1026) we will end up adding more text about "keepalive".

comments.body:
When discussing #1026 in Toronto, the wg agreed Expires does not extend on publishing an object, so I don't think there's any intersection there.

Unless someone can articulate why a _Relay_ needs this signal, I suggest we close this with no action.

issues.title: Proposal for REQUEST_OK message
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
I'd like to add a generic REQUEST_OK with the following structure:

```
REQUEST_OK {
  Request ID (i),
  Length (16),
  Number of Parameters (i),
  Parameters (..)
}
```

This would immediately replace PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_OK and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE_OK, while adding an extensibility point (parameters) to those messages.  I would also use REQUEST_OK (along with #1157) to address #1003.

Assuming we reach consensus on moving Content Exists/Largest and Expires to parameters (#1052 #1012), we would also replace TRACK_STATUS_OK with REQUEST_OK, which would solve #1064 and #1144.

SUBSCRIBE_OK, PUBLISH_OK and FETCH_OK seem to have enough specific fields to warrant being specialized messages.

issues.title: Determine if/where we should use TV instead of TLV
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
@fluffy presented on extensibility [slides](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/interim-2025-moq-25/materials/slides-interim-2025-moq-25-sessa-exentions-00) and pointed out there were some cases when TV made more sense, because it's reasonable to require the peer to understand the codepoint.

Victor pointed out that this is true of SUBSCRIBE, where we say you shouldn't just forward the SUBSCRIBE upstream with the params.  As a result, it seems true for SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE as well.

Possibly it's true for more control messages, but @afrind didn't think it was true for PUBLISH.

I don't have a clear proposal at the moment, but I do like the idea of sending only fields you know the peer can process in control messages.  This has worked well for QUIC messages, in my opinion.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The current set of params are _mostly_ already TV, because they are varints so the L is already implicit/embedded.  The exception is Auth, but Auth definitely needs explicit length because the contents are variable length.

If we param Group Order or Priority, which are currently 8 bits rather than varint, TV might make sense there, since there's no need for the varint flexibility.  We're already planning to tweak the encoding of key-value (see #794), so we can reserve part of the range for TV values.

SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE and PUBLISH_OK are hop-by-hop messages, not end-to-end (at least there's never a guarantee they will go past one relay hop), so they don't need the same kind of "pass through unknown" params.  SUBSCRIBE_OK / PUBLISH could be considered end-to-end, see #1176 which uses this to convey track level extensions via a parameters in these messages.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
If we assume the following Fields are Parameters, which includes:

MAX_CACHE_DURATION
DELIVERY_TIMEOUT
AUTH_TOKEN
SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY (#1210)
PUBLISHER_PRIORITY (#1056)
GROUP_ORDER / PUBLISHER_GROUP_ORDER_PREFERENCE (#1210)
EXPIRES (#1012)
LARGEST_OBJECT (#1052)

Then I propose using TV for the these:

SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY -> uint8
PUBLISHER_PRIORITY -> uint8
GROUP_ORDER / PUBLISHER_GROUP_ORDER_PREFERENCE -> enum (encoded in uint8)
LARGEST_OBJECT -> Location

These will be varint:

MAX_CACHE_DURATION
DELIVERY_TIMEOUT
EXPIRES

These be length prefixed:

AUTH_TOKEN

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I thought moving to TV would be worthwhile, but for the Parameters we have today, it's basically a no-op on the wire.

I'm fine to make this change, but I'm also not sure it's worth the change?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
After discussing with @fluffy we agreed that the most straightforward way to make these required and not skippable was to use TV.

Also, SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY and PUBLISHER_PRIORITY are slightly better as TV, since they'd commonly need a 2 byte varint.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Based on discussion in Boulder, the plan is to move forward with TV for Parameters.

Sec. 2.3.1 of -v14:

> SUBSCRIBE and FETCH delivery use Group Order, so a FETCH cannot deliver Groups out of order and a subscription could have unexpected delivery order if Group IDs do not increase with time.
> 

This sentence is a bit confusing. "so a FETCH cannot deliver Groups out of order" does not seem to be consequence of "FETCH delivery uses Group Order". Was "so a FETCH cannot deliver Groups out of order" intended to be "so a FETCH _could_ deliver Groups out of order"?

issues.title: What does "A Subgroup is received with two or more different final Objects" mean?
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
In Sec. 2.5 of -v14:

> 4. An Object is received whose Object ID is larger than the final Object in the Subgroup. The final Object in a Subgroup is the last Object received on a Subgroup stream before a FIN.
> 
> 5. A Subgroup is received with two or more different final Objects.
> 

Given that the final Object in a Subgroup is "the last Object received on a Subgroup stream before a FIN" (per item 4), what does it mean by "A Subgroup is received with two or more different final Objects" (as in item 5)? Does it mean that there were multiple instances of FIN received when receiving the Subgroup, each FIN is associated with a final Object, and the final Objects are different Objects (i.e., the Objects are associated with different Locations)?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Does it mean that there were multiple instances of FIN received when receiving the Subgroup, each FIN is associated with a final Object, and the final Objects are different Objects (i.e., the Objects are associated with different Locations)?

Yes, it's intended to describe this pattern:

```
Stream A: Group=10, Subgroup=0, Object=1; FIN
Stream B: Group=10, Subgroup=0, Object=0; FIN
```

Do you have an editorial suggestion?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
I am not yet fully understanding the situation yet. Let me try to understand better first.

In Sec. 2.2, we have:

> Objects from the same Subgroup MUST NOT be sent on different streams, unless one of the streams was reset prematurely, or upstream conditions have forced objects from a Subgroup to be sent out of Object ID order.

So it seems possible and not an error that in certain conditions Objects from the same Subgroup are sent on different streams. And if more than two of the streaming carrying Objects from the same Subgroup are associated with FINs, then the pattern would happen. 

So my first question is, in that case, something is wrong?

Second question: This seems to be a result of how the track is transmitted, not really how the track is formed/created, therefore why determine that the track is a malformed track?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> So it seems possible and not an error that in certain conditions Objects from the same Subgroup are sent on different streams.

Correct.

> And if more than two of the streaming carrying Objects from the same Subgroup are associated with FINs, then the pattern would happen.

No, a FIN on the underlying stream carries semantics at the MOQT layer and only one Object can precede a FIN for any give Group+Subgroup.  If a publisher needs to end a stream on a non-final object, it MUST NOT terminate that stream with a FIN.  It either waits for the ACK and sends RESET_STREAM, or uses RESET_STREAM_AT.

> Second question: This seems to be a result of how the track is transmitted, not really how the track is formed/created, therefore why determine that the track is a malformed track?

In this case the publisher is trying to say that the subgroup has two final objects, which is malformed.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
Got it. Thanks!

In your example, two streams are used for the same Subgroup. If the case of receiving multiple final Objects of a Subgroup can only occur when multiple streams, maybe it is better to have that stated in the sentence? Other than that, I don't have any editorial suggestion regarding this sentence.

BTW, regarding "or upstream conditions have forced objects from a Subgroup to be sent out of Object ID order" in Sec. 2.2, one of the conditions when the same Subgroup can be sent on different streams, I know that the control messages may indicate ascending or descending Group order, but I cannot figure out what upstream conditions would force objects from a Subgroup to be sent out of Object ID order. I'd appreciate if you could enlighten me on that. Or it might be even better to clarify that a bit in the draft.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> BTW, regarding "or upstream conditions have forced objects from a Subgroup to be sent out of Object ID order" 

This is a rare edge case that involves graceful publisher failover.

```
P -> R (session 1): Open stream A, send Group 10, Subgroup 0, Object 0 (delayed in network)
Publisher initiates graceful failover (wifi->cell), opens a new session to R
P -> R (session 2): Open stream B, send Group 10, Subgroup 0, Object 1 (arrives before Object 0)
P -> R (session 1): MUST NOT FIN Stream A
R -> S: Open stream C, send Group 10, Subgroup 0, Object 1
Object 0 arrives at R
R -> S: Open stream D, send Group 10, Subgroup 0, Object 0 (MUST NOT FIN)
```

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: @afrind Thanks! Understand now. I leave it to you on whether some editorial improvement on the sentence "A Subgroup is received with two or more different final Objects." should be made or not. If no, please go ahead to close this issue.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Maybe:

> A Subgroup is received over multiple transport streams terminated by FIN with different final Objects.

issues.title: Calculating of the length of a Full Track Name
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
In Sec. 1.4 of -v14, we have:

> This document extends the RFC9000 syntax and with the additional field types:
> 
> x (b):
> Indicates that x consists of a variable length integer encoding as described in ([[RFC9000](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-14.html#RFC9000)], [Section 16](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000#section-16)), followed by that many bytes of binary data
> 
> x (tuple):
> Indicates that x is a tuple, consisting of a variable length integer encoded as described in ([[RFC9000](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-14.html#RFC9000)], [Section 16](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000#section-16)), followed by that many variable length tuple fields, each of which are encoded as (b) above.

Minor question: Should "encoded as (b) above" be "encoded as x (b) above"?

In Sec. 2.4.1 of -v14, we have:

> The maximum total length of a Full Track Name is 4,096 bytes, computed as the sum of the lengths of each Track Namespace tuple field and the Track Name length field.

Therefore, a tuple field is one data structed coded as (b) or x (b), and consequently the length of a Track Namespace tuple field would include the length of the Varint-coded value itself at the beginning of the tuple field, not just "that many bytes of binary data" following the Varint-coded value.  

On the other hand, a Track Name is represented by the following two elements in the control messages that use it, i.e., PUBLISH (9.13) and standalone FETCH (9.16.1):

>   Track Name Length (i),
>   Track Name (..),
> 

The elements are essentially "Trarck Name (b)" (BTW, why not use this form since the coding of x (b) is defined?)

So, in the current definition of the total length of a Full Track Name, the length of the varint of each track Namespace tuple field is counted, but the length of the varint of the Track Name is not counted. That's odd.

It is therefore suggested to change 

>   Track Name Length (i),
>   Track Name (..),
> 

In both the syntaxes of PUBLISH (9.13) and standalone FETCH (9.16.1) to 

>   Track Name (b),


And it is also suggested to change 

> The maximum total length of a Full Track Name is 4,096 bytes, computed as the sum of the lengths of each Track Namespace tuple field and the Track Name length field.

to

> The maximum total length of a Full Track Name is 4,096 bytes, computed as the sum of the values of the varints at the beginning of the Track Namespace tuple fields and the varint at the beginning of the Track Name field.

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
Response to question 1: In Section 1.4, “x (b)” is a pattern showing how any field x is encoded when it uses the (b) form. When the tuple definition says “each of which are encoded as (b) above,” it is referring to that encoding form (varint length followed by that many bytes), not to a literal field named x. If you want to make it even clearer without changing meaning, you could say “each of which is encoded in the (b) form described above,”

Response to question 2: Yes, from a wire-format standpoint it is fully equivalent. Changing to “Track Name (b)” would be an editorial simplification.

Response to question 3: That would work, but here's a slightly more compact and clear version that I'd prefer: "The maximum total length of a Full Track Name is 4,096 bytes, computed as the sum of the values of the variable‑length integer length fields for each Track Namespace tuple element and of the Track Name; the varint encoding bytes are not counted."

comments.body: @sharmafb Thanks! If there is no objection, I will integrate the refined changes suggested above by @sharmafb to PR #1192.

issues.title: Clarify Objects from different subgroups can be sent on the same FETCH stream
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
Can Subgroups be used in a FETCH response? My current understanding of the MOQT draft is no. Is that understanding correct?

If so, why? It seems to me there is no such an essential difference between sending Objects of a Group as a response to a FETCH or as a response to a SUBSCRIBE that would determine the use or not use of Subgroups. Appreciate any clarification!

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: The subgroup ID is sent, but you cannot break the fetch response into multiple streams by subgroup, as is done in subscribe responses.  One of the functions of FETCH is to help the receiver understand where the gaps of non-existent objects are in the track.  Splitting into multiple streams makes this very difficult.  Another purpose of the single stream is to make the response easily flow controlled by the receiver.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: @afrind Thank you! I can understand the first reason. For the second reason (i.e., to make the response easily flow controlled by the receiver), what is the difference herein between FETCH and SUBSCRIBE?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: BTW, Sec. 2.2 includes the following sentence: "Objects from two subgroups cannot be sent on the same stream." I did not check whether such sentences exist also in other places. A clarification should be made to the text to make it clear that such statement(s) do not apply when Objects are sent as a response to a FETCH request.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  what is the difference herein between FETCH and SUBSCRIBE?

Let's say a Track uses an object per stream and the underlying transport has a 1000 stream maximum and an initial max stream data of 64k.  A FETCH over a wide range could result in the publisher immediately opening all 1000 streams and sending 64MB of data.

By forcing FETCH to a single stream, the most the publisher can send without the peer sending additional credit is a single max stream data.

To some degree SUBSCRIBE _also_ has this problem **however** it's limited to the publisher's ability to produce the data for this track at the live edge.  We felt like FETCH was worse since it can be used to request a very large amount of past data.  That said, there's also #869, to which we don't really have an answer yet.  I think we discussed this a bunch at the interim last October in Boston, I'm sure the YouTube recording is very entertaining.

[Minutes Session 1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/minutes-interim-2024-moq-18-202410021330/).  You can find additional minutes for sessions 19,20 and 21.
