@martinduke , 

You are right, it shouldn't have, but it does because MOQT group and object ID are not session specific... If object id was QUIC session specific, then it would be simplistic as you suggest. In the MOQT case, group-id and object-id are track specific, which spans (aka global) relay peering sessions and many subscriber sessions.  In order to sync all of them, the object GAP header and location information is required to compute the publisher original object ID from received objects. 

> [!NOTE]
> Datagram does not follow this, so this is very strange that only streams now have to deal with delta values, to which is used to compute an object id.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  In order to sync all of them, the object GAP header and location information is required to compute the publisher original object ID from received objects.

I think you are misunderstanding Object ID delta compression in draft-14.  It is intended to be completely independent of the Gap extension headers -- the delta encoding is local to a point-to-point session -- in fact confined to a single stream.  Gap extension headers are clues for caches and other subscribers that if they don't have object X, it's because it doesn't exist -- don't waste time fetching it.

Perhaps the crux of your issue is that you are trying to forward stream data through a relay _without_ decoding it?  It's true that delta encoding does restrict this capability -- but only when a subscriber joins a group late.  As long as the subgroup is relayed from upstream to downstream starting from the beginning, the delta encoding doesn't change.  Further, if a subscriber does join late, only the _first_ forwarded object needs to be re-encoded as a delta from 0, and the remainder of the stream can be forwarded without decoding/re-encoding.

One intersection between Prior Object Gap and delta encoding is that they can conflict -- eg: the delta is 0 but the gap is 1.  Such a conflict results in a malformed track.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
It is possible for inconsistency with object GAP extension and delta value.  They may not be the same unless MOQT addresses when to use which and what should be done when there is a delta and GAP header exists or doesn't exist.

> the delta encoding is local to a point-to-point session 

Computing a local object id as written is just a count of received objects plus the received delta value. This can result in the same content being identified with a different object IDs in cache on different relays because the received count is not the same for every relay and subscriber. You would have to sync and start the object with the correct delta value and/or GAP object header, hop-by-hop.   Otherwise, the receive side will start at zero thinking it's object zero when it's actually object id 123456.    As written, standalone fetch will not work correctly unless the object IDs are correct. 

> "If the Forward State is 0, the publisher does not send objects for the subscription. "

@afrind , do you consider a publisher still sending a malformed track and/or protocol violation?  How do you handle the race condition where the publisher hasn't processed the forward state change and still sends objects when the relay has indicated fwd=0?   We allow this and discard.  This results in object gaps because the publisher sent objects when forward state is zero. We are okay with this in our apps, but this becomes more of a problem with delta values as the original object ID would be lost by the receiving relay.. it would just assume, **incorrectly**, that the object ID resumes when fwd=1 again. 

The application object ID is now lost and the receiver cannot rely on object ID anymore. 
**If the application needs an object ID, I supposed now the app has to use an extension header.** This seems to be counter productive in that it's now more bytes wire encoded than it was before.   In other words, using delta resulted in more wire encoded bytes.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
In section 2.1, 

> An object is uniquely identified by its track namespace, track name, group ID, and object ID, and must be an identical sequence of bytes regardless of how or where it is retrieved.

Considering objects IDs for streams are locally significant to the session using `previous_object_id (init at zero) + received_object_delta + 1`, what ensures caches and subscribers that join at different times stay in sync with the original publisher session computation of object ID?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> Considering objects IDs for streams are locally significant to the session using `previous_object_id (init at zero) + received_object_delta + 1`, what ensures caches and subscribers that join at different times stay in sync with the original publisher session computation of object ID?

Object ID is Group-specific, i.e., the first Object in each Group has Object ID equal to 0, and Object ID of an Object does not depends on an Object of another Group. Also, caches and subscribers join at Group boundaries.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> They may not be the same unless MOQT addresses when to use which and what should be done when there is a delta and GAP header exists or doesn't exist

They may not be the same because there may be more than one subgroup for the group.  Eg:

```
SG=0: 0, 2, 4, 6
SG=1: 1, 3, 5, 7
```

Here there is no Prior Object Gap, because the object space is contiguous, but the Object ID Delta is always 1 (except the first object).

You could also have two subgroups with gaps:

```
SG=0: 0, 3 [gap=1], 6 [gap=1]
SG=1: 1, 4, 7
```

Here the gap markers indicate the non-existence of Objects with ID=2 and ID=5.  The Object ID Delta values are always 2 (except the first object per subgroup).


> Computing a local object id as written is just a _count of received objects_ plus the received delta value. 

This is not correct.  Here's the specification text:

> The Object ID Delta + 1 is added to the previous Object ID in the Subgroup stream if there was one


> do you consider a publisher still sending a malformed track and/or protocol violation? How do you handle the race condition where the publisher hasn't processed the forward state change and still sends objects when the relay has indicated fwd=0? 

No I don't, but this sounds like a separate issue.

>  but this becomes more of a problem with delta values as the original object ID would be lost by the receiving relay.

Let's take a concrete example, where fwd goes from 1 to 0 back to 1.  The upstream is sending object with sequential Ids, all delta encoded as 0.  

```
Up->R: 0, 1, 2, 3
R->Down: 0, 1, 2, 3
// R processes fwd 1->0
Up->R: 4, 5, 6
// R processes fwd 0->1
Up->R: 7
```

Because the relay has created a gap in the subgroup, the correct behavior is to reset the existing subgroup stream to the downstream, and open a new stream to convey object ID 7.  

From 10.4.3 closing subgroup streams:

> A relay MUST NOT forward an Object on an existing Subgroup stream unless it is the next Object in that Subgroup. 

Since object 7 will be the first in its stream, it is not delta encoded, but sent in absolute form.

>  The Object ID is the Object ID Delta if it's the first Object in the Subgroup stream.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Considering objects IDs for streams are locally significant to the session using previous_object_id (init at zero) + received_object_delta + 1, what ensures caches and subscribers that join at different times stay in sync with the original publisher session computation of object ID?

I think you are confusing changing the object ID of an object with a compression scheme to transmit it over a single hop.  The logical object ID needs to be preserved across relay hops for all the reasons you suggest.

> // mean that the object IDs stop. Instead they will continue to increment, resulting in a gap.

I think I'm with you.  This is a case where Prior Object ID Gap would be _useful_ (but not necessary) - in the case that objects 4, 5 and 6 will _never_ be published or available.

> // Relay sends fwd=1 to PUB

Now you've lost me.  First, if the downstream subscriber received the entire stream from the beginning, even the relay blindly forwarding 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0 would result in the subscriber receiving 0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9.  If the subscriber had joined late, the onus is on the relay to correctly encode the first Object ID sent in the subgroup stream.  eg: if the subscriber joins during the pause, it should receive 7, 0, 0 = 7, 8, 9.

Whole objects certainly don't need to be maintained.

Regarding subgroups - please take that conversation to the list as it is orthogonal to this issue.  I believe the wg has consensus on them and a discussion to reopen would be counterproductive.

issues.title: Are error codes best-effort or mandatory?
issues.author: michalhosna
issues.body:
I have the impression that there is currently a lack of consensus on whether error codes, or errors in general, may/should be explicitly handled. See related discussion in #1175 and #1162. There should be an explicit discussion about this.

Should recoverable, i.e., explicitly handleable and/or retryable states, be expressed using
a) an error and a specific code, or
b) should those states always be expressed using a different mechanism?

See [#1036 FETCH_ERROR + No Objects](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/1036) as an example of this.

I don’t have a strong personal preference, but I believe the WG should reach a clear consensus and update the draft accordingly. The current draft is, in my view, not entirely clear on this point, as shown by the number of recent comments about error handling.

I want to note that once the spec defines a set of error codes, it is inevitable, in my opinion, that implementations in the wild will match on them and build specific handling around them.

We can learn a bit about how HTTP has evolved, for example 429, the Retry-After header etc.

issues.title: Semantic FIN and Filters / Forward
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
Currently, we use FIN to indicate that a subgroup stream has been completed; this FIN has a semantic meaning (relays have to forward it).

How does this interact with filters?  If I have a filter that stops at `(15, 10)`, but the subgroup goes on, the publisher is expected to send a FIN after `(15, 10)`, which is not where the original publisher would put it.

How does this interact with forward?  Assume I have a really long group.  If I send Forward=0, does the publisher has to cleanly fin the subgroup stream, reset it or what?  What happens if I set Forward=1, and that subgroup is still open?  Or if it's been closed so long ago that the relay evicted all the information about it from the cache?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Presently you cannot set an end object in a filter, only an end group. I think this issue might have been one of the motivations?

If we land a proposal like #1164 and the last object in a subgroup is omitted, I think the answer is - you wait for an ack and reset, or send reset_stream_at.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I missed the second part of your issue

> How does this interact with forward? Assume I have a really long group. If I send Forward=0, does the publisher has to cleanly fin the subgroup stream, reset it or what? What happens if I set Forward=1, and that subgroup is still open?

Relays/publishers don't have to immediately terminate open streams when Forward goes from 0->1.  The only normative rules are you can't send a FIN if you didn't send the final object in the subgroup, and a relay MUST NOT forward an Object on an existing Subgroup stream unless it is the *next* Object in that Subgroup.  But if Forward=0 causes an object to be missed - the logical thing to do is reset it.  If Forward=0 and the end of subgroup is reached _and_ the final object has been sent, I think it's fine to FIN the stream.

> Or if it's been closed so long ago that the relay evicted all the information about it from the cache?

I think the same logic applies.

Are you asking for editorial clarification or a design change?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: I am not sure if it's editorial or design, but we definitely should describe what happens to existing streams when Forward changes.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think we can address this with an Editorial PR.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
I don't think we should bake routing logic into the core transport. 

This won't work well in hierarchical distribution networks that are more than one layer deep.  A relay network may have several peers it must connect to in sequence to find the the original publisher. While you could code the first hop into the first tuple of the namespace, the namespace must remain consistent going upstream, but the MOQT URI of each the intermediate hops will need to differ.

I do think we might want to use the first (few) tuples of the namespace for routing, but these will be more of a routing ID. Each relay will then look that ID up in a local (and dynamic) routing table, which will return the actual MOQT URI that it should use to go upstream to the next node.

issues.title: How to serve a partial-hit FETCH when the original publisher is unavailable
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
If a cache has some objects in a FETCH range cached, but a range of objects with unknown status, and the original publisher is offline/unavailable, the cache must stop serving the FETCH at the first unknown object.  The subscriber has no way to know how many objects are unknown, so doesn't have an efficient way to skip over the gap.

FETCH_OK may have already been sent, so can't necessarily send a FETCH_ERROR when this happens
RESET_STREAM only carries an error code and can't encode any information about the unknown range
The absence of the OP may be either temporary or permanent

We could have an Object Status like "unknown" or "unknown range", but we just tentatively agreed to remove serving object status in FETCH responses.

```
and later

Presumably MOQT is using network byte order (big endian). RFC 9000, which MOQT borrows from defines it upfront so consider pulling this in too https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-1.3-5

issues.title: REGISTER requirements are poorly organized.
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
IN 9.2.2.1:

> If a registration is attempted which would cause this limit to be exceeded, the receiver MUST termiate the Session with a AUTH_TOKEN_CACHE_OVERFLOW error.


IN 9.3.2.5:

> If a server receives an AUTHORIZATION TOKEN parameter in CLIENT_SETUP with Alias Type REGISTER that exceeds its MAX_AUTH_TOKEN_CACHE_SIZE, it MUST NOT fail the session with AUTH_TOKEN_CACHE_OVERFLOW.

I don't think it's good for one section to say "you MUST always do this"  and have a completely different section say that "you MUST NOT in this very specific circumstance."

At the very least, the sentences above should have hyperlinks to each other. Or we could consolidate this.

issues.title: Clarify whether Message Parameters are hop-by-hop or end-to-end
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
I thought all control messages and the parameters associated with them were hop-by-hop.  If that was true, it'd be possible to use TV for all of them if we wanted and not do an even/odd parameter space algorithm.  I don't have a strong opinion that this would be better, but it would be possible.

@vasilvv  said that Parameters on PUBLISH (and SUBSCRIBE_OK) like MAX_CACHE_DURATION are end-to-end, which was initially surprising, but I agree that MAX_CACHE_DURATION should be preserved down the caching hierarchy.  Though that doesn't inherently mean it's end-to-end.

It seems pretty clear that parameters for most messages should not be blindly propagated upstream (ie: SUBSCRIBE params), but is PUBLISH different?  Or is it the fact that MAX_CACHE_DURATION is part of the base transport spec?

Possibly we're mixing two different things: Parameters on subscriptions and properties of a Track? (ie: Track Extensions)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
SUBSCRIBE / PUBLISH_OK params are definitely hop-by-hop, because of possible fan-out at the relay.

I agree there's ambiguity in publisher specified parameters like MAX_CACHE_DURATION and DELIVERY_TIMEOUT.  I also think there's value in Track properties/extensions, but #781 / #1176 has been parked.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think it'd be really nice to separate things that are hop-by-hop from E2E and make all the hop-by-hop things TV and the end-to-end things more like HTTP Headers.  MAX_CACHE_DURATION seems like a track property, since it's only sent by the publisher, but DELIVERY_TIMEOUT does not.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I think they're all hop-by-hop and are not guaranteed to be stable along the entire path, but in practice there is no reason for relays to alter some of these values.

In the case of delivery timeout, a relay *could* actually make it shorter due to memory limitations.

I think splitting up

issues.title: Parameter order of operation
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body: A subscribe, subscribe update, and publish_ok can specify both `forward=0` (aka paused state) and parameter NEW_GROUP_REQUEST.  How are we do handle this when a new group is requested at the same time the subscription is disabled from receiving data?

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body: It probably does not make sense. But on the other hand, it is up to the subscriber to decide, so it does not seem that bad. But of course, it is worth a discussion on whether the spec should prohibit the combination of sending both the parameter NEW_GROUP_REQUEST and the parameter FORWARD = 0. To me, prohibiting that is OK.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think FORWARD and NGR are orthogonal.  FORWARD is about whether you want the relay to send you objects.  NGR is whether you need a new join point created.

Would you prohibit this pattern:

SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE NGR
SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE FORWARD=0

?

I can imagine something like there are simulcast tracks, I SUBSCRIBE and find them both at object 500,000.  Then discover my bw is only enough for the smaller one, but maybe want to upswitch soon. I SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE NGR for low-res and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE NGR, FORWARD=0 for the other.

That said, I don't feel strongly.  If folks want to prohibit NGR and FORWARD=0 (or whenever FORWARD=0??) I can live with it.

comments.author: TimEvens
TimEvens
comments.body: +1 @yekuiwang

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
We don't expect relays to blindly forward subscriber messages, the spec has text already about subscriber priority, group order, and forward taking on different values when crossing relays.  The NGR text says that the Relay "MUST send a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE", not forward one.  With #1283, the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE probably won't even have a Forward -- meaning "unchanged".

There was some discussion of this at Wednesday's interim as it pertains to #1278.

>  as long as we have subscribers still with forward=1

I'll note that the spec has a SHOULD set to 1 regardless of downstream forward state, but I expect most implementations to ignore this when it's too expensive.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
> We don't expect relays to blindly forward subscriber messages

The issue with blindly forwarding was called out in our implementation because **we do not blindly forward.** We re-generate MoQT control messages which CAN result in defaults being used and params stripped upon regeneration because it's not defined in MoQT how a relay aggregates conflicting/unknown params/settings/knobs. 

It's great to see that the following were removed from `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE` after draft-14:

```
Start Location (Location),`
End Group (i),
Subscriber Priority (8),
```

as we just zeroed these out when sending NGR northbound.  Forward was in question and it seems that the expectation is that the relay (or MoQT update) will have to do one of the following:

1. Upon receive of NGR, check forwarding state of all subscribes and set northbound NGR SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE to forward=1 if at least one subscriber is in forward=1
2. Hard-code it and always set forward=1
3. MoQT define that if NGR is present forward value is irrelevant and implicitly sets `forward=1` because after all we are requesting a new group of objects to be received, to which is used to clear the NGR pending state

Parameters are still an issue considering we would not forward them. Only the NGR would result in a new generated SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE.  In fact, if we receive a PUBLISH_OK or SUBSCRIBE with NGR, that would be converted to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE with all those params not forwarded. In other words, we generate a general basic SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE with NGR.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> will have to do one of the following:

No we are planning to remove `Forward` as a mandatory field in SUBSCRIBE_UDPATE, and omitting it means "don't change" (#1283).

> Parameters are still an issue considering we would not forward them. Only the NGR would result in a new generated SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE. In fact, if we receive a PUBLISH_OK or SUBSCRIBE with NGR, that would be converted to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE with all those params not forwarded. In other words, we generate a general basic SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE with NGR.

This all sounds correct to me.  Parameters from the subscriber should all be destined only for the first hop.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body:
> This all sounds correct to me. Parameters from the subscriber should all be destined only for the first hop.

Agreed.  To confirm... PUBLISH messages sent to SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE requestor follows the same pattern where the PUBLISH is generated by the relay and does not contain the original params or exact value settings in the PUBLISH message.?.?

comments.body:
> A subscribe, subscribe update, and publish_ok can specify both `forward=0` (aka paused state) and parameter NEW_GROUP_REQUEST. How are we do handle this when a new group is requested at the same time the subscription is disabled from receiving data?

issues.title: There is no way for the publisher to cancel SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Say that a subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE with a valid authorization and the publisher OKs it.

Some time later, the authorization expires. Alternatively, the publisher is a relay that has an upstream subscription to a namespace, but that session suddenly dies.

How can the publisher signal this? It can PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE or PUBLISH_DONE anything that was delivered, but that's a different thing from canceling the subscribe.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Somewhat related to #1267 

I'm loathe to make new messages but I fear we have to for consistency of the state machine here.

```mermaid

stateDiagram-v2 
    [*] --> Idle: Initial state
    Idle --> Pending: SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (sub)
    Pending --> Established: REQUEST_OK (pub)
    Pending --> Terminated: REQUEST_ERROR (pub)
    Pending --> Terminated: UNSUSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (sub)
    Established --> Terminated: SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE_DONE (pub)
    Established --> Terminated: UNSUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (sub)
```

comments.author: suhasHere

issues.title: Discovery of MOQT publishers is always done out-of-band?
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
In Section 6 of the editor's copy, we have:

> Discovery of MOQT servers is always done out-of-band. Namespace discovery can be done in the context of an established MOQT session.
> 
> Given sufficient out of band information, it is valid for a subscriber to send a SUBSCRIBE or FETCH message to a publisher (including a relay) without any previous MOQT messages besides SETUP. However, SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, PUBLISH and PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages provide an in-band means of discovery of publishers for a namespace.
> 

First, in the first sentence of the first paragraph, "MOQT servers" should be changed to "MOQT publishers"?

Second, the first sentence of the first paragraph says "always done out-of-band", then the second sentence in the second paragraph describes how the discovery can be done in-band. They seem contradicting with each other?

comments.body:
> First, in the first sentence of the first paragraph, "MOQT servers" should be changed to "MOQT publishers"?

No, I think servers (publishers or subscribers -- eg ingest server) is correct.  We don't tell you where to connect.  Except in GOAWAY.  Sometimes.

issues.title: A single Subgroup stream (not a single Subgroup) has a single publisher priority
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
In Section 7 of the editor's copy, we have:

> A single subgroup or datagram has a single publisher priority. 

However, we know that Objects in a fetch response can have publisher priority present on Object level thus Objects of the same Subgroup could have different publisher priorities.

It is therefore suggested to change the above sentence to be as follows:

> A single Subgroup stream or datagram has a single publisher priority.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
A fetch response can encode a different publisher priority per each object in a single subgroup, but such a subgroup might be malformed?  In response to Subscribe, you can only have one priority per subgroup.

We thought about preventing this encoding in FETCH compression PR, but decided it was too much complexity because of receiver state.

So I think the original text is in the right spirit, and we can make it an error to specify different priorities in a fetch response subgroup.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
OK, I will make a PR for this. 

BTW, I just checked which error code should be used, and figured out it should be "MALFORMED_TRACK", and when I searched for "MALFORMED_TRACK" in the editor's copy, I noticed that are two different error codes, code values 0x12 and 0x07, with the same name of "MALFORMED_TRACK". comments.body: BTW again, if all Objects of each Subgroup in a fetch stream must have the same publisher priority, it would be so much more efficient to signal the publisher priority values in the fetch header, one value for each Subgroup. Would that be a very bad idea?

comments.body:

> BTW again, if all Objects of each Subgroup in a fetch stream must have the same publisher priority, it would be so much more efficient to signal the publisher priority values in the fetch header, one value for each Subgroup. Would that be a very bad idea?

I agree it would be better to disallow encoding something that is not possible in our object model.  We tried and failed to come up with a satisfying encoding though.  It can't go in the FETCH_HEADER, since that requires foreknowledge of all retrieved subgroups before opening the data stream.  We tried making it only in the first object for any subgroup also, but it requires unbounded state on the receiver, so we bailed.

comments.body:

To add to Section 5.2 (Fetch State Management)?

Give them the same value seems better to me, as malformed is one error, and the context (FETCH_ERROR, PUBLISH_DONE, fetch data stream resetting) is already clear by the source of the error code.

So bummed! I just don't feel great that there was a great goal/wish of MoQ being able to unify the worlds of conversational, live streaming, and on-demand streaming applications (https://www.ietf.org/blog/moq-overview/), but on-demand streaming has not been given enough attention in the MOQT design. issues.title: Joining FETCH as a separate control message creates edge cases and feature gaps
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
The point of joining FETCH is to save the round trip, therefore the only time its valuable to send a joining FETCH is immediately after sending the SUBSCRIBE.

There are the obvious edge cases, such as referencing a subscription that no longer exists (#1261) or failed for some reason. There are probably more that I'm not thinking of.

~~Additionally, there's no FETCH_UPDATE today, so I can change the priority of the SUBSCRIBE, but not the corresponding Joining FETCH.~~

I also don't think the transition is handled well in some cases, as I commented in a now closed issue: https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/598#issuecomment-2603109830. They key problem being that the latest Object could have greatly increased between the time the SUBSCRIBE+JOINING_FETCH are made and when the JOINING_FETCH catches up realtime.  If they were a single message, it would be relatively simple to say that if Objects greater than the Largest Object have been published since the subscription started, they MAY be sent on the FETCH stream.

Merging the two messages simplifies this, and makes it clear how to correctly use this feature.  This would lose a slight bit of functionality in terms of being able to separately prioritize or cancel the FETCH and SUBSCRIBE, but in practice you could cancel either by narrowing the SUBFETCH (or whatever the combined verb is called) with SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE

Somewhat related to #1039 and #861

comments.body:

You can send it after receiving a PUBLISH also?

As for the "subscribe+joining fetch -15 seconds" use case, can you elaborate more on what is actually broken?  It seems to me that in the worst case, the relay buffers live subscription data until the fetch completes, then delivers it.  Also, I think the scenario (backfill the buffer) works better as:

At time T:
SUBSCRIBE Largest Object, Pri=1
FETCH -15s, Descending, Pri=2 // lower priority
... 
FETCH_CANCEL // once total buffer len = 15s

If it takes 1s to download 5s of track data (fetch or subscribe), I'll have a 15s jitter buffer after 3s, starting at **T-12**

issues.title: Possible improvements on MoQ support of VOD applications
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
There was a great goal/wish of MoQ being able to unify the worlds of conversational, live streaming, and VOD applications (https://www.ietf.org/blog/moq-overview/). As side topics, @afrind and I touched a couple of times, e.g., in #1205 and #1309, on support of VOD applications in MOQT. From the discussions, I learned that:

1. For support of VOD applications based on MOQT, only FETCH requests can be used, as for VOD all Objects are "already published" or "from the past", while SUBCRIBE is only for "newly published or received" Objects.
2. Because of bullet 1, multiple streams cannot be used for VOD, unless Subgroup or Priority based Object filter, e.g., as discussed in #1164, is added to the MOQT draft and allowed to be used with FETCH.
3. Because Subgroup based streams cannot be used, signalling of priority cannot be in the stream header, while all Objects of one Subgroup are required to have the same priority. (@afrind does not think this is a major issue, which is probably true, but it would be very nice if this aspect can be improved.)
4. @afrind mentioned, in both #1205 and #1309, that due to lack of information about the consumption/playback rate, a relay cannot effectively serve past content, but rather VOD support with MOQT has to rely on use of many FETCH requests, just like use of many HTTP requests in HTTP adaptive streaming (e.g., DASH and HLS). 

Bullet 2 depends on #1164, and bullet 3 somehow depends on bullet 2. 

On bullet 4 above, I can think of the following possible ways of conveying information about the consumption/playback rate (i.e., media bitrate) such that relays can use it:
a) Require that catalog tracks are not encrypted, which ensures that relays can access all information in the catalog tracks, including the Bitrate field.
b) Add an Object Extension Header to convey the bitrate information.
c) Add a Bitrate Parameter to conveying the bitrate information, and allow this parameter to appear in a TRACK_STATUS_OK and whatever other control messages that deemed useful to have this parameter.

Opinions?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: CC: VOD enthusiast @wilaw

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
+1 to ensuring that MOQT is robust over the VOD playback use-case. 

>  VOD support with MOQT has to rely on use of many FETCH requests

I view this as a benefit, not a constraint. The client has full control over what it is FETCHING. Since the relay is going to burst the FETCH'd data as fast as possible, the client risks buffer-bloat if it asks for the entire track at once. So it will likely FETCH smaller amounts in order to constrain the forward buffer size. It could mimic HLS/DASH and request every group individually, or it could utilize a more optimal or dynamic reqeusting scheme. 

> Require that catalog tracks are not encrypted, which ensures that relays can access all information in the catalog tracks, including the Bitrate field.

This is a bad idea, as catalogs are not a part of MOQT, but rather of WARP, which is one particular streaming format. So it is not a generalized solution for MOQT payload delivery. 

> I can think of the following possible ways of conveying information about the consumption/playback rate (i.e., media bitrate) such that relays can use it:

I'll give a 4th option - add in a parameter to FETCH that allows the client to specify the rate at which the response SHOULD be returned. This would allow a client to FETCH the entirety of a 2-hr track encoded at an average of 2Mbps by specifying a rate just slightly above that, for example 2.1 Mbps. This does require us to standardize the timebase over which this rate is calculated, but that is solvable.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> I'll give a 4th option - add in a parameter to FETCH that allows the client to specify the rate at which the response SHOULD be returned. This would allow a client to FETCH the entirety of a 2-hr track encoded at an average of 2Mbps by specifying a rate just slightly above that, for example 2.1 Mbps. This does require us to standardize the timebase over which this rate is calculated, but that is solvable.

I like the idea of client-based rate control. 
The Subscriber should know the average bitrate of the track, which it can typically extract from a catalog (if any) or offline. However, it requires the Relay to have rate management (which may be complicated as you mentioned), and it does not work well with Variable Bit-Rate.
Another idea: the Subscriber indicates in the FETCH the expected time between two consecutive Group transmission. Group duration is an information that the client can extract from the catalog too (group_duration = 2sec), and it is much simpler at the Relay side (it is a timeout between consecutive group delivery). However, and I note it, one can also argue that, in VOD, group may be of different duration.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> > VOD support with MOQT has to rely on use of many FETCH requests
> 
> I view this as a benefit, not a constraint. The client has full control over what it is FETCHING. Since the relay is going to burst the FETCH'd data as fast as possible, the client risks buffer-bloat if it asks for the entire track at once. So it will likely FETCH smaller amounts in order to constrain the forward buffer size. It could mimic HLS/DASH and request every group individually, or it could utilize a more optimal or dynamic reqeusting scheme.

@wilaw Thanks! Good to learn. In HLS/DASH, both live and on-demand streaming scenarios are client-controlled, while in MOQT live streaming is based on subscriptions which does not use many requests. Why for on-demand streaming based on MOQT client-controlled is better but that is not the case for live steaming based on MOQT?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> In HLS/DASH, both live and on-demand streaming scenarios are client-controlled, while in MOQT live streaming is based on subscriptions which does not use many requests. Why for on-demand streaming based on MOQT client-controlled is better but that is not the case for live steaming based on MOQT?

In MOQT, both SUBSCRIBE and FETCH are initiated by the client (the subscriber) and are therefore 'client-controlled' . The difference with a live subscription is that the rate of sending is inherently controlled by the original publisher, as the relays are forwarding as fast as they can. With VOD, the content is immediately available, therefore the relay will send as fast as line speed allows. That is why in the live case a MOQT client will just make one subscribe request, but likely multiple fetches for VOD. The multiple fetches are to prevent the buildup of excessive forward buffer in the client. The multiple fetches are not required. For short content, such as a 15s advertisement, the client would likely just make a single FETCH.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think there's a use case for both a 'bitrate' Extension Header that can be used on Tracks as the default for the Track as well as for Objects if there's a need to override the Track's default value.

But I don't think that's sufficient, because it's going to be some sort of average over time, and you really want to ensure you're delivering content at the correct rate and maintaining the correctly sized buffer.  Also, there are use cases where people play back media at 1.5x or 2x the original rate.  I wouldn't optimize for those, but they're worth considering.

If I had whatever API I wanted for what you're describing, I think I'd want a way for the subscriber to keep bumping out the end of the subscription, and when the publisher hits the end, it pauses for some period of time (15s or 30s) in the expectation the subscriber may want to extend the end again.  In theory you could use multiple streams for Subgroups or Datagrams in this model as well.  In retrospect, this is a potential approach to solve #869.

One could imagine communicating enough information to the publisher to deliver media at exactly the right rate, but I think that information is probably larger and more complex than a simple SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE that increases the end Group.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> I think there's a use case for both a 'bitrate' Extension Header that can be used on Tracks as the default for the Track as well as for Objects if there's a need to override the Track's default value.
> 
> But I don't think that's sufficient, because it's going to be some sort of average over time, and you really want to ensure you're delivering content at the correct rate and maintaining the correctly sized buffer. Also, there are use cases where people play back media at 1.5x or 2x the original rate. I wouldn't optimize for those, but they're worth considering.

I think my proposal of indicating "a delay between consecutive Group fetches" is good for this use-case. The Subscriber gets the expected group duration from the catalog. Thus, it knows that, for example, a Groups on this track is a 2s video (if playback rate is 1x). The Subscriber can indicate FETCH with an extension parameter "consecutive_group_delay = 1.8s", which means "after you send one group, wait 1.8s before sending me the next group". Interestingly, if playback rate is 2x, then it can simply reduce the "consecutive_group_delay = 0.9s" to get data on time. I think it is reasonably simple to implement at Relay side (timer)

issues.title: Enable Subgroup stream across Groups
issues.author: yekuiwang
issues.body:
My reading of the MOQT draft is that each Subgroup stream conveys a Subgroup within one Group.

For video, typically a temporal sublayer lasts across independently coded group of pictures. Therefore, assuming one Subgroup corresponds to one temporal sublayer, and one Group corresponds to one independently coded group of pictures, then a Subgroup lasts across Groups. This would be the most common allocation of Groups and Subgroups for video.

In this case, it seems to me that allowing a Subgroup stream to convey the same Subgroup across multiple Groups would reduce the need of opening Subgroup streams at the start of each Group and closing of Subgroup streams at the end of each Group.

To add this capability, a flag can be added to SUBCRIBE and associated control messages to specify whether Subgroup streams are within one Group and across all Groups within the Start Location and the End Group.

Opinions?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The wire encoding of subgroups compresses the group ID out to the subgroup header, so you would also need a data plane change in order to communicate the new group ID.  Would you allow a priority change?  Do these encodings have dependencies on each other, or would single object subgroups be a better fit?

Opening and closing streams should not be that expensive, and should be infrequent compared to the transmission of object data.

I'm inclined to keep the object model and mapping as is.

comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> The wire encoding of subgroups compresses the group ID out to the subgroup header, so you would also need a data plane change in order to communicate the new group ID.

Yes.

> Would you allow a priority change?

No need to change the design herein; if a priority change is needed, then it can be controlled by using multiple control messages with different Start Location and End Group. 

> Do these encodings have dependencies on each other, or would single object subgroups be a better fit?
 
No need to have dependencies on each other. Whether single object subgroups be a better fit depends on the whether the complexity of opening and closing streams is high and whether opening and closing streams at Group boundaries has a negative impact on the continuity of the final playing back of the groups.

> Opening and closing streams should not be that expensive, and should be infrequent compared to the transmission of object data.
> 

This is the aspect I don't have a feeling; I trust yours. I assume you also think that opening and closing streams at Group boundaries does not have a negative impact on the continuity of the final playing back of the groups?

> I'm inclined to keep the object model and mapping as is.

OK (if you also think that opening and closing streams at Group boundaries does not have a negative impact on the continuity of the final playing back of the groups).

comments.body:
> I was referring to publisher priority, too. Here was what I meant. For example, for a particular Subgroup ID, if from Group N to Group N+1 the publisher would like to change is desired, then Group N and Group N+1 can be requested using two different SUBSCRIBE messages.

But this also makes me wonder, would you make subgroup ID be global across all groups in the Track? comments.author: yekuiwang
comments.body:
> If this is the case then the publisher would just create a different subgroup in the next group with the correct priority. But this also makes me wonder, would you make subgroup ID be global across all groups in the Track? How would a relay know when subgroup ID X in group N is the same/different from subgroup ID X in group N + 1?

Good question. Let's say a subscriber requests (using SUBSCRIBE) a range covering Groups N and N + 1 from a publisher. Regardless of whether the subgroup ID X applies across the two Groups or not, if the publisher wants to transmits the Subgroup with Subgroup ID = X for Group N in one Subgroup stream and the Subgroup with Subgroup ID = X for Group N+1 in another Subgroup stream, the publisher needs to send two SUBSCRIBE_OK, the first with a filter covering Group N, and the second with a filter covering Group N+1. Or SUBSCRIBE_OK is updated to allow the presence of multiple instances of the filter parameter to achieve the same effect. In this case, downstream relays treat Groups N and N + 1 as if the Subgroup ID = X  does not apply across Groups N and N + 1. However, if the subgroup ID X does apply across the two Groups and the publisher does want to transmit the Subgroup with Subgroup ID = X for both Groups N and N + 1 in one Subgroup stream, the publisher sends a SUBSCRIBE_OK with no filter. In this case, downstream relays treat Groups N and N + 1 as that the Subgroup ID = X  does apply across Groups N and N + 1.

issues.title: What happens if both endpoints try to establish a subscription to the same track?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
Current text (in SUBSCRIBE definition) 

> A subscriber MUST NOT establish multiple concurrent subscriptions for a track within a single session and publishers SHOULD treat this as a protocol violation.

1. We should move this restriction to the subscriptions section, since it applies to PUBLISH also
2. It's possible for the publisher and subscriber to race establishing a subscription to the same track.  This probably shouldn't be a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION. Instead we can clearly say which one wins, and which one gets a REQUEST_ERROR.  Publisher wins?

> If a publisher receives a SUBSCRIBE request for a subscription in the Pending state, it MUST reject that request with a REQUEST_ERROR with code DUPLICATE_SUBSCRIPTION.  If a subscriber receives a PUBLISH for a subscription in the Pending state, it MUST first terminate its pending subscription UNSUBSCRIBE before sending PUBLISH_OK.

comments.body:
Looks good to let the publisher win. 

> If a subscriber receives a PUBLISH for a subscription in the Pending state, it MUST first terminate its pending subscription UNSUBSCRIBE before sending PUBLISH_OK.

If the subscriber receives the REQUEST_ERROR with code DUPLICATE_SUBSCRIPTION before trying to terminate its pending subscription using UNSUBSCRIBE, then it no longer needs to terminate its pending subscription using UNSUBSCRIBE before sending PUBLISH_OK, right?

comments.body:
S->P: SUBSCRIBE id=1
P->S: PUBLISH id=0
P->S: REQUEST_ERROR id=1

If the subscriber processes the REQUEST_ERROR, that subscription moves from `Pending (subscriber)` to `Terminated`, so there's no need to UNSUBSCRIBE.

If a subscriber receives a PUBLISH for a subscription in the `Pending (subscriber)` state, it MUST transition the subscription to `Terminated` before sending PUBLISH_OK.

issues.title: Cancelling a subscription can be slow
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
In HTTP/3, we made sure that one could cancel a HTTP request at the QUIC layer, in case the upper HTTP layers were busy.  This was informed by experience with the importance of TCP reset working.

In MoQ today, UNSUBSCRIBE is on the control stream, so it's HoL blocked behind other messages.  Today this is made worse by the fact that there might be a number of PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages, but even without that, it'd be nice to be able to immediately cancel a Subscription without waiting for any pending SUBSCRIBE_UPDATEs/etc to be processed.

issues.title: No way to avoid PUBLISH when using SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE
issues.author: kixelated
issues.body:
> If the FORWARD parameter ([Section 9.2.1.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-15.html#forward-parameter)) is present in this message and equal to 0, PUBLISH messages resulting from this SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE will set the FORWARD parameter to 0. If the FORWARD parameter is equal to 1 or omitted from this message, PUBLISH messages resulting from this SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE will set the FORWARD parameter to 1, or indicate that value by omitting the parameter (see [Section 5.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-15.html#subscriptions)).

What this means is that `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE` will trigger both `PUBLISH` and `PUBLISH_NAMESPACE`. There's no way to get only `PUBLISH_NAMESPACE`.

Currently, I have to send `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE forward=0` and `PUBLISH_ERROR` all of the incoming `PUBLISH forward=0` messages. I don't want to learn about every (currently known) track within a namespace, and will `SUBSCRIBE` to tracks when I actually want them. comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Chatting with Lorenzo, it sounds like this was an intentional change to `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE` around when `PUBLISH` was added. I'm using `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE` to discover namespaces ONLY, and I don't want a `PUBLISH` when a relay discovers a new track.

ex. let's say I have 50 people in a conference room. I'm using `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE` to learn about each participant and issuing a `SUBSCRIBE catalog.json` for each. I have a bunch of optional tracks, like `captions.txt`, that the relay doesn't know about because they exist in the catalog only. The first participant to `SUBSCRIBE captions.txt` will cause a `PUBLISH captions.txt` to all 49 other participants, who then reply `PUBLISH_ERROR` because they're not interested in the subscription.

This behavior also makes dynamic track names quite problematic. If we implement something like SSAI using unique ad tracks, every subscriber will get a PUBLISH for each unique ad...

issues.title: Do we need stricter text for Request IDs?
issues.author: lminiero
issues.body:
The draft currently says:

>  The client's Request ID starts at 0 and are even and the server's Request ID starts at 1 and are odd

and

> The Request ID increments by 2 with each FETCH, ...

It also says

> If an endpoint receives a Request ID that is not valid for the peer, or a new request with a Request ID that is not the next in sequence or exceeds the received MAX_REQUEST_ID, it MUST close the session with INVALID_REQUEST_ID.

I know many, me included, have translated to our stacks mandating 0 as a starting point for clients, 1 for servers, and mandatory increment steps of +2, meaning that if I get a Request ID different from 0 as the first ID from a client, I'll close the connection, and I'll do the same if I get 0 first and 4 next.

The issue I see is that there's no MUST for the starting points, and for the increments either. This means that a loose interpretation could have people see them as a generic starting point and a need for always going up, but not as strictly as they should: meaning that 4, 10, 68 could be seen as a valid always growing sequence of Request IDs from a client. I did meet such a use case in my interop, where one of the clients that hit my relay was using Request ID 8 as the first ID, rather than 0.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think MUSTs here are fine.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Closing the connection if the first Request ID isn't 0 is overly strict, in my opinion.  The idea behind MAX_REQUEST_ID is to limit the number of requests, not dictate the exact order in which Request IDs are used.  There are valid cases where they might not be strictly in order.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I am also ok saying any ID is fine as long as it's the correct parity and under the limit.  But the current text is ambiguous and leads to interop failures.

issues.title: SUBSCRIBE does not need a forward parameter if we have filters
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
Currently within SUBSCRIBE you can set a [forward parameter](https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#forward-parameter) of 0 (don't send me anything) or 1 ( send me everything, default).

If we implement FILTERS (see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1164 and also Filter design team results), then we can remove this flag as:

a forward flag of 0 is syntactically equivalent to a FILTER that blocks everything
a forward flag of 1 is syntactically equivalent to a FILTER that allows everything 

Forward state can be managed by SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE and adjusting the FILTER.

issues.title: Why do we need a dedicated SWITCH message?
issues.author: acbegen
issues.body:
To date, numerous discussions have been held to understand and devise meaningful solutions for track switching in MOQT. The following is the list of open issues tagged with the ABR label.

- #259 
The challenge involves a publisher providing multiple quality versions of the same content (e.g., 360p and 720p video), where the subscriber needs to receive only the best quality version they can handle. The argument is that the publisher knows what it can send and should decide what to send.

- #370 
Previously, we implemented this through a probing track and whenever the subscriber needed a probing test, it would subscribe to this track.

- #471 
In client-side ABR streaming, the decision to switch to a higher quality stream can lead to excessive bandwidth usage, potentially causing network congestion and degrading the overall user experience. To address this, the proposed solution introduces a "Less than Best Effort" (LBE) mechanism. With LBE, higher-quality (but lower-priority) content is transmitted only if the congestion window (CWND) remains below a specified threshold, such as 1.5 times the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP). This approach ensures that LBE data does not compete with or crowd out higher-priority traffic, thereby maintaining network stability and prioritizing essential data delivery.

- #475 
There's no effective way to keep two subscriptions with identical priority in sync, which becomes problematic when one subscription experiences delays (such as during transcoding), potentially causing them to drift out of sync and impact the quality of experience, especially for low-latency use cases.

- #534 
The author proposes allowing for at least padding unidirectional streams, which can then be used for probing.

- #1101 
The issue raises concerns about how to achieve a smooth, gapless switch between two synchronized media tracks in MOQT, such as switching video quality (ABR) or audio languages, using the existing SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE methods, possibly with track priorities. The goal is to avoid both interruptions and duplicate delivery of the same content during the switch, particularly for live streaming. Previous attempts to address this issue with track priorities have led to conflicting approaches, highlighting ambiguities and limitations in the current protocol. The discussion aims to identify and address these shortcomings and initiate work on protocol improvements to enable reliable and seamless track switching.

**What we have now:**

As advocates of client-side ABR and server-assisted ABR techniques, we implemented the following:
- The first ABR demo that used client-side information, such as client bandwidth measured on the client side and some congestion signals, such as late-arriving MOQ groups. 
- Bandwidth probing from the relay to assist the client in doing ABR.

We also proposed a [solution](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-gurel-moq-track-switching/) to merge subscribe and unsubscribe operations and do an atomic track switch on the relay and published our results [here](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11152184) ([Stockholm interim slides](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/interim-2025-moq-09/materials/slides-interim-2025-moq-09-sessa-track-switching-made-easy-in-media-over-quic-transport-00)). Our results showed advantages of letting the (edge) relay control the switching process.

We believe that a SWITCH message in MOQT is necessary to address the track switching problem properly and pave the way for developing robust ABR implementations. 

This message ensures smooth transitions between alternative tracks, eliminating any gaps or overlaps in content download and transmission during the switch. It also handles cases where the groups/objects are not necessarily arriving at the relay at the same time.

A demo showing ABR with the current messages and parameters is available [here](https://abr.moqtail.dev/). The same demo, featuring a SWITCH message, will be available soon.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Just to re-explain one of the key problems. It happens when a Subscriber is "far from live", i.e. at a given time the Subscriber is receiving an Object that the Relay received some time ago. Furthermore, the Relay has received one or more Objects since.

Example: 
a Relay receives one new Group per second. It receives 28, 29, 30, 31...
a Subscriber is aligned with the Relay until group 28, and then it experiences some network troubles, its bandwidth is only half of the video bit-rate. It has a buffer of say 8 seconds of video, so it can survive. After 4 seconds of bad experience, the Subscriber observes buffer depletion and would like to switch. **The Relay just received Group 32, while the Subscriber is receiving Group 30.**

The subscribe/unsubscribe option does not work: 
Subscribe to track B starts with Group 33 - 34 - ...
Unsubscribe track A 33 means that the the Subscriber must still receive Groups 31 and 32
It is awful: 1/ the switch operation generates an increase of the amount of data on the line, 2/ the switch happens too late, 

So, no @ianswett I disagree with your claim that "_Track switching in the future is quite good_". I also disagree with "_By sending the SUBSCRIBE+SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE at the same time with an explicit Group ID in the future, prioritization is easy_". In my example, the Subscriber would send a Subscribe track B group 31, ... which would generate an error at the Relay. And no, prioritization is not easy. #1101 explained that we tried to find some way to address the problem with priorities but we did not find the way. Prioritizing track A during two whole groups will generate an accumulation of track groups at Relay and little chance to catch up for the Subscriber.

The solution that @wilaw and I have presented a long time ago is to Subscribe track B, get largest group, realize the gap, emit a joining FETCH at the next group, unsubscribe track A asap... but, as we mentioned at that time, it includes a number of pitfalls: 1/ it is overly complicated, 2/ it requires the Relay to be fast to get past objects (especially if was not previously subscribed to track B), 3/ it requires the Subscriber to guess the location ID in the future, 4/ it inevitably generates some objects in the line at the same time, with prioritization issues.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Alternatively, what if the client was subscribed to a timeline track with the highest priority?

The player could them know how far behind the live broadcast it is and choose a concrete switch point (SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE + SUBSCRIBE). This approach would work with unaligned groups, unlike SWITCH. It would also be able to tell the difference between broadcaster congestion and viewer congestion: if the timeline stops making progress then switching down a rendition won't help.

A GROUP_END message (separate from the data streams) with the number of objects would accomplish something similar. It would also help the subscriber/relay know how much of the group was dropped (and may need a FETCH), because the current group FIN status is literally the first object that can be dropped.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body: And I'm not saying that SWITCH is a bad idea, but it feels off that the player doesn't know the live playhead yet has still come to the conclusion that a SWITCH is necessary. Plus I really want to support unaligned groups.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> Alternatively, what if the client was subscribed to a timeline track with the highest priority?
> 
> The player could them know how far behind the live broadcast it is and choose a concrete switch point (SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE + SUBSCRIBE). This approach would work with unaligned groups, unlike SWITCH. It would also be able to tell the difference between broadcaster congestion and viewer congestion: if the timeline stops making progress then switching down a rendition won't help.

It addresses one of the points (identifying gap between Relay's live and Subscriber's status). But it does not say whether the Relay has an ongoing subscription to the target Track, nor if the Relay cached the past objects of track B. If not to any of these questions, the Relay will take more time to get the requested Objects from the Publisher, and may generate other problems.

Note that this problem can be addressed by preemptively subscribe to track B with forward=0 (and "force" the Relay to cache some recent objects of this track). I would argue that 1/ sometimes bandwidth drops unexpectedly. In my example, the Subscriber was perfectly fine until Group=28, so no reason to warm up a second track; 2/ if every Subscriber requests both up and down tracks just in case of a possible switch in the future, it would be a bad design with respect to network consumption and Relay resource management.

And overall, forcing timeline subscription + extra-track warm-up + switch point choice management. It does not address the "overly complicated" point.

With a SWITCH message, the Subscriber offloads the switch responsibility to the Relay, who has a better view of the system. The Relay knows both Subscriber status (from the SWITCH message) and its own status. It knows what it has in cache; it knows track group alignment; it knows the size of the groups in both tracks.

Oh absolutely. I don't think warming the CDN is necessary, especially at this stage of the draft. At best is a minor optimization that should be backed by production experiments before entering an RFC. 

Joining FETCH should absolutely be replaced with subscriptions that start at group boundaries. It's so gross writing a subscriber right now.

You're (probably) going to want the timeline track anyway for cross-rendition metadata.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Joining FETCH should absolutely be replaced with subscriptions that start at group boundaries. It's so gross writing a subscriber right now.

+1 

> You're (probably) going to want the timeline track anyway for cross-rendition metadata.

Timeline tracks are not a part of MOQT. They are an application construct, in this case of MSF. We should depend upon their presence for what should otherwise be a native functionality of payload-agnostic MOQT - namely the ability to switch from one track to another at a non-duplicating join-point. 

> it feels off that the player doesn't know the live playhead yet has still come to the conclusion that a SWITCH is necessary

The player is the only component which knows the length of its forward buffer and hence how much time it has before it rebuffers. Therefore  it knows when a SWITCH is necessary. This is independent of any notion about live playhead. 

> With a SWITCH message, the Subscriber offloads the switch responsibility to the Relay, who has a better view of the system. The Relay knows both Subscriber status (from the SWITCH message) and its own status. It knows what it has in cache; it knows track group alignment; it knows the size of the groups in both tracks.

+1

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
And some quick use-cases from Twitch when we wanted "unaligned" renditions:

1. Source quality is transmuxed and may not have a fixed keyframe interval. It would be nice if our transcoded renditions could insert keyframes when needed/optimal.
2. Would be nice to spin up/down independent transcode instances. Makes it more difficult when keyframe boundaries MUST be aligned across instances.
3. Truly redundant ingest, sourced from different (unaligned) encoders.
4. Server side ads lul. You have to rewrite sequences on a per viewer basis across all renditions. Would be nice to do ABR based on timestamp instead and avoid that.
5. Server side ads v2. When ads don't have a duration evenly divisible by the keyframe interval, they increase latency by the remainder.
6. Transcoded renditions have higher latency than transmuxed renditions, so switching to them needs to be sooner.

I think SWITCH based on PTS might work, if that was available at the MoQT layer, but aligned sequence numbers are meh.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Apologies, I've completely derailed the conversation. Nobody cares about unaligned groups and it would be many years before a service even attempts it. I just have fun brainstorming ways to improve HLS/DASH.

That being said, ABR in MoQ is currently worse than HLS because of the lack of a timeline (provided by the HLS playlist). SWITCH could alleviate that, but I would be worried implementing it as a CDN vendor given the independent nature of QUIC streams. You would have to really prescribe what a relay should do, like does it have to check how much of a QUIC stream has been buffered/transmitted/acked and how would it make any SWITCH decision.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
About SWITCH complexity at Relay, we had a simplified flowchart at the end of [this slidedeck (presented in Feb 2025)](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1YPLTpHjrJpNUtjvw58fAvE2NhiWHjuptDwTcjaRvVcI/edit?usp=sharing) but it was mostly informative. 

At reception of a SWITCH (oldSubscriptionID, newSubscriptionID, trackAlias, track B, newAuthInfo), the main decision of a Relay is about the "transition" (the group at which Track B rather than Track A is delivered downstream). We proposed the transition to be at "the next mutual group boundary" (slide 13), which depends on the situation, in particular whether the Relay is already subscribed to Track B. It is possible to implement some optimization, for example to FETCH some missing Track B's groups if the Subscriber is late, so that the transition can be effective earlier, but these are optional operational details. 

With a SWITCH, no need to implement complex priority management, nor even more complex QUIC buffer management. The Relay app sends Objects one by one as usual. Just that, at the transition, Track B is sent instead of Track A.

Some errors can happen though. For example, the Subscriber is very late and, for any reason, the Relay has no way to FETCH missing Groups to fill the gap between both Tracks. We can document it.

It may be worth issuing a PR to make the discussion more to-the-point.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Yep yep @gwendalsimon, best to keep it simple. If the relay always switches at the next group then that's super easy to implement.

But I don't think that will be good enough. "There are some possible optimizations in which an earlier group boundary may be used" (slide 13) and "determine transition strategy" (slide 14) are what scares me. 

That's because the SWITCH decision should made based on the client's view of the world, not the relay's view of the world. If the client is struggling to download group 31 and the relay decides to switch at group 34 (latest+1), that's far too late. The client will be stuck downloading multiple groups at an unsustainable bitrate; it needs a switch ASAP. 

It's not reasonable to expect the relay to reconstruct the client's buffer state based on QUIC acknowledgements. I think there would need to be an explicit group number in SWITCH instead.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> That's because the SWITCH decision should made based on the client's view of the world, not the relay's view of the world.

No. The Relay is the only one who knows everything: the status of track B, what he has in cache, the objects that are currently sent to the Subscriber (so, he has almost the view of the Subscriber), the gaps in the tracks... The Relay is in a waaaay better position to apply the best switch possible.

> If the client is struggling to download group 31 and the relay decides to switch at group 34 (latest+1), that's far too late. 

I 100% agree with you... but a good Relay will never do it. A good Relay should do whatever it can to switch that client at group 32. Yet, it depends on many parameters: is the Relay subscribed to track B? does the Relay has 32 and 33 in cache? If not, how long will it take to FETCH 32, 33? Is the Relay a good Relay that implements this optimization or is it a dumb Relay that simply switch at the next Track B boundaries? Is it even possible to do even better and switch at 31 retrospectively? ... The Relay can take such decisions.

On the one hand, I don't want to force all Relays in the world to implement smart optimization.
On the other hand, the situation you describe requires smart Relays.

I think it should be left as a differentiator between CDN vendors. The basic requirement of a Relay is to switch at the next possible boundary. An improvement requirement may be to switch as early as possible.

> It's not reasonable to expect the relay to reconstruct the client's buffer state based on QUIC acknowledgements. I think there would need to be an explicit group number in SWITCH instead.

No. The Relay is the only one who knows what it will be capable of sending to the Subscriber in a smooth transition. The Subscriber has zero knowledge. It does not even know if there is a gap in the coming groups nor the status of Track B. 

When we discussed it with @wilaw six months ago, we considered adding a parameter such that "Please I'm in panic, do it ASAP or die" but it does not really change the behavior.

> I 100% agree with you... but a good Relay will never do it. A good Relay should do whatever it can to switch that client at group 32. 

Ya, I'm saying that in order to switch at group 32, a "good" relay would need to inspect QUIC streams to figure out what byte offsets have been queued/transmitted/acknowledged, and remember what byte offset corresponds to which objects. That's the only way it can tell if group 32 should be canceled and replaced with another track, based on some heueristic.

The "default" relay would write each object to a QUIC stream as they arrive, subject to flow control. It would always switch at the next group 34 because it has no information about the client's progress, unless flow control limits are low enough. QUIC libraries usually don't expose ack information so making a "good" relay would require tighter QUIC bindings.

IMO, a "default" relay will make a worse switching decision than a client. The client will try to switch at group 32, regardless of how much data the relay has queued for group 33.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> What if SWITCH was an extension so a smart relay could opt-in?

Why an extension instead of a core and basic functionality? Groups are defined as access points in tracks. A media agnostic capability of switching between tracks at the next mutually numbered group seems like a conceptually simple and useful capability for the transport. 

I'd support more complicated intra-group or early switch optimizations being relegated to an extension (or pushed to the client), but argue strongly for retaining simpler next-group switching in the core protocol.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:

Yeah exactly. A "dumb" switch at the next group ID could totally be in the base spec. 

I don't think it's good enough for higher latency targets, specifically when the jitter buffer is larger than the GoP/segment duration. If the client's buffer size is 5s and GoPs are 2s, then by the time the client's buffer depletes it is multiple groups behind. 

You want the "next" group from the client's perspective, not the relay's perspective. It's the same concept with HLS: the client switches at the most recently downloaded group +1, not the tail of playlist +1 (aka "dumb" SWITCH).

But if SWITCH is only meant for real-time clients then it's fine. Simple enough.

I think picoquic does that (?) but not quiche, quinn, quic-go, and W3C WebTransport (for what it's worth).

comments.author: laiDisney
comments.body: I haven't caught all the threads here, but want to pop an idea here to discuss: could an atomic operation on multiple control messages work here? Like we always meet an issue that the gap between the messages, so if we can group multiple messages, then make it perform as one, can this be a solution?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> I haven't caught all the threads here, but want to pop an idea here to discuss: could an atomic operation on multiple control messages work here? Like we always meet an issue that the gap between the messages, so if we can group multiple messages, then make it perform as one, can this be a solution?

We don't propose SWITCH to simplify the emission of two/three messages in a row. We propose it because the Subscriber must offload part of the switching decision to the Relay for a smooth transition. Let me get back to the example of a Subscriber getting a track A:

a Relay receives one new Group per second. It receives 28, 29, 30, 31...
a Subscriber is aligned with the Relay until group 28, and then it experiences some network troubles, its bandwidth is only half of the video bit-rate. It has a large buffer of video, so it can survive. After 4 seconds of bad experience, the Subscriber observes sustained buffer depletion and would like to switch to track B. The Relay just received track A's Group 32, while the Subscriber is only receiving Group 30.

Let's say that MOQT authorizes sending multiple messages all in once.

_Subscribe B / Unsubscribe A_ does not work --> the Subscriber would never receive 31 
_Subscribe B 31 / Unsubscribe A 31_ does not work --> it generates a Subscribe_error because 31 is in the past for track B
_Subscribe B / Joining_Fetch 31 / Unsubscribe 31_ does not work --> two data flows are sent on the wire in the same time (32 due to subscribe + 31 due to fetch) which increases the throughput (the opposite the Subscriber wants) + the Subscriber does not know if the Relay cached 31 for B so it does not know how long it will take to get 31

With SWITCH, the Relay receives the notification to switch from A to B. It knows this Subscriber is currently getting 30. It knows that it just received track A's 32, and, more importantly, it knows its own status related to track B. So the Relay can decide:
If it is already subscribed to track B and 31 is in its cache, it can do the transition from A to B at group 31
If it is already subscribed to track B but it does not have 31 in its cache, it can decide if it is worth Fetching B 31 and accordingly transition at 31 (if it is possible) or 32
If it is not subscribed to track B, then it subscribes to B (possibly with joining fetch) and transitions when possible
