Section 10.4.3 of the spec says "If a sender will not deliver any objects from a Subgroup, it MAY send a SUBGROUP_HEADER on a new stream, with no objects, and then send RESET_STREAM_AT with a reliable_size equal to the length of the stream header. This explicitly tells the receiver there is an unsent Subgroup."

We might want to be a little more clear about how this affects the stream count in a PUBLISH_DONE message, since section 9.15 says "If the track had only Objects with Forwarding Preference = Datagram, the publisher MUST set Stream Count to 0."

If, within a specific track, a publisher just sends objects within datagrams, but also opens up an empty subgroup, what effect should this have on the stream count? What about a publisher that has sent objects within subgroups?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm not sure I remember why we think we might ever send an empty subgroup.

The purpose of stream count is to ensure the receiver can guarantee delivery of everything that was sent to the application.  I'm not sure we need to include a stream with no objects in the count.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> I'm not sure I remember why we think we might ever send an empty subgroup.

I guess it could be a case that an impl opens a stream and sends the header, but objects never get prioritized and/or timeout, so it shouldn't be an error to receive it.

issues.title: Object Datagram: Status != Normal and contains extensions allowed?
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body:
Section 10.2.1.2 states: "If an endpoint receives extension headers on Objects with status that is not Normal, it MUST close the session with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION."

Section 10.3.1 lists disallowed datagram types, but types such as 0x21 that have both the STATUS and EXTENSIONS bit set are allowed. Is there a reason for allowing this for object datagrams and not objects? Should we disallow it for object datagrams by adding to the list of disallowed datagram types?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
With datagram type 0x21:
 - EXTENSIONS bit (0x01) = Extensions present
 - STATUS bit (0x20) = Object Status field present, no payload

If Object Status = 0x0 (Normal), this is valid - it's a Normal object with
extensions and explicitly _no payload_.

If Object Status = 0x3 or 0x4 (non-Normal), the rule from 10.2.1.2 should still
apply - it's a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

So the answer is:
 1. Type 0x21 isn't actually a special case - the rule from 10.2.1.2 applies to all Objects
 including datagrams
 2. Type 0x21 with Status=Normal is allowed (extensions + empty payload)
 3. Type 0x21 with Status=non-Normal should still be a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION per 10.2.1.2

issues.title: There is no way to turn off DELIVERY_TIMEOUT
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
As a subscriber, say I start with DELIVERY_TIMEOUT = 1 sec, but then decide I want everything and want to set it to Infinite.

There is no way to express this in REQUEST_UPDATE. '0' could have a special meaning, but it is currently disallowed. If REQUEST_UPDATE omits the parameter, it's unchanged.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I open to the idea that there is no use case for this, so we don't need it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Using 0 for this seems sensible, especially since it's currently disallowed.  I can't remember why we didn't make 0 mean infinite before, or if we just didn't discuss it.

issues.title: Lack of clarity in updating the EXPIRY
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body: Section 9.2.2.6 says "The receiver of the parameter can extend the subscription by sending a REQUEST_UPDATE". However, in that same section, REQUEST_UPDATE isn't listed as a message that allows the EXPIRY parameter. Should we add it in, or is there some other mechanism through which the REQUEST_UPDATE can request that the subscription be extended?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I don't think REQUEST_UPDATE should include EXPIRES; the requester can't generally extend the expiration of something.  I think REQUEST_OK probably should have it - eg if you update an auth token, you might get a new expires.  Or if you updated something else, it may extend the peer's idle timeout.

PUBLISH can include expires - this is for the relay to client direction expressing e.g. idle timeout.

comments.author: sharmafb
comments.body:
I might be splitting hairs here, but do you think that a better rewording of that sentence could be "The reception of a REQUEST_UPDATE (for example, one containing a new auth token) may cause an extension of the expiration."

This makes it more clear that one can't directly request a postponement of the expiration by sending a REQUEST_UPDATE (e.g. using an EXPIRES parameter), but that certain properties of that REQUEST_UPDATE may result in an extension of the expiration.

issues.title: We Need MOQPACK
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Now that Auth Tokens can arrive on the SUB_NS stream, Token Registry operations are no longer HOL blocked. The draft needs language for how to handle this case.

I don't really care which of many solutions we choose.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The band-aid solution to this problem is you can't use a TOKEN_ALIAS until you've seen the response (OK or ERROR) to the request that had REGISTER.  This would prevent pipelined requests from using aliases.

Another reasonable option is to remove token compression from the draft, and move it to an extension.

If we need the full complexity of the QPACK dynamic table, with sending requests that may block on the arrival of an out-of-order request, we would do better to find a way to import that (also likely via an extension) rather than recreate it.

See #969

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: SUBSCRIBE_NS can safely reference token aliases in CLIENT_SETUP, right?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: yes -- I think anything registered in CLIENT_SETUP is globally safe.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Yes, the issue in 16 is tokens registered in SUB NS can’t be reliably referenced elsewhere until after a response, and those registered on the control stream can’t be referenced in SUB NS until a response.

issues.title: Should REQUEST_ERROR Codes have GOING_AWAY?
issues.author: sandarsh
issues.body:
>Upon receiving a GOAWAY, an endpoint SHOULD NOT initiate new requests to the
peer including SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH, FETCH, PUBLISH_NAMESPACE,
SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE and TRACK_STATUS.

>Sending a GOAWAY does not prevent the sender from initiating new requests,
though the sender SHOULD avoid initiating requests unless required by migration
(see ({{graceful-subscriber-switchover}} and {{graceful-publisher-switchover}}).
An endpoint that receives a GOAWAY MAY reject new requests with an appropriate
error code (e.g., **SUBSCRIBE_ERROR with error code GOING_AWAY**).

This reads like there should be a REQUEST_ERROR code GOING_AWAY, that will be sent when GO_AWAY has already been received and then we receive a new request.

Currently it is only part of PUBLISH_DONE codes which might not be sufficient. Thoughts?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This seems fine to me, want to make a PR?

comments.author: sandarsh
comments.body: Will do

issues.title: What happens when a client subscribes to a namespace that is too large?
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body: I imagine that at some point the namespace can reach the number of active publishers (1000? 10000? 100000?) where it is too large for the relay network to handle.  We should have some story for what happens in that scenario.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
I really need to see a case where we have numbers in that range.  Also nothing stops from a subscribing  to 100000 tracks. 

Having said that, we need to be able to have a way to subscribe namespace to be rejected if the resource consumption issues arise. I would expect the same thing to happen on individual subscription too.

May we adding this in securiy consideration sections is good and perhaps add a error code in SubscribeError/SubscribeNamespace bidi response ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
We don't have much in our security section, but we have this:

> A Relay SHOULD have mechanisms to prevent malicious endpoints from flooding it with PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE requests that could bloat data structures. It could use the advertised MAX_REQUEST_ID to limit the number of such requests, or could have application-specific policies that can reject incoming PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE requests that cause the state maintenance for the session to be excessive.

> A Relay can use authorization rules in order to prevent subscriptions closer to the root of a large prefix tree. Otherwise, if an entity sends a relay a SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE message with a short prefix, it can cause the relay to send a large volume of PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages. As churn continues in the tree of prefixes, the relay would have to continue to send PUBLISH_NAMESPACE/PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE messages to the entity that had sent the SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.

So to some degree, it's expected that this be handled by auth.

Let's assume that there are 100k tracks published under one namespace and a client issues SUBSCRIBE_NS with publish option.  This will likely run out of Request IDs unless the client has very generous limits.  Perhaps the relay also needs a way to protect itself from opening too many (eg: client has MAX_REQUEST_ID 100000), but the relay won't do that.  See also #1262.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This may be a duplicate - @vasilvv to investigate.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Elsewhere I proposed that we have a TOO_FAR_BEHIND error. Namespaces that the relay already has will be in a tree structure. If the whole tree cannot fit in the initial bidi stream credit, I believe it will be difficult to keep track of that state.

Admittedly, I haven't implemented it yet so maybe I'll find a way around these problems, but in any case it's a reasonable thing for relays to panic about.

I haven't implemented a FETCH relay either, but if there is any sort of fanout instead of piping all FETCHes back to the original publisher or full cache, I believe similar considerations are in play.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm not sure fetch is in play here - if there's too much in the cache, the relay needs to wait for more credit and resume.  Yes the cache state can have changed out from under it, but you have to handle that case.  It's more tractable because there's a fixed iteration order for fetch.  You can pin the current object to prevent it's eviction while waiting, and pick up at the next object.  The ns tree changing out from under you and the obligation to deliver future updates as well as current state makes it different.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Victor articulated two specific asks to me besides #1452:

1. A specific error code for SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE - NAMESPACE_TOO_LARGE
2. All using TOO_FAR_BEHIND when a SUB_NS response stream blocks on flow control

These seem quite reasonable.

issues.title: Clarify which extensions are immutable
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Non-editorial comment: extension types should be either immutable or mutable, it should say in the draft, and it should be a malformed track if it's in the wrong spot.

Editorial comment:

The section numbering is a little messed up in Section 11, which makes it hard to tell what categories are where.

More broadly, it would be nice to understand if any of the defined extensions are immutable or not. AFAICT all of the track extensions are mutable and the gap ones are immutable. Or, the draft could make it clear that there are no immutable extensions defined in the draft.

So I find this to be pretty confusing. I would reorganize as follows:

11.1 Mutable Extensions - must be in the "first level"

11.1.1 Delivery Timeout...

11.1.X The "Immutable Extensions" Extension

11.2 Immutable Extensions -- must be in the 11.1.X extension

11.2.1 Object Gap

11.2.2 Group Gap

11.2.3 Max Cache Duration?

but there are other ways to do it that would make sense too.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the design of immutable was intentionally flexible, because what goes in there becomes input to an end-to-end AAD.  So even though Object Gap can't be removed or modified (the text says so), the e2e scheme may not care to authenticate that.  But maybe @fluffy or @suhasHere have different thoughts and we can say that certain MOQT defined extensions can _only_ be carried in the immutable block.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed with Authors/Editors:

inclined to allow Gap headers to appear in either place
we need text to indicate that when looking for an extension value, processor needs to search both mutable and immutable lists
we might need text explaining what happens if an extension appears in both?

issues.title: Draft rendering error for ZERO_OBJECT_ID
issues.author: lminiero
issues.body: The markdown says ``` * The **ZERO_OBJECT_ID** bit (0x04) indicates when the Object ID field is present. When set to 1, the Object ID field is omitted and the Object ID is 0. When set to 0, the Object ID field is present. ``` but in the draft it's rendered as My guess is that the `0.` on the new line is interpreted by Markdown as the beginning of a new ordered list, and so it's turned to `1.` This causes the text to change, as it suggests that when no Object ID property is there, it defaults to 1 instead of 0.

issues.title: Define session reuse rules and improve scope definition.
issues.author: michalhosna
issues.body:
With the current draft text, I am not sure how to implement the following:

Given two different connection URIs, how can a client/subscriber decide if they may share a session? 
Given two different downstream subscriptions from two different sessions, how can a relay decide that they may share a session to a original publisher? 

The problem is

1. `AUTHORITY` and `PATH` are sent in `CLIENT_SETUP` 
2.  Scope is defined as "An MOQT scope is a set of servers (as identified by their connection URIs)."

As I read the current text, it would imply that a session may be shared only when AUTHORITY and PATH match exactly. Is this intended? 

## MOQT Scope

This leads to a general question of what defines MOQT scope. As I read the current draft, when two different clients connect to a connection URI with the same AUTHORITY and same PATH, they are guaranteed to be in the same scope. That is, one client should be able to subscribe to a track the other client is publishing under the same full track name. 

Do I read this right? Is this intended behaviour? 

The draft later says, "It is up to the application using MOQT to define how broad or narrow the scope is". I can imagine widening the scope by defining that even different connection URIs with, e.g. different PATHs share scope. I am not sure how to narrow the scope? 

Making this application specific somewhat limits the usability of application agnostic relay, which, as I understand, is the goal of this spec; not only does it limit connection reuse but also caching scope. 

I heard opinions from people here, that the intention was to have more of a global scope or CDN-scope, ignoring the AUTHORITY and PATH altogether, and doing multi-tenancy on 3rd party relays (i.e. commercial CDNs) using, e.g., namespace prefixes given out by that 3rd party. I would rather not misrepresent those ideas, so I am not summarizing those ideas here, please comment.    

------

Sorry, editors (Alan), for opening new issues, especially this long one, I tried to withhold opening this can of worms, but the consensus doesn't seem to be there. I am not sending a PR given that it's unclear what the WG's intended behavior is. I could not find any prior discussion regarding this problem recent enough so that they cover the current text.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
WebTransport sessions inherit Authority and Path from the enclosing WT session.  One way to merge disparate scopes is to pool WT sessions on a QUIC connection.  This is not a widely supported feature yet, but it does make it clear that the scopes are isolated from each other e.g. from a prioritization perspective and works with the specification as designed, I think.

Raw QUIC sends these parameters explicitly in SETUP, and doesn't have a pooling concept.  We _could_ think of these parameters like defaults that can be overridden with Message Parameters?  But then you might have disparate applications using priority differently and starving each other.

comments.author: michalhosna
comments.body:
Pooling WT sessions still adds a setup roundtrip, which may be a fine tradeoff? And it may be potentially resolved with 0RTT discussion. 

Moreover, all the other limits (MAX_REQUEST_ID, MAX_AUTH_TOKEN_CACHE_SIZE) are now separated, which has a positive effect of not being able to starve each other, especially important on "upstream" connections.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Repeating comment from interim: "host/path uniquely identifies a scope, but a given scope may have more than one such name."

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I feel that different scopes should not share a MoQ Connection. ( I understand multiple Moq connection might be multiplexed into one quic session in some cases but that is separate )

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I believe @vasilvv agreed to update the text here

issues.title: Can multiple SUBSCRIBE_UPDATES be collapsed into one, and then applied?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
When discussing potential DoS/Resource issues in MoQ with @englishm I wondered if we could merge a sequence of SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE messages into one, and then apply that one message to reduce churn and resource consumption, whether it's an attack or just a noisy subscriber (ie: re-prioritizes every few ms with no hysteresis)?

I believe that all existing Parameters have the property that applying a sequence of SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE messages is equivalent to applying one SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE where a later Parameter value overwrites a prior value.

For example, for sequence of updates to the Subscriber Priority or Forward value, only the latest value matters.

If we can state this MUST always be true in the draft, I think it makes parameters easier to reason about, but importantly for DoS, it allows a publisher that's behind on SUBSCRIBE_UPDATEs to enact only one SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE to catch up.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the answer is Yes - a publisher can coalesce a sequence of REQUEST_UPDATEs into a single REQUEST_UPDATE, and any conflicts are last one wins.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Oops, REQUEST_UPDATE has a response, so you can't return one response for N REQUEST_UPDATE.  You could theoretically use REQUEST_OK of latest UPDATE to OK all of them, but that's a bigger change.

issues.title: Are varints part of extension immutability?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 11.2 says the "Immutable Extensions" Extension (0xB) "MUST NOT be modified or removed."

In general, an encoded value is equivalent no matter the length of the varint. So if a 2B varint with value 6 comes in and I compress it to 1 byte, have I "modified" the extension?

There are two possible scopes of the answer to this question:
- the extensions inside the 0xB extension must not change expression, but values 0xB itself and the length field can be altered to isotropic expressions.
- the 0xB extension also cannot be altered in any way even if the semantic value is unchanged.

@vasilvv suggested that the answer was that the inner extensions cannot change varint lengths, but the 0xB extension can.

I would find locking of the 0xB fields to be annoying to implement, but don't have strong feelings about it otherwise.

Regardless, this ought to be clarified.

comments.author: nils-ohlmeier
comments.body:
I would argue that anything which relies on end-to-end data to be not modified, should not depend on the encapsulation header. Everything it needs should go into the payload of 0xB.
And yes clarifying this in written form sounds like a good idea.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The immutable extension is expressed as: Type | Length | Value

I think the intent is that Value cannot change, nor can Type or Length, but their varint encoding can (though you SHOULD always use the minimal encoding anyways).

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: OK, so the varint lengths with the 0xB extension cannot change.

issues.title: Absolute Object IDs
issues.author: birneee
issues.body:
The current MoQ addressing is hierarchical: (Track, Group, Object), where Object IDs are relative to a Group. I propose shifting to Absolute Object ID addressing, where every object in a track is assigned a unique, monotonically increasing ID from the start of the track. This means an object would be uniquely identifiable by its namespace, track name, and Absolute object ID, regardless of how or where it is retrieved.

Motivation & Use Cases:
1. Track Switching: Objects IDs would be consistent across multiple alternative tracks. The groups can now depend on the encoding and do not have to align with other tracks. Absolute Object IDs allow a subscriber to request AbsoluteStart = N regardless of how the encoder has partitioned groups for different tracks. This also works across different object rates, if known by the subscriber.
2. Multi-Track Sync: Synchronizing audio and video tracks becomes trivial, with a known object rate. Object N in the audio track can be directly mapped to Object N (or by simple multiplication) in the video track without manifest-level mapping of relative indices.
3. Relay Probing: When a subscriber probes multiple relays for the same track, the Absolute Object ID allows for a simple comparison of arrival times.
4. Time-Based Skipping:  Absolute IDs make jumping through a stream much simpler. Skipping 10 seconds ahead on a track, with a known object rate, is a simple addition. Currently, jumping with a dynamic group sizes requires additional jump metadata.

I am curious about the original design intent behind the current hierarchical addressing with group-relative object ids.

I would love to hear the thoughts or if there are pitfalls I might be overlooking.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: CC: @vasilvv who proposed something similar in 2024 but ultimately did not gain consensus.

comments.author: birneee
comments.body:
I think I found the related issues: #772 #808

Although I was not part of the original discussion, I can see many advantages in keeping the object addresses flat, as I mentioned above (switch,sync,probe,skip).

I agree that the ability to address Groups must be preserved (for random access), but that doesn't necessitate making Object IDs relative. 
This functionality can be preserved by additional Subscription Filters AbsoluteGroupStart (start at the group id) and GroupOfAbsoluteObjectStart (start at the group containing the specific object).

I still don't see a strong reason for relative object ids.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: Just to note, the above functionality is helpful only if the object rates are known and uniform

comments.author: birneee
comments.body: True, but if your application signals the object rate and that it is uniform, no additional location metadata is required.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: I think this assumes that all media is CFR, which is not necessarily the case.  I think putting an extension into a timestamp (#475) and then using a filter on that timestamp (#1401) would address this use case while making less assumptions about the media involved.

comments.author: birneee
comments.body:
You are absolutely right, time and object IDs should not be strictly coupled at the protocol level. However, for tracks where they are linked, that relationship could be signaled by the application to simplify addressing for CFR media.
The question is: Would absolute object IDs hurt VFR?

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: It would not, but any solution that works correctly for VFR would work for CFR too.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> I am curious about the original design intent behind the current hierarchical addressing with group-relative object ids.

The intent was to provide a design which allowed for the fact that not all Objects are valid join points to a track. IDRs are a good example of such a use case. In this case Groups are introduced, such that the first Object in a Group is always a valid join point for a track. This is true independent of any application signaling. 

You can achieve your stated requirement of "_every object in a track is assigned a unique, monotonically increasing ID from the start of the track_" by simply placing all your Objects in the same Group. This will give you a track with monotonically increasing object IDs starting at zero.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Making Object IDs absolute is a constraint on the current design, in my view.  One could do that with the existing design if you wanted to.

So my question would be what we gain by making Object IDs absolute? We could Filter only by Object ID and ignore Group ID, but I can't think of any key functionality that enables?

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
So this have been discussed in the WG prior, and applying the constraint on MOQT level has been judged to not be compatible with the full set of use cases the protocol intend to support. However, particular usages of MOQT could apply the constraints as several has commented. This might limited the potentials for what the issue opener desired, but this trade-off has to be accepted at this time. 

As Chair I make the decision that this is past deadline and the issue have an rough consensus. Thus this issue is closed.

issues.title: Qlog for MOQT
issues.author: yuyou
issues.body:
There’s a [QLog](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-qlog-main-schema/) specification for QUIC, plus [QUIC event definition for qlog](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-qlog-quic-events/)

I’m curious if it’s necessary and useful to have a similar log spec and viewer implementations, like MOQT log (mlog), that follows the same convention but logs the control messages of MOQT. It would be very useful for interoperability tracing and auto-testing, like tools for quic-introps.

comments.author: mengelbart
comments.body:
We have this draft: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-pardue-moq-qlog-moq-events/ 

The draft was not (yet?) adopted by the working group, by iirc last time Lucas presented it at IETF 124, the feedback was generally positive.

issues.title: What is Implicit in the SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE stream?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
When a SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE stream closes, what is Implicit?

- do all open NAMESPACE messages have an implicit NAMESPACE_DONE? I would say yes.
- do all open PUBLISH messages have an implicit PUBLISH_DONE? I would say no, because the PUBLISH is on the control stream, and PUBLISH_DONE has important information that cannot be implicit. The endpoint that killed the stream has to manually clean up PUBLISH.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I agree with both of your statements.  It definitely can't change the state of PUBLISH, since those are their own separate Subscriptions.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Hm, #1458 seems related.  If we decide we need to allow overlaps, then closing a stream implying NS_DONE could be problematic because two SUB_NS have received NS.  Single control stream, where have you gone?

I suppose you could refcount namespaces by Namespace/Done.

issues.title: There should be a Stream Error Code for TOO_FAR_BEHIND
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: If a relay is spewing NAMESPACE messages and the subscriber isn't keeping up, it's going to need this code.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Another option is the publisher can detect backpressure on this stream and wait to send more.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
The problem is there is a FETCH-like and a SUBSCRIBE-like component to this.

part 1 is that I go through all the outstanding namespaces and send them. part 2 is forwarding new ones that arrive.

say that I only get halfway through part 1; it is not immediately clear to me how to keep track of the fact that some of the namespaces in my data structure are unsent.

likewise, if a subscriber is way behind on newly arriving namespaces, it's hard to track an unbounded backlog of stuff in the data structure that still has to be sent

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Hrm, I don't like the idea of "your SUB_NS just too big there is no way to answer you", but I see the challenge in, e.g., pausing your enumeration of the subtree for backpressure, only to have the tree change before the client grants more credit.

That said, I don't have a problem with a stream error code for TOO_FAR_BEHIND since subscriptions can use this, and maybe the SUB_NS problem goes in #1428?

issues.title: Send Rate parameter
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
Standard congestion control algorithms download data as fast as possible. Since throughput between client and server is typically much higher than the encoded rate of the content (Netflix report an average of 13x higher), this leads to bursty downloads at either the Object or Group . Bustiness leads to buffer bloat and packet loss. Instead of downloading data as fast as possible, a better goal for CC is to download as fast as needed. In the ABR content, the "as needed" refers to a rate which prevents the player's ABR algorithm from switching down and simultaneously allows it to switch up. In their testing, a rate of 3.5x encoded birtate satisfied these goals

Delivering "as fast as needed" produced performance benefits (in Netflix study presented at MHV26 Conference by TY) in throughput, retrans and RTT. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b0c56fd-0ab8-40d2-b1dd-f7f0ba188b13)

To allow similar gains in MOQT, we should enable a new "send rate" parameter to accompany a SUBSCRIBE or FETCH. This parameter specifies the rate at which the client wishes to have the content sent by the relay.. The value of the parameter is the rate in kbps at which the content should be paced. A client can adjust the send rate using a REQUEST_UPDATE message. A value of 0 has special meaning and it disables any pacing.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The SCONE WG has investigated significant effort in defining how to communicate "throughput advice". I expect QUIC implementations will be able to support acting on the advice independent of the signal delivery mechanism. 

If MoQT wants to take advantage of a feature like this, keeping the model similar to SCONE is likely to reduce friction

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Do we like "kbps" or rather something more moq-ish like "milliseconds per group".

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Per Lucas's [comment](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/1453#issuecomment-3837637787) , SCONE defined a logarithmic scale with a 6-bit or 7-bit Rate Signal field. The bitrate is determined by a formula where the signal value (n) acts as an exponent. For the most common version (0xSCONE1):

Bitrate = b_min \times 10^{n/20}
b_min (Base Rate): 100 Kbps.\
n: The value provided in the SCONE packet header.
Range: This allows the protocol to signal everything from 100 Kbps (n=0) up to ~199.5 Gbps (n=126).

Rate Signal (n) | Calculated Bitrate
0 | 100 Kbps
20 | 1 Mbps
40 | 10 Mbps
60 | 100 Mbps
80 | 1 Gbps
120 | 100 Gbps

My concern with this is that it only provides throughput limit steps which are multiple of 10. For optimal efficiency with MOQT, I'd like to be able to provide more precise limits - such as 5.7Mbps, 3.2 Mbps. 

The key question is do we expect the pacing to be implemented at the QUIC layer, or at a higher MOQT application layer? If the former, then aligning with changes in QUIC dues to SCONE makes sense. If the latter, then Alan's suggestion of milliseconds-between-groups would be preferred.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks Will. That step granularity doesn't sound quite right by my understanding (which is admittedly small). If we check https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-scone-protocol-04.html#table-1, you'll see _some_ examples of values based on various rate signals. For instance, rate signal 20 is 1 Mbps while 21 is 1.12 Mbps. 

I didn't do any more maths but my memory is that ylthe design provides fine enough granularity to address common video-streaming throughput targets

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Ah, reading the spec always helps me. Thanks for the guidance Lucas. Rate signals do provide sufficient resolution to meet pacing needs. Here are some useful bitrate limits for signals 20-50. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dfa19230-37ca-4e9d-bc06-7c7b716bbcb6)

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The way SCONE works, the subscriber's QUIC stack might receive a signal that says "23 - 1.41 Mbps" -- this indicates an average over a very long window (67s), and it's best used to select the appropriate track to SUBSCRIBE to, rather than attempting to apply a rate limit on the publisher side (SUBSCRIBE to a 10mbps stream, but rate limit to 1.41 Mbps is not going to work). 

For FETCH, there's more applicability of a subscriber sent parameter.  I imagine that the subscriber still wants to allow for bursts, particularly at the beginning of a group.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
For what it's worth, modern network transports already handle this issue on the congestion control level (see, e.g., [RFC 9002 Section 7.7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9002#name-pacing) for QUIC).

There are some advantages to pacing data to a known application data rate, but this also has a lot of edge cases (mostly related to time horizon over which to average the rate), and some noteworthy drawbacks (e.g. burst sending is generally more CPU-efficieny due to the data being in cache).

Edit: another thing I forgot to point out is that SUBSCRIBE is naturally less-prone to this, as in the ideal scenario, data is forwarded as soon as it's generated, and it's at the frame (and in the ideal case, byte) granularity.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> For what it's worth, modern network transports already handle this issue on the congestion control level (see, e.g., [RFC 9002 Section 7.7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9002#name-pacing) for QUIC).

But the intent here is to pace well below the limit that the congestion controller thinks is appropriate for the conneciton. For example, the CC may estimate correctly that it can send you data at 100Mbps, however we would like to pace to 7Mbps. 

> Edit: another thing I forgot to point out is that SUBSCRIBE is naturally less-prone to this, as in the ideal scenario, data is forwarded as soon as it's generated, and it's at the frame (and in the ideal case, byte) granularity.

Valid observation, SUBSCRIBE is delivered at the encoded rate, which is typically far lower than channel capacity. So any pacing effort is primarily targeted at FETCH'd content which can burst above the encoded rate.

>  (SUBSCRIBE to a 10mbps stream, but rate limit to 1.41 Mbps is not going to work).

It would 'work'. The subscribe would fall behind live by 8.59s every 10s. That is a silly behavior for a subscriber, but it should not invalidate the case for clients which want to implement valid pacing constraints, such limit my 10Mbps stream to 30Mbps.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The subscribe would fall behind live by 8.59s every 10s. 

Relay implementations can't afford the memory to let subscribers fall behind by 8.5Mbps for very long.  If they are caching relays and implemented well, it may not cost that much net new memory... until the data would other wise be evicted.

You will get PUB_DONE with TOO_FAR_BEHIND at some point, and the client needs to switch to FETCH.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Pacing at a rate below the congestion controller's max pacing rate has real value, as Netflix experience shows.

For SUBSCRIBE, at least as it stands now, I don't think this should be necessary?

For VoD/Fetch, pacing at a lower rate is very relevant.

The publisher can already pace at a lower rate if it wants to, so the question is whether the Subscriber needs to specify anything to the publisher or the publisher can just do the right thing? The SCONE signaling model requires the Subscriber to send information to the Publisher, so allowing the Subscriber the specify it fits well with SCONE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Even if the track has an extension specifying the rate, I think you probably still need an opt-in in FETCH right?  Maybe you want to FETCH it faster or slower than the rate.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Even if the track has an extension specifying the rate

While the original publisher could set an extension saying "never deliver this FETCH'd content at more than 10Mbps", the real utility comes with subscriber-based control. A subscriber that is starting to play back some long form content may well wish to burst it at 50Mbps for 5s, in order to quickly build a robust buffer, before throttling it back to 10Mbps. A subscriber that knows it is on a mobile network with high throughput jitter may well choose  a higher paced rate than one that is on a stable connection. The original publisher, which is feeding thousands of downstream clients, can't make an optimal pacing decision for each client. 

A solution in which the subscriber adds a simple pacing request parameter to a FETCH would enable client flexibility and would comply with the SCONE workflow.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I've been thinking more about where to put this feature and how it might be implemented.

I expect most congestion controllers have a pacing engine builtin or available.  However, that's for the entire connection.  I don't think people have application data pacers readily available today.  Obviously, that can change or we can suggest a simple implementation approach that achieves the desired goal.

If this rate was for the entire connection, it's be trivial for us to implement, but that seems like a layering violation of sorts?  That being said, SCONE is for the entire flow.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I envisioned this working at the application layer, pacing data into the FETCH stream (subject to backpressure).  If someone has a per-stream pacer in their QUIC stack, that works too.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> But the intent here is to pace well below the limit that the congestion controller thinks is appropriate for the conneciton. For example, the CC may estimate correctly that it can send you data at 100Mbps, however we would like to pace to 7Mbps.

If CC has estimated 100Mbps and if the application can send at 100 Mbps, why to slow it down ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> If CC has estimated 100Mbps and if the application can send at 100 Mbps, why to slow it down ?

I believe there are use cases articulated in the OP and elsewhere upthread.

Pulling media much faster than you can play it (for FETCH) is detrimental to qoe, and might be speculative, so unworthy of full CC capabilities.

SCONE is another use case- network advice

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I'm increasingly unsure if we want to add this as a client controlled feature, at least now.

If we want a way to convey the SCONE bandwidth, it'd be better to have a dedicated message on the connection control stream or something similar, since SCONE applies to the entire flow, not a FETCH.

Adding a Parameter like this is fairly straightforward from a spec perspective, so we might want to park this until someone implements and deploys Netflix style pacing that uses MoQ.  My guess is that it'd be built into a sender-side ABR algorithm, which would take a lot more than the client's max send rate in mind (client buffer depth, etc).

issues.title: Location Structure with Subgroup ID
issues.author: yuyou
issues.body:
The Object’s [Canonical Object Properties (10.2.1)](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-16.html#section-10.2.1) defines Subgroup ID. However, the [Location Structure (1.4.1)](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-16.html#section-1.4.1) specifies that a location can only be expressed in the form of {GroupID, ObjectID}. 

Since objects within a subgroup must be delivered together and exist within the scope of Group IDs (“The scope of a Subgroup ID is a Group”), could the Location structure be modified to accommodate SubgroupID? For instance, could a location be expressed in the new format {GroupID, SubgroupID, ObjectID}?

comments.author: sandarsh
comments.body:
Open to being corrected here--

I believe the intent for sub-group is different from identifying object within a track. Objects within a track are uniquely identified by {GroupID, ObjectID}. From what I understand, sub-group is a delivery mechanism choice, not an inherent property of the object's location in the track. Including that in the absolute location notation might not be correct.

Also, datagrams don't have subgroups, which further clarifies that sub-groups are basically a transport level construct.

For example a track could be delivered as:
- ONE_SUBGROUP_PER_GROUP
- ONE_SUBGROUP_PER_OBJECT
- TWO_SUBGROUPS_PER_GROUP
- DATAGRAM (which doesn't use subgroups)
or any other configuration..

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: So far, in the places where we communicate Location, we only need the group/object.  Do you have a use case where you need to know the subgroup also?  As @sandarsh points out, it's not part of the actual location of the object, but rather a delivery property.

comments.author: yuyou
comments.body:
Thanks for the clarification.

The idea of including an optional SubGroupID within the location structure “`{GroupID, [SubgroupID], ObjectID}`” is intended to facilitate convenient filtering (5.1.2) and control messages (9.x) where Locations are utilized.

We haven’t implemented anything yet; we’re just checking if the concept is valid.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: With #1401 you can filter by subgroup ID.  Are you saying eg you need LARGEST_OBJECT also to communicate its subgroup ID (if any, could be a datagram).

comments.author: yuyou
comments.body:
I’m aware of the #1401. The new design looks cool.

Good question to the largest object. The largest object, IMHO, could be communicated by the location plus one. The definition of “location plus one” could be one of the following:
1. {Largest Object.Group, Largest Object.Object + 1} (with SubGroup Id is not present in the Filters, e.g.);
2. {Largest Object.Group, Largest Object.Object, Largest Object.SubGroup +1} (when SubGroup ID is present in the Start Location in the Filter).

These changes should be minimal and not conflict with the ongoing filtering design. However, they should allow some extensions to the existing subscription filters to filter objects based on their subgroups.  The definition of the location structure could indicate that the subgroup id should not be defined and would be ignored when objects are sent as datagrams.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @yuyou : today, Location appears in Start Location (Subscribe), Largest Object and Start/End for FETCH.  What are the use cases where you need subgroup specifically in one of those places that wouldn't be addressed by 1401?

comments.body: Alright, the intention was to make it easier to subscribe to the subgroup levels within a track. If the design (#1401) supports subscriptions or filtering on the subgroup level within a track, we can close this issue and no changes are needed.

issues.title: Track Namespaces can have zero fields now
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
A NAMESPACE has a track_namespace_suffix field. If it's announcing the whole namespace, the suffix will have zero elements.

Section 2.4.1 is very clear that if Number of Track Namespace Fields is zero, it's a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION. 

That's not true anymore. Either track_namespace_suffix needs an explicit exception, or the rules have to be relaxed.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
We can't use that to eliminate PUBLISH_NAMESPACE however.

PUBLISH_NAMESPACE goes from client publishers towards relays (this carries auth).
NAMESPACE goes from relays towards client subscribers.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: You could have relays send SUB_NS(all) as a matter of course.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I agree with @afrind I think the draft is inconsistent and we intended to allow empty everywhere.

issues.title: Edge Cases around updating SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Now that SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE has an option, there is not much flexibility to control the option type.

Say I want namespaces for "Foo" but PUBLISH and NAMESPACE for "Foo/bar". I could express this as two separate SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACEs but I can't have overlapping prefixes, so there's no legal way to do it.

Say I start out just wanting NAMESPACE for "Foo" but later want PUBLISH as well. I can't send another message because that would be overlapping prefixes. I believe the only to proceed is kill the stream and start over. This is fraught because I have no way of guaranteeing that the Reset arrives before the new SN unless I wait for an RTT, and even then assumes the QUIC API gives me packet granularity.

And of course, a RESET/SUBSCRIBE pattern introduces latency in getting stuff while waiting.

Some possibilities:
- we could just get rid of the option altogether, as it's got serious problems.
- we could make the option a parameter, which would at least solve the second problem but not the first one.
- we could lift the "no overlapping prefixes" rule, which has its own can of worms
- there could be entirely separate namespace trees for PUBLISH and NAMESPACE. At that point, it's basically a different message and should probably be split as such.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: The no-overlaps rule existed before because it would always lead to duplicate data being sent on the same stream (eg the same PUBLISH_NAMESAPCE).  Now that the response is isolated to a stream, and there are the options, I don't think it's so fraught to lift the restriction.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
IIUC you are suggesting that I can subscribe to foo and foo/bar, and NAMESPACE foo/bar/baz would arrive on both streams.

That would allow me to keep only one namespace tree per relay instead of two per session, so that's good.

It is probably workable, but introduces new issues. A man with one watch always knows what time it is. A man with two watches is never sure.

Say a relay regularly alternates between NAMESPACE and NAMESPACE_DONE, maybe because the upstream is intermittent. Furthermore, foo is a big namespace and its stream is flow controlled. So the two streams are out of sync. Can I access the namespace or not?

Likewise, one of the streams closes. Is that an implicit NAMESPACE_DONE?

And of course this is wasteful of bandwidth.

All the options are bad, but if we don't want the fix to be another issue fountain, we have to think through all the edge cases.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Relatedly: I think duplicate SN can be no more than a REQUEST_ERROR, not a Protocol Violation. As mentioned above, if I unsubscribe and then resubscribe there is no way to guarantee these arrive in the correct order unless the QUIC API tells you exactly when the peer acknowledged the RESET frame.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in Authors/Editors meeting and we think it might be easiest to just allow duplicates.  There should be eventual consistency for Mr. Two Watches.

issues.title: Request ID validation is broken in draft-16
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In Section 9.1 it says

The client's Request ID starts at 0 and are even and the server's Request ID starts at 1 and are odd. The Request ID increments by 2 with each FETCH, SUBSCRIBE, REQUEST_UPDATE, SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, PUBLISH, PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or TRACK_STATUS request. Other messages with a Request ID field reference the Request ID of another message for correlation. If an endpoint receives a Request ID that is not valid for the peer, or a new request with a Request ID that is not the next in sequence or exceeds the received MAX_REQUEST_ID, it MUST close the session with INVALID_REQUEST_ID.

But now there's no way to verify the order in which request IDs arrive, because SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE is on a different stream. The simplest fix is probably to just let the request ID in SUB_NS to be literally anything, and it's those on the control stream that have to be in order.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I'm going to implement, for now, the "only control stream has to pass validation" thing, but this can break interop

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: The real fix would be to eliminate request_id from SUB_NS, REQUEST_OK, and REQUEST_ERROR when on the namespace stream.

comments.author: TimEvens
comments.body: I would prefer we remove request ID in SUB_NS instead of allowing anything.  We currently track in a map the request IDs that is not specific to which control bidir we received them on. In other words, using anything could cause collision. It would seem excessive to start tracking request IDs by bidir stream.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: We should remove it in the next draft but we need to agree on -16 behavior before we faceplant.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Exactly how to fix this depends on the bidirectional stream consensus call.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:

In draft-16, please validate only the parity of the request ID, that it is smaller than MAX_REQUEST_ID and do not validate the sequential nature.  You can also check for duplicates.

Leaving open for visibility until we ship draft-18.

issues.title: Validating END_OF_GROUP bit in a subgroup header
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body:
Section 10.4.2 of the specification says "The END_OF_GROUP bit (0x08) indicates that this subgroup contains the largest Object in the Group. When set to 1, the subscriber can infer the final Object in the Group when the data stream is terminated by a FIN. In this case, Objects that have the same Group ID and an Object ID larger than the last Object received on the stream do not exist."

Let's say that an endpoint sends a subgroup header with an END_OF_GROUP bit, terminates it with a FIN, but then sends a larger object on a different subgroup of the same group. How is the receiver supposed to handle this? The specification doesn't have clear language on this. Is this a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION?

> An Object is received in a Group whose Object ID is larger than the final Object in the Group. The final Object in a Group is the Object with Status END_OF_GROUP or the last Object sent in a FETCH that requested the entire Group.

I guess we need to tweak that slightly to include EOG bit cases?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Yes, you can SUBSCRIBE with an End Group, or REQUEST_UPDATE to add one once you know it.  The publisher won't send you any objects larger than that group.

An Original Publisher can also send you a PUBLISH_DONE once they know they are done with your End Group.  A relay can in some limited circumstances, but generally not, because it requires knowledge of all objects that exist in the subscriber's range and their delivery status.  Your application might still need to UNSUBSCRIBE after you detect that you have all the objects from the that group.

issues.title: Inconsistency on Message Parameters
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In Sec 9.2 

Each message parameter definition indicates the message types in which it can appear. If it appears in some other type of message, it MUST be ignored.

In 9.11

The receiver MUST close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION if the sender specifies an invalid Existing Request ID, or if the parameters included in the REQUEST_UPDATE are invalid for the type of request being modified.

I hope 9.11 is an oversight, because I've written a lot of code assuming I can just ignore irrelevant parameters.

In theory, you could be totally accepting according to message type but super-strict within a type based on the other type that it's modifying, and then both texts are correct. But that seems really perverse.

issues.title: End_Of_Group flag is still problematic
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
I seem to recall filing this issue, and others remember me doing it, but I can't find it.

The END_OF_GROUP bit, as written, introduces problems.

When I receive an object without anything else on the stream, I have to introduce latency before delivering it. If I deliver it and then a FIN arrives, I have to change the status of the object, which breaks immutability. If a byte from the next object arrives, then it's safe.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body: "end of group" as an object property adds a frame of latency unless the publisher is 100% certain the next frame will be a keyframe.

comments.body:
It was closed by #1342

I don't know why you think this is true.  When I receive an object, I deliver it.  The EOG bit does not affect the status of any object.  The way I think about it is "this subgroup contains the last object in the group".  My implementation has a separate "endOfSubgroup" API call (eg FIN received) that coupled with "containsLastObject" is a meaningful signal.

This information is only useful to caches (to insert gap markers) and end subscribers (who want to know when the group is over).

#1342 attempted to clarify that the "end of group object" is more of a virtual construct.  An actual object with Location (X,Y) status END_OF_GROUP is a signal that all objects from [X,Y - X+1,0) do not exist.  It is equivalent to open a subgroup with the EOG bit, send object X,Y-1 followed by FIN.  If your cache tracks gap ranges, you can insert this gap range and if there was an END_OF_GROUP object you can effectively discard it.

issues.title: Does a REQUEST_OK (FETCH_OK) need to contain Largest Object?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
For a cache that has enough Objects to serve the FETCH, does the FETCH really need to go upstream?

One can easily imagine cases when the FETCH could be completed quickly, but finding out Largest Object is relatively slow.

This is partially motivated by the fact that it'd be nice to be able to return REQUEST_OK as the start of a response stream and then follow it with the Objects being Fetched.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: It's called "largest object" but it's actually not always the largest object - it's more like the "fetch endpoint".  It's only something other than what you specified as Fetch End if Fetch End spans the true largest object.  Maybe the right behavior is to make this optional and only include it when the range spans the end.

issues.title: Clarify that Joining Fetch needs to wait for all REQUEST_UPDATEs to be processed for the dependent Subscription
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
When talking to Alan today, the new Joining Fetch + REQUEST_UPDATE requires the Subscription to be in state Forward=1. PR #1335 

The current control stream guarantees delivery order, but not processing order.  In this case, it's critical that the REQUEST_UPDATE(s) be processed before the Joining Fetch.

Possibly this is implied by the existing Joining Fetch design, since Joining FETCH needs to wait for the SUBSCRIBE to be processed before it can proceed?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think if the track is live and in fwd=1 upstream, this is not a big deal. Largest object is immediately available and correct. If the upstream subscription is in fwd=0, the largest object (if known) is stale. This is similar to the joining fetch when the subscription is not fully established upstream.

We probably need text to explain - the best bet in this case is to forward the joining fetch upstream.

Hmm, but this could result in refetching cached content. Might need a filter? Or wait?

issues.title: Can use PUBLISH_NAMESPACE in lieu of NAMESPACE? Is this a security issue?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
If a subscriber has an open SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, can a publisher send PUBLISH_NAMESPACE on the control stream (or PUBLISH_NAMESPACE stream in the editors' draft) instead of NAMESPACE on the SUB_NS stream if the namespace is within the SUB_NS prefix?

This seems like annoying behavior, but there's an edge case where the SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE or its REQUEST_OK is in flight and a PUBLISH_NAMESPACE is in flight as well.

Also, in principle I might not want to have PN remain in effect even if the SUB_NS goes away (as closing that stream is an implicit NS_DONE). Don't know if this is a real use case or not.

So I'm afraid the answer may have to be yes even though I very much want it to be no.

Relatedly: how does AUTH work in SUB_NS streams?

If I SUBSCRIBE_NS * to Alan, and then he sends NAMESPACE for us-govt, do I just have to accept that as truth? Is the ability to send AUTH a reason to use PUBLISH_NAMESPACE, or do we have to add parameters to NAMESPACE? And if we add to NAMESPACE, does that mean we need REQUEST_OK/REQUEST_ERROR

A relay has no reason to send a publish_namespace in draft-16. If we’re talking about direct publisher to subscriber connection, then yes, it’s possible the ships pass in the night.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
+1 to having this, to assisting clients with making ABR decisions. 

One solution is for the client to issue a PROBE message. This is necessary if your throughput estimate is application limited (you are playing 32 kbps audio and you want to know if you can play 4k video). The PROBE response could also return the throughput (goodput) estimate. 

Another option would be for the relay to append an extension to each object it sends to that client, each holding the current throughput estimate for the connection. This would give the client a near constant stream of throughput estimates, without having to ask for each one.

It could be a flag on SUBSCRIBE/FETCH  and could be turned on/off using REQUEST_UPDATE.

comments.body:
Something like this is useful. I would propose a feedback track 
" ./well-known/<connection-specific-id>/feedback"

Such a design can be extended to get other send side / relay side measurements that might be useful for end-subscribers and probably between relays too.

comments.author: acbegen
kixelated
comments.body:
> Something like this is useful. I would propose a feedback track
" ./well-known//feedback"
at each relay and define payload types such as BitRateEstimation and a mechanisms of its periodicity and so on.

We should also have some way to trigger probing, so it'd be cool to combine the two.

```
 -> PROBE target_bitrate=3.0 
<-  PROBE_RESULT bitrate=2.5
<-  PROBE_RESULT bitrate=3.2
 -> PROBE_UPDATE target_bitrate=6.0
<-  PROBE_RESULT bitrate=4.5
<-  PROBE_RESULT bitrate=6.0
```

Set `target_bitrate=0` if you just want to know the bitrate without enabling probing.

> [@kixelated](https://github.com/kixelated) what info are you suggesting to put in there? Something obtained from the QUIC layer or something you measure through probing (which is not trivial)?

We should report the estimated send rate from the QUIC congestion controller. `CWND / RTT` for Reno/CUBIC and `PacingRate` for BBR. It's the exact number of bits/second that QUIC is allowed to send; no guess-work required.

My MoQ implementation should send QUIC PADDING packets (transparently discarded) when BBR enters the PROBE_BW phase (1/8th of the time in BBRv1). The congestion controller knows the exact number of packets it needs to send and knows exactly when the target bitrate is reached. The benefit of letting the publisher drive the probing is that you don't waste any bandwidth by going over the indicated amount.

> Also, I don't think we need this carriage per hop between the original publisher and end subscriber. The last mile is sufficient for this (just like we use with CMSD), as subscriber-side ABR should occur only there.

Agreed, the estimated bitrate is a connection property and it's not associated with any publisher. One connection can serve multiple namespaces, so it's not even clear how this could go upstream. 

I would hesitate to make a special `feedback` track because it doesn't behave like any other MoQ track. It should never be propagated/cached/fanned out by a relay. A wire extension makes it impossible to mess up.

issues.title: varint encoding using min size possible
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body:
we have 

** To reduce unnecessary use of bandwidth, variable length integers SHOULD be encoded using the least number of bytes possible to **

This seems to be something that can contributes to bug by allowing something that is seldom tested because most software does the SHOULD. 

I think this would be better as a MUST. I do not understand when it would be reasonable for software not to do it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think we copied this language from RFC 9000. Unsure if anyone remembers the thought process there?

I agree with you that now there’s 9 ways to say “0” and that may not be great.

It does create an extra error check on the decode path - today I can look at the first byte, wait for that many more bytes to arrive, and I’m guaranteed to decode a valid integer, which is very likely going into a uint64_t.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-16 says

> Values do not need to be encoded on the minimum number of bytes necessary, with the sole exception of the Frame Type field; see [Section 12.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#frames).

Which states

> The Frame Type field uses a variable-length integer encoding (see [Section 16](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#integer-encoding)), with one exception. To ensure simple and efficient implementations of frame parsing, a frame type MUST use the shortest possible encoding. For frame types defined in this document, this means a single-byte encoding, even though it is possible to encode these values as a two-, four-, or eight-byte variable-length integer. For instance, though 0x4001 is a legitimate two-byte encoding for a variable-length integer with a value of 1, PING frames are always encoded as a single byte with the value 0x01. This rule applies to all current and future QUIC frame types. An endpoint MAY treat the receipt of a frame type that uses a longer encoding than necessary as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.


There was a fairly length discussion about the topic of minimal encoding in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2299. If you want to make it a MUST then surveying implemeneters for feasibility first would make sense.

comments.body:
I've purposely used more bytes than needed with QUIC VarInts. Specifically, encoding the packet size as 0 with two bytes. After the packet is fully encoded, then I update it with the correct size, which might not actually need two bytes. 

I think MoQ should keep the SHOULD.

comments.body: Control messages us 16 bit length not varint - or you mean something else?

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> Control messages us 16 bit length not varint - or you mean something else?

It was just an example, but yes it would have been useful before the switch to u16 control message lengths. I guess you could do the same optimization for object payload lengths since those are still a varint, but I don't have any concrete use-cases at the moment.

comments.body: There might be some cases a SHOULD can be valuable, particularly for lengths like Luke's example, but I can't see a problem with making Message types use the minimal length encoding like QUIC did.

comments.body:
Meh, I wrote a PR just making it an error.  It says "MUST close" if you receive a bad one, maybe some impls will skip that, maybe they won't.

I don't really see a spot where you'd two a one-pass-and-rewrite-length in the protocol anymore.  Object Payload Length in a subgroup is kind of it, but how far are you going to get into sending your object bytes before you want to write the length -- the length has to go out first on the wire.  An application would do better to make more objects with known lengths.  If this is really a use case, we can go back to draft-02/3 which allowed you to say "this whole stream contains one object and has no explicit length".  That's a separate issue with no driving use-case though.

comments.body:
@suhasHere commented in a duplicate issue:

> I think the spec must specify that relays must not modify encoding of values it receives when forwarding or caching. This is the context of recent open issues with secure objects and loc ..

comments.body:

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed at 125 - room indicated we don't want to require minimal lengths.

The Object ID, for example, isn't even sent on the wire in most cases.  Instead it's a varint compressed _delta_.  I opened https://github.com/moq-wg/secure-objects/issues/72 to track necessary changes to secure-object.

issues.title: Improve design of requests blocking on other requests
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
We need to at least add the text about how request ID dependencies interact with timeouts and stream being reset, also add a note that one cannot rely on those because of this.

I also have an alternative design I would like us to consider, quoting from #1389:
> * A message `WAIT_FOR x` causes the receiver to stop reading control stream until `x` is triggered, or timeout occurs.
> * A message `UNBLOCK x` causes all `WAIT_FOR x` messages to unblock.
> * Messages can occur on any control stream.
> * We need some text about state tracking.

The main advantage is that it decouples the blocking from request processing, and you can move it to the parser level (where it arguably belongs).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Consolidating from #1603:

From Cullen's post to the mailing list regarding use-cases:

---
1) Swap tracks. In a video conference, a subscriber is subscribe to track for Alice and Bob’s video and is watching Alice with Bob paused, but wants to pause Alice and unpause the track with Bob. It’s pretty common to want to ensure to pause the current one before unpausing the new track to not have congestion.

2) client side ABR

3) a stream being paused and unpaused in rapid succession and requests reorders on the wire resulting in the opposite of the desired state.
---

I'll note that #3 is already handled because REQUEST_UPDATE for a given subscription happens on a single control stream.

Could someone add more color on the specific ordering requirements for "Client Side ABR"?  Is that a special case of 1 (Swap tracks) when the tracks have the same content?  To what extent would SWITCH handle both?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Some approaches for ABR:
1) Subscribe to the new Track at a specific group and also end the current subscription. (could be downswitch or changing audio tracks or ?)
2) Subscribe to the new Track and ensure you actually have enough bandwidth before ending the current subscription. (upswitch)
3) Use SWITCH or DTS

For 1, I think the potential use case is "I really want the Subscribe to succeed before I end the existing subscription"?  But if it fails completely, do we still execute the REQUEST_UPDATE to set forward=0?  What if the control message succeeds quickly, but the actual data is slow to arrive?  You definitely have an active subscription.  No content, but you know what Largest Object is.

For the "pause before unpause" the case that I believe is potentially problematic is they're in two separate packets and the pause gets lost. If you send them in a single packet, I believe you'd achieve the desired outcome?  ie: It's still ok if the two messages were processed in parallel.  It might take longer to start sending the new track than pause the existing subscription anyway.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> If you send them in a single packet, ...

Most MOQT stacks don't really offer direct application control of "send these two requests in the same QUIC packet".  I think 99% of the time that's just going to happen -- the control streams should have highest priority, and they are not large.  Are we ok saying "this is mostly fine" or do we need a MOQT mechanism to collect the related requests on the receiver side.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I'm saying "this is mostly fine". I think MoQ libraries might want a way to encourage batching anyway, otherwise if you send 10 Messages in sequence, they'll end up in 10 packets.  We have something like this for HTTP/3 that delays flushing until its popped off the stack.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in London: use cases reduce to "stop track A, start track B" in a coordinated manor -- similar to #1354.

Proposal is to introduce a SWITCH_FROM parameter, to be used in SUBSCRIBE or REQUEST_OK, identifying the "stop" track, and some related processing instructions.

Preview PR: https://github.com/afrind/moq-transport/pull/18

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
The preview defines two options:

Mode=Hard (set forward=0) and Soft (set filter end=Start Group - 1)
Publish Done=0/1

Discussed other options "medium" or "soft boiled" with slightly different behaviors.  Goal is to land something relatively simple and let data drive additional functionality.

comments.body: Fixed by #1674

I'm really confused by the word "delivered", and what does it mean to have the application involved?

"delivered to the application" is intended to mean that the MOQT layer has parsed the message and used whatever mechanism to notify the application that the message has arrived - put it in a message queue or fire a callback or whatever you do/did when the control stream was a single stream.  It's not intended to force you to wait for the application to _respond_ to the message.

In other words, if you always set Required Request ID Delta=1, you recreate the draft-15 control stream ordering properties.
