issues.title: Draft-17: properties type encode format
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#section-14.4-3.1.1   says about properties  type:

`0x40 to 0x37FF: Specification Required (2-byte encoding)`


However, according to the vi64 encode rules:
- `0x40` is in range 0-127, so it can be encoded in 1 byte, not 2 bytes.

does draft-17 about properties(type 0x40) is wrong?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Ah yes, I guess we split the range there.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think the intent was to reserve the last 8 1 byte code points, but we used 6 bit max instead of the new 7 bit.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
Based on our practical implementation experience, reserving only 8 one-byte values for application-specific extensions may be insufficient in practice, especially considering future extensions and experimentation.

We suggest reserving one quarter of the one-byte extension space:

- For a 0–63 one-byte extension range, reserve 16 values (0x30–0x3F).

- For a 0–127 one-byte extension range, reserve 32 values (0x60–0x7F).

> I think the intent was to reserve the last 8 1 byte code points, but we used 6 bit max instead of the new 7 bit.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm not sure we want to reserve 48 of our 128 1 byte code points for application use, but I am amenable to more than 8.  Can you explain why your application has so many length sensitive extensions?

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
I also agree that reserving more than 8 values for application-specific extensions would be helpful.

In our product environment, we currently use WebRTC, and in standard WebRTC deployments there are already several commonly used RTP header extensions, for example:

Video Orientation – defined in RFC 8834-https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8834.html#name-coordination-of-video-orien

Playout Delay-https://webrtc.googlesource.com/src/+/refs/heads/main/docs/native-code/rtp-hdrext/playout-delay

Video Content Type-https://webrtc.googlesource.com/src/+/refs/heads/main/docs/native-code/rtp-hdrext/video-content-type

In addition to these standardized extensions, real deployments often introduce private extensions. For example, in our case we also use extensions such as: audio codec related metadata、video decode timestamp(for B frame)、extra application data which is related with audio/video

Currently, 8 application-specific extension values are sufficient, but reserving a slightly larger space could be better for future.
Perhaps the working group could consider reserving 16 values instead?

> I'm not sure we want to reserve 48 of our 128 1 byte code points for application use, but I am amenable to more than 8. Can you explain why your application has so many length sensitive extensions?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Do all these app specific extensions need to be 1 byte?  Anything attached to a video frame is not going to notice an extra byte.     Are any proposed app specific extensions common enough to warrant an IANA registration that could be used across multiple applications (timestamps)?  In that case there's still more than 100 available.

If you really think an app is going to run out of 1-byte app specific codes, open an issue and we can discuss bumping to 16.  Unsure if it will get consensus, but I'm pretty sure we won't go any higher.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
In our case, current 8 reserved application-specific values are sufficient. If we eventually run out of the 1-byte space, we would simply use the 2-byte extension format, so this is not a strict limitation for us.

Video Orientation and Video Content Type, which are already widely used, could potentially be considered by the working group for IANA registration.

issues.title: Draft-17:  Add Request ID to response messages for better request–response correlation
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
[https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#section-9.1-1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#section-9.1-1) says:
`Only request messages include a Request ID; response messages do not, since they are sent on the same bidirectional stream as the request.`

In draft-16, response messages included the same Request ID as the corresponding request.

The current draft assumes that each request is sent on a separate bidirectional QUIC stream, so responses can be implicitly correlated with the request by the stream itself. However, this assumption may not always hold in practice.

For example, consider a meeting scenario where a new participant joins a meeting with 30 existing tracks and sends 30 SUBSCRIBE requests. If these requests are sent on the same QUIC stream, the server may process them concurrently (e.g., in different threads) and respond with SUBSCRIBE_OK or REQUEST_ERROR messages in any order. Without a Request ID in the response, the endpoint cannot reliably determine which request a response corresponds to.

Using separate QUIC streams for each request would solve this problem, but it may not always be desirable or possible. 

Suggestion: Consider adding the corresponding Request ID field to response messages as was done in draft-16. make request–response correlation explicit and robust.  
The Request ID is encoded as a vi64, so the additional bandwidth overhead is minimal, in return, it simplifies implementations and makes the protocol more robust

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: We no longer use Request ID for correlation and instead use the QUIC stream ID.  In draft-17 all requests use their own bidi stream.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: @yuanchao-chris  Do you want to close this as a misunderstanding, or are you objecting to the draft-17 design?

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> If these requests are sent on the same QUIC stream...

That's the fundamental change, you can't do that any longer. Open a new stream for each SUBSCRIBE, and the corresponding SUBSCRIBE_OK returns on the same stream. Effectively we're using the stream ID as the request ID now.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
I understand MOQ is designed to run over QUIC, and sending requests on separate quic streams works well.

However, in real product environments, UDP may sometimes be restricted or unavailable. In such situations, an application might fall back to a TCP-based transport while still reusing the same MOQ object model and semantics. Switching to a completely different protocol stack (for example WebTransport over TCP) is certainly possible, but in practice some implementations may prefer to reuse the same request/response model.

In a TCP-based fallback scenario, multiple requests be sent over the same connection. In that case, having an explicit Request ID in the response could make request–response correlation clearer and more robust.

If this is not aligned with the current design goals of MOQ, feel free to close this issue.

> [@yuanchao-chris](https://github.com/yuanchao-chris) Do you want to close this as a misunderstanding, or are you objecting to the draft-17 design?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I think to run moqt over TCP, you'll want something like [WebTransport over HTTP/2 ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-webtrans-http2/)or [QMUX](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-qmux/) as your substrate, which will require no changes to the MOQT layer.

issues.title: Subscribe Namespace and Subscribe Overlap with RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
Due to the introduction of rendezvous timeout for Subscribe,  we have a situation where a relay might have the below scenario: 

Subscriber sends 
SUBSCRIBE to ns:           (a,b,c) name: d 
SUBSCRIBE_NS to ns:    (a,b,c)

Publisher sends
PUBLISH to.                  ns: (a,b,c) name: d 

Now the relay sees  2 possible way to react to the incoming publish
1. Forward PUBLISH as a response to SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE due to prefix match
2. Send SUBSCRIBE_OK to fulfill the SUBSCRIBE

There are few options we can deal in this situation
1. Publisher Wins  ( so option 1 above). This 
2. Subscriber Wins ( so option 2 above). 
3. Add a parameter to SubscribeNamespace called `excludedSuffixes': [], a list of suffix that the subscriber wants not to be bothered about when sending Publish.

I am inclined to option 2 since it let's the end subscriber influence the choice. 

I also like option 3 since it allows to attain such functionality generically. 

Thoughts ?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This is similar to a publisher and subscriber racing -- one sending PUBLISH A and the other sending SUBSCRIBE A.  The current draft text says publisher wins, and subscriber get REQUEST_ERROR.  I think it was somewhat arbitrary that we picked publisher wins.

I'm also inclined towards 2 in this case.  If you resolve the subscribe first, then at least my implementation logic would skip sending the PUBLISH, since this subscriber is already subscribed to the track.  Are we ok with the inconsistency with the above, or should we flip that to subscriber wins also?  It is slightly different - in the above the publisher _already_ sent the publish when the subscribe arrives.

I'd prefer not to add more machinery as in 3 at this time as long as 2 solves the problem.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: excludeSuffixes mimics Namespace model and allows one to not know about its own namespace, if needed.

issues.title: Draft-17: How to associate PUBLISH_DONE with the correct PUBLISH track
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#name-publish_don says:
`PUBLISH_DONE is sent on the control stream`

The format of PUBLISH_DONE is as follows:

> _PUBLISH_DONE Message {
>       Type (vi64) = 0xB,
>       Length (16),
>       Status Code (vi64),
>       Stream Count (vi64),
>       Error Reason (Reason Phrase)
> }_

However, if a client sends multiple PUBLISH requests on different bidirectional QUIC streams (each corresponding to a different track),
how the receiver can determine which track a PUBLISH_DONE refers to.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think it should read:

PUBLISH_DONE is sent on the control stream _associated with the subscription being terminated_.

In draft-17 there is a 1:1 mapping between control stream and subscription.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
draft-ietf-moq-transport-17 https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#section-3.3-2 says in Section 3.3:

> In addition to the control streams, this specification uses bidirectional streams to carry requests. A request stream begins with one of these six message types: TRACK_STATUS, SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH, FETCH, PUBLISH_NAMESPACE, and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.

and https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#name-publish_don says:

> PUBLISH_DONE is sent on the control stream

Previously, I understood that control messages could be sent on two types of streams:

- Control stream: a unidirectional stream used for messages such as SETUP, which do not contain a Request ID.

- Request stream: a bidirectional stream used for request/response style messages with a Request ID, such as PUBLISH.

Based on this, when the draft says “PUBLISH_DONE is sent on the control stream”, I initially interpreted PUBLISH_DONE would be sent on a separate control stream (different from the PUBLISH request stream).

However, according to your reply, PUBLISH_DONE is actually sent on the same QUIC stream as the corresponding PUBLISH message.

Thanks for your clarification

issues.title: Invalid varints (implementation experience tracking)
issues.author: vasilvv
issues.body:
I've started implementing some of the draft-17 varint syntax, and wanted to note some of the experience / thoughts I've had while doing this.

The good is that there is no longer an invalid value case when serializing uint64 as a varint.  This simplifies serialization logic.

The annoying but not really new part is that now it is much easier to hit integer overflows in all of the delta-encoded fields.

The main downside occurs on the parsing side.  The output of a varint parsing is now a ternary state:
1. Varint parsing is successful.
2. Varint parsing is unsuccessful because there is not enough input data.
3. Varint parsing is unsuccessful because the varint is invalid.

In a lot of cases state 2 and state 3 lead to the same result (e.g. when parsing the contents of a control message), meaning those can be handled the same way.  In other cases, failing to distinguish between the states 2 and 3 leads to a deadlock (i.e. if you naively replace the old varint parser with the new one, and then someone writes an invalid varint on the data stream, it is permanently stuck).  @martinthomson has [pointed out](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1016#discussion_r2743708235) this on the original PR.

Given all of this, I'd like to hear from other implementers about how much complexity they've encountered integrating this change.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I was kind of planning to not check for invalid varints in my implementation.  You want to send me a 7 byte varint or a non-minimal encoding, that's fine, I'm not the protocol police.

issues.title: Draft-17: Handle redirection before session establishment on the control stream
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
In draft-ietf-moq-transport-17, https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#name-unidirectional-stream-types
the first message on the control stream MUST be a SETUP(Type=0x2F00) message.

However, consider the following scenario:
A server receives the client's SETUP request and determines that the session itself is valid, but the client should connect to another server instead (for example, due to high CPU load, load balancing, or deployment topology).
In the current specification, the server need send two messages:

  1. SETUP
  2. GOAWAY

This results: client set to an established state when receive the server SETUP, and then immediately close the session when receive the GOAWAY. This behavior introduce unnecessary state transitions and complexity in implementations.

In https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#name-termination:
Section "Termination" allows the server to close the session if a specific error occurs (for example UNAUTHORIZED). However, in the scenario described above, the SETUP itself is valid and successful, but the server prefers the client to connect to another server.

Proposed change:
1. allow send GOAWAY as the first message on the control stream
2. Alternatively, add new SETUP Option to indicate a new URI(like GOAWAY)

Would the working group consider the proposed change?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I like that control always starts with SETUP, and this mirrors HTTP/3 (SETTINGS).

Is it a hardship to ensure SETUP (which can be empty) goes out before GOAWAY?

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
Ensuring that SETUP is the first message is not difficult. The server can always send an empty SETUP before GOAWAY.

However, from the client's perspective, receiving even an empty SETUP generally indicates that the session has been successfully established. At that point, the client may immediately trigger other actions, such as notifying the application that the session is established, publishing tracks, or starting to send audio/video data.

For example, the client may already start sending media after receiving SETUP, and some audio/video data might be transmitted before GOAWAY is received. In this case, that data would likely be dropped when the session is closed.

In scenarios such as redirecting the client to another server(similar to http 302), it may be prefer for the client to receive this information directly, before the session is considered established.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body:
As you suggested, my understanding is that:
if the server sends an empty SETUP, the client could delay performing other actions.
However, if the server sends a valid SETUP (with options), the client would normally treat the session is established and proceed to do other actions.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
In draft-17, you do not need to wait for peer SETUP in order to send requests, as long as the requests do not use any features that depend on a SETUP Option.

Instead I wonder if we need a field in GOAWAY similar to HTTP that indicates the smallest unprocessed Request ID.  So an exchange might be:

0-RTT:

C->S: SETUP
C->S: PUBLISH id=0

S->C: SETUP
S->C: GOAWAY id=0 // no requests were processed

1-RTT:

S->C: SETUP
S->C: GOAWAY id=0

C: sends no messages

@ianswett

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'm going to make a PR that adds a request ID to GOAWAY.  But the core issues here I think we will leave SETUP as required as the first message on the control stream.

comments.author: yuanchao-chris
comments.body: SETUP as the first message is acceptable. In our implementation, SETUP is not used to indicate application status. Instead, a separate (custom-defined) message type may be used to convey the application-level status.

issues.title: draft-17: Properties Type collision between moq-16 and loc-01
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
In draft-ietf-moq-transport-17 Section 14.4 https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17.html#name-properties-2 Property Type are registries, including `0x02` and `0x04`. the scope is "Track"
```
| Type | Name               | Scope | Specification |
|------|--------------------|-------|---------------|
| 0x02 | DELIVERY_TIMEOUT   | Track | Section 11.1  |

issues.title: draft-17: On which stream type should the GOAWAY message be sent?
issues.author: shanyutongxue
issues.body:
According to the Unidirectional Stream Types definition in draft-17: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#name-unidirectional-stream-types. Only three types of data can be sent on unidirectional streams: FETCH_HEADER, SUBGROUP_HEADER, and SETUP. Since the GOAWAY control message has ID = 0x10, which overlaps with the SUBGROUP_HEADER range (0x10–0x1D), GOAWAY can only be sent on a bidirectional stream.

ID | Type
-- | --
0x05 | FETCH_HEADER ([Section 10.4.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#fetch-header))
0x10-0x1D | SUBGROUP_HEADER ([Section 10.4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#subgroup-header))
0x2F00 | SETUP ([Section 9.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#message-setup))

ID | Messages
-- | --
0x10 | GOAWAY ([Section 9.5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#message-goaway))

However, according to Section 3.3 (Session Initialization): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-17#name-session-initialization. A bidirectional stream must begin with one of the following message types: TRACK_STATUS, SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH, FETCH, PUBLISH_NAMESPACE, or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE. This means GOAWAY can only be sent after one of these messages has already been initiated on a bidirectional stream. If a server or relay needs to send GOAWAY for redirection immediately after the session is established — before any of these messages have been exchanged — the timing would be too late.
Proposal:
Would it make sense to allow GOAWAY to be sent on a unidirectional stream, without requiring it to follow a SETUP message? This would also require assigning GOAWAY a new stream type ID that does not conflict with the SUBGROUP_HEADER range (0x10–0x1D).

However, the current GOAWAY ID (0x10) conflicts with the SUBGROUP_HEADER range (0x10–0x1D), making it impossible to distinguish between the two.

issues.title: Section 13: Grease formula 0x7f should be 0x1f
issues.author: Vaisman
issues.body:
Section 13 currently states that grease values follow `0x7f * N + 0x9D`, but this is inconsistent with the examples in the same sentence (`0x9D, 0xBC, ...`) and with the stated upper bound `0x3ffffffffffffffe`.

For `N=1`: `0x7f * 1 + 0x9D = 0x11C`, not `0xBC`.
The stated maximum also fails: `(0x3ffffffffffffffe - 0x9D) mod 0x7f = 32`.

By contrast, `0x1f * N + 0x9D` matches both:
- Examples: `N=0 -> 0x9D`, `N=1 -> 0xBC` 
- Upper bound: `(0x3ffffffffffffffe - 0x9D) mod 0x1f = 0` 

This is also consistent with the QUIC grease pattern (`0x1f * N + 0x21`, RFC 9000 17.2.1) which uses the same multiplier.

This pattern is referenced by 7 IANA registries (Section 13), the current text can cause implementations to generate different grease values depending on whether they follow the formula or the examples.

**Proposed fix:** In Section 13, change the multiplier from `0x7f` to `0x1f`:

> Grease values follow the pattern **0x1f** * N + 0x9D...

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: We changed the grease multiplier to be larger to reduce the number of grease code points on purpose. I think we can change the examples

issues.title: Section 7.1 conflicts with Section 9.3.6 on GROUP_ORDER value 0x0
issues.author: Vaisman
issues.body:
Section 7.1 states that a subscriber can set Group Order to `0x0` to defer to the publisher's preference:

> "the publisher's preference is used if the subscriber did not express one (by setting Group Order field to value 0x0)."

However, Section 9.3.6 defines the GROUP_ORDER parameter as:

> "The allowed values are Ascending (0x1) or Descending (0x2). If an endpoint receives a value outside this range, it **MUST** close the session with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION."

and separately provides a mechanism for deferring to the publisher:

> "If omitted from SUBSCRIBE, the publisher's preference from the Track is used."

A subscriber following Section 7.1 will send `GROUP_ORDER = 0x0`. A publisher following Section 9.3.6 will terminate the session with `PROTOCOL_VIOLATION`, since `0x0` is outside `{0x1, 0x2}`. This is a interop break between two implementations on every SUBSCRIBE that uses a default group order.

**Proposed fix:** Remove the reference to `0x0` in Section 7.1 and align with Section 9.3.6, which already defines the correct mechanism (omitting the parameter). Something like:

> "the publisher's preference is used if the subscriber did not express one (by omitting the Group Order parameter)."

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Are you confused why there's 3 concepts?

Setup Options: only in SETUP, used to negotiate and initialize extensions and features
Track/Object Properties: part of the Track/Object
Message Parameters: convey information specific to the message

Or maybe you are asking why there are different encodings?

Options and Properties can be extended without negotiation, so they have length, so unknown values can be skipped over.
Parameters cannot be extended without negotiation - you have to understand every property in the message or you can't parse it.

Or maybe you are asking why there's different ways to delineate the block?

Options and Object Properties are length delineated, it's just that for Setup the length is the frame length (there are no other fields)  For Track Properties, you need to subtract the other parts of of the containing message to find it.  There was a reason to make it length delineated -- you can skip over them if you don't do anything with them.

Parameters parsing is totally different.  I think count is slightly easier to deal with - you don't need to reserve space or make two passes.

issues.title: Setup Parameters and Extension Negotiation Again
issues.author: yuyou
issues.body:
The issue #1407 is closed but still current specification (V17) Is unclear (at least to me) how a new parameter with a complex structure can be negotiated in SETUP Options.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Don’t use the GREASE values. These will be discarded by the receiver.

Do pick a large random non-grease code point for your custom setup options. We will set up a registry later.

The semantics of your “foo” extension are not negotiated - they are declared by some specification or convention— never hurts to write a draft.

The namespaces of setup options, message parameters, and track/object properties are all independent, as are stream types, datagram types and all other enumerations in the spec. Everything starts with Setup Options to let the peer know that you have extended capabilities.

I will add an example

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Example Extension: HIPPO               
                                                                                           
  This example illustrates an extension that uses multiple extensibility points together.  
                                                                                           
  Setup Option                                              

  The extension defines a Setup Option HIPPO_CONFIG 0xf3a891. The value is a JSON blob:

```
  {
    "versions": [1, 2, 3],
    "max_hippo_weight_kg": 3200
  }
```

  Each endpoint includes this option in its SETUP message. Since SETUP is sent unilaterally
   by each side, there is no request/response negotiation — each endpoint independently
  declares its hippo preferences. The endpoints determine the agreed-upon parameters (e.g.,
   highest mutual version, maximum weight) from the two SETUP messages.

  New Message Type

  The extension defines a new control message HIPPO (type=0xb74d02):

```
  HIPPO {
    Type (0xb74d02),
    Length (16),
    Request ID (i),
    Number of Parameters (i),
    Parameters (..) ...
  }
```
  The extension defines two new parameter types:

  - 0xa219f6 — Weight (varint, in kg)
  - 0xa219f8 — Aggressiveness (uint8, 0-100)

  A peer sends a HIPPO message whenever it has hippos to report. 

  Unidirectional Stream

  The extension opens a unidirectional stream with type 0xd583a0. This carries bulk hippo data:

```
  Hippo Uni Stream {
    Stream Type (i) = 0xd583a0,
    Request ID (i),          // correlates with a HIPPO message
    Total Hippo Bytes (i),
    Hippo Data (..)
  }
```

  The Request ID ties the stream back to a specific HIPPO message on the control stream.

  How It All Fits Together

  1. Setup: Both endpoints independently declare hippo preferences via Setup Option
  0xf3a891 in their SETUP messages, then derive agreed-upon parameters from the pair
  2. Mid-session hippos: Either side sends a HIPPO message on the control stream with
  parameters for weight and aggressiveness
  3. Bulk hippo data: The sender opens a unidirectional stream (type 0xd583a0) correlated
  by Request ID

  An endpoint that does not support HIPPO simply ignores the setup option. The peer that
  supports it cannot send HIPPO messages, streams or parameters -- doing so is a
  PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

issues.title: Can the same Track be published multiple times into different namespaces?
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
I have a question regarding whether the same Track can be published under multiple namespaces

### Use case

In a typical application scenario, a single MoQ client may need to publish the same real media source (e.g., one audio track) to multiple namespaces.
For example, in an online education scenario, one teacher may simultaneously serve multiple classes from a single device:
The publisher publishes the same audio track to both namespaces:
- Publish to /room1/user1/audio_track
- Publish to /room2/user1/audio_track

Subscribers in different rooms consume independently:
- Users in room1 subscribe /room1/user1/audio_track
- Users in room2 subscribe /room2/user1/audio_track

### Questions

- Is it allowed for a publisher to publish the same Track (same media source) to multiple namespaces?

- If allowed, the same underlying Track would have multiple full names, should implementations treat one full track name as the unique key

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
@yuanchao-chris - some answers:


  *   Is it allowed for a publisher to publish the same Track (same media source) to multiple namespaces?

Yes.
  *   If allowed, the same underlying Track would have multiple full names, should implementations treat one full track name as the unique key

The globally unique key for any Object  (as a cache key for example), would be comprised of
scope + namespace + name + GroupID + ObjectID
If an implementation is trying to differentiate tracks, then it would use this as its unique key

scope + namespace + name

Each combination of this key would get cache separately, even if they hold the same binary payloads.

It is illegal to publish different binary payloads under the same cache key.

The scope  is defined as the universe within which the Full Track name (i.e. namespace + name)  is unique. If the ‘implementation’ is client side (i.e a player), it may not know the scope under which the namespace was allocated. In this case, it would use namespace + name as the unique key.

 For more info, view the scope<https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-scope> section of the spec.

Cheers
Will

issues.title: Joining FETCH session errors are subject to a race condition
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
The draft says Joining FETCH to a forward = 0 subscription is a session error.

But the forward state and the FETCH are on different streams, so there's a race condition. If the REQUEST_UPDATE that carries forward = 1 is delayed, that can kill the whole session.

This cannot be a session error!

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: IMO we should just have joining fetch on the same stream. It eliminates tons of error cases and the gross buffering mechanic.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: You are supposed to use Required Request ID to address this see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1577

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Does this completely solve it though? Here's an edge case:

1. SUBSCRIBE (id = 0) with forward = 1
2. Send JoiningFetch with min_request_id = 0.
3. Send REQUEST_UPDATE with forward = 0 due to changed requirements

#3 arrives before #2 -> explosion

issues.title: Joining Fetch should be on the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH stream
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
This solves a bunch of problems:

- no need for an annoying buffer in case the FETCH arrives before SUBSCRIBE
- no need for matching request IDs, looking up the subscribe context, etc
- solves the race condition #1601, which I don't think the current solution completely does
- neatly handles the case where the Unsubscribe happens before SUBSCRIBE_OK but after Joining FETCH
- eliminates tons of error cases and therefore test cases

If the use case where SUBSCRIBE ends but joining FETCH is still going is important, then we don't want to do this. I suspect this is not a real use case.

I might do a PR once REWIND is out of my hands.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Can you enumerate any downsides?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
As I said, there'd be no way to end the SUBSCRIBE and still get FETCH objects, except to send a standalone fetch for whatever remains.

My Joining FETCH implementation is partial at this point. If I had more code I might think of something else.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Oh, if we put the fetch objects in the bidi stream (which I'd like to do) that complicates things.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: One issue is that REQUEST_UPDATE is ambiguous.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Ok, this REQUEST_UPDATE problem is pretty hairy. I think the answer may be that SUBSCRIBE and JF need to share parameters, if the parameter applies to both message types

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Another pain point: REQUEST_ERROR on the Fetch shouldn't kill the SUBSCRIBE.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This is a duplicate of #1313

issues.title: What is the use case for required-request-id
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
I see that draft-17 has required-request-id in every type of request. I don't see the value of this.

REQUEST_UPDATE might need it to sequence forward modes, etc

FETCH needs it for joining FETCH, obviously

Other than that, the only dependencies are on request termination, which doesn't have a request ID.

If there are this many dependencies we shouldn't have separated out the control stream.

I propose we eliminate this field except for REQUEST_UPDATE and FETCH (unless #1602 makes the FETCH dependency obvious)

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: Another annoying thing: I need to keep a scoreboard of all received request IDs to check if I processed them, even if the request is long-dead. A malicious client could use every other request ID to maximize my state.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Another annoying thing: I need to keep a scoreboard of all received request IDs to check if I processed them, even if the request is long-dead. A malicious client could use every other request ID to maximize my state.

Your state is bounded by QUIC max bidi streams, which are implicitly opened if received out-of-order (receiving 8 implicitly opens 4).  So the every-other peer will run out of stream credit, I think.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: are stream IDs bound to request IDs somehow?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Stream IDs in WebTransport and some QUIC implementations aren't exposed to the application.  Which is sometimes annoying.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
required-request-id was added to achieve 'feature parity' with the single control stream model, but given there's no guarantee you finish processing one request before the next one, even when they're on a single stream, it was never clear exactly what functionality this provided.

HTTP requests don't depend upon one another and I'd like to follow that model if possible.

Joining FETCH is annoying, and it having a dependency on another Request is one big reason I dislike it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Aside from Joining FETCH, you can use this to enforce ordering with REQUEST_UDPATE fwd changes for independent subscriptions, and initiating new SUBSCRIBEs.  Sadly you can no longer order request cancellation (e.g. UNSUBSCRIBE) but that was advertised as a feature of moving to bidi streams.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> > Another annoying thing: I need to keep a scoreboard of all received request IDs to check if I processed them, even if the request is long-dead. A malicious client could use every other request ID to maximize my state.
> 
> Your state is bounded by QUIC max bidi streams, which are implicitly opened if received out-of-order (receiving 8 implicitly opens 4). So the every-other peer will run out of stream credit, I think.

I think this is incorrect; I can have any number of request IDs in a single stream thanks to REQUEST_UPDATE.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Here is what I would propose:
1) eliminate RRID and Request ID REQUEST_UDPATE
2) if you want to swap forward modes on two subscriptions, use SWITCH, or risk getting REQUEST_ERROR if you don't.
3) If you want to open a sub depending on ending another one, use SWITCH, or risk getting REQUEST_ERROR if you don't.
4) Put Joining FETCH in the SUBSCRIBE stream as in #1604 
4a) If we really want the SUBSCRIBE and Joining FETCH to have unshared parameters, add a "modified request ID" field to REQUEST_UPDATE that points to the original SUBSCRIBE or FETCH.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I have all these aesthetic concerns, but I do want to highlight that there is a DoS vector in here that IMO we must address

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Yeah, I don't understand why it's on so many messages either.

One use-case could be to make sure that you don't issue a duplicate `SUBSCRIBE track=video` until the previous one has finished (FIN/RST received), but that doesn't even work. It did work when UNSUBSCRIBE was a separate message. IMO it needs a rethink.

And I +1 Martin's concern about DoS. I don't think it's a major issue in this instance because of MAX_STREAMS, but I'm not a fan of blocking on arbitrary IDs like Track Alias and Required Request ID in general (oops forgot a timeout).

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
From today's interim:
Conclusion was to remove required-request-id from draft 18 and fix Joining Fetch (if necessary?)

Those who believe some functionality in this space is useful, such as for make-before-break, should explore those use cases in more detail and further describe what, if any, dependency structure between requests is needed in MoQ.  Tentative plan is to discuss these at the London hybrid interim in June.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
From Cullen's post to the mailing list:
---
1) Swap tracks. In a video conference, a subscriber is subscribe to track for Alice and Bob’s video and is watching Alice with Bob paused, but wants to pause Alice and unpause the track with Bob. It’s pretty common to want to ensure to pause the current one before unpausing the new track to not have congestion.

2) client side ABR

3) a stream being paused and unpaused in rapid succession and requests reorders on the wire resulting in the opposite of the desired state.
---

I'll note that #3 is already handled because REQUEST_UPDATE for a given subscription happens on a single control stream.

Could someone add more color on the specific ordering requirements for "Client Side ABR"?  Is that a special case of 1 (Swap tracks) when the tracks have the same content?  To what extent would SWITCH handle both?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: This is now tracked in #1519

issues.title: What happens to Joining FETCH if fwd changes to 0?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
The spec says I can't send Joining FETCH if the subscription has fwd=0. What if I send it and then fwd changes to 0? Does that cancel the joining FETCH?

I don't really care what the answer is, but the spec should say what happens.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Changing the subscription from 1 to 0 after joining fetch has no effect on the FETCH.  We can update the spec.

Though now it seems like requiring fwd=1 is causing a lot of problems.  I wonder if we should just allow fwd=0.  I think we disallow because the Joining Location could be stale.

issues.title: (JOINING) FETCH + SUBSCRIBE prioritization
issues.author: kixelated
issues.body:
Making a separate issue instead of hijacking #1358

When starting a subscription for a real-time use-case, the goal is to always deliver the most recent GoP and cancel/deprioritize any older GoPs.

We do this via `SUBSCRIBE order=desc`, and of course we need to issue two requests to start the subscription: 
```
SUBSCRIBE track=video order=desc filter=LatestObject
JOINING FETCH track=video
```


However, as it stands in the current draft, it's implementation specific how to prioritize these two requests. Ideally, we want the `JOINING FETCH` first, otherwise we're wasting bandwidth/RAM on undecodable frames from `SUBSCRIBE`, hurting TTV. We could explicitly request this:

```
SUBSCRIBE track=video order=desc filter=LatestObject priority=5
JOINING FETCH track=video priority=6
```

However, this doesn't work properly when NextGroup starts. The higher priority `JOINING FETCH` takes precedence over `order=DESC`. That means we're stuck downloading all of the old segment up until the original `LargestObject` before we can skip to the next group.

---

Here's a concrete example. The largest object is 1.5s into a 2s GoP (group 6), so it's almost done. Let's say the the media is encoded at 3Mb/s and our network speed is 4.5Mb/s.

It takes 1s to download the higher priority JOINING FETCH (1.5s of media). However, at this point the live playhead is already 0.5s into the next group (group 7). Now SUBSCRIBE is the highest priority request and skips to the next group, delivering the first 0.5s (in 0.33s) and then delivering the next 0.33s that was generated in the meantime (in 0.22s or whatever), etc. IDK of the exact math but it would take something like 1.5s to catch up to the live playhead.

But if we did a LargestGroup SUBSCRIBE, it would only take 0.5s to catch up to the live playhead. We would spend the first 0.5s downloading the largest group (6), but the instant there's a new group, the SUBSCRIBE immediately prioritizes the next group (order=desc) instead.

---

Basically, we need `order=DESC` support for JOINING FETCH. Either some way of prioritizing between the SUBSCRIBE + JOINING FETCH, or cancelling the JOINING FETCH if the next group starts (kinda gross), or add back the LargestGroup filter (pls).

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
Effectively, I want to race to determine if it's faster to:
- Download all of the current group (at network speed).
- Wait for the next group.

`SUBSCRIBE filter=CurrentGroup order=DESC` does this perfectly. I don't think it's possible in the current draft.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This came up during yesterday's discussion:

```
10  11a | 11b  12
        ^
        |
   Largest Object
```

It sounds like the goal is "11a 11b 12", *unless* 12,0 is available before the end of 11, in which case you want 12 to starve 11a or b.

I think the #1642 Group Order "FillDescending" almost does this: as written the Fill starts from the _Current Group - 1_ going backwards, Subscribe starts at Current Group going forwards.  Instead you want that split at Current Group.

CC: @fluffy since I think this is also the case you were mentioning.

issues.title: Request ID in GOAWAY isn't useful
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
After more thought (yes I approved #1559), I don't think the Request ID in GOAWAY is actionable in MoQ.  My intuition was "We have a Stream ID in HTTP/3, so we should have one in MoQ".  But MoQ is not HTTP, and that's intentional.

A possible exception is TRACK_INFO, but even then its safe to replay on another session and you're not guaranteed to get the response back before the session is closed.

Now that we're removing Required Request ID (#1615) and we've already removed Request ID flow control, GOAWAY is one of the two remaining uses of Request ID (the other is Joining Fetch).

Filing this now because #1559 landed relatively recently (hasn't even been published in a draft) to address #1549.  I'm also not completely sure #1549 is addressed by #1559, but I'd have to think about it more.

@vasilvv noted reluctance to relying on Request ID (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1559#issuecomment-4064673351) on the PR as well, but I think we all thought this would be useful at the time.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: My counter is - it's trivial to put the request ID in goaway, and might be useful.  If nothing else it can speed up retry when a new request is racing a GOAWAY.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Perhaps we want to use the Request ID slot to convey a Group ID when sent on an individual subscription or fetch stream.

issues.title: Track-level codec switching semantics
issues.author: yuanchao-chris
issues.body:
It seems that a MoQ Track is generally assumed to carry a single stable codec configuration for its lifetime.

However, in real-world RTC systems, codecs may need to change dynamically during an ongoing session, for example:

* H265 -> H264
* AV1 -> H264

In RTP/WebRTC, this is commonly handled within the same SSRC by changing Payload Type and updating decoder configuration.

In MoQ, it is unclear how mid-session codec migration is expected to work.
If codec changes require publishing a completely new Track, this may introduce several issues for low-latency RTC scenarios:
* subscribers need to subscribe to a new Track
* switching timing may not align perfectly
* frames may be lost during migration

Is there an expectation that codec reconfiguration could happen in-band within an existing Track?

Currently REQUEST_UPDATE appears mainly targeted at resynchronization/keyframe generation, but it is unclear whether it could also play a role in codec migration workflows.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Seems like you could have the publisher make a new group in an ongoing track, and include codec information on properties communicated on Object 0 in the new group - or the Object 0 payload.

Would something like that work?

comments.body:
yes, this can work in stream mode.

1. now we use datagram mode, the new codec information is added in object properties, and at subscriber side, we also add a "ACK" semantics(use REQUEST_UPDATE) to tell publisher stop add the property
2. track information in catalog also need update. https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-msf-00.html#section-5.1.24
