issues.title: Should we allow more than one concurrent subscription per Track
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
There's been a PR open on this for a while #1451 - but no specific tracking issue.  The editors have had slides on the topic since IETF 125, but we've never had enough agenda time to discuss.

I'm copying the text of the slides here, which includes proposals.


---
Primary Use Case: Preventing Relay DOS via “needle-in-a-haystack”

Subscriber 1: SUB t=huge track, range={100000,100000}-{100000,100001}
Subscriber 2: SUB t=huge track, range={200000,200000}-{200000,200001}

Relay has to either open 2 upstream sessions with narrow filters, or 1 session that is unfiltered or under-filtered.

Problem exists today but #1518 filters will create more opportunities
	Filters has been updated with “AndSets”

---
Secondary Use Case:

	SUBSCRIBE to a Track
	Cancel the Subscription by closing the request stream
		The RESET_STREAM is lost or delayed
	SUBSCRIBE to the Track again (for whatever reason)
		Peer closes the Session

Today, can avoid closing the Session by waiting for the Request Stream to fully close, but that’s slow and somewhat complex.

---
Considerations:

Wire Deduplication or Double Work
- Do subscriptions with overlapping filters receive the object once, or once per subscription?
- If it’s only once, both the publisher and subscriber both have to filter

Deduplicating multiple subscriptions is an illusion created by the publisher coalescing subscriptions and doing a union of the filters

The same effect could be created by expressing the union in a single subscription

Multiple subscriptions can have conflicting params that affect delivery
	Group Order, Priority, Delivery Timeout

---
Proposal 1a:

Allow multiple subscriptions, each with a unique Track Alias; no deduplication.
Subscriber/relay is responsible for minimizing overlaps/duplication and mapping correctly from upstreams to downstreams.

Proposal 1b:

Allow multiple subscriptions, all get the same Track Alias
Publisher coalesces these as a single subscription with a union of filters
Conflicting parameters ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Proposal 2:

Keep single subscription per track
Allow unions of all filter filter types in control messages
Can’t specify conflicting parameters (Delivery Timeout, etc) 

Proposal 3:

Status Quo

Editors’ Recommendation: 1a

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Thanks for filing an issue, I was about to.  @martinduke was discussing this with me today and liked 1b better.

Can you remind me what the issue is with conflicting parameters in 1b?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Can you remind me what the issue is with conflicting parameters in 1b?

I can subscribe to the same track with overlapping filters and different DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, PRIORITY, GROUP_ORDER, AUTH, etc.  If the publisher is deduplicating by using a single track alias, its unclear how to apply these.

For me, the bigger issue is the subscriber has to re-filter the arriving objects.

> Wire Deduplication or Double Work

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Yes, 1b.

The non-silly use case for this is make-before-break or just avoiding a session_error because of a lost RESET_STREAM. If a client does this it's going to have to deal with an object that maps to two local subscriptions and/or figure out under which handle to pass it up the stack. The answer is ~always the new subscription.

If you're doing something goofier, you can deal with the consequences. If it doesn't want to do the work, don't subscribe twice.

I don't think conflicting parameters matter. Parameters don't affect the content of objects, just what objects get delivered. If either subscribe's filters match, the object should go on the wire. I'm not sure if that means "intersection" or "union" but that's the correct behavior IMO.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
With Subgroup filters, one clear usecase is starting the enhancement layer Subgroup at the next group boundary.  I believe the easiest way to accomplish this is to end the current Subscription at the end of the current Group and start a new one at the next Group with the updated Subgroup filter.

This means relays don't have to do special handling for different types of updates of filters/etc.  It does make joining at a group boundary an even more important thing to get right, but hopefully we have a path to getting that figured out.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
yeah, that's a make-before-break.

It also highlights that the group-as-join-point thinking in the design is still pretty muddled. Why can't a REQUEST_UPDATE be triggered to start on the next group?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think a REQUEST_UPDATE could be triggered to start on the next group, but doing that for arbitrary parameters/filters might be quite complex?  I think a simpler option might be to start a new Subscription with the new filters you want, but I could be wrong.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Conclusion in London is that 1a to allow multiple Subscriptions for the same Track, and if you do you get duplicates if they overlap.  But we advise against overlapping, partially because the publisher might use the same track alias for the two Subscriptions, so you won't know which Objects are for which Subscription.

issues.title: [draft-18] What semantics do FIN or RST on a request stream carry?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The spec indicates that the way to cancel a request with bidi streams is to send a STOP_SENDING:

> 4.5: "The subscriber terminates a subscription in the Pending (Subscriber) or Established states by sending STOP_SENDING."

Of course the send side needs cleanup to, so there's:

> 3.6: "Implementations SHOULD cancel requests by abruptly terminating any directions of a stream that are still open by resetting or sending 
  STOP_SENDING."

What action should a receiver take, if any, when receiving only a FIN, or only a RST_STREAM, but no STOP_SENDING?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I'm inclined to say FIN almost always isn't a cancellation from the sender of the request.

For TRACK_STATUS an early FIN is perfectly normal - there's never anything else to say.  

For requests like FETCH, PUB_NS, SUB_NS, SUB_T and SUBSCRIBE, an early FIN can mean "I don't plan to REQUEST_UPDATE" - both sides can clean up some state.

PUBLISH is the odd duck, because sending a FIN on a subscription stream seems like it ought to mean something like "quiet PUBLISH_DONE" - with an inferred error code and stream count (maxint?).  See also #1635.

From the responder side, I'm less sure.  Since the requester _can_ send a REQUEST_UPDATE, closing the response channel proactively seems like a cancellation.  So I'd say FIN from the responder _is_ a cancellation.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Discussed in London.  If either direction of the bidi stream is closed (RESET or STOP_SENDING), the request is being cancelled.

It makes sense to send a FIN immediately after TRACK_STATUS, because you can't update a TRACK_STATUS.  That principle applies to other request types as well.  FINing a stream on the publisher side before sending a PUBLISH_DONE or other response message is potentially a protocol issue, but it's another issue. #1635 

For each message type, describe which messages can/should be immediately followed by a FIN.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: A FIN by the _sender_ after any message except PUBLISH is not cancellation, only a signal that no further updates will come.  STOP_SENDING is the preferred way to cancel after FIN.  PUBLISH requires a PUBLISH_DONE before FIN and that does terminate the request.  FIN by the receiver of a message MUST be preceded by a terminal message (_OK, REQUEST_ERROR, PUBLISH_DONE) and does signal the end of the request.

issues.title: [draft-18] Should a subscriber treat FIN/RST on a bidi stream as equivalent to PUBLISH_DONE?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
PUBLISH_DONE conveys error information as well as stream count.

Seems like FIN without PUBLISH_DONE is entirely avoidable and could be a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Discussed in London.  "MUST send PUBLISH_DONE before a FIN."

issues.title: Empty namespace clarification
issues.author: RichLogan
issues.body:
I was just reading the draft-18 text regarding namespace prefixes and full track names and wanted to clarify the rules for our implementation. 

I understand the use-case for zero element namespace prefixes, but wanted to check that publishing a track with a zero element namespace is allowed, and in theory, given the text as it is today, a track with a zero element namespace AND an empty name is also allowed?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
With apologies for answering your question with AI:

  Track Namespace (for tracks): Line 511 says "between 1 and 32 Track Namespace Fields" and line
  544-546 explicitly states: "If an endpoint receives a Track Namespace consisting of 0 or greater
  than 32 Track Namespace Fields, it MUST close the session with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION." So
  publishing a track with a zero-element namespace is NOT allowed — it's a protocol violation.

  Track Namespace Prefix (in SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE): Line 3107-3108 says "between 0 and 32 Track
  Namespace Fields." A zero-element prefix is explicitly permitted here — it acts as a wildcard
  matching all namespaces.
  
  So the rules diverge intentionally:
  - SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE prefix: 0-32 fields (zero is valid, matches everything)
  - Track Namespace (in PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, etc.): 1-32 fields (zero is a protocol violation)
  
  Regarding empty track name: Line 548 says "Track Name is a sequence of bytes, possibly empty." So
  yes, an empty track name is explicitly allowed. A track with a 1-element namespace and an empty
  name would be valid.

  The combination you asked about — zero-element namespace AND empty name — would not be valid for
  an actual track, because the namespace needs at least 1 field.

comments.author: RichLogan
comments.body:
@afrind forgive me if I'm missing (and it's late for me) but I'm not sure that's reflective of the text in the draft today. I can't see any mention of "between 1 and 32 Track Namespace Fields", only "between 0 and 32".

E.g See here the Track Naming section: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-18.html#section-2.4.1

> Track Namespace is an ordered set of between 0 and 32 Track Namespace Fields, encoded as follows

And any reference to Track Namespace I believe just links back to 2.4.1 - such as PUBLISH:

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-18.html#name-publish

Or Subscribe: 

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-18.html#name-subscribe

I am totally fine with it being 0 elements and/or empty btw, I just wanted to double check on it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Wow, that is pretty embarrassing.  I apologize.  It spit out that sentence about 1 and 32 and that seemed familiar I didn't double check it.  Ouch.

Per the current draft you are 100% right it's allowed to have 0 fields and a 0 length name.  I'm unclear if I think it's a good idea to forbid it or not, but maybe I'm inclined to allow it.  It's sort of like path=/ in HTTP?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
My intuition is that I don't like Tracks with no name or namespace, partially because I worry they're confusing.

How did we decide that an empty Track Name is ok?  Is there a real use case for that?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Discussed in London.  We might need to clarify this, but the group wanted to keep the status quo and continue to allow both Track Namespace and Name to be empty.

issues.title: What does MOQT do without bidi stream credit?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
I don't think the text is clear about what happens when there isn't enough bidi stream credit to send a request. Specifically, does the responsibility to retry lie with MOQT or with the application?

We got rid of REQUEST_BLOCKED, and it would be sad to pipe OnCanOpenBidiStream() from QUIC all the way up to the application, so it seems worthwhile to just have MOQT track pending bidi streams.

But we have PUBLISH_BLOCKED, which I guess is a way for a subscriber to SUBSCRIBE (where it might have credit). But this is the inverse of SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED, where the publisher could potentially deliver the stream, but there's no SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED message.

At the very least, the draft should spell out what is required for interoperability, and ideally what MOQT is doing vs. what applications do, so
(1) What request streams are retried by MOQT vs. requiring the application to do something?
(2) When is the peer expected to try the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH inverse because the other direction is blocked?
(3) If both directions are blocked, who is responsible for finally opening it? Will we just let the messages cross and let the tiebreaker rules in 5.1 do their thing?

It would be nice to actually clean this up conceptually as well.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Another thought:

If there were no PUBLISH, all pending streams could be ordered by subscriber priority. a PUBLISH in response to SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS could use the SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS priority. But there is no subscriber priority for other PUBLISH messages, so how should these be ordered?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Should MOQT act on PUBLISH_BLOCKED or is this punted to the application?

Can MOQT send PUBLISH_BLOCKED and also keep trying to open the PUBLISH stream?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
> Should MOQT act on PUBLISH_BLOCKED or is this punted to the application?

Typically, I'd expect MoQT to act on it, unless it became obvious it was going to be way too many PUBLISHes.

> 
> Can MOQT send PUBLISH_BLOCKED and also keep trying to open the PUBLISH stream?

No, you don't send a PUBLISH after PUBLISH_BLOCKED for a given track: "The Publisher MUST NOT send a PUBLISH for a Track after PUBLISH_BLOCKED has been sent. " from section 6.1

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-moq-transport-18.html#section-6.1

That section might be clearer if it was reorganized now that SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE is split into two.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
> I don't think the text is clear about what happens when there isn't enough bidi stream credit to send a request. Specifically, does the responsibility to retry lie with MOQT or with the application?

Probably, or create a new MoQT session.

> 
> We got rid of REQUEST_BLOCKED, and it would be sad to pipe OnCanOpenBidiStream() from QUIC all the way up to the application, so it seems worthwhile to just have MOQT track pending bidi streams.

I'm not sure that's so sad, I'm pretty sure we do that in HTTP/3 today.

> 
> But we have PUBLISH_BLOCKED, which I guess is a way for a subscriber to SUBSCRIBE (where it might have credit). But this is the inverse of SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED, where the publisher could potentially deliver the stream, but there's no SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED message.

PUBLISH_BLOCKED is there to avoid the publisher having to queue up a ton of pending Subscriptions for some unknown period of time.  Once it sends PUBLISH_BLOCKED, the subscriber knows the Track name and can ask for it if it wants.

SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED is the same as FETCH_BLOCKED or any other request, which is if you don't have any bidi streams available, you can't start a new request.

> 
> At the very least, the draft should spell out what is required for interoperability, and ideally what MOQT is doing vs. what applications do, so (1) What request streams are retried by MOQT vs. requiring the application to do something? (2) When is the peer expected to try the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH inverse because the other direction is blocked? (3) If both directions are blocked, who is responsible for finally opening it? Will we just let the messages cross and let the tiebreaker rules in 5.1 do their thing?
> 
> It would be nice to actually clean this up conceptually as well.

I'm not sure what the conceptual problem is?  Maybe we should rename PUBLISH_BLOCKED to PUBLISH_SKIPPED to make it clearer what the intended semantics are?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> > I don't think the text is clear about what happens when there isn't enough bidi stream credit to send a request. Specifically, does the responsibility to retry lie with MOQT or with the application?
> 
> Probably, or create a new MoQT session.

Since HTTP/1.1 we've been trying to prevent multiple sessions.  it also doesn't work if the requester is the server, or if the requester is the client and the servers are load balanced, when requests are dependent on each other.

> > We got rid of REQUEST_BLOCKED, and it would be sad to pipe OnCanOpenBidiStream() from QUIC all the way up to the application, so it seems worthwhile to just have MOQT track pending bidi streams.
> 
> I'm not sure that's so sad, I'm pretty sure we do that in HTTP/3 today.

I dunno, having all applications implement retry instead of doing it at the MOQT layer is wasteful.

> 
> > But we have PUBLISH_BLOCKED, which I guess is a way for a subscriber to SUBSCRIBE (where it might have credit). But this is the inverse of SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED, where the publisher could potentially deliver the stream, but there's no SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED message.
> 
> PUBLISH_BLOCKED is there to avoid the publisher having to queue up a ton of pending Subscriptions for some unknown period of time. Once it sends PUBLISH_BLOCKED, the subscriber knows the Track name and can ask for it if it wants.
> 
> SUBSCRIBE_BLOCKED is the same as FETCH_BLOCKED or any other request, which is if you don't have any bidi streams available, you can't start a new request.

But it's symmetric. The publisher *could* simply send a PUBLISH instead of granting more stream credit.

> 
> > At the very least, the draft should spell out what is required for interoperability, and ideally what MOQT is doing vs. what applications do, so (1) What request streams are retried by MOQT vs. requiring the application to do something? (2) When is the peer expected to try the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH inverse because the other direction is blocked? (3) If both directions are blocked, who is responsible for finally opening it? Will we just let the messages cross and let the tiebreaker rules in 5.1 do their thing?
> > It would be nice to actually clean this up conceptually as well.
> 
> I'm not sure what the conceptual problem is? Maybe we should rename PUBLISH_BLOCKED to PUBLISH_SKIPPED to make it clearer what the intended semantics are?

The naming isn't important. The spec should just say if the receiver is supposed to grant stream credit or send SUBSCRIBE. Does my publisher implementation have to queue it for retry or not?

The conceptual problem is why NAMESPACE-stream PUBLISH instead of regular PUBLISH, or a blocked SUBSCRIBE. There may be good reasons it's so narrowly scoped but I'm not sure what they are.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Discussed in London.

AI for @ianswett is to rename PUBLISH_BLOCKED to PUBLISH_SKIPPED or something similar and clarify that if a subscriber wants that Track, it has to send a SUBSCRIBE.

For the flow control issue as a Relay, @martinduke or @afrind are going to add a REQUEST_ERROR error code.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: It is a little more complicated than just REQUEST_ERROR because a single request can result in multiple FETCH streams. The fix is just to reset the FETCH stream or declare unknown blocks within it.

issues.title: EXPIRES should be allowed in more REQUEST_OK sub-types.
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
IIUC EXPIRES is basically saying "this is how long your auth token is good for." If that's the case, this parameter is useful for any response for a request that contains an auth token, which is all of them.

I can squint and say that FETCH_OK is an exception, because all the objects are in the past and therefore the token can't expire. That's a design question I don't have the answer to.

Similarly, TRACK_STATUS is ~ instantaneous so maybe EXPIRES doesn't make sense.

The EXPIRES text also mentions PUBLISH_DONE, which is not applicable if the parameter is applicable to a wide range of request types, so that language would need cleanup.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I'd say all except TRACK_STATUS and FETCH.  I think those only get one chance to auth since they are not expected to take a long time.

issues.title: Publish DONE, control stream or request stream?
issues.author: TimEvens
issues.body:
https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/blob/cb2e772fd8ca8cbe7550b1765c269be89fb1c886/draft-ietf-moq-transport.md?plain=1#L3181


> Because PUBLISH_DONE is sent on a control stream, it is likely to arrive at the receiver before late-arriving objects, and often even late-opening streams.

Should this be removed considering the PUBLISH_DONE is sent on the bidir/request stream?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Request streams are considered "control" streams in most of the text, but we can probably crisp this up.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Fixed in #1649

issues.title: [draft-18] Is it a request or session error to FIN a response bidi stream without a control message first?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
eg: publisher responds to FETCH with FIN but not FETCH_OK/ERROR?

If I read HTTP/3 correctly, this is just a stream error there.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Discussed in London: "MUST send a response message (REQUEST_OK, REQUEST_ERROR, etc) to a SUBSCRIBE prior to sending a FIN."

issues.title: Duplicate Track Properties on repeated SUBSCRIBE_OK / FETCH_OK
issues.author: kixelated
issues.body:
I don't think this is an issue worth fixing for v1, but I wanted to raise it.

Track properties are meant to be fixed for the lifetime of a track. They can be cached indefinitely, at least in theory.

However, each SUBSCRIBE_OK and FETCH_OK transmits a fresh copy of the Track Properties even if the subscriber already has that information cached. The most egregious example would be a FETCH for each group; we keep transmitting redundant track properties. 

This could get quite inefficient if track properties get large, like for folks using them as a replacement for the catalog. Imagine a FETCH for an audio group and each FETCH_OK contains the full codec/description/timescale/etc information.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
The most radical solution would be to remove Track Properties from SUBSCRIBE_OK / FETCH_OK and require a parallel TRACK_STATUS request, only requested by the subscriber if track properties are not cached.

A more balanced solution would be a flag indicating if they should be included in the SUBSCRIBE_OK / FETCH_OK.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> Track Properties : A sequence of Properties. See {{properties}}. The length of Track Properties is the remaining length of the message after parsing all previous fields. Track Properties are populated in TRACK_STATUS_OK; they are empty in PUBLISH_OK, REQUEST_UPDATE_OK, SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE_OK and PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_OK. If an endpoint receives Track Properties in one of these messages it MUST close the session with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

And just a quick editorial note, it's kinda weird adding Track Properties to REQUEST_OK. I paniced seeing Track Properties it on every REQUEST_OK until you read the fine print and realize... it's only for TRACK_STATUS_OK.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Discussed in London: Add a parameter to request/not request Track Properties to save bytes on the wire.  Maybe we can get rid of it later if we do the new Joining Fetch proposal.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Proposal: INCLUDE_PROPERTIES 1/0 -- default=1

Add some text about property (non)malleability.

issues.title: Application-specific property codepoints conflict
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body: Section 2.5 reserves 0x38 to 0x3F and 0x3800 to 0x3FFF for application use, but section 15.8 reserves 0x78 to 0x7F.

issues.title: [Loc] TIMESTAMP and SUBGROUP_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT have same value
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body: See section 15.8

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
>  0x06 | SUBGROUP_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT | Track, Object | Section 12.1

>  0x06 | TIMESTAMP | Object | draft-ietf-moq-loc

Despite our best efforts to not stomp on LOC, we did it _again_.  @mzanaty @suhasHere 

I recommend that LOC move all its properties to the high end of the 1-byte varint space and count down to avoid this in future drafts.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This is LOC's problem: https://github.com/moq-wg/loc/issues/20.  Once they correctly assign their numbers, they can make a PR against moq-transport so we don't keep making the same mistake.  Closing this for now.

CC: @mzanaty

comments.author: mzanaty
comments.body: This issue was caused by a bad merge in MOQT PR#1605 making MOQT internally inconsistent in adjacent tables for 0x06 (Subgroup Delivery Timeout and LOC Timestamp). LOC-03 fixed this by moving its Timestamp to 0x0A. MOQT is still internally inconsistent and needs a fix.

issues.title: Forward Handling SHOULD set Forward=1 upstream is too strong
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
> 9.2. Forward Handling
> 
> Relays SHOULD set the Forward flag to 1 when a new subscription needs to be sent upstream, regardless of the value of the Forward field from the downstream subscription. Subscriptions that are not forwarded consume resources from the publisher, so a publisher might deprioritize, reject, or close those subscriptions to ensure other subscriptions can be delivered.

Sending a subscription with fwd=0 causing the relay to open an upstream subscription with fwd=1 is another DOS vector.  In real production environments this is going to be a policy decision that involves factors like current load, the size of the subscription, the popularity of the Track, etc.

I propose we drop the normative SHOULD and instead explain that relays have discretion, and highlight some of the possible tradeoffs (faster join vs possible attacks).

comments.author: zafergurel
comments.body:
I agree with @afrind. Eventually, the relays end up implementing optimizations not to open upstream subscriptions. 

As an additional note, FORWARD parameter may appear SUBSCRIBE_OK, so that the relay can transmit its decision to the subscriber whether it opened an upstream subscription or not.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
I agree with removing the ability to pre-warm the cache.

It's a pre-mature optimization that causes upstream work without downstream work.

comments.author: acidseed
comments.body: I agree with this. Is pre-warming the cache that big of a concern, as eventually you will be bound to the publisher's connection.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Discussed in London - agree to remove the SHOULD in favor of giving relays more discretion and info about tradeoffs.

issues.title: How does GROUP_ORDER interact with PUBLISH?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In SUBSCRIBE, the subscriber dictates the group order. If it doesn't specify, the Publisher's default wins.

Notably, GROUP_ORDER is not allowed in REQUEST_UPDATE, presumably because it would be disruptive to update mid-subscription. For one thing, it would involve re-prioritizing all streams in the subscription.

Given this, I don't understand how it's supposed to work with PUBLISH.

The Publisher has no subscriber input when it starts pushing objects so it uses its default group order. But then, a PUBLISH_OK arrives and it's supposed to change the group order?

This would be a lot cleaner if (1) GROUP_ORDER was not allowed in PUBLISH_OK or (2) it was allowed in REQUEST_UPDATE. As an implementer, I would prefer (1) as it's less painful.

I'm happy to write a PR if everyone agrees.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @afrind proposed that GROUP_ORDER be allowed in SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS, and that should be used if applicable.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Discussed in London: Should be able to specify GROUP_ORDER in SUBSCRIBE_TRACKs and that gets copied to any PUBLISHes that result.  Should not be able to specify GROUP_ORDER in PUBLISH_OK, because we want to continue with the property that Group Order can't be changed mid Subscription.

issues.title: SETUP - extensions negotiation
issues.author: kvasilye
issues.body:
Looking at Draft 18

Section 3.2

```
3.2.  Extension Negotiation

   Endpoints use the exchange of Setup messages to negotiate MOQT
   extensions.  Extensions can define new Message types, new Parameters,
   new Properties, or new framing for Streams and Datagrams.
```
However `Section 10.3. SETUP` including `Section 10.3.1.  Setup Options` does not seem to define the exact mechanism for extension negotiation.

We are currently designing our MoQ stack and will need to use extensions for some features.

Would it be possible to clarify the extension negotiation mechanism please?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I wrote an extension draft a couple months ago: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-frindell-moq-moqpack-00.html if that is helpful.

The general mechanism is to have each peer declare its extension support in SETUP - when both peers declare support - the extension is negotiated.

Once that’s true you can for example send new message types, new parameters, new enum values, new stream types, etc.

There is also one extensibility point that does not require pre negotiation- Track/Object Properties (sent by the publisher). These will be forwarded unmodified towards subscribers even if not understood.

comments.author: kvasilye
comments.body:
Thank you

Looking at your doc - are we supposed to send numeric extension IDs in the SETUP message?

Or there negotiation of IDs based on some string key values (which could be assured to be unique be deriving them from domains for example)?

comments.author: yuyou
comments.body:
Also the v18 spec says:
> The client and server MUST include all Setup Options [Section 10.3.1] required for the negotiated MOQT version in SETUP.

In a chain of relays, would it be helpful to clarify that all Setup Options, including those reserved for application use as  newly defined extensions, must be forwarded along the path?
 
e.g. 

`A -- (SETUP with extention a ) --> Relay1 -- (SETUP with extension a) --> Relay2 (SETUP with extension a) --> B
`

Suggest to add something like:

`To ensure consistent SETUP negotiation, a Relay must propagate all SETUP options, including extensions, to the next endpoint in both the upstream and downstream directions.
`

comments.author: kvasilye
comments.body:
> The general mechanism is to have each peer declare its extension support in SETUP - when both peers declare support - the extension is negotiated.

Sorry but I don't see where the mechanism for "declaring its extension support" is documented, can you point this out?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: > Each endpoint declares the extensions it supports and provides any initial values required by those extensions as Setup Options in SETUP. Once an endpoint has both sent and received SETUP messages, it determines the set of negotiated extensions.

comments.author: laiDisney
comments.body:
> A -- (SETUP with extention a ) --> Relay1 -- (SETUP with extension a) --> Relay2 (SETUP with extension a) --> B

What will happen when a relay has multiple upstreams? I believe that a relay may have its own extension supported.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> What will happen when a relay has multiple upstreams? I believe that a relay may have its own extension supported.

That is correct.

Multi-hop extension negotiation is a hard problem and we're not going to try to solve that here (note e.g. HTTP doesn't have a solution either).  For the most part, the applications that need to use multiple relays will coordinate out of band to ensure all relays deploy necessary extensions.

You can also use the Mandatory Track Properties code points to enforce certain tracks do not pass through relays which do not understand their associated extensions.

issues.title: [draft-18] REQUEST_OK in response to REQUEST_UPDATE lacks Request ID
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
If I send multiple REQUEST_UPDATE at once on the same bidi stream, there's no correlator in the response.

I suppose in draft-18 that means the updates MUST return in the order sent.  This smells of HTTP/1.1.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I think that SGTM! If we can handle all the cross-dependencies some other way, it'd be great to get rid of request ID.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Discussion in London and people agreed that the only way to guarantee correct behavior is to process REQUEST_UPDATE in order. 

SWITCH_FROM could make the REQUEST_UPDATE consume a substantial amount of time before a REQUEST_OK can be returned, and auth might have similar delays.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Can we think of a use-case where we want to change something during SWITCH_FROM before it's ok comes back?  For most of the things you can change (forward, priority, range filters), having that update serialized on the publisher after the switch completes seems mostly fine?

Do we think that all parameters in REQUEST_UPDATE need to be applied at the same time, or can we model them as all completely independent (eg: UPDATE A, B, C is equivalent to UPDATE A, UPDATE B, UPDATE C)?  If so, we could limit FIFO blocking on a per-param basis -- it's fine to update priority while waiting for a new auth token to validate.

issues.title: Tighter language around GOAWAYs on a request stream
issues.author: sharmafb
issues.body:
Section 10.4 says "A GOAWAY MAY also be sent on a request stream to initiate migration of that individual request." and "A client MUST send a zero-length New Session URI in any GOAWAY, as clients cannot instruct servers to initiate connections."

We may want to add some further restrictions to this:
- Only the recipient of a SUBSCRIBE can send a GOAWAY for it.
- Only the sender of a PUBLISH can send a GOAWAY for it.
- Only the recipient of a FETCH can send a GOAWAY for it.

In general, only the endpoint that is sending the data for the track should be able to send a GOAWAY. I don't really see why the other endpoint would want to send a GOAWAY for it.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think either end of a subscription can send GOAWAY.  The relay server can be a subscriber (client sent PUBLISH) or a publisher (client sent SUBSCRIBE).

I think that is true of PUB_NS, SUB_NS and SUB_TRACKS (long-lived requests).  But only the receiver of a FETCH or TRACK_STATUS can GOAWAY those, and maybe those don't make any sense.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Discussed in London.  The group was leaning towards the idea that only the receiver of a request message can send GOAWAY, but Mo also asked if we could allow it for either direction.

There was also a suggestion that only the server could send it, because the client can't send the server somewhere else.

Alan to make a more specific proposal.

issues.title: Add generic support for handling AUTH Challenges
issues.author: suhasHere
issues.body:
The REQUEST_ERROR message currently only carries a UTF-8 Reason Phrase for diagnostic information. Authorization schemes like Privacy Pass (draft-ietf-moq-privacy-pass-auth) need to convey structured binary data (e.g., MoQAuthChallenge
  containing TokenChallenge structures) back to the client on auth failure. 

These structures contain opaque binary fields
  (redemption_context, origin_info, cryptographic material) that cannot be cleanly represented in a UTF-8 string.

  For SETUP-level errors, the QUIC CONNECTION_CLOSE reason phrase is also constrained to UTF-8, but for MoQT-level  REQUEST_ERROR there is no reason to force binary challenge data through a text encoding.

  Related: https://github.com/moq-wg/privacy-pass/issues/14, 
                 https://github.com/moq-wg/privacy-pass/issues/15

  Proposal

  Add an opaque Error Payload field (length-prefixed) to REQUEST_ERROR, whose interpretation is defined by the Error Code.
 
 This allows:
  - Authorization schemes to carry token challenges as binary without base64url overhead
  - Future extensions to attach structured error metadata without overloading Reason Phrase
  - Endpoints that don't recognize the Error Code to ignore the payload

  Additional minor clarifications:
  - UNAUTHORIZED session termination: note that clients MAY reconnect with credentials

issues.title: SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS should contain SUBSCRIBE parameters
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: In London, we agreed that SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS can/should contain parameters that only apply to SUBSCRIBE, and resulting PUBLISH messages should act as if those parameters had been included in a SUBSCRIBE.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This seems to overlap with #1777, but is a more general change.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
People didn't like the idea of SUBSCRIBE parameters occurring in PUBLISH, so there are some options here.

1) Assume that people can figure out what the initial parameters are, so omit them.
  - Pro: Easy  Con: If you update SUB_TRACKS, then how do you know which params are in use?
2) Reference the Request ID of the SUB_TRACKS or subsequent REQUEST_UPDATE to indicate which params are in use
  - Pro: Only one field. Con: Instead of being racy, now you need to store all params ever sent on a SUB_TRACKS for an unknown time
3) Repeat all the SUBSCRIBE parameters in the PUBLISH (PR #1788)
  - Con: Some parameters don't make sense in the PUBLISH and aren't allowed today.  Pro: It's easy, no new framing or codepoints. They also don't conflict, so there's no ambiguity.  We'll probably want to allow some of these in PUBLISH in the future (filters?)
4) Create a parameter that contains all the parameters the Subscription was initialized with (ie: SUBSCRIBE_PARAMS?)
  - Con: Another nested parameter.  Pro: Don't have to think very hard about whether a Parameter might have a different meaning depending on which perspective it comes from (it probably shouldn't anyway, though?)

I liked 3 because I think we're heading to a world with Switch/DTS/etc where subscribers will give publishers instructions and they will update the filter ranges or publisher priority on their behalf. Admittedly, 4 also works in that way, since it could be used by Switch/DTS in a REQUEST_UPDATE message.

I think 1 and 2 are quite unappealing, and they don't help Switch/DTS, which I think we should keep in mind here.

issues.title: How does auth work
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body: Is is hop by hop or can an end subscriber send an auth token to an original publisher? What is the overal architecture for authorization. What things can be authorized. When are tokens, re-evaluated. Note tokens can have time and geo ranges.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> Is is hop by hop or can an end subscriber send an auth token to an original publisher? 

On this question specifically, I feel like it's been discussed multiple times including recently (#1462) when we added this:

> Message Parameters are only intended for the peer only and are not forwarded by Relays, though relays can consider received parameter values when making a request. 

AUTH_TOKEN is a Message Parameter so falls under this guidance.  Most messages can be coalesced at a relay, there's no guarantee that an AUTH_TOKEN will ever go any farther than the first hop.  Including the first subscriber's auth token(s) on the upstream subscribe, then attaching subsequent subscribers seems wrong in many cases.  I think at one time Luke had proposed a separate "AUTH" message for delegating the verification upstream before attaching to a coalesced subscription, but this didn't go very far.

PUBLISH is an exception to coalescing, though see #799 - blindly forwarding a PUBLISH AUTH_TOKEN through a relay to clients that have sent SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE might not be correct, since those clients may not have the means to verify that token. I now vaguely recall discussions where there could be multiple tokens with different destinations (relay, end subscriber).  It seems like what gets included on subsequent hops of these control messages is likely a policy rather than a protocol decision?

In any case, I'm glad we have formed the Auth design team to work through all the scenarios.

issues.title: Clarify that object ID gaps in subgroups and datagrams do not imply non-existence
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body:
The draft has the text 

> The Object is known to not exist. This state is permanent. All
> signals that an Object does not exist are authoritative.

I think the above is correct. 

The draft also has contradicting text bellow that I think is wrong/out of date. 

> Since Objects can be delivered out of order, an endpoint can receive
> an Object after it has already recorded that the Object does not
> exist (e.g., via a FETCH gap from one source and later delivery via a
> subscription). This is not a protocol error and the Track is not
> malformed.

I think we need some text along the lines that says object can arrive out of order and thus just the fact that objects 4 and 6 are received does not mean 5 does not exist.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> The draft also has contradicting text bellow that I think is wrong/out of date.

This text was specifically added relatively recently (#1566) to address #1376 and I believe it is correct.

> I think we need some text along the lines that says object can arrive out of order and thus just the fact that objects 4 and 6 are received does not mean 5 does not exist.

This text is not talking about object 5.  It's capturing the following case:

S->P: SUBSCRIBE from 0,0
P->S: Object 0 ... delayed in flight
S->P: FETCH 0,0
P->S: has thrown away object 0, returns empty --> Object 0 DOES_NOT_EXIST
Object 0 arrives via subscription --> this does not contradict the permanence of DOES_NOT_EXIST, and is not a malformed track condition.

Doest that make sense @fluffy?

To return to this point:

> I think we need some text along the lines that says object can arrive out of order and thus just the fact that objects 4 and 6 are received does not mean 5 does not exist.

I agree.  I found this way down in the Prior Object ID Gap definition:

> If Prior Object ID Gap is not present, the receiver cannot infer any information about the existence of prior objects (see {{model-object}}).

But we should have something in Object Model explaining that even within a subgroup, a gap in the object ID space does not imply any information.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
This partially overlaps with our logic that says "try moqt and h3, and if you get h3, treat the URL as an https url".  That is, any rules we define for the structure of the query needs to be convertible to https.  I suppose if an application doesn't support MOQT over webtrans it can use any query form it likes.

I am not a URL expert, but isn't FCFS reserving query params a little like reserving parts of the path (e.g. isn't this for the _application_)?

Can you give examples of the kinds of uses you have in mind for this?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in Vienna: we made some progress on the issue _as written_, until we realized that @fluffy actually wanted something different -- more structure to the format of the _fragment_ not the query.

To capture the discussion - there was at least some interest in requiring more structure to the query (eg x-www-url-form-encoded), and there wouldn't be any problems converting _to_ https URLs, only from https to moq, but no one expressed a use case for that.  There was a concern, raised by @englishm-ietf / @englishm, about how adding structured query params would impact scope.

As I understand, the entire path -- including the query -- are part of the scope.  If there are query params that are structured, do we need to say anything about canonicalization (e.g. is foo.com/path?a=b&c=d the same as foo.com/path?c=d&a=b)?  It may be fine to leave this up to the individual resource?

I talked to @fluffy post session, who offered to write a PR for what he has in mind for structuring the fragment.  From what I understand, it was changing our single <fragment-id>:<fragment-id-specific> format to allow multiple, particularly for versioning, e.g. `#msf-v1:...&msf-v2:...`.  I suppose the alternative is to let versioning of msf, etc happen inside the type specific portion.  CC: @wilaw who may have MSF opinions?

For the part of this issue discussing FCFS - I think we already have an IANA table for registering fragment-id's, so I don't think anything more is needed?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: CC: scope enthusiast @michalhosna

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
IMO the fragment "type" indicates the general class of application and not the version. Different types can have complex versioning structures (Major, Minor, and Patch semantic versioning, or strings). These are best left to the application to define and transmit. Within MSF for example, we already have a versioning capability. The application should be responsible for backwards compatibility with its versioning for a given registered application type. If MSF decides in the future to make a completely different catalog type which would require a different parser to extract the version, thus breaking the backwards compatibility, then it can register a new  application type for MOQT, for example "MSF2". 

Note that because the current type prefix is a string, it can already accommodate prefix versioning in the form

```
#msf-v1:
#myotherformat-23.056.2843:
```

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
So I think what Alan is proposing is:

MoQ Transport 1.0 get published as RFC 1000. 

Then after an extension that modifies the replay behavior such as Top-N gets published as RFC 2000. 

Then before that can really be used we have to wait for MoQ Transport 2.0 to get published as RFC 3000. 

That seems like very hard way to do things because people will want to make many changes in RFC 3000 not just add RFC2000. 


I think a better proposal would be like this. 

We have an IANA registry ( probably requiring a standards track RFC to update it ) that has a table that is roughly registers a MoQ Transport version number and maps it to a base transport RFC and to the extentions that are required to be supported. So in the example above, 

RFC 2000 would create an version entry that looks like 
Moq_1.0 => RFC 1000

Then RFC 2000 would add an entry like 
Moq_1.1 => RFC  1000 + RFC 2000

Then RFC 3000 would add an entry like 
Moc_2.0 => RFC 3000 + RFC 2000 

I would view this as probably need a PR that tagged as "design" in the general area of extensibility

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I removed the NoTransport because I think this does need to dealt with as part of transport extensibility

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> MoQ Transport 1.0 get published as RFC 1000.
> Then after an extension that modifies the replay behavior such as Top-N gets published as RFC 2000.
> Then before that can really be used we have to wait for MoQ Transport 2.0 to get published as RFC 3000.

No that's not the idea.  I think it's like this:

MOQ Transport gets published as RFC 1000.
Extensions that go out in this cluster say "Can be used with MOQT v1, or subsequent versions that are wire compatible with v1".

Sweet Extension gets published as RFC 2000.  It says "Can be used with MOQT v1, or subsequent versions that are wire compatible with v1".

MOQT v2 gets published as RFC 3000.  It's backwards wire compatible with v1 and says "All extensions that work with MOQT v1 work with MOQT v2".

MOQT v3 gets published as RFC 4000.  It makes fundamental changes to e.g. the object model.  Future us might enumerate known extensions that work and don't work, as well as considerations for extension authors about whether they need to make changes to support v3.

Neat Extension gets published as RFC 5000.  It says "this only works with MOQT v3".

In general, I'm not even sure we need to say anything in MOQT v1.  The point of the text is really advisory -- if we are revving MOQT or someone is defining an extension, just need to think about the sensible compatibility matrix.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
We cannot move .session to an extension.  We already reserve every namespace that starts with '.'

`.` --> DOES_NOT_EXIST
`.session`:

> The Application MUST NOT publish tracks or namespaces whose first field is .session. Relays MUST NOT forward requests for session-level tracks and namespaces to other sessions

> Session-level tracks and namespaces are managed by the MOQT implementation, not the Application. **They provide a mechanism for extending MOQT transport functionality using existing subscription and object delivery machinery, without defining new control messages or stream types**.

issues.title: Updating cache fields / properties
issues.author: fluffy
issues.body:
draft has text that says 

> Relays MAY ignore subsequently received Objects or MAY use them to
> update certain cached fields. Implementations that update the cache
> need to protect against cache poisoning. The only Object fields that
> can be updated are the following:
> 1. Object can transition from existing to not existing in cases
> where the object is no longer available.
> 2. Object Properties can be added, removed or updated, subject to
> the constraints of the specific property.

I think this is going to turn out be a bad idea on two axis.

1. it is going to be insanity to allow things to go from non existing to existing. Other places we say that is not allowed 

2. allowing properties to change is going to be a very brittle particularly if only something do it. I think these need be described as the relay ignore any future properties from objects that are currently in cache and uses the cache values. 

We need to phrase carefully because a relay might add a property like the NTP time it sent the object but for what it stores in cache, I think it need to never change. We also don't want clients relying on cache behavior that not all relays support.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> it is going to be insanity to allow things to go from non existing to existing.

Agree, but this text does not allow that.  It says the opposite:

> Object can transition from **existing** to **not existing** in cases where the object is no longer available.

> allowing properties to change is going to be a very brittle particularly if only something do it. I think these need be described as the relay ignore any future properties from objects that are currently in cache and uses the cache values

This carve out is explicitly for ephemeral properties like time, tracing extensions, etc.

There's also this sentence which is buried back in 2.5 Properties, and either needs a reference or to move to the caching section:

> If a Track or Object arrives with a different set of unknown properties than previously cached, the most recent set SHOULD replace any cached values, removing any unknown values not present in the new set. Relays MUST NOT attempt to merge sets of unknown properties received in different messages.

So we explicitly agreed in draft-16 that the cache SHOULD get updated (see #1395 / #1380)

Editorial - text only changes

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> if an publisher does not know if an object has existed in the past, or may exist in the future, it MUST not singalling that indicates it does not exist.

I don't find this to be practical for the past - effectively it means every publisher needs to retain every object ever published forever, or relays will never be able to cache non-existence for objects that expire. issues.title: upstream fetch for multi publishers

Right now the draft has

> When more than one publisher is available, the Relay MAY send the
> FETCH to any of them.

The question is should this be MUST send to all of them like subscribe. 

If the use case is each is only responsible for part of the track, then you want all. If the use case each upstream is a fully redundant copy of the full track, then you want any of them. 

Even in the the second case, you probably want MUST send to at lease one of them, not "MAY send to any of them. 

I think this topic is particularly important if we are trying to replace fetch with subscribe.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
FETCH can go to any publisher (see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1117 / https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1165) -- @fluffy you approved https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1117.

> If the use case is each is only responsible for part of the track, then you want all. If the use case each upstream is a fully redundant copy of the full track, then you want any of them.

There's unfortunately no way for a relay to know the answer to "each is only responsible for part".  The consensus we arrived at is that if you have that design (I think most people have abandoned these designs in favor of newer mechanisms in the draft), you have to have an aggregating entity that presents itself to the relay as a single source of truth for the Track.  If you think about this problem, merging arbitrary fetch responses is very complicated, and we agreed to _not_ foist this problem onto every MOQT relay.

This has passed multiple consensus calls.  I recommend we do not reopen this topic.

issues.title: Fill Timeout reduction by relay
issues.author: fluffy

> the subscriber specifies a Fill Timeout larger than the relay is

I don't like the idea that relay can use a shorter time, perhaps 0, without the subscriber knowing that happened. Could we design a way to inform what was used, or negotiate a lower bound that will not be shortened, or return an error when this happens.

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body: I don't think the PR resolved my issue, I'm fine with the relay rejecting the request becaue the fill time is too long but it is going to be very hard to build apps where the relay changes this without telling the subscriber what happened.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
@fluffy do you have a specific use case that is going to break in mind, or are you arguing based on experiences of things going badly in other protocols?  It would really help me understand if you can give concrete flows and negative outcomes if a client issues a FILL_FETCH timeout of 5s and the relay times out after 1s instead, with no notification?  I can't see one.

Let's walk through the options:

Current draft:

```
C->S:  FETCH FILL_TIMEOUT=5s
S->C:  FETCH_OK, data, data, TIMEOUT (after 1s), data.
```

> relay rejecting the request because the fill time is too long


```
C->S:  FETCH FILL_TIMEOUT=5s
S->C: REQUEST_ERROR FILL_TIMEOUT_TOO_LONG, MAX_FILL_TIMEOUT=1s
C->S: FETCH FILL_TIMEOUT=1s
S->C:  FETCH_OK, data, data, TIMEOUT (after 1s), data.
```

This is the **same outcome** as the current draft, with additional complexity, **1 RTT later**.

>  add a setup parameter that indicates the relay's max

S->C: SETUP MAX_FILL_TIMEOUT 1s
C->S: FETCH FILL_TIMEOUT 1s
S->C:  FETCH_OK, data, data, TIMEOUT (after 1s), data.

This is the **same outcome** as above, with additional complexity.

It also seems inconsistent because every publisher has 12 _other_ internal timeouts (see IETF 126 slides) it didn't broadcast to the subscriber.

I see only complexity downsides and no problems being solved here.
