comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
> This explicit flag in SETUP is a lot better than crashing if an unsupported message is sent by the peer.

Having a flag in SETUP doesn't stop from someone sending unsupported messages. A faulty implementation or intentionally malicious endpoint can send unsupported messages. A receiver should be prepared to handle unsupported messages regardless.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> > This explicit flag in SETUP is a lot better than crashing if an unsupported message is sent by the peer.
> 
> Having a flag in SETUP doesn't stop from someone sending unsupported messages. A faulty implementation or intentionally malicious endpoint can send unsupported messages. A receiver should be prepared to handle unsupported messages regardless.

Right, an implementation is still going to crash if it receives an unsupported message, but there's a difference between signaling that upfront and yolo.

A one-sided implementation will look something like this:
```
receive(message) {
  switch (message.type) {
  case SUBSCRIBE:
    // ...
  case UNSUBSCRIBE:
    // ..
  default:
    throw PROTOCOL_ERROR
  }
}
```

The purpose of the ROLE parameter is to avoid accidentally triggering that default, as it will close the connection.

For example, I absolutely want to have a way to get per-viewer feedback: a `feedback` track produced by each viewer. Without this ROLE field, a viewer might cause a crash if it sends an `ANNOUNCE feedback` to the server, or the server might cause a crash if it sends a `SUBSCRIBE feedback` to the viewer. It will only work if both endpoints explicitly flag `ROLE=both`. 

The only alternative to the ROLE field is to implement the entire protocol, but that's unnecessarily restrictive. Take HTTP for example, it's almost taken for granted that an implementation is for a client or a server, but rarely both. I imagine that will also be the case with MoQ with the sole exception of relays. OBS is not going to implement subscribing, and VLC is not going to implement publishing.

Even in my MoQ.js library that does support both modes, I ran into a deadlock because of ROLE=both. My publisher was not consuming ANNOUNCE messages because it was not expecting them. Explicitly signaling ROLE=publisher would have prevented this, making it a protocol violation to send half of the messages in the draft.

> **Every client has to be built to be resilient to arbitrary incoming messages**. It can't break because the other side said their role was subscriber but then they send you an ANNOUCE.

pulls.title: Delivery Preference for VOD and reliable live (and absolute start/end offsets)
pulls.author: kixelated
pulls.body:
The default behavior for live streams will be `prefer-skip` as encoded in the priority field. This doesn't work for VOD and reliable live, as they want to receive objects in creation order instead.

This is a counter-proposal to the FETCH keyword which attempts to accomplish something similar, but in a way that won't work for reliable live.

This PR also removes relative start/end offsets because SUBSCRIBE was getting too complex. An application that wants to start N groups back needs to use use #425 or a timeline to learn about the absolute group/object IDs.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
After reviewing fully, yeah I don't think we can decouple drops from resets.

When any publisher (including a relay) decides to drop an object, it will also reset the associated QUIC stream. Otherwise, the publisher has to delay writing the object to streams (like TCP low watermark) so it retains the ability to drop it.

And the problem with TCP low watermark in MoQ is of course... _priorities_. Newer content is usually more important, so even if we already have N bytes queued in the QUIC layer, our new content needs to skip the queue. The only way to do that is to actually write to the QUIC stream marked at a higher priority... or reset streams currently queued. The PR doesn't allow either of these as I understand.

This is intended to be complementary to #429 by adding a SUBSCRIBE specific mechanism to indicate hop-by-hop Objects that will not be delivered.  Because this is specific to a SUBSCRIBE, it's not intended to be cacheable.

> 
> That way OBJECTS_DROPPED would only block SUBSCRIBE_END, which almost sounds like a feature?

I can easily imagine something like that but I think we need to deal with the following requirements one way or another:

1. If we have three subscribes for three tracks A, B, C and A is always more important than B , which is more important than C.  You don't want the OBJ_DROP messages for B to have stop all the data on A track from flowing. (and I will hand wave the what is newer / older / priority etc but you can see how as we dig into that, we will still need to solve some version of this ) 

2. If a publisher is sending a ton of OBJ_DROP to a subscriber on a badly congested link,  it  must not result in a situation where the subscriber can not tell the publisher to end the subscription. Even when the bandwidth each direction is highly asymmetrical.

I don't think this works when multiple groups are specified.

Could we specify a specific `group_id` instead of a range? It's fine sending multiple messages.

Do we want to allow gaps? I don't really want to support dropping the middle of a group, especially when using a stream per track/group.

I think we should only allow dropping the tail of a group. You can still prioritize objects separately, but eh it's just a pain to support dropping them out of order. Is there a use-case?

If so, then we can remove this `Last Object` and `Fin` since it's implied.
A flag indicating as such would be good to prevent spurious retries. 404 versus 409.
If they're permanently unavailable, that should be cacheable and Cullen's PR can handle that.
If one prioritizes sending certain Objects over others, at some point, you can imagine dropping them, in which case we'd want a mechanism to indicate that.
I can go either way on this.

That's true. It's fine.

I really don't like the temporal scalability use-case because it creates these jagged edges. At some point I think we should explicitly rule it out and require that SVC layers are separate tracks, not interleaved objects within a group that can be prioritized/dropped separately.
I don't understand the relation to Cullen's PR then. I thought this PR effectively replaced status codes 0x0 - 0x3?

No, the intent is only to replace the case when it's not deliverable due to congestion/etc, which I believe we cannot/should not cache.  If the Objects are immutable/cacheable, then they'd be delivered on unidirectional streams, even if they're missing/length 0.

I think that's almost the case, but not quite.

A broadcaster will produce an OBJECT size=1234 and keep it in an internal cache for 5s. A subscriber might need it immediately so we sent it. But if a fetch comes in later, after the 5s expiration, then it sounds like you want the broadcaster to send OBJECT size=0 instead (or with an equivalent status code)? Otherwise there's no way of indicating that an object is permanently gone.

That kind of breaks the immutable property, and it gives a mixed signal because the object used to exist but no longer. IMO the broadcaster should send OBJECTS_DROPPED instead, just with a flag saying please don't try again; trust me.

If an object goes from available to permanently gone, then that new status is cacheable.  The object didn't change, it's availability did.

From a functional perspective, we could definitely add a flag indicating the Objects were permanently dropped, but I think that mixes up the Track specific information with the Subscription specific information.

OBJECTS_DROPPED is intended to be specific to a subscription, and Objects sent on unidirectional streams are part of the track.

I have one sort of meta issue about this and proposal to fix. 

Imagine a case that is audio only where each audio packet is on a new group and where the relay is dropping a large percentage of theses. The objects dropped message are pretty large and comparable in size to the actual audio packets that are getting dropped. 

I'm worried about the priorities - and yes, I know I am the person always saying lets leave the priorities to the next interim meeting.  I am assuming we will set the control channels at the highest priority because it is bad to loose the control messages that allow you shut off the flood of data from other things. ( I've seen phones where video is higher priority than control messages and you get on a congested link and you can not hang up - really funny ). My worry here is that in audio case above will cause the control link to become swamped with these messages. 

So few ideas on how to fix this... 

1. in this PR, make it so these happen on some to be determined in the future stream that is lower priority than control stream and we can sort out what stream that is and what priorities as part of the upcoming priority discussion 

2. Make it so "objects dropped" message could only be sent at a max rate over every 100 ms per stream and instead of trying to describe all the gaps, just indicated that on or more object were dropped between the start group/object and end group/object range. 

I'm trying to think about how this will be used and it seems like in most cases, it will be used to know to move on an where the good data that was not dropped is the key thing, not the fine grain details of what got dropped. 

All the details of the proposal other than this seem reasonable and a fine starting point.

I think this highlights something that may require additional discussion; I get the sense different wg members have different assumptions about how streams move through relays.

My view is that when a publisher chooses to deliver objects in stream-per-group or stream-per-track modes, it is doing so because it wants the reliability and ordering guarantees QUIC provides to streams.  Therefore, a relay **can't** remove an object from the middle of such a stream, since this changes the reliability properties my app depends on.  The current draft has language reflecting this:

> A relay MUST not reorder or drop objects received on a multi-object stream when forwarding to subscribers, unless it has application specific information.

With this in mind, I'm inclined to agree with the stream-per-group restrictions in this PR - if a relay is delivering a group on a stream, and encounters an object that has exceeded the delivery timeout and won't deliver it, the only option is to close the stream and move on.  I'm also in favor of some kind of restriction on dropping objects using stream-per-track (either disallowing it entirely, or closing the stream).

If reordering or dropping objects at relays is important to application behavior, I would think the publisher would choose datagram or stream-per-object forwarding preferences.

**Is there a use case for using stream-per-group/track, but allowing the relay to drop or reorder objects?**

If so, how is it better than using a stream-per-object or datagram mapping?

To me, this is the key question, not just in this context, but re: caching expectations as a whole. 

What behavior do we expect when a relay is serving active subscribers at the live edge, but a new subscribe comes in so far behind the live edge that all of the delivery timeouts have expired and none of the objects are in cache any longer? In order to implement per-session ad insertion, we may want to give certain edge-servers the ability to read and modify catalogs in a edge-compute type of implementation. In this case it might better to say

> The payload portion may be encrypted, in which case it is only visible to the Original Publisher, End Subscribers and application-authorized relays.

Some edge relays may be authorized to modify content. Therefore we should relax this constraint to

> A relay MUST NOT combine, split, or otherwise modify object payloads unless authorized to by an application.

While I agree that manipulating catalogs with edge compute is a valid use case, I don't think we should blur the lines of what a relay is here, but instead consider that node something different. One way of framing it would be to consider it both an end subscriber for the original catalog track and an original publisher for the modified catalog.
As above, I'd rather we keep this strict and consider any modifying entity to be something other than a relay. We need a very minimal baseline for what's necessary to provide simple fan out capacity.

Follow up based on in-person discussion just now: my concerns here are primarily about whether other entities in a system can rely on immutability of objects within tracks of the same name regardless of where they received them from, or if that immutability guarantee is more limited. 

If we allow application-authorized modification to occur, I think it would be helpful to have a name for such authorized entities that is clearly distinct from simple fan out relays to make it more explicit when they are in play and when applications and systems designers may need to account for additional variability.

comments.body:
> We agreed on highest at this point, the latest is for other part.

This was part of the discussion from Wednesday's call.  The consensus was that using highest priority value in the track to select a track does not work well.  If you use highest, then priority can only be increased and not decreased.  

Example, assume two tracks, stream-per-group and each has 2 groups to send from:
Track A: group1, pri=1; group2, pri=2
Track B: group1, pri=2; group2, pri=1

Using max, the algorithm would treat these tracks with *equal* priority, and move to another tiebreaker.

The room felt (I think unanimously) that the most recent value should set the track priority, so in the above example, Track B would be higher than Track A.  Which group from Track B is determined by the group-send-order.

Reflecting more, I think logically what bits we want to send in the above example depends on the group order.  If using ascending groups, a track's priority is the priority of it's lowest group to send and if descending, a track's priority is the priority of it's highest group to send.  Now, if Track A and Track B are both ascending, A > B.  If they are both descending, B > A.  If they mismatch, it is a tie.

When using stream/datagram-per-object, the priority of a group is the highest priority among queued object for that group.

That feels right to me but the implementation might be complex to implement.

> This seems like a really complicated way to limit the subscribes. I understand how it mirror streams but that had pretty different constrains. Why don't we just have an subscribe error of "too many subscriptions"?

Unfortunately, that makes it much more difficult for the server to tell abusive clients from valid ones, as we discovered with the recent HTTP/2 rapid reset attacks.  In the end we did develop heuristics, but they're imperfect and in the process we broke a bunch of applications in an effort to defend against DDoS attacks.  In contrast, QUIC had a system like this and experienced no issues and we didn't need to develop any new heuristics.

The language is confusing because Peeps don't have priority, Objects do.  All objects in the same peep have the same priority, so you can call that the priority of the Peep, but the wording isn't totally clear.

Mandating increasing object ID within a peep is a good thing, but using object ID as the tie-breaker between peeps with equivalent object priority is not good.

Consider this case, where all objects have priority 128:

Peep/Stream 1:

Object 1, Object 3

Peep/Stream 2:

Object 2, Object 4

Let' assume all data has been written to the QUIC stack.  At the point when all the bytes of Object 1 are sent, the priority of Peep/Stream 2 needs to change to be higher than Peep/Stream 1.  This is way more complex than most implementers what to deal with.

So we can:

1. Make Peep ID the tie-breaker - with the same priority, lower peep ID goes first
2. Collapse Peep ID and Priority:

  2b. Use 8 bits - restricts maximum peeps per group, which probably breaks some object-per-stream cases

So a MOQ Application interfaces with moq object model and assigns priorities to the objects. The moq stack has a new object to send ( output of the priority decision algorithm), it looks at the object priority and does one of the following to match moq object priority to QUIC Stream.  
   - create a new stream , set the priority of the stream to match the priority of the object or
   - If there is already a stream created (as per first step) , pick that stream and send the object over that stream.
   
When relays receive the objects, the canonical object has priority saved as well. So relay for downstream can apply the similar logic.

pulls.title: Remove normative restriction on relays forwarding decision input
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
I removed this sentence:

Relays MUST NOT depend on OBJECT payload content for making forwarding decisions and MUST only depend on the fields, such as priority order and other metadata properties in the OBJECT message header.

We already have text explaining that the object payload content can be encrypted (section 2.1).  I think that makes it clear that a relay can't do anything with the object payload unless it has the encryption keys or a priori knowledge they are cleartext.

The sentence itself was overly restrictive (relays could use other inputs, for example out of band information from configuration or business relationships).  The preceding sentence explains how to find subscribers to this track, the subsequent one says "MUST forward", and we have an entire section explaining what to do with priority order now.

Fixes: #217

pulls.author: wilaw
pulls.body:
This PR adds an extensible header to Objects, as well as updating the SETUP parameters to allow negotiation of required extension header parameters. Extensible headers have types which are IANA registered. A new Extensible header is defined and reserved with type 0x0, allowing name/value data to be passed in a manner compatible with HTTP headers. The wider problem I see with this design is that extension negotiation is hop-by-hop (HTTP has similar problems with SETTINGS).  What happens when, say, the publisher and relay negotiate use of an extension, but one of the subscribers to the relay does not?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> The wider problem I see with this design is that extension negotiation is hop-by-hop 

Fair comment. We have the same problem with our MOQT version. It is negotiated hop-by-hop and there is nothing currently to enforce a MOQT version (or a extension support) across a delivery chain. 

One solution on the extension side would be that Object Extensions, from a relay perspective, are always optional within a given moqt version. If we require an new Object header in a future version, then whichever spec defines that new version would also define the new object header as a first-class header and not an extension.  We could  remove the SETUP component. Any node (relay, or end subscriber) could test for the presence of the Extension , in much the same way that a HTTP server tests for the presence of a request header.

comments.author: tianji-sdo
comments.body:
**A 5G use case to justify the support of the PR (Problem description & Requirements on MoQT per-object metadata header extension)**:
========
As we have presented in the IETF-121 MoQ session @ Dublin, the 3GPP 5G has standardized the solution of applying the MoQT to address the transmission of encrypted XRM media streams between MoQ server(s) and client(s) via MoQ relay. A MoQ relay is deployed in the 5G UPF. The corresponding 3GPP 5G specifications are TS 23.501 and TS 26.522. In the MoQT-based solution, there is per-object (or so-named per-PDU in 5G term) related metadata that is used to identify the PDU-set (i.e., a set of PDUs) related metadata information to 5G system. These PDU-set meta-info is identified and marked at a 5G UPF (i.e., where a MoQ replay runs) for RAN-based resource scheduling and optimization. Our IETF draft (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-defoy-moq-relay-network-handling/)  has clearly explained the mechanism.  

Because an XRM media stream is encrypted (and so is the RTP header extension associated with an XRM PDU), the PDU-set metadata has to be mapped to the MoQT metadata field in an object header. The MoQ-based solution (as in 3GPP TS 23.501) is repurposing those object header fields, which leads to two problems: mapping accuracy and future extensibility.
 
Based on the discussions & rough consensus from the IETF-121 MoQ session, we think that the logics as specified in PR#502 , targeting at providing the OBJECT Extension Header, can address exactly the XRM ciphered stream challenges with a new revision of the MoQT draft. 

Those logics include REQUESTED-EXTENSION parameter, Object Extensions, as well as {{IANA}} part, and possibly more, in the current PR.

comments.author: xdfy
comments.body:
I'd like to give more details on the use case described in https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/502#issuecomment-2471516973. 
 
There are basically 2 phases: (1) client and server negotiate the use of the extension and (2) the media sender includes XR metadata in the object headers.
 
For (2), the existing PR text is sufficient for our needs: we can register a MOQ extension header type "A" with IANA (just not sure if we should use the 0-127 space or the 128-16383 space).
 
For (1), our understanding is that the same MOQ extension header type "A" is used to set a varint value in the REQUESTED-EXTENSION parameter in the SETUP messages. 
 
Additionally, for (1), the 5G XR use case introduces a potentially new interesting aspect: this extension does not relate to a monolithic set of metadata fields. It can include multiple sets of metadata, e.g.:
 
•	So-called "Release-18 (R18) metadata", which is a fixed set of metadata defined in by 3GPP.
•	"R19 metadata", which is a second fixed set of metadata defined by 3GPP
•	Potentially, both sets may be communicated together, or in some cases only one set may be communicated.
 
Additionally, some metadata fields of the R18 metadata set are optional.
 
To address this need, our IETF draft ( https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-defoy-moq-relay-network-handling/) has defined bitfields (2 varints) that are included in a new TLV parameter in the SETUP messages. Client and server use these varints to negotiate their supported/requested 5G XR metadata set.
 
This requires registering a new TLV type for use in the SETUP messages. This may be okay if our case of "negotiable extension format" is rare. 
 
For the sake of discussing the MOQ extension mechanism design, here are multiple options for handling this situation, that we can think of (as a starting point -- we don't have a strong preference)
 
Option A (used in our draft so far) : when adding an extension with a negotiable format, a new TLV type is registered, for use in the SETUP message. The value of the new TLV contains bitfields or any other parameter useful to negotiate the actual content of the per-object metadata of the extension.
 
Option B (not used in our draft so far) : MOQT defines a new "extension description" TLV that is used in SETUP messages. Its value starts with a varint, which holds the MOQ extension type. The remainder of the TLV value (beyond the initial varint) depends on the extension. Multiple such TLVs can be present in a SETUP message. Such a method would avoid having to register a new TLV by each extension with a negotiable format.
 
To conclude, option A works and does not require a change in the PR. Option B may make it easier for some future extensions but it would require a small change in the PR.

### Relay Extension Processing Rules

@Suhas - I agree on point 1 (processing rules are defined by whatever spec defines the extension). 

> but relay doesn't support such an extension, it is treated as protocol violation.

A protocol violation can only be triggered by behaviors defined by the MOQT spec. It cannot be a protocol violation to not support some future optional extension. It may be a protocol violation of the 3rd party spec that defines the extension, but that spec will need to deal with that outcome as these are, after all, optional extensions as far as MOQT is concerned. 

> Now on the point on how to know if a relay understands an extension or not ,

We have the setup negotiation already in place. This informs the client whether the server "supports" a given extension. By 'support' we mean that it understands any processing rules that are defined by the 3rd party spec. minor: s/part of the Object/part of the Object payload/

I can live with SHOULD here; perhaps RECOMMENDED is also ok?  My reasoning is that if the transport will never look at the extension, it shouldn't waste any time parsing out the fields.  However, as Suhas pointed out, it's unenforceable, and a relay cannot distinguish between an unsupported extension and payload.

@wilaw - I think that MoQ should be changed to work the way you think it works (see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/549)  but it does not

Right now the encoding is defined in section 16 of RFC 9000
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000#section-16

And for 1 byte, you only get 6 bits of data not 7.

The problem with serializing in the object is that the object will be end to end encrypted in many cases and thus the rely can not read it. Take the example of capture timestamp for media. Relay can look at this timestamp to figure out how much lag. Then  metrics dashboard can take differences of lag to figure out the latency between two relays. This type of operational information is supper useful on running real systems. SRTP which we are trying to replace with MoQ is explicitly designed to keep that type of timing information in the readable hops along the media path. I feel very strongly we need the same sort of thing here. 

We could introduce two types of option , relay options, and client options so that the relay did not need to parse the client options. Or another design could be to introduce object headers that were not end to end encrypted.  But all of these options end up using another byte even if there are no headers and that is a big impact for audio only applications. 

I don't buy the parsing time problem. Anything reasonable relay is going to be able to parse to the level to check if it is interested in any of the extensions on single core at a rate that greatly exceeds whatever networking technology it uses and probably exceeds the bandwidth to non cached memory so you can probably parse this as fast as you can memcpy it. Either way, I just don't see any performance problem. 

I could live with this saying 

"Any metadata which will not be read or logged by any relay ever including use for operational or diagnostic reasons, 
 SHOULD NOT be sent in an extension header."

pulls.title: Simplify SUBSCRIBE as a follow-up to FETCH
pulls.author: ianswett
pulls.body:
This is another effort at the SUBSCRIBE vs FETCH concept.

I've reduced the number of modes for SUBSCRIBE to 3, and only one of them subscribes to Objects in the future.

I removed Latest Group because the other two modes operate on the latest Object and I wasn't sure how practical it is to expect every relay to cache all of the latest group.  And if they don't, implementations get complex.

This is an opinionated approach, but it has quite a bit of flexibility now that the new priority design has landed.  In particular, it gives the subscriber lots of control over what order Objects on either side of the live head are delivered.


Fixes #368 
Could be extended to fix #350

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
This PR does not simplify subscription for non-real-time live stream clients (i.e live sports). These players need a variable buffer before start-up. To achieve this, they need to request several groups behind latest and then all future groups. The suggestion in the PR is for these clients to "it can send a SUBSCRIBE for the Latest Object followed by a SUBSCRIBE of type AbsoluteStart or AbsoluteRange.". The trouble with this is that it complicates the player's handling of the received data. It must first make a request for Latest Object. This will give it the latest and future objects and data will begin to flow immediately after it makes this request. However the player cannot place this data in a decode buffer. It must store it in a temporary buffer and hold it. Based the info it receives in the SUBSCRIBE_OK, it can then make a second request for the absolute range preceding this latest object. That data it can place it its decode buffer and begin decoding and it must then continuously copy data from the first receive buffer in to the decode buffer. This is unnecessarily messy, especially as the recommended workflow. 

A cleaner and simpler approach would be for the player to be able to make a single SUBSCRIBE request and be able to pipe that response directly in to its decode buffer. This can be achieve by either modifying the proposed AbsoluteStart filter so that it doesn't stop at the Latest Object, or adding a new filter type which is "AbsoluteStart and carry on" (bikeshead away). So the player wanting to start behind live would first make a TRACK_STATUS_REQUEST, which would give it the latest Group and Object. With this information it could calculate where it wanted to start behind live and then make a SUBSCRIBE request with the "AbsoluteStart and carry on" filter. It could pipe the response of this request directly in to its decode buffer and begin playback.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
Agree with @kixelated 

My proposal would be:
 
1. Keep LatestGroup and LatestObject in subscribe with the restriction that only one of each can be issued. Remove other filter types.
2. Remove AbsoluteStart altogether.
3. Define new Fetch API with just the AbsoluteRange. 

Applications using Fetch and unaware of the group information can use TrackStatusRequest to find the range of groups to request for. They can optionally specify a control parameter for flow rate vs the network rate for delivery. Fetch api also will attempt fill holes by requesting upstream as needed, Also specifying group delivery order might still be useful.

This will allow players to use appropriate buffer for starting from history and at the right time ( when they know they have right amount of data in buffer to move onto live data, for example) shall issue Subscribe to continue from the live edge.

pulls.title: Remove track per stream
pulls.author: ianswett
pulls.body:
As discussed at the Wednesday virtual interim.

Fixes #480
May fix #490
May fix #476

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
IMO multiple peeps per stream is even worse than a stream per track. You inherit all of the problems (priorities, head-of-line blocking, inability to reset) but now it's implicit rather than explicit.

Even worse, the text doesn't require that peeps share the same track/subscription.

I don't think MAX_STREAMS is an issue worth degrading the protocol. Make implementations raise the limit rather than impose unnecessary HoLB.

So IMO just delete a track per stream and offer no replacement. Make a stream for each group, and if you're blocked by MAX_STREAMS before MAX_DATA then the limit needs to be raised.

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body:
I think we just landed a PR saying a PEEP == Stream. I am bit confused on the wording of multiple peeps per stream. 

I am not saying we definitely need Stream per Track or not. However I tend to disagree that it makes implementation complicated.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
> IMO multiple peeps per stream is even worse than a stream per track. You inherit all of the problems (priorities, head-of-line blocking, inability to reset) but now it's implicit rather than explicit.

The intent is that you'd only use this when it's beneficial.

> 
> Even worse, the text doesn't require that peeps share the same track/subscription.

I clarified that, but the intent was always that they're Peeps from the same subscription.
> 
> I don't think MAX_STREAMS is an issue worth degrading the protocol. Make implementations raise the limit rather than impose unnecessary HoLB.

I'm a lot less concerned about MAX_STREAMS and more concerned about memory usage and buffering when a subscriber requests a large amount of Data/Objects from the past (aka Fetch) and there is a real need for backpressure/flow control of some sort.  Inventing a new mechanism in MoQ to do that is complex, but caching HTTP proxies deal with this today quite well for large requests. 

> 
> So IMO just delete a track per stream and offer no replacement. Make a stream for each group, and if you're blocked by MAX_STREAMS before MAX_DATA then the limit needs to be raised.

I'm fine with just deleting track per stream as well, and we can limit this PR to only that if people prefer.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
I'm not sure falling back from multi-stream to single-stream is a good idea: there is no good reason for the server to have large per-stream buffers but small total limit on streams, so I think the preferred approach here would be to buffer outgoing peeps until the credits appears.

Otherwise this looks good, though you might need to remove Track as a forwarding preference from other places in the spec.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body: Another problem is that if we ever assign semantics to closing a peep via a FIN, or require resetting a stream upon certain events (e.g. timeouts), "multiple peeps in a single stream" completely breaks that.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
I definitely don't want a relay converting N streams into 1 stream by coalescing peeps, introducing HoLB in the process. The reverse is probably fine but it's still extremely situational; the broadcaster is trying to send more concurrent peeps than the QUIC connection allows?

But in general this just seems extremely fishy. We're worried about too many streams so we invent our own stream within a stream abstraction. Use fewer peeps or raise MAX_STREAMS.

reviews.body: Individual Comment

comments.body:
This implies that publisher priority trumps subscriber group order.  That was not how I read the previous algorithm.  Higher publisher priority would *select a subscription* to send from, then you go through to group order.  This is how we got min.

I like the property that says group order is ascending or descending *only*, and priority doesn't influence group order.  Trying to use the object priority as both intra and inter track is weird.

reviews.author: ianswett
reviews.body: Some nits, but I think this is very close.

comments.body:
```suggestion
A _priority_ is an unsigned integer with a value between 0 and 255.
```

nit: Can we just call it priority?

```suggestion
Since a single peep or datagram has a single publisher priority, it can be
useful to conceptualize this process as scheduling peeps or datagrams
instead of individual objects on them.
```

> Trying to use the object priority as both intra and inter track is weird.

I agree that it might feel a little bit weird, but if priority is applied before group order, this makes sense, since this should be more expressive than just having two of those.

As to publisher priority vs group order, I feel like for the use cases that I can think of, the group order should always apply _after_ the publisher priority.  E.g. for the active vs non-active speaker case, you'd always want to prioritize the more-useful audio over less-useful regardless of stream position; or for SVC, you'd probably rather have all of the base layer frames than have the newest group in the best quality and a missing group right before it.

(Of course, even if that is not true, you can choose the opposite behavior by setting publisher priority as the same for all track, and then using peep IDs to prioritize those within the group.)

The problem that I see if that the publisher gets the final say on group order here -- if the subscriber asks for one track with pri=0 and order=asc, but the publisher sets the peep priorities for each group in descending order, the data will be delivered dsc.  I'd find it more consistent and easier to think about if we separate publisher track priority from peep/object priority (Martin's Option 3).  Then it's `sub pri -> pub pri -> group order -> peep/obj pri -> peep ID`.

In any case, this PR doesn't feel like a clarification so much as a change to the algorithm.

Adding an explicit track priority is completely reasonable, though it'd be good to understand what cases it was necessary?  For SVC, I'm quite sure you'd want the peep priority to be more important than group order.

We only have 256 priority values, so your example won't last that long for most use cases.  Also, your example is somewhat adversarial, so I'm not sure how realistic it is?
I created https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/519 to discuss the question of whether publishers should specify a priority in addition to the subscriber priority.

reviews.author: fluffy
reviews.body:
This is a huge improvement and I like it. 

I do have one questions about if we need the concept of scheduleable that I would like to get to resolution on.

comments.body: change "to be sent" to "to be sent on from this peep"

I would add here something along lines of "when it is changed, in a relay it is implementation dependent on how it will apply to object that the relay has already received".

Clearly if a something had been pushed into the QUIC stack but not yet pushed to the wire, it would be pretty hard to change. I think it is fine to leave this very implementation dependent because this is something that is happening for a short time on the edge of the change and weather a given object gets the old or new priority during the switch over does not matter much to apps.

Let me ask a questions first.  If every object was a schedulable object, does it change the algorithm in the rest of this in any way ? When I read the rest of this I think the answer is No but I feel like others might feel the answer is yes and that I am missing something that is a key issue for other people. 

The way I would implement this is put all the object on a priority queue where the priority on the q was an integer basically formed by concatenating subscriber priority, publisher priority, and either the group id or reverse group id based on direction, then peep id, then object id.  Then when there is space available send an object, you grab the next object out of queue and and send it.  I want to understand if this is wrong. If it is wrong, I am probably fine with what people want but I think it will help me get to understanding why people keep saying this is complicated. If this is right, then I don't think we need the concept of a schedulable object.
Not a big deal but I would have a preference of limiting peep ID to 8 bits if they are going to be used as one of the priority fields.

I do not see any reason to add peep into this. If the publisher wanted the object in one peep to be delivered ahead of another peep, it should have set the publisher priority. I can probably live with this but I'd like to understand why we need it.

Looking at wills slides from seattle interim it is clear that publisher priority override group id other wise nearly all the uses cases that use publisher priority don't work. I think if we just step back and look at uses cases, we can reason our way though the conversation we have had several times and end up back at the space spot of what Victor has in the PR now 

There are not enough priorities codes for a publisher to even do the example Alan raised at top of this thread. I view that sort of use cases as just a broken application if the publisher and subscriber are trying to do totally conflicting things and does not bother me much that weird things happen in that case.

Individual Comment:

I agree the Seattle proposal was: pick a track by sub priority, then min(pub-priority-of-pending-objects), select a group by group order, order by object ID.

There's a complaint that min priority is too hard to implement.  Sounds like the new proposal is:

Pick a track by sub priority, then pub priority, then group by group order, order by peep/object ID.

Here's what I think is a weird case:

The subscriber asked for ascending groups.
In group 1, all objects have the same pub pri = 100.
In group 2, some objects have pub pri 100 but some are more important and get pub pri 90
  -> The publisher wants to express relative priority of the objects *within the group*

The new algorithm will deliver group 2 pri=90 objects first and that seems wrong.  The Seattle algorithm would send group 1 object in obj ID order, then group 2 pri=90 objects, then group 2 pri=100 objects.  This seemed more correct, if harder to implement.  You can sort of fix this by incrementing the base priority of objects in every group, but you will run out of priority levels after 256 groups.

There seemed to be general consensus that groups would only be delivered ascending or descending and I think we should try to preserve that property -- do people care less about this now?  I'm inclined to think we need to set aside some time to discuss at the hybrid interim next month.

One observation about ascending / descending order is that it seems the use case for it are all times where it is a fetch not a subscribe. It also seems that for flow control reason fetch will likely flow over one stream. I wonder if we could just remove descending order for subscribe.  I've pointed out in the past it is totally useless and in most cases where the things are not congested and the subscribe is on the live edge, the subscribe will get things in the order the publisher published them regardless of how any of the priorities and orders are set. This will mean a subscriber asks for things in reverse order and will then get most things in forward order with perhaps a few object in reverse order then there was a bit of congestion. I don't object to it being here if others want it because it is all trivial to implement but I remain of the opinion order is unless for subscribe and critical for fetch.
@vasilvv - This question here is the only question I have of significance on this PR. Love the PR - thanks.

well ... I suspect this is going to fall in policy for relays region. Lets say you have 10 million viewers of a Taylor Swift livestream that can all publish text comments to various chat tracks. reviews.author: afrind
reviews.body: Individual Comments

comments.body:
I think a SHOULD will probably work?  Keeping state of everything sent to every client is not scalable, but in some common cases it should be pretty easy (eg within a peep, if you see the same object ID or it goes backwards from the most recent, just drop it).  Implementation experience will help us see what's possible.

I'm thinking of a make-befrore-break case, during the point when the publisher has 2 connections to the relay, it would be nice if the relay is deduplicating as much as it can as it forwards.

My concern is that without a normative default for what to do, there's very little interoperability.  The only other normative behavior I can think of is "MUST reject any subscribe with authorization info", but that seems less functional.

I 100% agree that CDNs are going to have policies and such that govern this and we should acknowledge that, but it should also work "out of the box".

We will likely revisit some of this when we tackle auth in more detail too.

I was hoping SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE would solve some of that problem -- all 10M viewers have their own namespace `tswift/chat/unique_id`.  We may need to indicate here what limits are likely to exist, because it influences how higher level protocols will use moqt in terms of namespace and track naming.

Agreed the max will be different, but is there a min that we need to specify to get basic interop, eg: for make-before-break, min=2.

I mean, 2 publishers have announced track T, and published some objects into the cache.  A subscriber issue a subscribe for track T but whatever is specified as the start and/or end is already in cache - there's no need to forward subscribe.  Maybe you can reword this to say - if you would send a subscribe to pub 1, you MUST send it to all N.

Rather than drop the later arriving object, I would rather that it overwrite the item existing in cache (i.e latest wins). This allows updating caches and purging corrupt content by overwriting. If we go with the proposal that the original write always wins, then we have no method for publishers to flush content from upstream caches other than waiting for its cache duration to expire.

> In the absence of such mechanisms, relays MUST forward SUBSCRIBE requests containing non-empty Auth Info parameters to the original publisher.


How is that expected to work if a thousand clients make the same subscription with different auth info to an edge? Normally we would want the edge to coalesce these requests and make a single upstream subscription. But it would now have to make 1000 upstream subscriptions? I don't think that is practical. I think Cullen's proposed text is fine.

> How is that expected to work if a thousand clients make the same subscription with different auth info to an edge?
 
 I see three possibilities:
 
 1.  pre-negotiated scheme for relay to perform auth
 2. forward the auth credentials to OP for validation 
 3. subscribe error (no way to auth)
 
If we dig into 2, right now, only SUBSCRIBE carries the auth field, so you'd end up blowing up your coalescing, unless you UNSUBSCRIBE duplicates immediately I guess. pulls.title: Reduce use of x(b) notation
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
This is a proposal to illustrate the changes needed to address one aspect of https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/536 .

In creating this, I realised that the [recent change](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/commit/b5ad15c1f4320271cd515b20e55275efe573256a) to add a length to control messages used the `x(b)` notation. This makes it awkward to then fully expand the full message structure as is done in RFC 9000 and RFC 9114 (and proposed for the `Type` field here on https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/541). Its also arguable if the "followed by that many bytes  of binary data" description for the `x (b)` notation is really supposed to apply to fields that are also formally defined but I think that debate is a distraction.

This PR reduces usage of `x (b)` by adding an explicit length field before the respective value. This reveals that some control message types have a redundant length field, which is rather pointless in some cases. For example, with this change we have

```
GOAWAY Message {
  Length (i),
  New Session URI Length (i),
  New Session URI (..),
}
```

this could be simplified to just 

```
GOAWAY Message {
  Length (i),
  New Session URI (..),
}
```

However, I avoided doing that in this PR because it is a breaking wire format change. 

I'd suggest we do the editorial changes in this PR first, and then survey the control types for opportunities to remove redundant lengths. We could even go so far as rearranging the order of fields so that the variable length ones go at the end, for example HTTP/3 does this with [HEADERS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#name-headers) and [PUSH_PROMISE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#section-7.2.5)

The last remaining usage of `x (b)` after this change relates to `x (tuple)`. I left that one since I didn't want to conflate things.

To detect a gap, the previous group id can be added by the original publisher to each group header. So,  incrementing group ids or incrementing by one is not necessary.

For instance we have group ids: 1, 3, 5. Using the previous group ids, the relay can understand that there is not gap when it receives  the groups in an arbitrary order such as 5, 3, 1. It can re-order them using the previous group ids as follows:

`1 <- 3 <- 5`

Even if the relay does not have 2 and 4 in the cache (which actually do not exist), the relay can understand there is no gap in the sequence above by looking at every previous group ids.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Individual Comment:

I don't like using FIN-ACK:

1. It moves the waiting period from the subscriber to the publisher.  The high-scale/long wait cases are likely when relays publish fan-out to client subscribers, and the relay is the one with reason to free up resources faster.  The publisher otherwise has no reason to keep this state around but the subscriber might.
2. Receiving a FIN-ACK does not mean the MoQ layer has received the stream, only the QUIC stack, which could be in the peer's kernel (or someday, NIC).  The SUBSCRIBE_DONE could still be racing delivery of the QUIC data and result in missed objects.  HTTP/3 explicitly chose *not* to use QUIC signals in QPACK for these reasons.
3. The subscriber doesn't have to wait around after SUBSCRIBE_DONE if it is uninterested in remaining data, but by withholding the signal, it doesn't get a choice.

I still prefer using RESET_STREAM_AT -- the downside from my perspective is pushing WebTransport to include this surface, which I think they should anyway, and perhaps that raw QUIC implementations MUST negotiate this extension.  Timers are inelegant and a waste when everything was already received.

comments.body:
@suhasHere The current DATAGRAM message has a status field that is present when length is 0.  Since this PR removes the length field, the only thing I could see was either 1) include the status in every datagram, wasting space in the common case, or 2) define a special datagram message that carries only the status.

Do you have an alternative encoding to what is here that is unambiguous and compact?

Here's an alternate with a "single" message (single in scare quotes because there are technically 5 code points):

~~~
OBJECT_DATAGRAM Message {
  TypeAndStatus(i) 0x00..0x04
  Track Alias (i),
  Group ID (i),
  Object ID (i),
  Publisher Priority (8),
  [Payload(..)]
}
~~~

The first varint in the datagram is TypeAndStatus.  Values 0-4 convey an Object.  If TypeAndStatus is 0, the Status is Normal and a Payload exists to the remainder of the datagram.  It is an error if the payload is empty.  TypeAndStatus 1-4 indicate the given object status and have no payload.  It is an error if the datagram has bytes beyond Publisher Priority.  TypeAndStatus > 4 are undefined.

pulls.title: Joining Fetch
pulls.author: englishm
pulls.body:
This PR adds the desired "Join" functionality as [discussed](https://meetecho-player.ietf.org/playout/?session=IETF121-MOQ-20241104-1730) [at IETF 121 in Dublin](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/121/session/moq)[^1]

Adding this functionality to Fetch unblocks further simplifications of Subscribe, allowing us to more clearly delineate between "past" (Fetch) and "future" (Subscribe). (see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/598, https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/510#pullrequestreview-2260597641, etc.)

There are several ways we could allow a publisher to "atomically" join a Fetch and a Subscribe.
At IETF 121, @wilaw presented [slides](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/121/materials/slides-121-moq-join-api-proposal-00) showing API options:
1. a new macro-like singular JOIN message that is decomposed at the publisher into both a SUBSCRIBE and a FETCH
2. a modified form of FETCH that can be joined together with an existing Subscribe 

The consensus of the discussion seemed to heavily favor the latter design, so, as was requested, this PR is written as a modified form of Fetch: **Joining Fetch**.

This PR:
- Adds "**Fetch Type**" field to Fetch messages
- Redefines pre-existing behavior as a Fetch Type: "**Standalone Fetch**"
- Defines new Fetch Type: "**Joining Fetch**"
- Defines new error code: "**Invalid Subscribe ID**"

[^1]: [21:18 ](https://youtu.be/zs5Y424tASE?feature=shared&t=1278) in the recording. Note: the [Meetecho page](https://meetecho-player.ietf.org/playout/?session=IETF121-MOQ-20241104-1730) includes the chat, synced to the video.

The intent is to define the fields of the Fetch range to be prior to and contiguous, but non-overlapping with the _resolved_ starting point of the corresponding Subscribe.

Here's the relevant text from the editor's draft's section on Fetch:

> Fetch specifies an inclusive range of Objects starting at StartObject
> in StartGroup and ending at EndObject in EndGroup. EndGroup and EndObject MUST
> specify the same or a later object than StartGroup and StartObject.

> If StartGroup/StartObject is greater than the latest published Object group, the publisher MUST return FETCH_ERROR with error code 'No Objects'.

and Subscribe (as it currently stands):

> Latest Group (0x1) : Specifies an open-ended subscription with objects from the beginning of the current group. If no content has been delivered yet, the subscription starts with the first published or received group.

> Latest Object (0x2): Specifies an open-ended subscription beginning from the current object of the current group. If no content has been delivered yet, the subscription starts with the first published or received group.

> AbsoluteStart (0x3): Specifies an open-ended subscription beginning from the object identified in the StartGroup and StartObject fields. If the StartGroup is prior to the current group, the publisher MUST reply with a SUBSCRIBE_ERROR with code 'Invalid Range'.

> AbsoluteRange (0x4): Specifies a closed subscription starting at StartObject in StartGroup and ending at EndObject in EndGroup. The start and end of the range are inclusive. EndGroup MUST specify the same or a later group than StartGroup. If the StartGroup is prior to the current group, the publisher MUST reply with a SUBSCRIBE_ERROR with code 'Invalid Range'.

and Subscribe OK:

> Largest Group ID: The largest Group ID available for this track. This field is only present if ContentExists has a value of 1.

> Largest Object ID: The largest Object ID available within the largest Group ID for this track. This field is only present if ContentExists has a value of 1.

So, at present it's not permitted to send a Subscribe (AbsoluteStart or AbsoluteRange) with a Group ID < Largest Group ID, even though you can't definitively know what that is ahead of time.

That said, I think we do still need to clarify this a bit further...

If we consider the case of Latest Group, then our "resolved StartGroup" for the Subscribe will == Largest Group ID and our "resolved StartObject" will == 0.

If we consider the case of Latest Object, then our "resolved StartGroup" will == Largest Group ID and our "resolved StartObject" will == Largest Object ID? Maybe? Let's assume for now the latter is true because we want to move in the direction of treating Subscribe more like an entry in a forwarding table and handle already "known" / "cached" objects with Fetch.

Examples:

Groups of 30 objects (0 through 29)
Contiguous, monotonically incrementing Group IDs
Largest Group ID = 20
Largest Object ID = 5

Subscribe(LatestObject) gets 20-6, 20-7, 20-8, ...
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=1) gets 19-0, 19-1, 19-2, ..., 19-29, 20-0, 20-1, ... 20-5
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=0) gets 20-0, 20-1, 20-2, ..., 20-5

And since we still have LatestGroup, let's look at that, too:
Subscribe(LatestGroup) gets: 20-0, 20-1, 20-2, ...
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=1) gets: 19-0, 19-1, 19-2, ... 19-29
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=0) gets: nothing, but not an error?

You wouldn't want to send PGC=0 with a LatestGroup Subscribe, but we'd have a similar case whenever Largest Object ID happens to fall on a group boundary so we should handle it gracefully.

I'll make a pass a rewriting this to match these examples and use "Largest Group ID" / "Largest Object ID" as our  points of reference since we have those defined for Subscribe OK already.

I think the Largest Group ID, Largest Object ID values in the Subscribe OK should be sufficient to resolve the ranges for the Joining Fetch from downstream into a Standalone Fetch to upstream as needed (depending on what the relay may have in cache). Am I missing a case we need to handle where even with a Subscribe OK we still lack sufficient information about the objects we might receive in response to a Subscribe?

As I'm revising these definitions, I've realized that there's an annoying boundary case we need to handle. 

Thinking aloud about how best to handle it...

Example:

Groups of 30 objects (0 through 29)
Contiguous, monotonically incrementing Group IDs
Largest Group ID = 20
Largest Object ID = 29

Assuming a Subscribe with Filter Type LatestObject gets the next object _after_ (Largest Group ID, Largest Object ID) then...

Subscribe(LatestObject) gets 21-0, 21-1, 21-2, ...
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=1) "should" get 20-0, 20-1, 20-2, ..., 20-29
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=0) "should" get nothing (because the subscribe already starts at an object 0)

But we can't know ahead of time that 29 is the last object in the group.

If we define our Joining Fetch range purely in terms relative to (Largest Group ID, Largest Object ID) consistently with the other examples above we'd end up fetching an entire extra Group.

Subscribe(LatestObject) gets 21-0, 21-1, 21-2, ...
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=1) gets 19-0, 19-1, 19-2, ..., 20-29
Fetch(JoiningFetch,PGC=0) gets 20-0, ..., 20-29

I think the simplest option would be to just accept that and say that the subscriber can always cancel the Fetch portion if we get "lucky" and find the Subscribe has given us what we need (an Object ID 0 and "sufficient" buffer depth for our purposes - which might be zero if we _really_ want to live on the edge).

In the future maybe we could consider a further optimization with a different Fetch Type that allows the _publisher_ to cancel the Fetch as soon as any Object ID 0 is sent, but there are only some circumstances in which that would be useful, and I don't think it's likely the common case for most live streaming applications.

Incorporated these suggestions, thanks!

> A Joining Fetch MUST be sent in ascending group order.

Why? See Alan's comment [here](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/598#issuecomment-2605532478). The suggests that the client execute the FETCH in descending order and waits until it has sufficient groups to start. Those groups are the sum of those delivered by the FETCH and those delivered by the SUBSCRIBE. If you go in ascending order, you are always forced to wait for the complete range to be sent before you can stitch them together. But by going in reverse, you assemble the fastest path to your starting buffer. This should be an option for the player.

When we originally discussed this, we had decided that supporting just one ordering would be simpler and assumed subscribers would prefer the Fetched portion to be in order of playback to avoid needing to reorder the received groups.

@afrind's suggestion is interesting - if the Subscribe portion returns a sufficient number of groups to contribute to meeting the target buffer size before the entire Fetch portion is delivered, it would be nice to be able to start playback at that point. This would allow the player to stay as close as possible (with its selected target buffer size) to the live edge. As you say, this would require Fetching groups in an order that allows them to remain contiguous with the Subscribe portion.

To be fair, I'm not entirely sure how likely this is to occur. If the first upstream relay from the end subscriber has a local cache of recently delivered objects then the Fetch portion could likely be delivered at line rate whereas the Subscribe portion will be limited to the application/media rate. Without doing the math, my gut sense is that depending on group sizes and available bandwidth this might be the difference of a group or two at most? And often not actually advantageous at all?

Despite that, Joining Fetch (and MoQT) as a whole are largely about allowing for possible optimizations of this sort, so it may still be worth allowing Group Order Descending here rather than precluding it—despite the extra complexity it would require to implement on the player side and the narrower set of scenarios when it would be advantageous.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
The flexibility built into this architecture can lead to routing loops.

Take relays A, B, and C, which are connected to each other.

C sends SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES for namespace Foo to B, but not A. B sends ("forwards") SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES to A for Foo.

Then A gets an ANNOUNCE for Foo from Upstream. it sends it to B, which passes it on to C. C forwards that ANNOUNCE unsolicited to A. Now A has a backup path to Foo, so even if its upstream session dies, it will not send UNANNOUNCE.

Even without SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCE, there could be this chain of events.

One way out of this would be to require SUBSCRIBE_ANNOUNCES to send an ANNOUNCE.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I'm closing this for now, and can always reopen if needed.

Individual comment:

For objects in the past, this is just another way of saying "subscribe + fetch" and it's fine.  For queued objects that are post-subscribe, I don't like the uncertainty of how many streams things are going to arrive on.

Furthermore, FETCH and SUBSCRIBE have different rules for omitting objects, and what to do with non-Normal objects. This introduces a lot of ambiguity that requires careful thought.

FETCH and SUBSCRIBE actually have quite similar rules for omitting objects.  The main difference is that SUBSCRIBE has more flexibility in the transmission order, since it can use more than one stream.

I agree with @martinduke here. I appreciate the sentiment that we could conceivably collapse subscribe and fetch into a singular message (again), but I think it would require quite a bit more articulation of the behavior than is currently written. I also agree that the difference in requirements for omitting objects is an important nuance we should not overlook because my current understanding is that Fetch is more likely to need to go upstream (potentially even back to the original publisher) to get a definitive answer about object non-existence. If we don't provide the same guarantee here, then we still need Fetch for that. If we do, we risk unduly increasing upstream requests for clients who may not need that same level of fidelity for the entire range of objects requested by a Subscribe.

Fair points.  The Joining FETCH PR is quite far along, and as long as we restrict it a bit more (ie: You can't join a SUBSCRIBE that starts 100 groups in the future), I think it will accomplish what we want without too much complexity.

comments.body: I wonder how does this support the flow in the demo use-case of synchronized video from Zafer, where the original publisher was indeed generating groupIds in different order than what is being proposed here ?

That can be accomplished by the synchronized clients all subscribing to a control track produced by the leader. That control track instructs them to play a VOD asset (play, pause, seek) in sync with the leader. The VOD asset group IDs run from {0,1,2,…,N}.

That demo could also show a live stream control, with (play,plause) controls if the relay has no caching, or (play,pause,seek) if the relay has caching. In this case the live streams Group IDs also run {0,1,2,…,N}.

Thanks for the re-wording.
Though, we are back to the point that it says nothing about the +1 issue (incremental increase of group_ID). 

Problem: if a Publisher publishes a track where group_ID contains only even incremental numbers. When a Relay caches the objects, it cannot know whether the missing odd group_ID are gaps or not. When receiving a FETCH(0,1000) request, it can serve the 500 objects from its cache but it generates 500 individual FETCH requests to the Publisher to check the 500 gaps. It may be exploited for DDoS attacks.

To reach a potential consensus, it was mentioned during Denver's interim meeting that we could add a track property which states whether the original publisher produces Group ID with gaps or not. I would be in favor of having such a track property.

yes .. we can do it in different ways .. but what we saw yesterday showed 2 learning points for me: 

1. Things work pretty well the way the protocol is defined today
2. Innovation happens in application space and can't wait to see what developers build in future.

One common use-case is, groupId start point is randomized to avoid reusing the same groupId when original publisher disconnects and rejoins a session due to intermittent network connectivity (happens several times when driving or changing from wifi to cellular)

From the relay perspective , there is discontinuity seen in the groupIds .. When a fetch happens on that track, relay needs to go upstream to find out the real status of the gap that was seen. Relays don't have sufficient information to really know what happens at the original publisher which might be 3-4 hops away from it.

It would make sense for your use-case to say "_this track may have gaps_" in the Track_Property. It is fine. It will significantly help the Relay to behave when dealing with FETCH and cache management.
And it will not prevent the use-cases where gaps are not supposed to happen (for example a TV live stream) to express "_this track must not have gaps_"; Relay would then be able to know exactly what to expect.
I think this Track_Property does not hurt anyone and it does help all the people that  have +1-ed the sequential increase for the past year.

@gwendalsimon  for my understanding, how will knowing that a group can have gaps help in relay implementation ?

Regardless, i agree anything we decide shouldn't make +1ed mode not impacted. If you can help me understand your thinking, it will be great.
Using previous group id in the group header can help. Please see #731 .

pulls.title: Adds AUTHORIZATION ALIAS parameter
pulls.author: wilaw
pulls.body:
The AUTHORIZATION ALIAS parameter allows a small alias to be associated with a larger AUTHORIZATION INFO payload, such as a token. This reduces message wireline size and token processing time (decryption etc) when future operations (such as rapid subscriptions and fetches) wish to reapply the same token. 

Also removes the restriction that AUTHORIZATION INFO is an ASCII string.

comments.author: afrind

comments.body:
> Would it be better to define a structure for Auth Info that has an optional alias? If we allow sending > 1 AUTH (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/issues/722), then there's no safe way to correlate them.

Since parameters have a serialization order, one alternative option is to specify that an AUTHORIZATION ALIAS refers to the AUTHORIZATION INFO which it follows. This would allow multiple auth blobs and aliases to be communicated in one message.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> I think we might want some text cautioning against storing an unlimited number of these aliases, since it causes the publisher to consume an unbounded amount of memory.

@ianswett  - the aliases are varints, so they're not the memory constraint. It would be the tokens they represent, which the relay is then forced to store for the remainder of the session.  We can set an arbitrary alias limit of 32 for example, but a single token of 1GB in size would consume more memory. So probably more reasonable to set a max total size of all tokens that should be stored per session, and then give content distributors flexibility to trade off count and size. How about 5MB limit per session? We can start off low and raise it once auth systems are deployed and we have some idea of token size & count in production.

Yes, you described it better than I did.  And yes, it's not really the number of aliases, but the total memory consumed by the aliases + tokens.

I think it's worth bringing this to the WG.  I would suggest a parameter in SETUP, which is similar to what HTTP/3 does for headers: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#header-size-constraints

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
>  I would suggest a parameter in SETUP

The problem with that approach is that the client is not making this token itself. It is given it ahead of attempting the connection. So its not like the client can adjust what token it sends after the result of the SETUP handshake. The entity that needs to know the max token size is the back-office system that created the token and it is not party to this handshake.

It might be more useful that if the client sends a token which is too large, that a 'Token limit exceeded" error gets thrown and this error carries an attribute which is the max limit being enforced by that relay. The client can then report that problem to its token issuer. 

I think the MOQT spec could define a max token size that SHOULD be supported, but allowing relays to vary that. For example, a CDN may wish to support a 5MB limit since they are dealing with millions of tokens, while a research relay on a private network might be happy with a 100MB limit.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Regarding introducing the notion of active/expired tokens into the moqt token cache:

We could add a specific error code "Authorization Token Expired" meaning an endpoint tried to use an alias for a token that the receiver has expired.  Receiving this error code is equivalent to deleting the token from the alias cache if Alias Type = USE_ALIAS.  The current size of the token cache has to be agreed on by both endpoints though, and the requesting endpoint may not know when the token expires.  It would have to assume it exists and occupies space in the cache until sending Alias Type = DELETE or it gets Auth Token Expired.

Separately, this PR needs to state what happens to the token cache when a request uses Alias Type = REGISTER but the token is invalid in some way (expired, or otherwise). If we say that the alias is not registered for some or all _ERROR responses, it introduces a condition where the endpoint pipelines two SUBSCRIBEs, one with REGISTER and one with USE_ALIAS, and the second fails - need to make sure that isn't a session error.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> I think this is largely reasonable. Does the token's permission get re-evaluated each time because what it authorizes might change on the back-end, or does the server do a single access check of the token and then remember what it grants access to? The difference is that the former requires storing the literal blob (whose size the client knows, as it sent it) while the latter requires storing information which the server extracted or looked up and whose size the client cannot gauge.

This is a good point. Since the definitions of the tokens are outside the scope of this document, I'm not sure we know.  Some systems might require storing the original token blob for re-evaluation (perhaps a URL that needs to be queried), while others might contain claims which could be stored which could be smaller, or larger if tokens are compressed.  In the absence of better mechanism to know how much storage the receiver is committing to, the length of the blob seems like a fine proxy?

> The discussion about removing expired tokens might lead to the latter in at least some cases, where a server forgets the blob and merely remembers the alias maps to an expired token. If either is a valid implementation, it might be worth discussing the trade-off.

I think either choice (storing the blob or storing the granted permissions) allows the receiver to clear the stored information if it detects expiration.  I think the PR can reflect something along these lines, but at least for now still require explicit deletion of the Alias by the sender.

pulls.title: Harmonizing serialization of Parameters and Extensions.
pulls.author: wilaw
pulls.body:
This PR applies extends serialization of Extensions (in which even types carry a varint payload and odd types carry a Length/Value payload) to parameters. The serialization is defined first for parameters and then referenced for Extensions.

The DELIVERY TIMEOUT parameter changes from a type of 0x03 to 0x02 as it carries a varint payload. 

The AUTHORIZATION INFO parameter changes from 0x02to 0x03 as it carries a TL payload. 

Renumbers the CLIENT_SETUP and SERVER_SETUP messages to make supporting both serializations easier.

No changes in type required for the SETUP parameters. 

Fixes #672

comments.author: fluffy
comments.body:
So here is requirements and then I will describe solution stolen from WebRTC>

Requirements when using E2E Encryptions (note many things will not use E2E Encryption):

* the whole payload is E2E encrypted - no more, no less. This makes it easier to reason about security proofs. 

* by default, MoQ headers extensions are *not* part of the E2E "extra authenticated data"

* it is possible to mark *some* of the moq headers extensions  as E2E authenticated. Relays can read these headers but can not change or remove them. 

* this does not increase bandwidth usage when it is not used 

The solution I would propose is roughly this:

There is a header extension called "start of authenticated headers". All the headers extension *after* that header are including in the E2E "extra authenticated data"  

Relays can not modify, or remove headers that follow this one but they can add, change, remove header extensions before the "start of authenticated headers".

pulls.title: Limit all the things
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
Created explicit limits for all variable length things in MoQT.

1. Control Messages have a max length of 2^16-1, changed the Length from varint to uint16.
2. Changed number of parameters from varint to uint8, so a max of 256 params per control message.
3. Changed number of supported versions from varint to uint8, so a max of 256 versions to offer.
4. Set reason phrase max to 1024 bytes.
5. Set max length of all extensions in streams and fetch to 2^16-1 (datagrams are limited to MTU, obvs).

Any length violation => close the session.

I'm open to different limit values, particularly for control messages if there's a compelling argument, though I'll point out that 64k is about the maximum size of an HTTP header block you can get across the internet.

Fixes: #473
Fixes: #554

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
@fluffy 

> If there is an internal error, I think we need to close the connection not the stream 

Internal error is really there as a catch-all and future proofing -- I know i want to kill this stream and I need to put *some* value.  We can bikeshed the name but without this, people will just make up their own reset codes and that doesn't really help anyone.  

One example in my implementation - if the publisher throws an exception while handling a FETCH request, but has already opened the fetch data stream, I reset it with INTERNAL_ERROR.

Most other examples happen when a publisher violates a rule when publishing - eg: tries to send an object ID smaller than the previous one on a stream.  I could be amenable to ending the _subscription_ if this happens, but I really don't want to kill the _session_, which can be shared by multiple subscriptions.

> It is not clear to me which things should reset vs close a stream.

This has a whole section in the current document (https://moq-wg.github.io/moq-transport/draft-ietf-moq-transport.html#name-closing-subgroup-streams).  FIN on a subgroup stream has a specific meaning: "I know I sent you the last object in this subgroup".  If you want to get rid of a stream for _any other reason_ - you have to use reset.

> I think we need some discussion around this and I think there are a bunch of bigger design questions around this.
> ... the issue here is what things cause reset vs somthing else.

Please file issues for what you think needs discussion if they are not already filed. This PR is just defining _some_ error codes and they are all based on a real implementation.
Are there cases in which the publisher can unilaterally close subscription?  Because in those cases, we'd need to close streams too, and "cancelled" does not quite fit in well

@vasilvv : CANCELLED seems fine to me in this case - what is the receiver going to do differently with a different code.  That said, tell me what you want and we can add it.  PUBLISHER_CANCELLED and SUBSCRIBER_CANCELLED?
It's actually a bit of the opposite case: I want a catch-all "subscription is gone so I am removing this data stream", since it does add complexity to track the reason why it was gone.
@vasilvv : can you make a specific counter proposal here?
Editorial nit: s/receiver/publisher

```suggestion
: The subscriber requested cancellation via UNSUBSCRIBE, FETCH_CANCEL or
```

@suhasHere : I think you mean subscriber.  eg: this is what the publisher includes in the stream reset if the subscriber sends UNSUBSCRIBE or FETCH_CANCEL on the control stream or STOP_SENDING on a DATA stream.
wondering, in what circumstances Cancelled and/or Session Closed will be sent by the publisher

For Cancelled, it's in the text - either the subscriber asked for it to be cancelled, or the publisher is ending the subscription for some other reason, specified in SUBSCRIBE_DONE.

> The subscriber requested cancellation via UNSUBSCRIBE, FETCH_CANCEL or
STOP_SENDING, or the publisher ended the subscription, in which case
SUBSCRIBE_DONE ({{message-subscribe-done}}) will have a more detailed
status code.

For Session Closed, my implementation sends this when the MoQ session is closed with open streams.  Might happen during shutdown or some other error condition is detected (eg: Protocol Violation on control stream).

To support multi-publisher, we need publisher ID as well.

Headers, specifically extension headers, are problem as some extension headers may be specific relay by relay (e.g., Relay 5 added headers that relay 14 never sees). Caching is a bit tricky in this sense where mutable headers are not the same relay by relay. In a distributed deep cache, the headers may not exist at all due to which relay populated the deep cache. When pulling from a deep cache (distributed, not directly on the relay), the fetch may not match what would have been there had the relay originally received the data based on subscribe. In addition, time to live needs to be taken into account. What is the retention policy and how will a subscriber/fetcher know that cache will never have requested data because they are asking for data outside of the retention policy?

> [!NOTE]
> While this example says 2 publishers, there could be more publishers... such as the same number of subscribers... they are all publishers and subscribers.
