pulls.title: Proposing `BATCH_SUBSCRIBE`
pulls.author: Johan511
pulls.body:
Often multiple channels of media such as subtitles, audio, base layer / enhancement layer video are subscribed to simultaneously.

It would make sense that they are all within the same track namespace

Consider the following object model

```
very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id/subtitles/eng
very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id/audio/eng
very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id/base_layer_video
very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id/enhancement_layer_video
``` 

Currently this would require 4 different subscribe messages to be sent, each with the same track namespace prefix of  "`very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id`"

We propose a simple fix to this redundancy with the `BATCH_SUBSCRIBE` message to subscribe to multiple tracks using a single message.

```
BATCH_SUBSCRIBE Message {
  Type (i) = 0x6,
  Length (i),
  Track Namespace Prefix (tuple),
  Number of Subscriptions (i),
  (
    Subscribe ID (i),
    Track Alias (i),
    Track Namespace Suffix (tuple),
    Track Name Length (i),
    Track Name (..),
    Subscriber Priority (8),
    Group Order (8),
    Filter Type (i),
    [StartGroup (i),
     StartObject (i)],
    [EndGroup (i)],
    Number of Parameters (i),
    Subscribe Parameters (..) ...
  ) ...
}
```

This also provides the implementation an hint that these subscriptions are related and possibly optimise delivery accordingly.

Answers to some possible questions
1. **Why not update the existing `SUBSCRIBE` message?** : Updating the existing subscribe message adds an overhead of 1-2 bytes in situations where no batched subscriptions are being made. I do not have a strong opinion on whether the 1-2 bytes are significant

2. **How do we handle the numerous interactions associated with `SUBSCRIBE`?** : The receiver of the `BATCH_SUBSCRIBE` must treat it to be identical to receiving multiple `SUBSCRIBE` messages, this means it should reply to it using multiple `SUBSCRIBE_OK`/`SUBSCRIBE_ERROR` messages and `SUBSCRIBE_DONE` when the subscription is fulfilled, allow updates or cancels on each of the subscriptions individually using `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE` or `UNSUBSCRIBE`. This removes much of the complexity associated with handling `BATCH_SUBSCRIBE` separately. 

3. **There are already talks of wildcard subscription, why do we need this?** : Assuming wildcard subscriptions to mean all tracks within a namespace; this might seldom be the right solution. Consider the above mentioned case, a wildcard subscription to all tracks within `very_long_namespace_prefix/media_id` would mean the client receives all subtitles and audio they are authorized to, this might include languages the client is not interested in receiving and data which would end up being discarded by the client. There might also be multiple post processed versions of the for censorship, better experience for specially-abled, etc.,

Does MoQT need a mechanism to supply this data when the app is not (eg padding streams?)

I'd rather not, because you can always request a higher quality at a low priority if there is one.

If there's not a higher quality, then you don't really need to discover more bandwidth.

Typically, I-Frames supply enough data to make the sender non app-limited for long enough to avoid completely under-utilizing the connection.

Senders control their congestion control, so client mechanisms to try to get their senders to unstick their congestion controllers are a bit scary.  This does remind me to read: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-ccwg-ratelimited-increase/

pulls.body:
This PR adds a 1-byte Serialization field to the FETCH object definition and defines 4 code points: 

0x0 - status quo - Group/Subgroup and Object ID fields are present. This would be used at the start of a track and adds 1 byte to the current serialization.

0x1 - The Group ID and Subgroup ID of this object are identical to those of the prior object and Object ID increments by 1. The Group ID, Subgroup ID and Object ID fields are not present.  This code point would most commonly occur in a FETCH response and would save 2 bytes per object.

0x2 - The Group ID field exists and Subgroup ID and Object ID are both 0. The SubGroup ID and Object ID fields are not present.  This code point would be used at the start of each new Group and saves 1 byte per object.

0x3 - The Group ID of this object is identical to that of the prior Object. Subgroup ID increments by 1 and Object ID increments by 1. The Subgroup ID and Object ID fields are not present. This code point would be used at the start of a new Subgroup and would save 1 byte per object. 


Fixes #660

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I like the idea of compression. From an implementation perspective, it would be great if we can map this to bits, rather than having 10 codewords whose capabilities have to be matched to a clumsy table, so that every check for "what element is next" requires multiple boolean checks against the integer. This is definitely an aesthetics/complexity complaint rather than a real performance one.

I would propose:
0x01 and 0x02: subgroup -- 4 permutations: 0, Prior, Prior+1, present
0x04: object -- present or prior+1. -- the "0" encoding saves at most one byte per group, which IMO is not worth the complexity.
0x08: Group --  prior or present.
0x10: publisher priority -- present or not. I know that the table is trying to enforce rules about when the publisher priority can actually differ, but that is futile. It's impossible to enforce this with encoding -- I still need to explicitly check, because the peer can make all the fields explicit and still send a subgroup with two different priorities. This is a false economy.
0x20: Extension header

I don't care about the ordering, except that subgroup should be the two LSBs.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
@martin - I like the bitmasking approach. Before I implement as a patch on this PR, do we have consensus to make this change? It would look something like that the tables below:

The two least significant bits (LSBs) of the serialization byte form a two-bit field that defines the state of the subgroup. To extract this value, a bitwise AND operation with the mask 0x03 MUST be performed.

| Bitmask Result (Byte & 0x03) | Meaning |
| ----------- | ----------- |
| 0x00 | Subgroup ID is zero |
| 0x01 | Subgroup ID is the same as the Subgroup ID of the prior Object |
| 0x02 | Subgroup ID is one more than the Subgroup ID of the prior Object |
| 0x03|  The Subgroup ID field is present |

The following table defines additional individual flags within the serialization byte. Each flag is an independent boolean value, where a set bit (1) indicates the corresponding condition is true.

| Bitmask | Condition if set | Condition if not set |
| ----------- | ----------- | -------|
|0x04 | Object ID field is present | Object ID is one more than the Object ID of the prior Object |
|0x08 | Group ID field is present | Group ID is identical to the Group ID of the prior Object |
|0x10 | Priority field is present | Priority field is not present |
|0x20 | Extension header field is present | Extension header field is not present |

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Discussed in 9/10 virtual interim

1. We'll go with "priority not present = priority from previous object in subgroup if present, otherwise previous object in FETCH response".  

Upon reflection, it does put the burden on a fetch decoder of a map from subgroup ID -> priority which can only be cleared when the group changes.  A malicious publisher can force the subscriber into keeping effectively infinite state.  When I write this up, I'll put a bound on the maximum number of subgroups per group that can use this compression flag (256?).

2. There wasn't sufficient interest in adding a bit for Object ID=0.  Suhas said they do FETCH datagram Tracks with one object per group, but the extra byte is not significant in a FETCH response.  This leaves 2 bits easily accessible for future versions.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> After a PR is approved, is there any more action needed from the PR submitter to have the change merged/committed? Is it generally the PR submitter who should close the PR? When should the PR be closed?

No action is needed on the submitter's part.  The editors (myself and @ianswett for this document) handle the merges.  For purely editorial issues, we can merge as soon as there is an approval.  For issues that impact Design, we keep them open a minimum of 2 weeks so the community has a chance to review.  We have a third category "Editorial and Minor Design" which can be merged after 1 week if they have 3 separate approvals.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
I am very not convinced by this parameter. I strongly call for more discussion on what we want to achieve here.

First we must disambiguate:
- **token re-validation time**: Today's CDN edge servers delivering ABR do not revalidate the claims of an already validated token because, by nature, requests arrive with a token every x seconds. However we need something different in the case of MoQ. We must revalidate the claims because the token is processed only at the connection and some characteristics of the client may change. Some ideas for notifying revalidation time are discussed [here](https://github.com/wilaw/CAT-4-MOQT/pull/9#discussion_r2073679318)
- **token expiration time**: It is an optional claim in CAT. Expiration time usually serves two purposes: 1/ right management (this content is available just for a given time); and 2/ prevent CDN leeching by forcing clients to re-authenticate. In MoQ, the second motivation is much less significant because the tokenized connection is established between client and server, so token replay is much easier to prevent.

Forcing a token renewal just for the sake of revalidating it is a particularly complex implementation (to not say a bad idea), especially with respect to how challenging token renewal is in practice.

Second, many content providers do not use expiration time in tokens.
- actually many content providers do not implement tokens at all. Public TV broadcasters for example do not need to protect content. The more viewers the better.
- some content providers serve content infinitely, for example a TV screen in an airport plays 24/7/365 and fixed video surveillance. We want a token identifier for various reasons at connection (analytics) but almost no claims.

Making expires a mandatory parameter is quite a forceful push. I am opposed to force everyone to use parameters just because a subset of cases need it.

Third, the token issuer and the token edge validator may want to keep their conversation (via token) secret. The Client and the Relay are regarded as possible leaks. The least information is revealed, the best. Encrypting tokens serves this purpose, Expiration time and (possible) re-validation time are crucial information, which the content protection scheme may want to keep encrypted.

comments.author: alficles
comments.body:
It seems to me there are two important problems to solve:

1. We need the recipient to know when they need to double-check that the token they have is valid, either by re-checking what they have (which requires that they hang onto it while the stream is open) or by asking the bearer to present a valid token (which might be a new token or a representation of the existing token if it remains valid).
2. We need the bearer to know when they need to get a new token.

These problems don't necessarily need to be solved inside the transport protocol, though. For the first problem, we could "solve" it by saying that authentication token processing is something that must be defined by the token definition. You could imagine a token format that always expires at midnight every day and had no way to express any restriction that could change over the course of the stream. You could also imagine a token format that requires checking in with a third party auth server at a specified interval, but never involved re-evaluating the token or asking for it to be re-presented. I'm not suggesting that these are _good_ tokens. (In fact, I have a strong opinion about some of their consequences, as expressed by the fact that the CAT doesn't work that way. :D) But I am suggesting that as people define new tokens, they may have meaningfully different semantics. And since any token format has to be implemented by the relay, it is safe to assume that such an implementation could also handle whatever revalidation is specified by the token format.

For the second problem, we can let the bearer deal with that. They already have to get the token somewhere, whatever hands it too them can also let them know when they need to come back for another one. A client with a signed or MACed token could even just read it and figure out when it's invalid. Or the client can let the server reject their token and then go get a new one. But we don't have to define precisely how this works, I think.

I think all we need is a way for the recipient to tell the bearer that their token is bad and they will not be getting any more data. And if the server is hanging on to the token, we need a way for the bearer to hand them a new one. (I think this is easily accomplished by just sending a new auth frame on the stream.) I like having the server hang onto the token, because it means it doesn't have to revalidate anything that can't have changed. Relevantly, this means that if the server knows that its list of acceptable keys hasn't changed, it doesn't need to revalidate the signature periodically.
There needs to be a default value to implementations to know when the parameter is omitted.

comments.body:
```suggestion
A subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE to a publisher to modify an existing
subscription. Subscriptions can only be narrowed, not widened, as an attempt to
widen could fail. If Objects with Locations smaller than the current
subscription's Start Location are required, FETCH can be used to retrieve
them. The Start Location MUST NOT decrease, and if it increases, there is no
guarantee that the publisher has not already sent Objects with Locations smaller
than the new Start Location. Similarly, the End Group MUST NOT increase, and if
it decreases, there is no guarantee that the publisher has not already sent
Objects with Locations larger than the new End Location.  A publisher MUST
terminate the session with a 'Protocol Violation' if the SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE
violates these rules or if the subscriber specifies a request ID that has not
existed within the Session.
```

There is a potential race condition with the design in this PR.  If SUBSCRIBE_OK set's default publisher priority to 10 but the objects arrive first without a priority field, then they will get Priority 128. comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Thanks for your review @TimEvens, comments inline:

> 1. `NEW_GROUP_REQUEST` param can only be sent by the subscriber IF the `SUBSCRIBE_OK` indicated that it's supported.  The keyword is **MUST** but there is no recourse stated if the subscriber violates this MUST.  Does the relay close the connection with protocol violation or should it ignore it, or should it `SUBSCRIBE_ERROR` ?

Good point, until we have a way to fail SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, the options are limited, I'd say it's a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION (close session) for now.

> 2. Value of zero is used when the subscriber doesn't know the group. Makes sense, but  is that really true? The subscriber could have had a `SUBSCRIBE_OK` with group id indicated as well could have been sent objects with group_id.  In this case the subscriber MUST know the group id, but because this PR doesn't clarify that,  the subscriber cloud always use zero. This PR does not require the subscriber that has previously been sent group_id via subscribe ok or via an object to honor that information when sending  `NEW_GROUP_REQUEST=<group_id + 1>`.

I can see it's a little nicer to include the group if you know it.  We can add some encouragement to this effect, it could be a MUST I suppose, but I'm ambivalent.  A client can always get the same effect by sending a random group ID larger than what's been delivered/known.

> 3. The way this is written, it suggests that ZERO will be sent to the publisher regardless of other subscribers that have requested specific group IDs. In inter-relay (peering), does the ZERO override sending a new group request with a value? In other words, if zero is received at the same time as other requests with group ids present, send only the zero?.?

The updated PR says you only send NGR upstream there's not already one, or if the value is greater than one already sent.  So the first 0 gets through but all other 0s are coalesced.  Specific values always override a zero.  If you are using zero properly, it's always fine to get coalesced to another NGR, since you're asking for _any_ new group.

> 4. A relay sends new group request but there is no ACK that it was actually delivered to the publisher. In addition, the publisher may have received it, but since there is no ACK with a status of try again later or ignored, the relay will no longer send new group requests to the publisher. Resulting in the publisher never starting a new group. The PR states that the publisher may delay the new group request, but it doesn't clearly state that the original publisher MUST maintain this request state because it will never receive a new request after this until it starts a new group. Suggest "**Original Publisher Handling:**"...  Some applications may not want to maintain this state and would prefer to get a request again from subscribers if it still needs it.

Yes, the OP can delay (indefinitely) but can't ignore. We may need to clarify that when the OP disconnects the relay clears the state too.  I think SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE responses are coming soon in a yet to be written PR.

> 5. Subscribe updates are not currently defined in MOQT to be queued and flooded or reconciled by the relay when peering/inter-relay communication is established. In other words, there maybe be a disconnect from the subscriber relay and the original publisher relay when new group request is sent. The PR does indicate that if the subscribe comes in with new-group request, that state would be maintained, but it does not mention anything about what happens to subscribe updates when there is this break of communication in the middle... This would result in the relay holding on to pending state that it sent new group request, but that actually was dropped in the middle with no feedback to the relay.

If I understand your scenario correctly you've got:

P -> R1 -> R2 -> S

but there's a break so either

P x R1 -> R2 -> S or
P -> R1 x R2 -> S

I think SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE responses will help here too, since R1/R2 can indicate that the update failed (because there's no OP).

> 6. There is lack of clarity mentioned for how the relay should handle multiple new group requests with different group ID's, which could be zero as well. If current group is 10 and subscriber 1 asks for 20 and subscriber 2 asks for 8 and subscribe 3 asks for 50, which new-group request group-id do we send to the original publisher?

It's pretty clear - you send if it's larger than the largest one you've sent and largest than largest group.  So in your example, it would send 20 and 50, but not 8.

> 7. Considering there is no ACK for the subscriber that new group will be handled or has been handled, the subscriber will have no choice but to continue to send new group requests when receiving objects that haven't changed to the new requested group. This would result in flood.

The relay would drop them because the value of the group would be the same.  The relay already needs to handle update floods (also, we added a separate Request ID to SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, which will limit the flood rate to N per RTT).

We can consider Parking this until SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE responses have landed since that might make the solution more robust.

```suggestion
complete. Subsequent NEW_GROUP_REQUEST received SHOULD be aggregated to a single request to the publisher that will be delayed by CLIENT_SETUP parameter TBD milliseconds from when the last request was sent. 
```

The below list will likely only be known by the origin relay.  The downstream relays do not have direct access to the publisher and the negotiated params for that publisher connection.  This is especially the case with multi-publisher. 

The text should say origin relay does this.

The original publisher is free to apply its logic on when and how to generate the new group. An application, say video conferencing app that supports non-static GOPs, will apply some hueristcs/batching logically at its end to decide when to generate a new group on the data stream.
Since the groupId is latching point and avoids using timers configured across all the relays. In the current proposal, the timers or such logic is moved only to the OP.

GroupID  is used to reduce the churn to the original publisher. A simple boolean along will not work . you need a combination of simple boolean + dampening logic ( like timers, for example). 

The goal with this proposal is to reduce signaling churn ( when requests can be latched) and to not to have arbitrary timers across the relay network.

Recall the implementation will apply this at the publisher edge relay only. Timers for such can be negotiated via parameters for such. Not complex or extensive to implement when considering publisher edge (aka origin relay).

Dampening IMO is required. Bool is totally fine and group id only complicates things with reconciliation between other subscriber requests. The net result is to start a new group, despite whatever the group id is. It’s a classic synchronization request to start anew.
+1 but a little vague and open ended

Can you explain the race conditions you see in detail?

I don't see why only the origin relay would know this:

> There is already an outstanding NEW_GROUP_REQUEST _from this Relay_

You are saying Largest Group = 10 and Relay gets NGR 15, then NGR 12? I think this is covered.

This algorithm will send NGR 15, but not send NGR 12 because there's an outstanding NGR.  If the relay sends NGR=15, receives Group 11, then receives NGR=12 it *would* forward it but that seems correct, since it could be a subscriber that's seen 11 and wants something new.

The group value is only for aggregation and not a command to mint a specific group number.

```suggestion

```

No, I am strongly opposed to any message that would force an Origin Publisher to create a New Group upon request, even delayed.

It was very clear since the beginning (and we collectively agreed) that this New Group Request is a great feature for video conferencing scenario but it is dangerous in any massive live streaming use case, so it must not be a forceful message. We agreed to debate on this topic at the condition that the Origin Publisher can decide to not apply a new group.

An Origin Publisher for the Superbowl or for moon landing does not want to pay any single attention to NGR messages.
@gwendalsimon the OP has to opt-in to NGR by sending DYNAMIC_GROUPS=1.  Does that mitigate your concern?

Not really. The OP should be free to decide whether it wants to create a new group, to delay this creation, or to ignore. There are cases where it makes sense to create a group (dynamic frames, small population, many resources...) and ten minutes later, it does not make sense any longer (static frames, large population, less resources...).
Imho, subscribers are free to send a NGR, and, well, they may get a new group soon, or not, ... but they have to understand that there is no "right to get a new group". The OP has a much wider understanding of the configuration and he may not fulfill all requests.

The only way to truly "ignore" an NGR is to _never_ make a new group.  If we retain the algorithm described here, an OP that silently drops an NGR and never starts a new group might never get another NGR.  Perhaps we can leave "ignore" in as a valid action with that caveat?

We can also fix this is by relaxing the restriction at the relay (as Cullen suggests), at the expense of losing some of the protection offered by the "one NGR at a time" rule.

If the NGR 15 had completed at the point the NGR 12 happened, there would not be an outstanding and at that point I thought it would send the NGR 12. I thought that was what was being proposed here but perhaps I had it wrong. I guess I might be unclear on what outstanding transaction means
@fluffy in case you missed my question here

@fluffy 

> If the NGR 15 had completed at the point the NGR 12 happened, there would not be an outstanding and at that point I thought it would send the NGR 12.

This is how it works. Per my example above:

```
Relay Largest = 10
S1->R: NGR 15
R->P: NGR
P->R: Object, Group=11
S2->R: NGR 12
R->P: NGR
```

Conceptually the NGR has _no group value_ when received by the OP (relays do include it in case next upstream is a relay).  See this bit:

>  The Original Publisher chooses the next Group ID; there are no requirements that it be equal to the NEW_GROUP_REQUEST parameter value.

> I guess I might be unclear on what outstanding transaction means

The definition is on line 1641:

> After sending a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST upstream, the request is considered outstanding _until the Largest Group increases_.

Can you articulate why you think this is a bad design?  And why this is a necessary requirement?

> it should also not send it if it has already sent a new group request that is equal too or larger than this

```suggestion
A relay that receives a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST for a Track without an active
subscription MUST include the NEW_GROUP_REQUEST when subscribing upstream.

A relay that receives a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST for an established subscription with a
value of 0 or a value larger than the Largest Group MUST send a SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE
including the NEW_GROUP_REQUEST to the publisher unless:

1. The Track does not support dynamic Groups
2. There is already an outstanding NEW_GROUP_REQUEST from this Relay with a
   greater or equal value

If a relay receives a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST with a non-zero value less than or equal
to the Largest Group, it does not send a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST upstream.

After sending a NEW_GROUP_REQUEST upstream, the request is considered
outstanding until the Largest Group increases.
```

Spoke offline with @fluffy.  The scenario where the "one outstanding" request does not work is as follows:


Largest Group seen in parens
```
C1 (22) -> R1 (22) -> P (24)
C2 (24) -> R2 (24) -/
```

R1 and C1 got behind.  Now C2 fails over from R2 to R1.

```
C1 (22) -> R1 (22) -> P (24)
C2 (24) -/
```

C1 sends NGR 23
C2 sends NGR 25

Under the original algorithm, the OP would discard NGR 23, because it has published 24, but R1 would discard NGR 25, because NGR 23 is outstanding (until the an object from 24 reaches R1).

The tradeoff is that a buggy or malicious client can send an unlimited number of NEW_GROUP_REQUESTs to the OP.  Cullen pointed out that a client can already send an unlimited number of FETCH requests that reach the OP as well.

reviews.author: TimEvens
reviews.body:
There are problems with this design as defined. There are conditions that are not handled and it leaves the relay stuck doing whatever the implementer decides (guaranteed inter-op issues). Unhandled items are stated below: 

1. `NEW_GROUP_REQUEST` param can only be sent by the subscriber IF the `SUBSCRIBE_OK` indicated that it's supported.  The keyword is **MUST** but there is no recourse stated if the subscriber violates this MUST.  Does the relay close the connection with protocol violation or should it ignore it, or should it `SUBSCRIBE_ERROR` ?

2. Value of zero is used when the subscriber doesn't know the group. Makes sense, but  is that really true? The subscriber could have had a `SUBSCRIBE_OK` with group id indicated as well could have been sent objects with group_id.  In this case the subscriber MUST know the group id, but because this PR doesn't clarify that,  the subscriber cloud always use zero. This PR does not require the subscriber that has previously been sent group_id via subscribe ok or via an object to honor that information when sending  `NEW_GROUP_REQUEST=<group_id + 1>`. 

3. The way this is written, it suggests that ZERO will be sent to the publisher regardless of other subscribers that have requested specific group IDs. In inter-relay (peering), does the ZERO override sending a new group request with a value? In other words, if zero is received at the same time as other requests with group ids present, send only the zero?.?

4. A relay sends new group request but there is no ACK that it was actually delivered to the publisher. In addition, the publisher may have received it, but since there is no ACK with a status of try again later or ignored, the relay will no longer send new group requests to the publisher. Resulting in the publisher never starting a new group. The PR states that the publisher may delay the new group request, but it doesn't clearly state that the original publisher MUST maintain this request state because it will never receive a new request after this until it starts a new group. Suggest "**Original Publisher Handling:**"...  Some applications may not want to maintain this state and would prefer to get a request again from subscribers if it still needs it. 

5. Subscribe updates are not currently defined in MOQT to be queued and flooded or reconciled by the relay when peering/inter-relay communication is established. In other words, there maybe be a disconnect from the subscriber relay and the original publisher relay when new group request is sent. The PR does indicate that if the subscribe comes in with new-group request, that state would be maintained, but it does not mention anything about what happens to subscribe updates when there is this break of communication in the middle... This would result in the relay holding on to pending state that it sent new group request, but that actually was dropped in the middle with no feedback to the relay. 

6. There is lack of clarity mentioned for how the relay should handle multiple new group requests with different group ID's, which could be zero as well. If current group is 10 and subscriber 1 asks for 20 and subscriber 2 asks for 8 and subscribe 3 asks for 50, which new-group request group-id do we send to the original publisher?

7. Considering there is no ACK for the subscriber that new group will be handled or has been handled, the subscriber will have no choice but to continue to send new group requests when receiving objects that haven't changed to the new requested group. This would result in flood.

comments.body: This dramatically complex inter-relay communication having to maintain state in more than one relay based on a publish that happened in the past where the relay had no subscribers.  It also is overly complex with multi-publisher where not all publishers will indicate new group or not. Tracking that state and sending to subscriber is more complex in that we have to send new group in OK to subscriber if at least one publisher supports it. When the subscriber sends it, I suspect we are to send it only to the publisher that said it would support it. This requires additional state with inter-relay protocol.

Params are ignored if not supported. The publisher should just ignore it if it doesn't support the param in the update or subscribe.  This is redundant to that and adds complexity where it's not needed.

In the case of peering/inter-relay, there is no ACK that new-group-request was actually sent to the publisher. `PENDING` state in this case could only be cleared if the relay receives a new group, which it may never receive if the publisher didn't get or decided to ignore it. This would result in subsequent requests for new group to be suppressed until then... which could be indefinitely.
Based on feedback from the working group, this is a must-have from the live-stream folks who want nothing to do with these updates.  The complexity is fairly minimal.

You are missing the second half of that sentence...

> ...if the publisher did not include DYNAMIC_GROUPS=1 when establishing the subscription

The subscriber sends PUBLISH_OK in response to PUBLISH.  Yes I believe this is correct.

See #781 - in effect, this parameter is part of the track state and has to be preserved.  We may end up with a slightly different design to address extensibility in which case we can migrate this parameter to that design.  Relays already have to track state about existing subscriptions so I can't believe that an additional bit is harmful.
Tim, it seems each relay would individually know this with no need to synchronize it across the relay mesh

There sort of is the ACK in the sense that all of the control messages are over a reliable transport but if some relay looses it, I agree but I don't see this as a problem. I think systems that use new groups at all are likely to pick a periodic update where they do a new group even if none were requested and it will be easy to see this problem in metrics.
I was imagining this happen on each individual relay with no sharing the info across the mesh of relays.

The key issue here is not if the original publisher supports it but if all the relays on the path support it. 

It might make more sense if we described it like publisher sets flag "FEATURE_NGR_SUPPORTED" to true and it is passed across the subscription path, any relays that does not support MUST change it to false, then subscriber can only use the feature it it is supported. It might make sense to make that a more generic mechanism that could be used to negotiate other features across the relay path.

@fluffy , I believe that makes an assumption that the inter-relay protocol is MOQT hop-by-hop. My understanding is that MOQT is not defining inter-relay protocol.  Has that changed? 

My two-cents are that this is a publisher capability exchange for subscribers, which is the first that needs to be conveyed to every subscriber via `SUBSCRIBE_OK`.  This is new and is pretty significant. If MOQT is going to start advertising capabilities of publishers to subscribers, then wouldn't there be more in the very near future? Either by this draft or by subsequent follow-up drafts that add publisher capabilities (aka params) that need to be made available to subscribers?  I'm supported of having that as a feature, but I do feel that this isn't solving how we sustain one or more publisher capability advertisements to subscribers. How we do that also needs to take into account multi-publisher for the same track.

Subsequent RFC/drafts to this protocol will likely add more params. Those params will end up going to the publisher, no different than new group request. Why go to this level just for new group? Sounds like the live-stream folks are interested in param/update filtering.  Basically, notify me of X but not Y.  Do not include params that I do not support.  This is classic capabilities exchange on params.

An issue here is that the publisher may not support NGR and the subscriber is unaware of that, resulting in repeated attempts for NGR from the subscriber to no avail. This causes a lot of churn for both the relays and publisher. 

The NGR capability being advertised appears like a good idea to notify the subscriber, but IMHO, this opens a bit of pandora's box. 

NGR is just one capability, there will likely be many more capabilities that are similar to NGR over time. 

MOQT should just facilitate the exchange of capabilities of a publisher to subscribers.

If the capabilities were made available to the subscriber, then the subscriber can act accordingly. If the edge relay can provide in-depth filtering (aka support the capability inspection and enforcement), then it can filter a subscriber sending NGR or other params that shouldn't result in notifying the publisher. 

I see this as an edge relay function, which requires publisher capabilities to be known.  If we go this route, then `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE` params  need to be marked on where they should go.   Some params are only meant for auth and to go to auth servers, others are meant for the local relay to control/influence the direct subscription delivery, some are notifications to the publisher, ...

Talking with @suhasHere, he indicated that the intent of group ID is another form of dampening. Basically, upon NGR, the relay will go into pending state for the NGR regardless of the group ID. Additional NGRs from other subscribers will be ignored if their NGR groupId is `less than or equal` to the current NGR group ID that is already pending.  Upon receiving `group != previous group`, the relay clears the state of any NGRs that were received during the initial pending request.  Thus allowing a new NGR to start the process again.

This works when NGR GIDs are high to low, but it gets really ugly when the NGR GID is low to high. 

For example: 

Subscriber 1 NGR group_id=100 (**forwarded to publisher with GID=100**)
Subscriber 2 NGR group_id=5 (ignored, less than previous pending)
Subscriber 3 NGR group_id=90 (ignored, less than previous pending)
Subscriber 4 NGR group+id=101 (**forwarded to publisher with GID=101**)

Publisher receives NGRs for group 100 and group 101.

Having the group id introduces complexity, causing arch self inflicted pain, which Suhas has slides on to describe why subscriber 4 NGR needs to be sent. Performing this function to send multiple NGRs while one is still pending  exposes, IMHO, a major DoS issue where there are no guards around max number of NGRs from a subscriber, allowing a subscriber or many subscribers to send unlimited `NGR++`.  

For example, a for loop of group_id++ sending NGRs.  Based on the current text in the PR, those all would be forwarded to the publisher and would require state updates for each in the relay.The publisher would have to deal with the churn of a for loop of NGRs... likely causing a publisher DoS. 

Nowhere in the PR text/spec does it say that the original publisher SHOULD NOT use the group id in the request. If the publisher application actually uses the group id sent in the NGR, then it would be feasible that the publisher may ignore ones that are either invalid due to current state or way off into the future.  If the publisher ignores it for one reason or another, it would cause a DoS in that relays would get stuck in PENDING state for group change that may not happen. The publisher may simply have dropped the invalid NGR, but would have accepted another that had a reasonable GID.  For example, had `NGR group_id=5` been sent the publisher would have responded with a new group.

I believe I'm on the same page as @gwendalsimon  in that NGR with or without GID is application/publisher specific. Timing is a factor as well as GID if GID is provided. Receiving a NGR too soon might result in no group change. Receiving a NGR for a GID that is too high or to low might also be ignored. Receiving a NGR that is in the correct range would result in actual group change. 

Having GID as part of NGR opens the door for all kinds of other uses, such as allowing subscribers to quiesce on a new group that might be +2 of HEAD.   If MOQT doesn't want the applications/publishers do to that, then it should be very clear that it MUST or SHOULD NOT do that.

@afrind, "since we forward DYNAMIC_GROUPS" is an assumption for inter-relay communication. AFAIK, MOQT is not defining inter-relay protocol.  As mentioned in other comments, DYNAMIC_GROUPS is a publisher edge relay side capability/filter. It is also only known when a publisher connects. We support lingering subscribers, where subscribers join before the publisher. We do this of course to support meetings where publishers (aka participant of a meeting) disconnects and reconnects, which will not result in resubscribe churn. Item 2 is more challenging in terms of DoS, which I mentioned in other comments. 

Talked with Suhas about this and it's a bit more of a problem than what I originally wrote. He is supposed to do an update to this PR to fix some of the issues with ZERO value regarding when we forward NGR (updates) or not. For example, `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE` NGR **CANNOT** have a **ZERO** value for group ID.  Only the `SUBSCRIBE` can have that. Allowing ZERO for `SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE` NGR using the text in the PR would result in applications just using ZERO all the time. After all, as an application subscriber developer, where does it say I can't use zero all the time and why would I care to use a group ID when ZERO is allowed and works to start a new group?   Per the text in the PR, this would result in flooding updates to the publisher(s) regardless of `less than or equal to last NGR`.

Reliable transmission of control messages is fine and not an issue. The issue is about how does the subscriber know that the NGR failed and should be reattempted and how to clear the PENDING state of NGRs on relays when new group doesn't happen?  There are many scenarios where NGRs will be ignored, suppressed, or lost.  The subscriber is completely in the dark and is left only to fire off attempt after attempt to get a new group started.  Relay is also completely in the dark if the publisher got the message and what it is doing about it. The relay just gets stuck in a PENDING state that results in suppression of NGRs, which likely will be a problem.

> Those params will end up going to the publisher, no different than new group request.

Similar to what Victor observed during the last interim, SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE params are all hop-by-hop, since there's no expectation that a new SUBSCRIBE will be sent past the first relay.  This PR defines special handling of NEW_GROUP_REQUEST, and uses SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE to avoid additional message machinery.  There's not a clear path for how we would add another param or message like this in subsequent MoQT versions, since it would require every hop on the path to have support for it.

I think @mzanaty and @wilaw looked hard at how to build something more generic or extensible, but ultimately did not produce a proposal.

> How we do that also needs to take into account multi-publisher for the same track.

I think in this PR, if there are two publishers with different DYNAMIC_GROUPS values for the same Track, I think it still works: one of them would get the NGR and one wouldn't.  I'm not sure that's likely though in the cases we care about.

> The key issue here is not if the original publisher supports it but if all the relays on the path support it.

The relay handling described here is a MUST for Relays, so all Relays on the path do support it.  It's really a question if the Original Publisher supports it.

> An issue here is that the publisher may not support NGR and the subscriber is unaware of that

That's why DYNAMIC_GROUPS needs to be conveyed in SUBSCRIBE_OK/PUBLISH.  If we feel like Params is not a good fit here, consider it a track-level Extension (see #1176).

Regarding Generic Capabilities Exchange:

I think additional Publisher -> Subscriber capabilities can be conveyed in future versions without any additional help from Relays.  However, Subscriber -> Original Publisher messages need some kind of relay support which is tricky.  I'd like to see a concrete proposal and PR to fully understand.

Ok, I see the problem:  If current group is 10 and someone sends NGR=1000000, the OP ignores it and keeps sending the current group.  Then legit subscribers cannot send NGR=11.

My vision is that #1182 / #1159 will soon positively or negatively acknowledge SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE.  In that case, the OP can send a REQUEST_ERROR for invalid NGR, which could clear the state at the relay.

> "since we forward DYNAMIC_GROUPS" is an assumption for inter-relay communication.

In MOQT we describe a single Relay.  If you have a mesh of Relays that act as a single Relay, then it needs to conform to the requirements in the spec.  So yes, in a way.

> MOQT is not defining inter-relay protocol

100% agree, but see above.  You can use any inter-relay protocol you want.  The requirement is if you are a Relay, you include DYNAMIC_GROUPS in the SUBSCRIBE_OK/PUBLISH if you received it.

> We support lingering subscribers, where subscribers join before the publisher.

I'm pretty sure sending the SUBSCRIBE_OK before having an upstream subscription is now disallowed.  If the subscriber shows up first it should use SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, and then it will get a PUBLISH.

> Per the text in the PR, this would result in flooding updates to the publisher(s) regardless of less than or equal to last NGR.

I'm not sure restricting 0 to SUBSCRIBE will prevent a DoS of the OP, since an attacker can just send SUBSCRIBE.  But also, if SUBSCRIBE has 0 but there's already a subscription, the relay needs to send SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE with NGR=0, so I don't think we can restrict it.
See above comment regarding REQUEST_OK / REQUEST_ERROR as a solution to #1003

> Ok, I see the problem: If current group is 10 and someone sends NGR=1000000, the OP ignores it and keeps sending the current group. Then legit subscribers cannot send NGR=11.

I don't think that's true.  A new subscriber can still send 11 and it will work .

> A new subscriber can still send 11 and it will work .

How?  11 < 10000000 and the relay has not seen a new group to clear the old request.

The OP supporting NGR cannot ignore the request. It will send the next group based on its application logic (may be delayed) and that should clear the one for 10000000.  

Yes something like this can cause subscribers to not get new group for a while until OP sends a new group, but it cannot block things indefinitely. 

However, if OP decides to never start a new group in which case the expected behavior on the subscriber is same regardless of what group Id is carried in  NGR.  This seems like application level issue and should not to be dealt at moq level and I think i did clarify this to Tim as well.

In this case a publisher saying i am capable of NGR is an optimization for the first hop and I am bit unsure of generic capabilities exchange as it defines its own sub protocol inside another protocol. Agree with @afrind a more concrete proposal/issue will help understand better

comments.body:
Is this original publisher?  Because this is required for relays, correct?

```suggestion
original publisher does not support dynamic Groups, it ignores the parameter in that
```
Fair point.
Is it valid to combine this with Forward=0?
You might send SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE before receiving SUBSCRIBE_OK, but I can infer that you mean the text to cover that case?
It seems a little mean to send NGR Forward=0, but not sure if we want to make it an error.
Good catch, can you suggest the change you want, if any?  Just allow it in SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE and the publisher can ignore?

This text applies to any publisher (including relays).  eg: 

```
P->R: PUBLISH (DYNAMIC_GROUPS=0)
// track discovery out of band
S->R: SUBSCRIBE (NGR)
// relay ignores NGR
```
I'm ok with leaving this as is, but it is odd.

```suggestion
The MAX_CACHE_DURATION parameter (Parameter Type 0x04) MAY appear in a PUBLISH,
SUBSCRIBE_OK, FETCH_OK or TRACK_STATUS_OK message.  It is an integer expressing
the number of milliseconds an object can be served from a cache. If present, the
relay MUST NOT start forwarding any individual Object received through this
subscription or fetch after the specified number of milliseconds has elapsed
since the beginning of the Object was received.  This means Objects earlier in a
multi-object stream will expire earlier than Objects later in the stream. Once
Objects have expired from cache, their state becomes unknown, and a relay that
handles a downstream request that includes those Objects re-requests them.
```

```suggestion
continue to attempt forwarding Objects after they have been received.  The start
time for the timeout is based on when the beginning of the Object is received,
and does not depend upon the forwarding preference. There is no explicit signal
that an Object was not sent because the delivery timeout was exceeded.
```

pulls.title: Security considerations on Relay: ANNOUNCE and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE considerations
pulls.author: sharmafb
pulls.body:
If an endpoint sends a relay a large number of ANNOUNCE or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE messages, the relay would be required to store the mappings, potentially forever. A flood of bogus namespaces could bloat data structures on a relay that store namespace tables. This PR adds some language in the "Security considerations" section in order to encourage implementations to guard against this.

Resolves #1094

comments.body:
```suggestion
A Relay SHOULD have mechanisms to prevent malicious endpoints from flooding it
with PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE requests that could bloat data
structures. It could use the advertised MAX_REQUEST_ID to limit the number of
such requests, or could have application-specific policies that can reject
incoming PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE requests that cause the state
maintenance for the session to be excessive.
```

```suggestion
A Relay connects publishers and subscribers by managing sessions based on the
Track Namespace or Full Track Name. When a SUBSCRIBE message is sent, its Full
Track Name is matched exactly against existing upstream subscriptions.

Namespace Prefix Matching is further used to decide which publishers receive a
SUBSCRIBE and which subscribers receive a PUBLISH. In this process, the tuples
in the Track Namespace are matched sequentially, requiring an exact match for
each field. If the published or subscribed Track Namespace has the same or fewer
fields than the Track Namespace in the message, it qualifies as a match.

For example:
A SUBSCRIBE message with namespace=(foo, bar) and name=x will match sessions
that sent PUBLISH_NAMESPACE messages with namespace=(foo) or namespace=(foo,
bar).  It will not match a session with namespace=(foobar).

Relays MUST forward SUBSCRIBE messages to all matching publishers and
PUBLISH_NAMESPACE or PUBLISH messages to all matching subscribers.

```

The original set of publishers matched may be different (changed) by the time ERROR response is received. > I can see how this might make sense for fetch but it seems to really complicate subscribe and I don't see the use cases it solves. To be specific, I can not imagine a subscriber where I want groups 100 to 200, then skip group 201 to 299, then give me groups 300 to 400.

Sparse non-contiguous ranges are really a filter use-case for FETCH. Since we want a common filter parameter between FETCH and SUBSCRIBE, these just won't be used much in SUBSCRIBE, but will be used with FETCH. 

For SUBSCRIBE, the use-cases for filters outside of Sparse non-contiguous ranges are quite real and some examples are described below. Additionally, when combined with extensions, we get some very nice behaviors. 

1. Sensors send temperature summary data in the first Object of each Group, then updates every minute as a new object. I want to monitor only the summary data by receiving only the first object in every group
FILTER ( =, object ID, 0 )

1. A live video feed codes its groups using unix epoch time. I want to subscribe to the feed starting  tonight at 7pm 
FILTER ( >, group ID, 1752138462)

1. Only forward me live security camera groups where the activity level is greater than or equal to 25%. The activity level is added to each object as the custom extension with a type of 400.
FILTER (>=, extension 400, 25)

1. Only forward me live temperature data from zip code 94925. The zip code is stored as the custom extension header 1444.
FILTER (=, extension 1444, 94925)

1. Only forward me log data from the media player with subscriber ID 847362511. The subscriber ID is sent in extension header 768 by the media player.
FILTER (=, extension 768, 847362511)

comments.author: mzanaty
comments.body:
In the Toronto interim, it was decided to setup a design team for object/track filters (PR#1164, I#441, 1068, 1206). Mo, Martin, Suhas, Victor, Will, YK volunteered. Please let me know if you want to join these meetings. Next meeting is Friday October 10 at 9:00am PDT.
Immediately after the interim, we had an impromptu initial meeting with the folks still lingering in Toronto: Mo, Victor, Cullen, Mike, Magnus. We converged on a simplified design.
- The 'Operands' were removed in favor of separate parameter types for each filter type.
- The 'Values' array was removed in favor of a single range, Start/End inclusive with no delta coding. End=0 means no end unless Start=0. For multiple ranges, use multiple parameters.
- The 'Negation' flag was removed. We discussed allowing Start>End to mean negation. Maybe unnecessary, since any desired ranges can be expressed without negation using an extra range. For example, not 3-7 can be expressed as 0-2 and 8-0.
- The track filter only specifies NumberOfTopTracks. The selection metric is a new Selector extension. Some folks preferred this opaque Selector to avoid leaking private info, so the relay network is not aware these are voice activity, temperature, etc. metrics. However, this means only a single metric can be the Selector for all subscribers. An alternative is to specify the extension ID as well, which can be the Selector or another extension. List feedback preferred this alternative.
- A setup parameter will negotiate the number of filter ranges supported, including 0 to disable support.

comments.author: mzanaty
comments.body:
Nov 5, 2025 design meeting with Martin, Mo, Suhas, Y.K.

On Wed, Nov 5, 2025 at 8:36 AM Martin Duke (martin.h.duke@gmail.com) wrote:

1. SUBSCRIBE and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE (and PUBLISH_OK and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE) in one PR, FETCH in a separate PR.
3. Add three parameters; start location, end group, and next group. If there is no start location or next group parameter, the default will be Largest Object. Mo will add text that makes Largest Object clearer to him.
4. We believe this retains all the capabilities of the existing framework in the editors' draft.
5. All parameters and filters have an AND relationship. To be delivered, an object has to comply with all parameters and filters.
6. For FETCH, we will retain start and end location fields. the new parameters do not apply. The filters do.
7. SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE can have all these filters and parameters. They are default applied to any PUBLISHes that arrive in that namespace. PUBLISH_OK is always sent, and can update the filters/parameters for a specific subscription in that NAMESPACE.
However, any SUBSCRIBE in that namespace does not inherit params/filters from SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE.
8. Add a field to track selection filter to SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE called 'latch-time' on how long a publisher should remain in the relay's table without publishing an update on its metric.
9. If two tracks have the same metric, the relay will continue to forward the one that it's already forwarding to break the tie.
10. There is a track selection filter field 'max deselected tracks'. When the number of open PUBLISHes exceeds the limit, the publisher MUST send PUBLISH_DONE to bound receiver state. The fields 'max tracks' is meant to bound incoming message traffic, which is a different constraint.

pulls.title: Parameters for Group Order, Subscribe Priority and Subscription Filter
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
Note: This is targeted against PR #1209.

This is a proposal based on the most recent discussion of parameters and extensibility.  

It moves Group Order and Subscriber Priority to parameters in SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, PUBLISH, PUBLISH_OK.  The PR specifies a value for the receiver to use if the parameter is omitted.

It defines a structure for a Subscription Filter as it exists today.  
  * The wire format for SUBSCRIBE and PUBLISH_OK use this directly (not as a param, no wire format change)
  * SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is changed to accept a parameter containing this filter when the subscriber wants to change it

Items of note:

1. This adds a new filter type "No Filter", addressing #1035.
2. Relative filter types are only allowed in SUBSCRIBE, because they require the SUBSCRIBE_OK containing Largest to communicate what actually happened, but maybe this could be relaxed?
3. The values used by Group Order are different depending on the message.  This preserves existing behavior while eliminating the "Default" wire value previously allowed in SUBSCRIBE.
4. Forward is retained as a Fixed field, rather than in all messages where it appears.  This is based on the fact that there's no sensible "common" value.
5. Other than Forward, everything that can be changed in SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is now a parameter, and omitted means "unchanged".

Fixes: #872 
Fixes: #878 
Fixes: #1035 
Closes: #1043
Closes: #1044 
Closes: #1059
Closes: #1046

> the weaknesses of this approach is that in the non caching relay case, it does not aggregate the upstream requests for new groups and in the other case of a caching relay, it does get a new group but instead floods the subscriber will all the objects in the group of to that point.

Both caching and non-caching relays can (and probably should) aggregate upstream fetches for the same data.

That said, I think the limitation that "min group duration == max cache duration" is significant. When to start a new group can be a bit more than just an sufficient time has passed. Publishers might want to sync with a camera angle change for example.

I think we would want a new parameter for this because many things will have cache durations that are much longer than the max group length. For example, a streaming video might want to make a new group every 30 seconds during normal playout but be willing to make them every 5 seconds when new people are joining and want to cache data for 30 minutes so viewers can scrub back and see older stuff.

But this will return all the frames that have been produced up to this point in the groups and that is a huge chunk of bandwidth which likely will not work. The app is trying to request a group to get a new join point exactly so it does not need to do a fetch of all this old frames and the bandwidth that requires.

In the case of many downstream subscribers all joining and roughly the same time and a non caching relay, this would result in each one of them creating a separate upstream request which we explicitly want to avoid because it causes "start of service" attack on the original publisher

pulls.title: Parameters for Group Order, Subscribe Priority and Subscription Filter (redo)
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
Note: this is a redo of #1210, targeted against main

This is a proposal based on the most recent discussion of parameters and extensibility.  

It moves Group Order and Subscriber Priority to parameters in SUBSCRIBE, SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, PUBLISH, PUBLISH_OK.  The PR specifies a value for the receiver to use if the parameter is omitted.

It defines a structure for a Subscription Filter as it exists today.  
  * The wire format for SUBSCRIBE and PUBLISH_OK use this directly (not as a param, no wire format change)
  * SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is changed to accept a parameter containing this filter when the subscriber wants to change it

Items of note:

1. This adds a new filter type "No Filter", addressing #1035.
2. Relative filter types are only allowed in SUBSCRIBE, because they require the SUBSCRIBE_OK containing Largest to communicate what actually happened, but maybe this could be relaxed?
3. The values used by Group Order are different depending on the message.  This preserves existing behavior while eliminating the "Default" wire value previously allowed in SUBSCRIBE.
4. Forward is retained as a Fixed field, rather than in all messages where it appears.  This is based on the fact that there's no sensible "common" value.
5. Other than Forward, everything that can be changed in SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is now a parameter, and omitted means "unchanged".

Fixes: #872 
Fixes: #878 
Fixes: #1035 
Closes: #1043

pulls.title: Allow joining FETCH for PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE forward=1
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
This also restricts joining fetch to subscriptions in Forward State=1, since joining a subscription in Forward State 0 does not have the intended "no gaps" effect.

This means that subscriptions initiated in Forward=0 need to update the join point when Forward transitions to 1.  Possible flow:

```
P->S: PUBLISH, Forward=0, Largest Object={10, 5}
P: Object 11,0
S->P: PUBLISH_OK, Forward=1
S->P: Joining FETCH
P->S: FETCH_OK, End=11,0 (inclusive)
P->S (fetch stream): 11,0
P->S (subscribe stream): Object 11,1
```

Note in the above flow, a standalone FETCH to Largest Object would miss 11,0.

This PR also allows re-joining a track that was temporarily in Forward=0:

```
S->P: SUBSCRIBE, Forward=1
S->P: Joining FETCH
...
S->P: SUBSCRIBE_UDPATE, Forward=0
...
S->P: SUBSCRIBE_UDPATE, Forward=1
S->P: Joining FETCH
P->S: REQUEST_OK, Largest={21,0}
P->S (fetch stream): Object 21,0
```

Addresses an issue raised in #1313

Fixes #1310
Fixes #1305

  1) Don't send REQUEST_ERROR on errors, QUIC RESET_STREAM with the application error code. Loses Reason Phrase

  3) Allow for subscribing to full Track names and not just Namespaces.
  4) Prohibit sending NAMESPACE_DONE before a NAMESPACE is received for a SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE
  5) Add a PUBLISH_BLOCKED sent on the response stream when a new PUBLISH couldn't be sent #1262

I was thinking maybe we should try to align with a scheme that already exists, so we don't need to write another encoder.  The proposed scheme is close to URL Safe encoding, which allows only 0-9, A-Z, a-z and these four characters:

- (hyphen) (ASCII 45)
. (dot) (ASCII 46)
_ (underscore) (ASCII 95)
~ (tilde) (ASCII 126)

But to use that, we can't select `.` and `-` as tuple and name separators.  So if we chose, say `/` and `+`, you could do:

`result = '/'.join(map(urllib.parse.quote, namespace)) + '+' + urllib.parse.quote(name)`

Examples:

```
namespace = ['simple', 'path', 'no-specials]
name = 'track'
```

`simple/path/no-specials+track`

```
namespace = ['path', 'with spaces', 'and special chars!']
name = 'hello world'
```

`path/with%20spaces/and%20special%20chars%21+hello%20world`

We discussed Largest Group quite a long time ago, didn't we?

One point is kind of philosophical: FETCH is for the past, SUBSCRIBE is for the present and the future. Largest Group for SUBSCRIBE breaks this rule.

More practically, we have the case where the Relay does not have the first Objects of the current group (because it does not have a cache, or because these Objects are too old to be delivered from cache, or because it did not have any active Subscription at the time these Objects were delivered). It may send the same request upstream, but the upstream Relay or the Original Publisher may have started a new Group. To be safe, the Relay should send a FETCH instead.

SUBSCRIBE returns Objects less than Largest Location today, since you can specify an absolute range.  This just avoids the latency of doing a TRACK_STATUS then issuing a SUBSCRIBE starting at the Group you want.

pulls.title: RFC: Fetch is dead
pulls.author: ianswett
pulls.body:
Removes Fetch and Joining Fetch in favor of moving to a Subscribe model that uses a single bidirectional control stream per Subscription.  Does not change how Objects are sent.

Removes Request ID from SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE, but not entirely.

Adds the 'Relative Past Group (0x5)' filter type to replicate the relative joining fetch functionality.

Some open PRs need to land for this to fully come together, so this is more of a proof-of-concept.

This is currently parked in favor of the more incremental change to move Requests to bidi streams, #1389

Fixes #1391
Fixes #1343
Fixes #1313 
Fixes #1168
Fixes #1039

May Fix #861

comments.author: acbegen
comments.body:
Having "fetch" functionality within Subscribe or as a separate message has been discussed in the past. Following the [slides](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/119/materials/slides-119-moq-subscribe-and-fetch) (slides 16-17) and then the subsequent [PR](https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/421).

I am curious whether we should reopen this discussion. Having something in the spec for 1.5 years and having people implement it, then changing it completely, I think, deserves some strong justification. Keeping Subscribe and Fetch separate, I thought, was also something those who did not want to implement Fetch wanted in the first place.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
I have to say this was not what I expected as a solution based on the earlier discussion. I thought the main solution to #1343 was to send control messages on different streams so there would be no HOL and you have a request context for updates. On #1313 I thought the obvious solution was to create a new verb that represents the combination. I think bunching all under subscribe have several impacts which I don't think necessary are in the best interest for the WG:

1. The name of the verb does not represent what the protocol does
2. It makes the separation into different implementation capabilities more unclear as it would not follow along the line of verb. A relay might only support subscribe, or subscribe+fetch, or be capable of joining fetch. Because I think it has been clear that there are usage of the protocol that has no need of caching or what was happening in the past, only what is being published after the end subscriber joined.
3. It will make it hard to discuss as we can't just subscribe, you have to make clear which mode of operations you are talking about.  
4. Although renaming all as part of Subscribe may in fact not be larger than keeping different verbs it still gives the impression that the WG is not making progress on the protocol and that we reshuffeling things completely again. 

So I have to ask is there actually a gain in deleting the verb names in favor calling all Subscribe? Are we actually getting anything additionally from that part of the change?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
> My biggest problem with FETCH is how it introduces head-of-line blocking. A relay has to merge N input streams (object ID ascending) into 1 output stream (group+object ID ascending).

This is only a thing if you are trying to FETCH live object, which is not something MOQT supports.  A FETCH response always ends at Largest Object, even if the requested end is larger.  So you construct the fetch response from your cache, or by sending a FETCH upstream, or some mixture of both.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> > My biggest problem with FETCH is how it introduces head-of-line blocking. A relay has to merge N input streams (object ID ascending) into 1 output stream (group+object ID ascending).
> 
> This is only a thing if you are trying to FETCH live object, which is not something MOQT supports. A FETCH response always ends at Largest Object, even if the requested end is larger. So you construct the fetch response from your cache, or by sending a FETCH upstream, or some mixture of both.

What I mean by interleaving N streams, is interleaving N sources of objects: 
- one stream might be a group from cold storage (ex. fetched from S3 via HTTP)
- another might be a cached group from a SUBSCRIBE (in RAM, not really a stream)
- another might be a FETCH for a potential gap within that cached group (ex. object 68 is missing, does it exist?)
- another might be an live group from a SUBSCRIBE **that is smaller than Largest Object**

The last one is because groups and objects arrive out of order on purpose. You can totally have a "live object" that it is smaller than Largest Object and should be served via FETCH, but it hasn't arrived yet due to congestion. Yes a relay *could* issue a FETCH instead of waiting for the stream to finish, but it's kind of silly to have a FETCH overlap with an active SUBSCRIBE (just wait instead of downloading it twice).

In general it's a pain in the butt being forced to serve objects in order. I think this all gets fixed if FETCH could serve sub-groups independently just like SUBSCRIBE. The end user experience would also be better because objects can be immediately served from cache (utilizing the network), instead of blocking on the fetch from cold storage. It's the same concept behind being able to serve HTTP/2/3 responses in parallel instead of HTTP/1 pipelining.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
>  I think this all gets fixed if FETCH could serve sub-groups independently just like SUBSCRIBE.

+1 . The original design of the FETCH response as a single stream was an imagined convenience stemming from the assumption that all the objects were in cache and therefore easily sequence-able. Implementation experience shows this to be otherwise. In many cases all the objects _will_ be in cache and easily sequence-able and the relay _may_ indeed use a single stream to return them. But in the case that they are not, flexibility should be allowed. A client that is capable of receiving SUBSCRIBE response can also correctly receive the FETCH across across multiple streams.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: One of the design requirements of FETCH was "I can tell I got everything" and "I know what does not exist".  Delivering subgroups out of order in different streams breaks this property.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> One of the design requirements of FETCH was "I can tell I got everything" and "I know what does not exist". Delivering subgroups out of order in different streams breaks this property.

That is a design requirement for SUBSCRIBE too. Otherwise, it's not possible to implement a HLS/DASH-like experience where media is buffered instead of skipped.

ex. A player issues a SUBSCRIBE and receives group 6 and group 8. The player buffers waiting for 7, but it may never arrive if the group was dropped or never existed.

I understand the design that head-of-line blocking acts an implicit signal that 7 doesn't exist because 8 was served next. However, you could have an explicit message instead: `OBJECT_DROPPED` or something. Same result but without the performance ramifications of HoLB and it would also work for SUBSCRIBE.

This would also take the guess-work out of PUBLISH_DONE's `Stream Count`. Every object between start-end would be accounted for, either received via a data stream or skipped via a `OBJECT_DROPPED` range.


why is UNSUBSCRIBE dead as well? Collateral victim?

pulls.author: gwendalsimon
pulls.body:
Fixes #1354 ... which addressed six previous issues.

Credits to @wilaw and @acbegen

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I would prefer a mechanism that supports at least simple server-side ABR as well as client-side ABR, and I think that's possible without much extra work.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> I would prefer a mechanism that supports at least simple server-side ABR as well as client-side ABR, and I think that's possible without much extra work.

I do not think that is a good approach. I support server-side switching, but it has some fundament differences with what is being proposed here. Mixing the two behaviors into the same message is going to complicate switching. Current SWITCH is executed once and requires only two inputs - the track you switch from and track you switch to. A server-side switch would have to be persistent and it requires threshold values at which the switches should be made. 

Server-side switching has many similarities to a persistent, conditional filter - it lets one track through at a time based on the estimated throughput. **And we already have a proposal to filter TOP N tracks. It is persistent.  If we extended the FILTER proposal to allow switching based on estimated-throughput (in addition to the current extension header) and we set N to 1, then we would have server-side ABR.** That seems architecturally a cleaner approach to implementing server-side switching with MOQT than overloading a message designed to implement clean client-side switching.

comments.body:
If i recall from a few ietf meetings on this topic, Absolute Joining Fetch was added to support this exact functionality . I am specifically referring to this slide here:

https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1YPLTpHjrJpNUtjvw58fAvE2NhiWHjuptDwTcjaRvVcI/edit?slide=id.g331a8043eb5_0_156#slide=id.g331a8043eb5_0_156

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> If i recall from a few ietf meetings on this topic, Absolute Joining Fetch was added to support this exact functionality . I am specifically referring to this slide here:
> 
> https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1YPLTpHjrJpNUtjvw58fAvE2NhiWHjuptDwTcjaRvVcI/edit?slide=id.g331a8043eb5_0_156#slide=id.g331a8043eb5_0_156
> 
> As per consensus call, we decided to add Absolute Joining Fetch. May be this is already discussed, is there a reason that will still not work or are we advocating that absolute joining fetch needs to be removed ?

You are right, we introduced Absolute Joining FETCH to implement a switch at the next transition group for subscribers who are behind the live stream. We note however:
- The whole process is circumvoluted ([slide 11](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1YPLTpHjrJpNUtjvw58fAvE2NhiWHjuptDwTcjaRvVcI/edit?slide=id.g350a88e60c9_0_0#slide=id.g350a88e60c9_0_0)) For a simple SWITCH, it requires the subscriber to send 4 messages, with risk at every step
- At some point of the switch, the link between relay to subscriber has 3 ongoing data flows (the subscribe of old track, the subscribe of new track, and the fetch). It is very bad especially for those who switch due to network congestion. At the time we presented this solution, it was said that priorities can handle this concurrency of flows but #1101 showed that, in practice, it is not possible
- The Subscriber does not know the status at the Relay, in particular it does not know whether the Absolute Joining FETCH is about Objects that are cached at the Relay or not. In practice, it happens that the Subscriber asks for Absolute Joining FETCH at the next group (which is not gap-friendly btw) and the Relay takes too much time to get it, or cannot get it at all.

Overall this solution UNSUBSCRIBE+SUBSCRIBE+Absolute Joining FETCH+SUBSCRIBE_UPDATE is overly complicated for a single operation and not efficient in practice.
