comments.body: Does this new “SWITCH” control message create a new bidirectional stream, similar to the other “six message types” defined in the v17 specification? If so, it would be good to include some clarification on this.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> Does this new “SWITCH” control message create a new bidirectional stream, similar to the other “six message types” defined in the v17 specification? If so, it would be good to include some clarification on this.

Thank you for the question. The PR has since been revised and this is now explicit.

SWITCH itself is sent on the control stream; it does not create a new bidirectional stream. In response to a SWITCH, the Relay opens a PUBLISH bidirectional stream for the target Track. The subscriber does not need to pre-allocate any Request ID; the Relay initiates the PUBLISH directly. In case of failure, the Relay opens the same PUBLISH stream and immediately sends PUBLISH_DONE with an appropriate Status Code.

This is now described in the updated PR.

comments.author: yuyou
comments.body:
The SWITCH is a key feature and addon to the Relay and the Subscriber as many  use cases need a feature like this.

Based on our experimental implementation, here comes with some suggestions for discussion:

1. Explicit timeout: Make the "`implementation-specific timeout  T_switch`” explicitly in the SWITCH message, either a new property or re-use RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT;
2. Explicit priority for catch-up: current PR says “`The Relay SHOULD assign a higher QUIC stream priority to this catch-up stream than to any concurrent SUBGROUP_HEADER streams for the target Track until the catch-up stream is closed`”: suggest adding a priority delta to the SWITCH message, if it helps.
3. Also for streams with large group sizes, switching at group boundaries may not always be the best option if a fast or hard SWITCH is needed. Please consider adding a way to instruct the Relay to do a hard and **deterministic** switch, as the switching may take **non-deterministic** time and wait for the next group boundary. It may be fast if the switching is already close to the end of a group; or be slow if the switching happens to the beginning of a long group.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> The SWITCH is a key feature and addon to the Relay and the Subscriber as many use cases need a feature like this.
> 
> Based on our experimental implementation, here comes with some suggestions for discussion:
> 
> 1. Explicit timeout: Make the "`implementation-specific timeout  T_switch`” explicitly in the SWITCH message, either a new property or re-use RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT;

Agreed. A dedicated `SWITCH_TIMEOUT` parameter would be cleaner than reusing `RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT`, which has different semantics.

> 2. Explicit priority for catch-up: current PR says “`The Relay SHOULD assign a higher QUIC stream priority to this catch-up stream than to any concurrent SUBGROUP_HEADER streams for the target Track until the catch-up stream is closed`”: suggest adding a priority delta to the SWITCH message, if it helps.

A good suggestion, though specifying the semantics precisely (units, baseline, interaction with `SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY`) adds complexity that may outweigh the benefit at this stage. The SHOULD gives relays sufficient flexibility; if experience shows otherwise, a parameter can be added in a follow-on.

> 3. Also for streams with large group sizes, switching at group boundaries may not always be the best option if a fast or hard SWITCH is needed. Please consider adding a way to instruct the Relay to do a hard and **deterministic** switch, as the switching may take **non-deterministic** time and wait for the next group boundary. It may be fast if the switching is already close to the end of a group; or be slow if the switching happens to the beginning of a long group.

Excellent use case. Worth noting that with the current spec, a subscriber at Group 10 can already set `Minimum Switching Group ID` = 10 to get an immediate switch: the relay opens Track B right away and delivers Group 10 from Object 0. The player is responsible for handling the buffered Track A data for that group. This is the fastest gapless path available today.

An idea is a `Request New Group` field: when set, the relay issues `NEW_GROUP_REQUEST` upstream on both tracks, forcing the publishers to start a new Group as soon as practical. For aligned ABR tracks this creates a synthetic common Group boundary within the publisher's keyframe interval. It would be deterministic and gapless.

In a related topic, @afrind suggested a `Hard Switch` flag. Concretely: subscriber is at Group 10, relay has Groups 11 from both Track A and Track B in cache, subscriber sends `SWITCH` with `Minimum Switching Group ID` = 11. By default, the relay finishes delivering Track A Group 10 before opening Track B at Group 11. It is the expected gapless behavior. With `Hard Switch` = 1, the relay terminates Track A mid-Group 10 and begins Track B at Group 11 immediately, at the cost of a content gap.

Both could be fixed fields in the `SWITCH` message wire format, or Parameters. The latter is the natural extension point, though parameters would require additional spec text to prevent them from being forwarded to the target Track `PUBLISH`

It is the subscriber's responsibility to know that these two tracks are switchable (for example, as part of a CMAF switching set). Being a CMAF switching set, it has sufficient requirements to ensure a seamless switch. If you are not aiming for such a seamless switch, then just use sub/unsub.

The relay does not need to check whether these two tracks are actually "switchable." The group IDs may not be aligned for different reasons and if the relay cannot complete the switch, it will return an error anyway. So, I don't think there is a need for a "disallow" check.

pulls.title: Move SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH, FETCH, TRACK_STATUS, and PUBLISH_NAMESPACE to bidi streams
pulls.author: ianswett
pulls.body:
Removes UNSUBSCRIBE, FETCH_CANCEL, and PUBLISH_NAMESPACE_DONE, replacing them with STOP_SENDING.

Removes MAX_REQUESTS and REQUESTS_BLOCKED.  QUIC Stream limits are used to limit the number of simultaneous requests.

Adds a 'Dependent RequestID' Message Parameter that allows one to make a Request dependent upon a prior Request to achieve the HoLB functionality that is lost by moving to multiple streams.

Fixes #1168
Fixes #1247
Fixes #1336
Fixes #1343
Fixes #1351
Fixes #1070

Could fix #632 if we moved the Fetch Objects to the Response stream
Improves Startup Latency #83 

This PR currently does not move FETCH response Objects to the response of the bidi stream, but it could.  The only negative is we'd be mixing response Objects and any REQUST_OK control messages that result from a REQUEST_UPDATE.

Potential future benefits:
* Provides an obvious place to put extensions like @vasilvv Object ACK proposal
* Could provide data on the Subscription or Track, such as the Largest Object in a Group, or Objects that weren't sent due to Delivery Timeout.

Closes #1505

I tried to write a concrete suggestion, but now I am not sure if we want to only disallow merging of the extension values or also forbid merging/union of the extension set.

Forbidding that would make it possible to drop whole extensions from the cache and make sure that the set is always sensible, but the behavior of known extensions may start to get weird.

Can you clarify what you mean by merging extension values or merging/union of the extension set?  I think the behavior we want is the following:

If the cached track/object has a set of supported extensions X and a set of unknown extensions Y, and we get another extension block for that track/object with supported extensions X' and unknown extensions Y'.  Then the cache SHOULD be updated to contain exactly:

merge_supported(X, X'), Y'

Anything in Y not in Y' is deleted.

"Merging values" (Appending): `{A=1} + {A=2} = {A=1, A=2}`. We don't want this. 

Merge/union of the extension set `{A=1, B=1} + {A=2, C=2}`
  1. Allow union/merge of the set = `{A=2, B=1, C=2}` 
  2. Disallow union/merge of the set = `{A=1, B=1}` or `{A=2, C=2}`. Either one is valid, with preference for the latter. 
  
The text recommends the 2nd option but is missing any hard requirements on the merge handling. I think we need a hard requirement (MUST) that forbids values merging/appending.

comments.body:
> "Filters are parameters in control messages that tell a publisher " ...

Given the possibility of additional filter parameters being defined in the future, it is unclear why all such parameters are restricted to integer values. This constraint limits extensibility, as any future filter that requires a different data type or comparison model would necessitate an update to this draft (or a subsequent RFC) solely to relax that restriction.

To avoid a sequence of follow-on drafts having to revise the core MOQT specification, would it be reasonable to relax this statement and allow each filter parameter to define its own value format and semantics? Allowing filters to specify their own data types and logical comparison behavior would improve extensibility and better accommodate future filtering use cases without requiring changes to the base protocol.

> "A filter parameter with zero length indicates no filter, which MAY
be used in REQUEST_UPDATE to remove the filter." 

Given this definition, allowing the parameter to appear more than once does not seem meaningful. As written, the parameter can be included at most once in a control message, where it replaces any previously received value. A zero-length value removes the previously applied filter, while omission of the parameter results in no change.

As currently defined, this behavior is restrictive and may complicate future extensions. In particular, adding enhanced or additional filtering capabilities in subsequent drafts could require changes to the MOQT draft itself, potentially forcing a MOQT v2 revision. Small design adjustments now—such as introducing filter subtypes or a more extensible structure—would provide better future-proofing and allow new filtering capabilities to be added without revising the base protocol.

Revise `TRACK_FILTER` to allow extendability with subsequent drafts... such as 

```
    TRACK_FILTER { Type=0x2D, Len, SubType, Len, [Filter Parameter Specific]}
```


While multi-publisher (aka one or more publishers send objects using the exact same namespace and name) isn't really handled in MOQT; when/if that does happen track filters would make sense to apply to `SUBSCRIBE` as well, where it could be applied to select which publisher to consume.

> “The TRACK_FILTER parameter (Type 0x2D) selects a specified Extension Type number, which MUST be even (single integer value).”

This definition further illustrates how the current approach is overly restrictive for a broadly scoped parameter intended to support track-level filtering. Semantics such as “highest,” “lowest,” or similar selection logic should not be baked into the base track filter definition. Instead, these behaviors are better expressed as specific track-filter subtypes, with the TRACK_FILTER parameter acting as a container for a set of filtering rules.

Separating the generic track-filter mechanism from subtype-specific semantics would improve clarity and make the design more extensible for future track-level filtering use cases.

The `TRACK_FILTER` parameter is well suited to act as a container for filtering rules that a relay uses to decide whether to forward a PUBLISH, based on subscriber-defined conditions. The relay can evaluate these rules in real time and dynamically adjust its `PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE` forwarding state as conditions evolve.

This model enables a highly adaptive behavior, allowing tracks to be selected or switched dynamically when the rules defined in the `TRACK_FILTER` parameter are satisfied.

By contrast, constraining the mechanism to a single extension-type match followed by “maximum tracks selected” and “maximum tracks deselected” addresses a narrow use case and limits applicability to others. Some filtering rules may not rely on extension header matching at all. For example, a rule could match on a namespace tuple position—such as interpreting tuple element 5 as a region identifier and selecting tracks based on membership in an allowed set of regions—without involving extension headers.

Maintaining an explicit list of deselected tracks is understandable, but it introduces additional complexity that could be avoided while still achieving the same goals of dampening and churn control. For example, consider a set of 100 tracks, of which only 30 qualify to establish state with a subscriber and therefore generate `PUBLISH` messages. Within those 30, only the top N tracks—say 6—are actively forwarded, resulting in 6 tracks with `forward = 1` and the remaining 24 with `forward = 0`. The other 70 tracks never reach the subscriber’s `SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE` at all.

This can be more naturally modeled as candidate selection. In this model, a dynamically ordered candidate list contains the 30 qualifying tracks, while only the top N candidates are marked as forwarding. As the ordering changes, forwarding state is updated accordingly. Tracks may enter or leave the candidate list entirely based on the filter rule logic, and those that no longer qualify are simply removed from the candidate set rather than being explicitly tracked as deselected.

reviews.author: TimEvens
reviews.body:
As written, `MAX_SEND_LOCATION` functions as a group/subgroup-level filter, but it is not clearly described as a filter on subscribed objects. It would be clearer to explicitly define it as an object filter, potentially renaming it to something like `OBJECT_FILTER_MAX_LOCATION` to align with that intent.

My concern with this parameter is that it will introduce churn due to repeated `REQUEST_UPDATE` calls to advance the limit. Additionally, increasing the limit could result in microbursting.

The PR also does not clearly describe the resume semantics when the limit is increased. As written, it appears to suggest that once the limit is raised, delivery resumes from where it previously stopped — effectively behaving like a joining fetch triggered by the limit increase.

For example, suppose the max is set to group 5, subgroup 2. The limit is not increased, but objects continue flowing and the track advances to group 10, subgroup 100. If the client later increases the limit to group 50, subgroup 1000, the sender would need to deliver all objects from group 5, subgroup 2 up to the current head. This would likely cause microbursting and would also introduce additional complexity around delivery timeouts, since these resumed objects would now be subject to timeout semantics based on the limit increase.

If the intent is not to perform a joining fetch on limit increase, then buffering would be required to support resumption. However, buffering is something many implementations try to avoid — especially given that cache already serves a similar role.

There are also use cases where `TOO_FAR_BEHIND` should not result in terminating the subscription. In those cases, it may make more sense to jump to head upon a significant limit increase rather than attempting to deliver the entire backlog. One possible approach would be to allow limit increases within a bounded delta; if that delta is exceeded, the subscription would skip ahead to head instead of replaying all missed objects.

> I'm a bit confused about this. I thought we wanted to use subgroup IDs for layer prioritization?

The primary way to prioritize subgroups as layers is with **Publisher Priority**.  The only reason to use SG-ID was for a group with 256+ subgroups that are logically the same priority, but sequenced.  You can still do that with this proposal since the SGs are likely single-object subgroups with the "sg-id == first object id" compression bit -- like datagrams but > than MTU and retransmittable.

Perhaps the most reasonable way to remove the "implementation dependent" comparison between Datagram Object ID and Subgroup ID is -- just compare them _anyways_.

2) This is the _third_ tiebreaker, these objects are in the same Track and Group and have the same publisher priority.  If the publisher cared, it would have set different priorities.

comments.body:
Here's a review I received from Ted Hardie via email:

So it looks you are registering three different URI schemes, "moqt", which you expect to handle either of the current two transports, and then a scheme for each specific transport , "moqt+wt", and "moqt+q".  This is not best practice, as you can see in the reviewer notes for similar approaches ([https://www.iana.org/assignments/uri-schemes/expert-notes/coap-expert-notes](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.iana.org/assignments/uri-schemes/expert-notes/coap-expert-notes__;!!Bt8RZUm9aw!_5-hIbdMPJadMK_ZcDZ0oCOeRyYFaTLD2qRIAUQIYoKkIzr5oWH52B0EYTpqXT7QYZfy3_9OZ75G$) is one).  You may also want to review [https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8323#section-8](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8323*section-8__;Iw!!Bt8RZUm9aw!_5-hIbdMPJadMK_ZcDZ0oCOeRyYFaTLD2qRIAUQIYoKkIzr5oWH52B0EYTpqXT7QYZfy37wv3L_C$), which describes why CoAP went that way; in essence, they were willing to see the distinct URI schemes as referencing fully distinct origins/resources.  Is that what you expect to?  Or do you expect that 

moqt://Alans_authority/some_resource
moqt+wt://Alans_authority/some_resource 

will reference the same resource since the moqt URI scheme implies support of web transport?  If so, it may not work as you expect by default.  Note that using +something after a scheme name has no semantics; the default comparison is by full scheme name, and going this way expects URI parsers to special case this. 

One way around this is to push that information out of the scheme.  It could have been encoded in a port had WS and QUIC chosen unique ports, but that ship has sort of sailed.  Another way to do it would be to make the query section mandatory, and specify that it must contain a parameter (from Cullen's comment, likely a key value pair) identifying the transports.  So

moqt://Alans_authority/some_resource?transport=wt; otherkey=othervalue; 

for a resource at Alans_authority, which supports only webtransport, and for which there is another parameter represented by a key/value pair.

In general, this looks a bit underspecified, because you just adopted the core syntax and didn't modify it.  But if you want any semantics beyond identifying resources, I think you need a bit more to explain syntactically how those semantics (like parameters) would be expressed.

> I suspect we almost certainly want different messages from redirecting a request in lieu of OK/ERROR, vs redirecting an active subscription.

That is already true in this PR:

Redirecting a request -> SUBSCRIBE_ERROR, code=REDIRECT + Redirect structure
Redirecting an active subscription -> REDIRECT message (contains redirect structure).

> Who can use the latter form of the redirect? The publisher? The request initiator?

The request initiator can _always_ redirect their _own_ request by cancelling the request and making a new one.  No action is required by the receiver.  The useful cases are:

* Publisher redirecting a subscriber (go subscribe here instead please)
* Subscriber redirecting a publisher (useful for client-publishers -> server subscriber says "please publish here instead")

I don't think we need a client publisher who initiates the request to ask the server to SUBSCRIBE to it at some other location.

So I think the answer is "the entity responding to a request can send a REQUEST_ERROR+REDIRECT or REDIRECT message".

> Is there any special handling required if I redirect a PUBLISH, but I already started sending objects?

I think you mean:

C->S: PUBLISH
C->S: Objects
S->C: ERROR+Redirect

?

In this case, we can add language that no objects will be processed by the server and the client can resend them.

C->S: PUBLISH
S->C: PUBLISH OK
C->S: Objects
...
S->C: REDIRECT

This is the more interesting case, since the client might like to know which of its objects were received and processed by the server.  We could add a field to REDIRECT which is the largest object received/processed.

This is not very actionable.

pulls.title: Allow framing single object subgroups without Subgroup ID
pulls.author: ianswett
pulls.body:
Allows single-object subgroups to be sent on streams with the same header as OBJECT_DATAGRAM, without explicitly encoding a Subgroup ID.

By introducing `OBJECT_STREAM` and allowing it to use the identical framing structure as `OBJECT_DATAGRAM`, single-object streams no longer require a Subgroup ID or an explicit Object Payload Length (the payload naturally consists of the remainder of the stream). To safely accomplish this, `FETCH_HEADER`'s stream type identifier was moved from `0x05` to `0x50` to avoid conflicts with the Datagram format type IDs `0x00..0x0F` and `0x20..0x2F`. 

An object received in an `OBJECT_STREAM` message retains an `Object Forwarding Preference` of `Subgroup`. This optimizes both wire space and simplifies single-object per-stream use cases.

Fixes #1405

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> I agree it's awkward. You can no longer have a different subscriber priority for your fetch and subscription.

I guess the most common use case for Publisher/Relay is to assign higher transmission priority to the FETCH data stream so the subscriber catches up to the live edge quickly, and lower priority to the live subgroup streams during that catch-up phase — then normalize once the FETCH data stream closes. A relay can implement this unilaterally by controlling the QUIC stream priorities of the streams it opens, without the subscriber specifying any parameter. So for this particular use case, the shared-parameter model does not block the right behavior. 

However, the problem occurs when a subscriber includes SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY in a Joining FETCH and expects it to apply only to past-content delivery. This issues a REQUEST_UPDATE on the live subscription, changing live delivery priority. There is no way for the subscriber to include a parameter in Joining FETCH and have it apply only to FETCH. We could make that UPDATES happening during a dual FETCH/SUBSCRIBE must be ignored?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
I want to share a concrete use case related to this PR: the SWITCH proposal (PR #1378).

In the SWITCH design, after the subscriber sends a SWITCH control message identifying the current and target Tracks, the Relay opens a PUBLISH bidi for the target Track. The PUBLISH includes a SWITCH_TRANSITION parameter carrying G_switch (the transition GroupID) and the Live Edge Group ID. The range [G_switch, Live Edge Group ID) is the "catch-up range": the past objects the subscriber needs to receive before it is aligned with the live edge of the target Track. 

If this range is non-empty, I propose these past objects to be delivered on the same PUBLISH bidi (alongside live objects arriving on PUBLISH subgroup streams) with higher QUIC transmission priority than the live streams (see https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1604#issuecomment-4254198238)

In practice this is achieved by having the Relay immediately follow the PUBLISH message on the relay-to-subscriber direction of the PUBLISH bidi with a FETCH_HEADER and deliver the catch-up objects inline, without any FETCH request from the subscriber.

In other words, #1378 is a relay-proactive variant of what this PR #1604 proposes: co-locating FETCH data on the PUBLISH bidi, but initiated by the Relay rather than by the Subscriber.

yes, the text could be revised.

On a SUBSCRIBE bidi: the subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE, then FETCH, in that order on the same stream. The publisher responds in order: SUBSCRIBE_OK (or REQUEST_ERROR for SUBSCRIBE), then FETCH_OK (or REQUEST_ERROR for FETCH). A REQUEST_ERROR that arrives before SUBSCRIBE_OK applies to the SUBSCRIBE and terminates the stream. A REQUEST_ERROR that arrives after SUBSCRIBE_OK applies to the Joining FETCH and does not terminate the stream.

On a PUBLISH bidi: the relay sends PUBLISH; the subscriber replies PUBLISH_OK, then FETCH. The relay's FETCH_OK or REQUEST_ERROR follows and unambiguously applies to the FETCH.

The revised text could be:
"On a bidi stream that carries both a SUBSCRIBE (or PUBLISH) and a Joining FETCH, the publisher MUST send the response to the SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH before sending the response to the Joining FETCH. A REQUEST_ERROR sent before SUBSCRIBE_OK terminates the stream and applies to the SUBSCRIBE. A REQUEST_ERROR sent after SUBSCRIBE_OK applies only to the Joining FETCH and MUST NOT terminate the stream."

It covers the case where Joining FETCH terminates without affecting the associated SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH. The reverse case is not addressed: what happens when the publisher closes the request stream (PUBLISH_DONE+ FIN on the PUBLISH bidi) while the Joining FETCH unidirectional data stream is still delivering objects?

The current wording "closing the stream terminates the FETCH request" means that if the relay sends PUBLISH_DONE + FIN before the FETCH data stream has finished, the subscriber loses any in-flight past-content objects.

We could say "A publisher MUST NOT send the final FIN on the request stream until the associated Joining FETCH unidirectional data stream has been closed (FIN or RESET_STREAM)."

This ensures the subscriber always receives the complete FETCH range before the subscription terminates.
@martinduke thoughts on Gwendal's proposal?

this is a general problem with REQUEST_UPDATE, so it's orthogonal to this PR.

pulls.title: [Draft/RFC] Add a `Largest Available Group` filter.
pulls.author: vasilvv
pulls.body:
This is similar to other proposals such as [Rewind](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-duke-moq-subscribe-rewind/), [CurrentGroupFill](https://github.com/afrind/moq-transport/pull/15), and [LargestGroup](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/moq/y5f5XZT005Y6ebrHYBOXtr4JojQ/). Distinct features of this approach:
* Only the current group is supported.
* It will always serve a complete group.
* It does not require any explicit backfill on the relay side.
* Probably really easy to implement.
* It has sensible semantics for cases when the groups are really large.

comments.author: kixelated
comments.body:
> At a higher level, I am tying to understand what use-cases this would solve in comparison to NextGroup filter. May be I am missing something, love to learn more.

One concrete use-case is the catalog track. `NextGroup` will never resolve; you MUST do a JOINING FETCH or SUBSCRIBE LargestGroup. A NGR for catalogs is extremely wasteful; every existing subscriber will get a duplicate copy of the old catalog.

> For static GOPs, if the duration is short, say 2s , then going to the beginning of the current group might be same effect as starting always at next group. 

Suhas, at Twitch we heavily optimized to reduce TTV. It's not acceptable to wait a random amount of time from 0-2s waiting for the next group.

Let's take the median and say we're 1s into a 2s group. We want to use LargestGroup to race:

1. Downloading/decoding 1s+ of old media (at network speed) to catch up from behind.
2. Or wait 1s.

As a concrete example, let's say the media is 1.5Mb/s (360p) and our network can do 3Mb/s. It'll take something like 0.66s to start playback instead of 1s if we waited, plus the congestion controller will be warmed. 333ms faster startup time is HUGE, and this is just for this median case.

> For larger GOPs or dynamic GOPs, next group may be too far to have applications wait. I do feel NGR might be a good solution that end subscriber may make such a decision.

You have to remember that NGR will be ignored if the group is too new, and NextGroup can sit there doing nothing.

Ideally, you combine CurrentGroup + NGR. Again it's a race:

1. Download/decode x seconds of old media at network speed.
2. Or wait for a new group.

This will warm the congestion controller much like LargestObject, but you also have the ability to WIN THE RACE and have faster startup time. I think it's a strict improvement over the status quo.

I have some concerns that mandating the Subgroup ID to always be identical to the first Object ID might restrict publisher flexibility.

**The Problem**: Tying the Subgroup ID directly to the first Object ID prevents applications from maintaining structurally consistent Subgroup IDs across multiple Groups. comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Passing an absolute or relative Group start in SUBSCRIBE is easy. Removing the current Joining FETCH section is easy too. That is not where the WG has been stuck. Some points have blocked consensus for months:
- Placement of catch-up Objects. Are they carried on a separate unidirectional stream, or in-band on the parent bidi? With an extra stream, boundary signaling, cancellation, and lifecycle are still split across streams.
- Cache gaps. If an Object is missing from cache, does the relay wait for it, with possible HoL blocking, or skip it, which makes catch-up unreliable? This needs an explicit rule. FILL_TIMEOUT looks like the right vehicle.
- Continuity model. Are past Objects required to be delivered before live Objects, to preserve continuity, or can past and live be sent concurrently? These are different semantics. 
- Drain behavior. If continuity is preserved by serving catch-up first, then live Objects accumulate while catch-up is being sent. Then the relay behavior must be defined: how backlog is drained, what “caught up” means, and what to do if drain does not converge (TOO_FAR_AWAY and TIMEOUT_DELIVERY seem good vehicles but they introduce gaps).
- Scope. This PR defines a SUBSCRIBE-side trigger. That may be fine, but it should not be confused with defining the catch-up transport itself.

In short, this PR simplifies the syntax. It does not yet define the semantics.

pulls.title: Add Sender-Side Track Switching (SSTS)
pulls.author: wilaw
pulls.body:
Adds the Sender-Side Track Switching (SSTS) feature, detailing subscriber operations, relay behavior, and bandwidth allocation algorithm.

Adds a new SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT parameter. 

Fixes #259

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
In the relay behavior section, all non-selected switching-set tracks have fwd=0 downstream. Per §9.2 (discussed in #1650), relays SHOULD set the Forward flag to 1 upstream regardless of the downstream value. However, this PR says nothing about upstream Forward State for non-selected tracks. The selection algorithm picks the best fitting track based on its configured throughput threshold _with no guard on upstream data availability_. What if a newly selected track has no upstream data flowing?

One option: "_When the algorithm selects a track for which upstream data is not yet available, the relay MUST forward using the highest-throughput available track and activate the upstream subscription for the selected track, switching at the next group boundary once data flows._" (note that this assumes the upstream subscription can be established before the next group boundary, which is not guaranteed with short groups and high upstream RTT)

Alternatively, this PR could require the relay to maintain fwd=1 upstream for all switching-set tracks, and rely on MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_TRACKS to bound the DoS exposure.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
I have some (D)DoS concerns with the PR. I have two independent (but related) comments.

`MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_TRACKS` bounds the number of tracks in a switching set, but not their aggregate throughput. A subscriber can assign a full ABR ladder to a single switching set. For example, Apple's HLS HEVC authoring spec defines 12 tiers from 145 kbps to 16.8 Mbps (~54 Mbps total). Per §9.2, the relay maintains upstream fwd=1 for all 12 tracks while the algorithm selects only the lowest tier downstream. A malicious subscriber throttling its network to minimum receives 145 kbps while the relay ingests 54 Mbps. Ingest-to-egress ratio: 372×

There is also a cache cost that is easy to overlook: the relay must buffer at least one full group per track to switch at group boundaries. At a 2-second group duration, the 12-tier ladder requires ~14 MB of cache per session, independent of what is actually delivered downstream.

As discussed in my earlier comment (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1638#issuecomment-4647283499), the spec does not require the relay to maintain upstream fwd=1 for all switching-set tracks. A relay aware of the subscriber's downstream bandwidth could limit upstream fwd=1 to tracks at or near that bandwidth. For a client consistently at 145 kbps, the top tiers could stay at fwd=0. However, this is not robust against malicious subscribers who continuously vary their apparent bandwidth.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
This second (D)DoS concern is related to but independent from my previous comment (https://github.com/moq-wg/moq-transport/pull/1638#issuecomment-4647768418).

`MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_TRACKS` is scoped per session (one QUIC connection or one WebTransport session). Multiple WebTransport sessions can be established over a single QUIC connection, and the MOQT spec sets no limit on how many a client may open.

Consider a relay configured with `MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_TRACKS` = 3, which is the most conservative possible setting, allowing only a minimal +1/-1 switching set. A single attacker opens 10,000 WebTransport sessions over one QUIC connection. With a 100 Mbps home connection, the per-session bandwidth estimate drops to ~10 kbps. Since it is below the lowest track in the ladder, the algorithm selects nothing and delivers zero bits downstream. The attacker's cost is only the one-time control-plane burst to establish sessions. Sustained bandwidth is negligible. Yet the relay must maintain state for 30,000 subscriptions and execute the allocation algorithm 10,000 times per group boundary. If each session targets a different channel, subscription aggregation does not apply and the relay must cache independently per session. For the three top Apple HLS HEVC tiers, we are talking around 100 GB of live group cache at the relay. If the Relay is smarter with its upstream `fwd` flag management, it still has computation cost and state management.

Should the PR consider whether DTS limits belong at the client level rather than the session level? Multiple WebTransport sessions over the same QUIC connection are identifiable as the same source. It would limit the risk of DoS. It would not fix potential DDoS though.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
>  Multiple WebTransport sessions can be established over a single QUIC connection, and the MOQT spec sets no limit on how many a client may open.

@gwendalsimon  - is this a DTS issue or a MOQT issue? I think its more the latter. I agree with the DDOS risk you describe. If the scare resource on the server is bandwidth more than connections, then we should probably consider replacing MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_TRACKS with MAX_DTS_CONCURRENT_THROUGHPUT, or else have noth of those together as negotiated settings. 


>  A single attacker opens 10,000 WebTransport sessions over one QUIC connection. With a 100 Mbps home connection, the per-session bandwidth estimate drops to ~10 kbps. Since it is below the lowest track in the ladder, the algorithm selects nothing and delivers zero bits downstream. The attacker's cost is only the one-time control-plane burst to establish sessions. Sustained bandwidth is negligible.

A similar risk situation occurs with Http/3 requests. However, both endpoints negotiate a MAX_STREAMS limit during the QUIC handshake, and HTTP/3 layers its own SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS on top of that. A typical server default is 100–1000 concurrent streams. We could apply something similar for MOQT?

This is subscriber decided value, because the subscriber has the knowledge of the bitrate of the track (say 1Mbps) and the throughput level it is comfortable switching to that track (perhaps 1.5Mbps). The relay knows neither of these values. 

If throughput threshold was communicated as the encoded bitrate of the track, then either different relays would choose different safety margins, or else the safety margin would need to be communicated as an additional parameter, which is less efficient than communicating the product of the two which is what we send now. Different clients will want different safety margins at different times (typically the closer you are to the live edge, the higher your margin), so baking a fixed value into the relay would not be optimal.

In prior meetings we debated the efficacy of specifying one bandwidth estimation algorithm that all relays must follow. before the current group, while delivering current and future objects via subscribe subgroups and
datagrams.

Changes:
- Remove Joining Fetch types, Joining Fetches section, Joining Fetch Range Calculation, Joining
   Location, and INVALID_JOINING_REQUEST_ID error code
- Inline Standalone Fetch fields directly into the FETCH message wire format
- Add new subscription filter types: AbsoluteStartFill (0x5), AbsoluteRangeFill (0x6), CurrentGroup
  (0x7), RelativeStartFill (0x8)
- Add Current Group Delivery section with publisher subgroup ordering and relay object accounting
  requirements, applicable to any filter covering the current group
- Add Fill Semantics section defining fill fetch stream behavior
- Add FillDescending (0x3) group order: descending for fill, ascending for subscribe
- Update LARGEST_OBJECT to serve as the fill boundary in SUBSCRIBE_OK
- Extend FILL_TIMEOUT to apply in SUBSCRIBE messages with fill filter types
- Add fill fetch stream cancellation semantics and relay guidance
- REQUEST_UPDATE with a fill filter type opens a new fill fetch stream using the REQUEST_UPDATE's
  Request ID
- Disallow fill filter types and CurrentGroup in PUBLISH_OK (stale LARGEST_OBJECT); recommend forward=0
   + REQUEST_UPDATE pattern instead
- Clarify PUBLISH forward=1 starts delivery at Largest Object

TODO: Resolve AbsoluteRangeFill behavior when end group is before current group.

Fixes #1039
Fixes #1313 
Fixes #1358
Fixes #1614

When the relay completes the current group via an upstream FETCH, the objects arrive on a single FETCH stream (FETCH semantics), but the relay must forward them downstream on subgroup streams. comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
Per @afrind request, adding a comment to remind him that he should add ability to fill-fetch to the largest object.

To elaborate on the use case:

If all objects on the enhancement layers are independent, the subscriber can subscribe at the largest object, and then do a fill-fetch up to that object for subgroup=0 only. A revision of #1642, this PR allows any range of objects passed to subscription to be satisfied.  The portion of the range before Largest Object comes on a "fill fetch stream" -- a unidirectional stream beginning with a FETCH_HEADER.

- Renamed AbsoluteStart/Range filters to AbsoluteStart/RangeFill, and added a new filter: RelativeStartFill.
- Defined the semantics of fill-fetch and the streams are opened and closed
- Added a FILL_PARAMETERS parameter, which carries the fill-specific versions of SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY, GROUP_ORDER, etc
- Updated the priority algorithm to explain how to order objects on fill-fetch vs the live portion of a subscription
  - Different Groups, same Group Order -> object's group determines
  - Different Groups and Different Group Order -> live wins
  - Same Group -> fill-fetch wins
- Explained how PUBLISH_OK and REQUEST_UPDATE work with new filter types
- Removed the Joining version of FETCH and removed the "standalone" monikker
- Minor updates to PUBLISH_DONE to include fill-fetch streams in stream count, and allow the publisher to delay the message
- INVALID_RANGE now only applies to FETCH

reviews.body: This is coming along well. There are few things we need to clarify/address though.

comments.body: +1. The boundary should be pinned to the Largest Object at the time the request is received, because Largest Object is otherwise a moving target. Concretely: every Group before the Largest Object is fill-delivered, and every Group from the Largest Object onward is subscription-delivered. Making this explicit removes the ambiguity.
+1. This paragraph is hard to understand, because it never explains what the duplicated Object is.

While the fill fetch stream is being delivered, the subscription delivers live objects (above the boundary) at the same time. The relay/publisher behavior during this window is not described, and it depends on Group Order:

- Ascending: older fill groups must precede live groups, so the relay has to buffer incoming live objects while the fill drains.
- Descending: live groups go first and fill groups last, so the relay must keep the fill objects in cache until they are delivered (they must not be evicted).

Could we specify this? It belongs here in fill-semantics and is inherited by the switch modes (see #1675).

+1. If a subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE whose Objects are all in the past — by mistake, or because it does not know the Largest Object — it should have used a FETCH. I do not see the value in keeping the subscription open in that case. I would prefer to close the subscription.

+1. I do not understand why the fill filter must be re-specified. If a subscription has a fill range at Forward State 0 and later moves to Forward State 1, why re-send the filter? For RelativeStartFill the filter already says "when it is time to start, give me N groups before now", and the Largest Object needed to resolve it is returned in REQUEST_UPDATE_OK at that moment, so the fill could be resolved automatically.

Also, what happens if the filter is not re-specified? As written, no fill fetch stream opens, so the fill range is silently dropped and only live objects are sent. Is that intended?

+1, "fill failure" needs to be defined. As a solution: since the only signal is a stream reset, could the reset carry a code that conveys the reason? RESET_STREAM already carries a stream reset error code, so if we define reset codes for the fill failure cases (for example an equivalent of INVALID_RANGE or not-found), the subscriber would learn why the fill failed, without needing a REQUEST_ERROR channel.

pulls.title: Track Switching via the SWITCH_FROM parameter
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
Introduce a new parameter SWITCH_FROM, that can appear in SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH_OK or REQUEST_UPDATE.  The parameter has a Mode enum which can control details of the switching algorithm.  The base algorithm and a single "Hard" mode that flips the Forward State are defined.  Subsequent PRs will introduce additional modes.

The parameter also has a "Publish Done" option which the subscriber uses to control whether the other track is closed or left open after Switch.

See #1354
Fixes #1519

pulls.author: afrind

I'm very against timeouts that the impact the client and the client can not discover the time or know it happened. So a few changes to propose here. Do it in a way the client knows, or can set, the timeout. Use an error if the timeout happens instead of treating it as all OK.

PUBLISH_DONE can safely be sent as soon as all subgroups in the group have been opened or otherwise accounted for in the Stream Count field.  The receiver knows upon receiving PUBLISH_DONE how many subgroups are still in flight, so it gets a clean handoff. We can adjust the text here to reflect that.

I’m ok with having a PUBLISH_DONE code that indicates that it was a) triggered by soft switch and b) timed out waiting to see an end of group object (which are not required or guaranteed to arrive) — SOFT_SWITCH_GROUP_END_TIMEOUT?

I also am ok with the client hinting the max time they are willing to wait, but relays can always have policy that takes precedence (no we’re not waiting 2 days for EOG). So both endpoints can state a max (in theory 2 maxes - one for pub and one for sub), but it’s an awful lot of machinery for a corner case, and this is not the only timeout in the protocol that is not advertised.
Probably the table belongs in the previous PR and this just adds an entry.

Thinking about this more, it's very difficult for a relay to know with certainty there are no more objects coming from upstream in a given _group_.  When upstream sends a PUBLISH_DONE, it has a StreamCount, but if the upstream has an ongoing subscription, that signal won't come.  The end-of-group marker helps, but only for cases where the relay can trivially scoreboard the object IDs in the group.  I think this is a retread of #641.

This is to say, that the relay's implementation almost certainly needs to have timers, so it likely makes sense to have the subscriber at least hint the timeout.

The text does not say what a relay does when the subscriber lags behind live.

Example: the relay is delivering Group 32 to the subscriber. Live is at Group 35 on both the suspending and activating tracks. Start Group is 34. Does the relay send 34 and 35 from the activating track immediately, without waiting for the suspending track to finish 32 and 33? That would not be the suitable behavior (two simultaneous tracks).

I think steps 4 and 5 (in #1674) must be strictly sequential. The relay should first finish the suspending track up to Start Group - 1 (33), and only then start the activating track from Start Group (34). During the drain it keeps groups 34, 35 (and any that arrive), so that at handoff it starts the activating track from 34 with a fill-fetch, not from live.

Could we reinforce this ordering, and state that the activating track resumes from Start Group and not from live? The ordering text probably belongs in #1674.

I do not understand why Start Group = 0 is treated like Hard mode.

I see one use case for Start Group = 0: the subscriber does not know where it is relative to live on the suspending track (for example it is receiving an old group while the live edge is far ahead), or the suspending track is at Forward State 0. In that case Start Group = 0 means "I do not know live; take the current group of the activating track as the Start Group."

But if the subscriber asks for Soft mode, it wants the suspending track to continue up to Start Group - 1 and then switch to the activating track. That is very different from stopping immediately. So treating Start Group = 0 as Hard does not make sense to me.

I needed to set some behavior for cases when `Start Group - 1` was invalid.  When the tracks are aligned, and the activating track is asking to start _before_ 0, I assumed it meant that everything in the old track should be cancelled (e.g. - the same as hard mode).

> I see one use case for Start Group = 0: the subscriber does not know where it is relative to live on the suspending track 

I disagree that is the use case for Start Group = 0. 

With fill fetch, setting Start Group = 0 will generate a fill fetch from the beginning; this is not what you want.  The subscriber should only specify one when they know an absolute group to start from, and this can be done when behind live (eg, live=35, you can SWITCH_FROM with start=33).  If the sub doesn't know a group to start from, they likely want RelativePrevFill(N) -- note RPF(>0) can also result in a computed Start Group < 0, which has the same behavior -- or NextGroup.

I see the problem you are describing, but I don't want to make steps 4 and 5 sequential in order to address it.  In MOQ, it is computationally impractical in the general case for a relay to know when it has received all objects in a group from the publisher.  So by forcing serial operation, we are necessarily introducing delay (the relay's group timeout).

Instead, I think it's better to try to handle this via prioritization.  Since suspending and activating tracks are aligned, they can be considered the same track for prioritization purposes (assuming publisher and subscriber priorities are identical) and fall back to group ordering.  Then, in your example, the relay will queue up 34, but 32 and 33 will always have priority.  There's an annoying edge if the subscriptions have opposite group orders.

This is much easier to write than to implement for most folks however.  I'm open to other suggestions.

I suppose one mechanism is to add end-of-group signaling to the subscription control channel.  eg: 

```
END_OF_GROUP { 
  Group ID (vi64),
  StreamCount (vi64)
}
```

Then relay can use this to know when to move to the other group (when it has all the streams and they have all terminated).  However, it's a bit heavy-handed to require such a message (3 MOQ bytes on the control stream every group).

pulls.title: Clarify FIN vs RST/STOP_SENDING semantics on request streams
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
## Problem

Three related issues asked what FIN, RESET_STREAM, and STOP_SENDING mean on a
bidirectional request stream:

- #1634 — What semantics do FIN or RST carry on a request stream?
- #1635 — Should a subscriber treat FIN/RST as equivalent to PUBLISH_DONE?
- #1643 — Is FINing a response stream without a control message first an error?

## Resolution (per London discussion + issue follow-ups)

A request stream's two directions close independently. The unifying model:

- **RESET_STREAM / STOP_SENDING = cancellation** (either endpoint, either
  direction).
- **A FIN is not a cancellation.** It only means "no more messages on this
  direction."
- An endpoint **MUST NOT FIN a direction until it has sent the messages required
  on that direction**:
  - the responder MUST send a response message (a `REQUEST_OK` variant,
    `SUBSCRIBE_OK`, `FETCH_OK`, or `REQUEST_ERROR`) before FIN (#1643);
  - the publisher of an `Established` subscription MUST send `PUBLISH_DONE`
    before FIN (#1635).
- A premature FIN fails the request; an endpoint MAY promote it to a session
  error per the existing escalation guidance in §Termination.

## Changes

- Rewrote **§Request Cancellation and Rejection** to state the FIN-vs-cancel
  model and list, per request type, which messages may be immediately followed
  by a FIN (#1634).
- Strengthened **§PUBLISH_DONE**: publisher MUST NOT FIN an `Established`
  subscription's direction before `PUBLISH_DONE`; receiver treats a premature
  FIN as a failed subscription (#1635).
- Fixed **§Subscribing to Namespaces**, which incorrectly listed FIN as a way to
  cancel SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE/SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS.

Fixes #1634, fixes #1635, fixes #1643.

this is still true when the publisher priority wasn't updated.

This opens an interesting quesiton:

If I started a subgroup with no priority (inherit default) and the default changed mid-subgroup, do newly received objects in that subgroup get the new priority?  If the answer is _yes_, then deleting the above _is correct_.  

If I'm a relay, should I reprioritize the matching outgoing subgroups?  If so, we need to state that.

> If applications care about the race, they could include priority in the object during the time of transition where the race can occur.

This covers the "too late" direction, but not REQUEST_UPDATE arriving *too early*.

When the publisher decides to change the priority, it can start stamping explicit priority on objects from that point on and send REQUEST_UPDATE. But objects sent before that decision, already in flight/submited to the QUIC stack can't be retroactively stamped. 

Since the bidi request stream is prioritized above data-plane, I’d expect this to be the most common form of the race.

I could see a mid-subgroup priority change being useful, but I think we would need a bigger update to the prioritization model. But reading the discussion here, we may need that anyway :/

It looks like SUBSCRIPTION_STATE_NOTIFY #1820 will land soon, in which case you could include Priority and the Largest Object/First Object with the new Priority there.  If we had that, I'm not sure we need to include it in the Objects as well?

pulls.title: Add PUBLISH_NOTIFY message
pulls.author: afrind
pulls.body:
Add a new control message, PUBLISH_NOTIFY (0x22), that a publisher sends on a subscription's bidirectional stream to notify the subscriber that subscription state has changed for a reason other than a subscriber-sent REQUEST_UPDATE. Unlike REQUEST_UPDATE, it is a unilateral notification: no REQUEST_OK/REQUEST_ERROR response and not subject to MAX_REQUEST_UPDATES. The FORWARD and LOCATION_FILTER parameters are updated to permit appearing in this message.

No existing mechanism in the draft sends this message yet. It is intended to support:

- SWITCH_FROM (#1674, #1675)
- Top-N (#1518)
- Possibly Default Publisher Priority (#1770)

High level thoughts:
- I think this version of the mechanism, like a lot of revisions of it before, does not allow for pre-computation of top-N.  We should design mechanism that allows relays to precompute top-N on publication whenever those are published.
- SELECTED/DESELECTED mechanism most likely should be shared with SSTS somehow.

comments.author: vasilvv
comments.body:
If I am a relay receiving three tracks from the original publisher, I should be able to precompute the top-N at that relay without knowing anything about subscribers.

I believe this is important because fundamentally, MOQT is a "small number of publishers to millions of subscribers" protocol, meaning that we almost never let information flow from the subscriber (relay) to the publisher (relay), and when we do (e.g. NGR), it's very carefully adjusted to scale.  The current design doesn't really allow that:
- You don't know what property the subscriber would compute top on, so you have to wait for the subscriber to tell you.
- Similarly, you don't know the N.
- One subscriber can subscribe for top-5, and then a later one can subscribe for top-10, causing a recompute on all relays in-between.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
There actually can’t be a stream count higher than 2^60 - 1, because you are fundamentally limited by the number of uni QUIC streams the peer can open, which is 2^62 / 4.

I’m going to assert that if the number is in excess of 2^60, or even 2^40, it’s almost certainly a bug or an attack, and everyone’s stack will wait for the timer and deliver pub done. 60 streams per second will get you 2^31 per year.

That said, if we want to remove ceiling entirely, I don’t see any harm.
